While the boys were not yet born, it was said: The elder shall serve the younger; as it is written: Jacob I loved, Esau I hated. So then he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills. The election obtained it, the rest were hardened. Concerning faith: Not all have faith. To you it has been given in the cause of Christ not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him. God works and [effects] to perfect. And as many as were ordained to eternal life believed. Concerning perseverance: The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are his. I give my sheep eternal life (eternal, says Christ, not for three days) and they shall never perish; neither shall anyone snatch them out of my hand. I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. False prophets will show great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, they would even deceive the elect. I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding, and revealed them to infants. Yes, Father, for so it was well-pleasing in your sight. These and similar mysteries of heavenly truth let them learn first to keep silent about, before they examine them by the fancies of their own brains, so that today they put their mouths against heaven.

units.la: Erat hic paucis indicaturus, quem Prothea Deum isti nobis fingunt: Qualem theologiam sudant: quæ principia conuellant: quas scripturas quam perulanter eludant. Sed chartæ angustia, quam typographus & tempus mihi nunc imperant, id facere non permittit. Nec possum tamen quin ex multis vnum saltem profligatæ audaciæ hominis istius breuiter inferam exemplum.
units.tr: Here I was about to point out briefly what kind of Proteus God these men fashion for us, what theology they sweat out, which principles they overturn, and how shamelessly they mock the Scriptures. But the narrowness of the paper, which the printer and the time now impose on me, does not allow this. Nor can I refrain from briefly giving one example, out of many, of this man's abandoned audacity.

units.la: Cum dicit Lucas de Antiochenis Pauli auditoribus: Et crediderunt, quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam æternam: manifeste indicat, qui & cur crediderint euangelio, nempe, qui ad fidem, conuersionem & vitam æternam ordinati seu prædestinati fuerant à Deo in Christo, ante iacta mundi fundamenta. In hoc summus Orthodoxorum omnium consensus. Ipse Chrysostomus: Crediderunt, inquit, quot-quot præordinati erant, hoc est, præfiniti à Deo.
units.tr: When Luke says of the hearers of Paul at Antioch: And as many as were ordained to eternal life believed, he clearly indicates who believed the gospel and why, namely, those who had been ordained, or predestined, by God in Christ to faith, conversion and eternal life before the foundation of the world was laid. In this there is the highest consensus of all the orthodox. Chrysostom himself says: As many as were foreordained believed, that is, were fixed beforehand by God.

units.la: Sed audite novum prophetam: Crediderunt, inquit, quotquot ordinati erant ad vitam æternam, hoc est, quotquot ordinem à Deo constitutum secuti, & per eum salvandi erant. seu, quotquot τάξιν ordinationem divinam amplexi sunt, et obedierunt, ab ordinatione non exorbitarunt, ut reliqui custoditi sunt ad vitam æternam. Impudentius os nemo vidit. Ofte dat nobis in scriptura, quod garrit de suo ordine: ostendat ordinatum esse ad vitam æternam, idem esse, quod ordinem sequi: Primam ergo nullam huius corruptelæ speciem ex tota Scriptura proferre potest. Deinde Catholicus interpretum veterum & recentium consensus eum refutat. Tertiò, Lutherus ipse frontem eius redarguit, vernacula versione: Vnd wurden glaubig, so viel ihrer zum ewigen leben verordnet waren: non autem: so viel ihrer sich selbst verordneten, oder der ordnung nachhielten. Quartò, clamat scriptura, credentes dici ordinatos ad vitam æternam in Christo, non propter observationem ordinis seu mediorum ad vitam: sed propter æternum Dei beneplacitum seu prædestinationem electorum ad salutem: nec ordinari eos nunc à seipsis, sed prœordinatos esse ab æterno à Deo: ita ut ordinatio hæc fidem & omnia media tempore & ordine causarum antegrediatur. Sic enim docet Apostolus ad Ephesios cap.1. Item Ro.8. Quos præsciuit hos & prædestinauit (nempe Deus). Lutherus vernaculè: Welche er zuvor versehen, die hat er auch verordnet, &c. Welche er aber verordnet hat, die hat er auch beruffen. &c. Et alibi: Non constituit nos Deus ad iram, sed ad obtinendam salutem &c. Quintò, erant ordinati ad vitam æternam, tanquam ad finem. Ordinatio autem nostri ad finem à Deo conditore est, non à nobis. Sextò, ait iste ordinem esse, ut credamus evangelio, & sic salvemur. Ergo secundum corruptelæ sensus erit: Crediderunt quotquot ordinati erant, hoc est, quotquot crediderunt: qua ταυτολογία[?] quid vanius? Denique, concedamus glossam, dicat nobis cur isti fuerint [illegible, ~3 letters] hoc est, ordine Dei observaverint: alij non obseruarint.Id enim illi fecerunt vel ex fe:vel ex Dei singula-ri gratia.Si ex fe:Pelagianum fe esse ne neget: Si ex Deo, manet quaestio,cur illis dederit, his non dederit gratiam Deus.nec potest elabi, quin vel gratiam ab hominis voluntate suspendat, quod fecit Pelagius: vel specialem Dei ordinationem fateatur.
units.tr: But hear the new prophet: As many, he says, as were ordained to eternal life believed, that is, as many as followed the order established by God and were to be saved through it; or, as many as embraced the divine order [taxis] and obeyed, did not stray from the ordinance, as the rest were kept for eternal life. No one has seen a more shameless face. Let him show from Scripture what he babbles about his own order: let him show that being ordained to eternal life is the same as following an order. Therefore he can produce no trace of this corruption from the whole of Scripture. Next, the catholic consensus of the old and recent interpreters refutes him. Third, Luther himself refutes his face by a vernacular version: And they became believers, as many as were appointed to eternal life [German]; not: as many as appointed themselves, or kept to the order. Fourth, Scripture proclaims that those who are called believers are ordained to eternal life in Christ, not on account of observing an order or of the means to life, but on account of God's eternal good pleasure, or the predestination of the elect to salvation; nor are they now ordained by themselves, but were foreordained by God from eternity; so that this ordination precedes faith and all the means in time and in the order of causes. For so the Apostle teaches in Ephesians chapter 1, likewise Romans 8: Whom he foreknew, these he also predestined (namely, God). Luther in the vernacular: Those whom he foresaw, these he also ordained, etc. And those whom he has ordained, these he has also called, etc. And elsewhere: God has not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation, etc. Fifth, they were ordained to eternal life as to an end. But the ordination of us to the end is by God the Creator, not by us. Sixth, he says that the order is that we believe the gospel and so are saved. Therefore, according to the sense of his corruption, it will be: As many as were ordained believed, that is, as many as believed; what could be emptier than this tautology? Finally, let us grant his gloss: let him tell us why those men were [illegible] that is, observed God's order, and others did not observe it. For they did this either of themselves, or by God's singular grace. If of themselves: let him deny that this is Pelagian if he can. If of God, the question remains why God gave grace to those and did not give it to these. Nor can he escape that he either makes grace depend on the human will, which Pelagius did, or confesses a special ordination of God.

units.la: Ista,viri amplissimi,magno cum dolore commemoro, tanquam enormia ingratitudinis exempla, pro tot tantisque bonis,& pro clarissima veritatis luce, cui dolendum est quidem mores ac vitam parum respondere: sed multò magis,audaces istos [illegible, ~8 letters] studiose tenebras offendere,ac venena peftilentiffima miscere, haereses ab orco reducere, veritatem proscindere, conseruos lacerare, sacrosanctam Theologiam in [illegible, ~10 letters] quandam conuertere:denique,quod caput mali est,Deum eiusque adoranda consilia cancellis ingenij sui circumscribere,in iis,quae ad [illegible, ~9 letters] suas non congruunt, eum mendacij, crudelitatis, [illegible, ~9 letters] iniustitiae accusare,hancque vulgo profanitatem instillare,vt hodie suspicienda haec & imperscrutabilia diuinorum consiliorum mysteria in popinis & tonstrinis irreligiosissime cribrentur & exsibilentur.Ista horribilis alicuius noctis ac tenebrarum impendentium, nec non grauissimorum malorum praeludia esse, boni ac prudentes omnes facile intelligunt: quo magis orandus est Deus,vt ecclesiam suam ab his pestibus clementer liberet: excitet piorum principum animos,qui has furias authoritate sua compescant,donec fideles doctores,qui vera & salutaria constanter doceant,vt in luce veritatis ambulantes ipsi grata facere studeamus.
units.tr: I record these things, most distinguished gentlemen, with great sorrow, as monstrous examples of ingratitude in return for so many and such great blessings, and for the most brilliant light of truth. It is to be lamented indeed that our morals and way of life scarcely match it; but much more do these bold men deliberately strike at the darkness, mix the most pestilent poisons, bring heresies back from hell, tear apart the truth, lacerate their fellow servants, and turn sacred theology into some kind of ... ; and finally, what is the root of the evil, they confine God and his adorable counsels within the limits of their own wit, and in those matters which do not agree with their own ... they accuse him of falsehood, cruelty, ... and injustice, and spread this profanity among the common people, so that these mysteries of the divine counsels, which ought to be revered and are beyond our investigation, are now sifted and hissed at in taverns and barbershops in the most irreligious way. Good and sensible people all easily understand that these things are the prelude to some dreadful night and gathering darkness, and also to the gravest evils; all the more reason to pray to God that he mercifully free his Church from these plagues, stir up the spirits of godly princes to restrain these furies with their authority, until faithful teachers who constantly teach the true and salutary doctrine are restored, so that we, walking in the light of truth, may strive to please him ourselves.

units.la: Nec dubium tamen est, passim in omnibus mundi angulis multos tales esse, qui inter suspiria & gemitus de communi [illegible, ~8 letters], illud ipsum omni animi cura & studio hactenus egerint & agant:quorum proinde [illegible, ~8 letters] scripta & sanctos labores ecclesia merito amat & veneratur.
units.tr: Yet there is no doubt that everywhere in every corner of the world there are many such men who, amid sighs and groans over the common ..., have hitherto pursued and still pursue that very cause with all the care and zeal of their minds; therefore the Church rightly loves and honours their writings and holy labours.

units.la: Atque in hoc genere minimè [illegible, ~8 letters], sed vere [illegible, ~9 letters], explicationes hasce catecheticas clarissimi viri D.ZACHA-RIAE VRSINI, qualicunque studio meo collectas & celebratas dubio procul boni omnes numerabunt, & gratas habebunt.
units.tr: And in this kind, not least ..., but truly ..., I am sure all good people will count and welcome these catechetical explanations of the most distinguished man, Dr. Zacharias Ursinus, which I have gathered and celebrated with whatever care I could.

units.la: Vobis vero,amplissimi & consultissimi viri, cur extremam hanc, quæ de Gratitudine est, partem confecran-dam exiftimarim non est quòd multis exponam.Etenim vos pro ea qua Deus Opt.Max.vos ornauit, quaque præclarè fungimini authoritate ac munere, in id omni ope, cura: & consilio incumbetis, vt in hac Sarepta Palatinatus ad Rhenum diminutus accensa veræ & incorruptæ doctri-nę lampas clarè effulgeat, magisque in dies nitorem suum proferat, ministerij honos ac dignitas conseruetur, illu-strissimorum Principum nostrorum maiestas legumque autoritas sacrosancta vigeat, aurea pax atque tranquillitas efflorescat, denique Deus Opt.Maxim. pro his summis bonis, quibus Palatinatum dignatur, Gratitudinem publicè priuatimque obtineat. Fuit etiam is vester in D.VRSI-NVM perpetuò amor & benevolentia, vt hi commentarij eius, amplissimi nominis vestri præsidium iure quodam requirant. Denique & in hanc scholam nostram, cuius u-sui cumprimis destinati sunt, & in me adeò, cui si illi nostra[?] omnia, certè ordinem ac lucem debent, vestræ Amplitudinis ea hactenus extiterunt merita, vt religio mihi fuerit de Gratitudine commentarios edere, nec aliquam grati[?] pro meritis in me vestris animi testificationem publicè ostendere. Accipite igitur benignè, hoc studium meum, & hanc scholam nostram patrocinio ac meritis porrò, quod facitis ornate, méque benevolentia vestra complecti petgite. Sic vos Dominus Iesus Reipublicæ diu incolumes præstet, & prudentissimis vestris consiliis cœlitus magis ac magis benedicat.Heidelbergæ, ex collegio Sapientiæ xv. Calend.Aprilis.Anno salutis humanæ MDXCI.
units.tr: As for you, most distinguished and most learned gentlemen, there is no need for me to set out at length why I thought this last part, which is on Gratitude, ought to be dedicated to you. For by the authority and office with which God, the best and greatest, has adorned you and which you exercise so excellently, you devote all your help, care and counsel to this end: that in this Sarepta of the diminished Palatinate on the Rhine the lamp of true and uncorrupted doctrine may shine clearly and show its brightness more and more each day; that the honour and dignity of the ministry may be preserved; that the majesty of our most illustrious princes and the sacred authority of the laws may flourish; and that golden peace and tranquillity may bloom. Finally, may God, the best and greatest, receive public and private Gratitude for these highest blessings with which he has graced the Palatinate. Your love and goodwill toward Dr. Ursinus have always been such that these commentaries of his rightly call for the protection of your distinguished name. Finally, your Dignity's merits toward this school of ours, for whose use they were especially intended, and toward me, to whom our school owes, if anything, its order and its light, have been so great up to now that I have felt bound to publish commentaries on Gratitude and not to show publicly some expression of gratitude for your merits toward me. Accept, then, kindly this effort of mine, and continue to protect and favour this school of ours, which you adorn, and embrace me with your goodwill. So may the Lord Jesus preserve you long unharmed for the Commonwealth, and bless your most prudent counsels more and more from heaven. Heidelberg, from the College of Wisdom, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of human salvation 1591.

units.la: DAVID PAREVS.
units.tr: DAVID PAREUS.

units.la: II. D. ZACHARIAE VRSINI Oratio EXHORTATORIA, AD DOCTRINÆ CHRISTIANÆ STVDIVM : HABITA Vratislauiæ in schola Elisabethana : cum examinis Theologici à Philippo Melanchthone conscripti, prælectionem exordiretur Anno Christi cIↄ Iↄ LVIII.
units.tr: II. Oration of D. Zacharias Ursinus, Exhorting to the Study of Christian Doctrine: delivered at Breslau in the Elisabethan school, when he was beginning the lecture on the theological examination drawn up by Philip Melanchthon, in the year of Christ 1558.

units.la: Postquam mihi consilio eorum, qui præsunt vestris studiis iniunctum est, vt doctrinæ Christianæ capita vobis compendio discenda proponam : equidem agnosco & fateor, opus à me requiri, cui nihil minus quàm infantia mea respondeat. Hæc enim doctrina est, quæ, non dico sapientissimis & acutissimis hominibus, nisi voce ecclesiæ & Spiritus sancti efficacia doceantur, perpetuò manet incognita, sed cuius magna pars etiam ipsis angelis, antequam per filium Dei ex arcano æterni patris sinu prolata fuit, ignota fuit. Ad quam explicandam & ornandam, si omnium angelorum & hominum perspicacitatis & eloquentiæ nerui omnes intendantur, nunquam tamen de illa pro rei amplitudine & dignitate dici possit. Mallem igitur, dum quantum in me desiderem cogito, has partes alteri demandatas esse, qui sal-tem aliquanto, quàm ego, melius & felicius eas sustinere posset, sed cum officii mei rationem expendo, mihi & saluti vestræ summa voluntate seruiendum, & Deo ad honestos labores vocanti obtemperandum esse, video, promittenti præsertim & auxilium, quo adiuti de nulla re desperare debent. Vult enim Deus efficax esse etiam per organa infirma & abiecta, iuxta sententiam Psalmi, 8.3. Ex ore infantium & lactentium perfecisti robur propter inimicos tuos, vt destruas inimicum & vltorem. Appellatio, qua vtitur, significat puerum, qui incipit intelligere & loqui. Nominantur autem vsitatè pueri non tantum ætate, sed etiam facultatibus siue intelligendi, siue alias actiones efficiendi. Sunt etiam ætate infantes, diuinæ bonitatis & prouidentiæ testes satis locupletes. Manifesta testimonia præsentiæ Dei in miranda sobolis propagatione, conseruatione & educatione satis refutant diabolos & Ios[?] & omnes atheos,negantes vel esse Deum,vel talem esse,qualem se esse dicit. Sed Christus in Euangelio Matt.21. 61.trahit sententiam ad confessionem,qua ratione in omnes nos coperit,qui de Deo aliquid cogitamus aut loquimur. Sumus.n.infantes intellectu & sermone de omnibus rebus divinis Discimus in hac vita exigua quaedam illarum initia,sicut pie & vere scribit Imperator Gratianus in sua confessione ad Ambrosium: Loquimur de Deo, non quantum debemus,sed quantum possumus. Etiam ipsi prophetae & apostoli de se idem fatentur, v. 1. Corinth.13 9. Imperfectè cognoscimus.imperfectè prophetamus, cum autem venerit perfectum, abolebitur imperfectio. Et 12. Videmus per speculum tanquam in aenigmate, tum autem de facie ad faciem.
units.tr: Since, by the counsel of those who oversee your studies, it has been enjoined on me to set before you the heads of Christian doctrine to be learned in summary form, I freely acknowledge and confess that the task demanded of me is one that my infancy is far from equal to. For this doctrine is one which, not to speak of the wisest and keenest of men, remains forever unknown unless it is taught by the voice of the Church and the efficacy of the Holy Spirit; and a great part of it was unknown even to the angels, before it was brought forth by the Son of God from the secret bosom of the eternal Father. Even if all the sinews of perspicacity and eloquence of all angels and men were devoted to explaining and adorning it, it could never be spoken of in a manner worthy of its greatness and dignity. I would therefore prefer, as I consider how far short I fall of my desire, that these parts had been entrusted to another who could sustain them at least somewhat better and more happily than I. But when I weigh the reckoning of my duty, I see that I must serve your salvation with the greatest willingness and obey God who calls me to honest labours, especially since he promises help, by which, being aided, we ought to despair of nothing. For God wills to be effective even through weak and despised instruments, according to the saying of Psalm 8:3: "Out of the mouth of babes and sucklings you have perfected strength because of your enemies, that you might destroy the enemy and the avenger." The term he uses signifies a child who is beginning to understand and speak. Children are commonly so named not only by age but also by their capacity either to understand or to perform other actions. There are also infants by age who are sufficiently rich witnesses of divine goodness and providence. The manifest evidences of God's presence in the wonderful propagation, preservation and upbringing of offspring sufficiently refute the devils and the Jews and all atheists, who deny either that God exists or that he is such as he declares himself to be. But Christ in the Gospel (Matt. 21:16) draws the saying to confession, in which way it applies to all of us who think or speak anything about God. For we are infants in understanding and speech regarding all divine matters; in this brief life we learn certain beginnings of those things, as the Emperor Gratian piously and truly writes in his confession to Ambrose: "We speak of God not as much as we ought, but as much as we are able." The prophets and apostles themselves also confess the same about themselves (1 Cor. 13:9): "We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect has come, that which is in part will be done away." And (1 Cor. 13:12): "We see through a mirror, in a riddle, but then face to face."

units.la: Etsi autem & initia quæ discimus,exigua sunt, & vox ministerij, nostro captui accommodata est, in quo Deus & ipse nobiscum tanquam cum infantibus s[?]ic loquitur,& nos de se tanquam infantes loquipatitur:tamen adeo vult Deus in hac vita doctrinam de se cognosci,vt non alio modo spem alterius vitæ nobis faciat.& hæc qualiacunq; initia tanto post se interuallo omnem humanam sapientiam relinquunt:vt eius ad hæc nulla fit collatio[?]. Sunt n.hæc rudimenta,rationem ignora sapientia,sit ad salutem æternam necessaria & sufficientia.Nō igitur tantū infantiā nostrā agnoscamus,sed etiā esse in lactentiū numero velimus. Vt n.non adolescet infans,qui lacte materno aut nutrimento cōueniente nō alitur:ita nos quoq; ne spe perfectionis nostræ excidamus.lac verbi diuini,quo ad vitā alimur & educamur,respuere non oportet.Hæc est infantia spiritualis, Deo placens, vt Christus testatur, cum obiurgat Pharisæos indignantes,quod in templo pueri canebant, Hosanna filio Dauid : Hi sunt infantes,quorum voce vult sese efficax,quorum ore vt addit Psalmus, perficit robur,seu, vt vertuntqui fontes cōsiderant, fundat regnum. Loquitur autē de robore seu regno,quod in hac vita cōspicit & nō minat regnū Christi,quod est filiū Dei instituere & con- seruare ministerium,colligere ecclesiā,viuificare credētes voce Euangelij,& sanctificare eos SS.ad vitā æternā,defendere ecclesiā in hac vita cōtra regnum Diaboli,& post- hanc vitam resuscitare sanctos ad vitam æternam,vt in cis regnet diuinitas palàm,non per ministerium.
units.tr: Although the beginnings we learn are small, and the voice of the ministry is adapted to our capacity, in which God himself speaks with us as with infants, and allows us to speak of him as infants do; nevertheless God so wills that his doctrine be known in this life that he gives us no other way to hope for another life; and these beginnings, however small they are, leave all human wisdom so far behind that there is no comparison of it with them. For these are the rudiments, a wisdom unknown to the world, yet necessary and sufficient for eternal salvation. Therefore we should not only acknowledge our infancy, but also wish to be counted among the sucklings. For just as an infant does not grow up if he is not nourished with mother's milk or suitable food, so too we must not fall away from the hope of our perfection. We ought not to spurn the milk of the divine Word, by which we are nourished and brought up to life. This is spiritual infancy, pleasing to God, as Christ testifies when he rebukes the Pharisees who were indignant that boys were singing in the temple, "Hosanna to the son of David." These are the infants whose voice God wills to make himself effective, and whose mouth, as the Psalm adds, "perfects strength," or, as those who consider the sources translate, "establishes the kingdom." He speaks of the strength or kingdom which he sees in this life, and which is the kingdom of Christ: that is, the Son of God establishes and preserves the ministry, gathers the Church, quickens believers by the voice of the Gospel and sanctifies them for eternal life, defends the Church in this life against the kingdom of the devil, and after this life raises the saints to eternal life, so that in them the divinity may reign openly, not through the ministry.

units.la: Fundamentum huius regni quod sit, Paulus explicat 1.Cor.3.11. dicens: Fundamentum aliud poni nō potest praeter id, quod positum est, qui est Christus. Fūdamētū Christus est, primum sua persona, quia omnia huius regni membra, id est, omnes sanctos, sibi copulatos & insertos gestat, feruat & continet, sicut fundamentum partes reliquas aedificij, sicut vitis palmites: Tum etiam doctrinā de se, id est, de persona & officio suo. Vt enim politici regni neruus sunt leges honestae: ita hoc regnum doctrinā de Christo colligitur, continetur, & gubernatur: & sicut sine fundamento non constat aedificium: sic nisi, quis sit Christus, & quid nobis praestet, teneamus, quaecunque reliqua videtur esse pietas aut consolatio, euanida, ficta, nulla est.
units.tr: Paul explains what the foundation of this kingdom is, saying (1 Cor. 3:11): "No other foundation can be laid than that which has been laid, which is Christ." Christ is the foundation: first by his own person, because he bears, preserves and contains all the members of this kingdom, that is, all the saints, joined and grafted into himself, just as a foundation holds the remaining parts of a building, or as the vine holds the branches. Then also by the doctrine concerning himself, that is, concerning his person and office. For just as the sinews of a political kingdom are good laws, so this kingdom is gathered, contained and governed by the doctrine concerning Christ; and just as a building does not stand without a foundation, so unless we hold fast who Christ is and what he bestows on us, whatever else seems to be piety or consolation is vain, feigned and nothing.

units.la: Hoc fundamentum ponitur ore infantium, dum credentes doctrinam auditam, excitati à Spiritu sancto discunt & ampleuntur, atque ita Christo inseruntur & coalescunt.
units.tr: This foundation is laid by the mouth of infants, while believers, roused by the Holy Spirit, learn and grow in the doctrine they have heard, and so are grafted into Christ and grow together with him.

units.la: Vtitur autem Deus ad hoc summum opus nostra infantia, vt illustretur ipsius gloria, dum operis magnitudo, & organorum imbecillitas, non nostra, sed Dei potentia & efficacia res tantas fieri & constitere, manifestū faciunt. Tum etiam, vt retundat superbiam eorum hostium, dum ingens ipsorum potentia nostra imbecillitate superatur, & nostra stultitiae species, ipsorum sapientia nihil esse stultius, tandem patefacit, sicut dicitur: In silentio & spe erit fortitudo vestra. Destruit enim filius Dei opera Diaboli, eripiens Diabolo credentes, remittens & tollens peccatum, inchoans iustitiam & vitam aeternam, defendens ecclesiam, accusans & detegens malitiam hostium, reprimens & puniens eos, & nunc & in posterum ecclesiae ab omnibus malis liberatione. Atque haec fomentibus inferorū portis, per miseras voces hominū partim efficit, partim testatur: quod 2. Cor. 10. 4. dicitur: Arma malitiae nostra non carnalia sunt, sed potentia Dei ad destructionem munitionum, quibus militamus, cōsilia destrue tes, & omnem altitudinem extollentē se adversus scientiā Dei, & in captivitatē redigētes omne intellectum in obsequium Christi, & in promptu habentes vltionem omnis inobedientiam, cum completa fuerit vestra obedientia. Vt igitur vasorum vilitas de mercium, quas continent, pretio nihil detrahit: sic vocis tenuitas & infantia doctrinam sonantis non ita negligenda videatur, vt quidquam de gravissimarum, quæ vos ad ardens Christianæ religionis studium hortantur, causarum pondere diminuat. Earum vero dum aliquas in hoc nostræ repetitionis exordio recensendas puto, immensa rerum maximarum molem sic obrui me experior, vt unde summam initium vix possim statuere.
units.tr: God uses our infancy for this highest work so that his glory may be made clear, since the magnitude of the work and the weakness of the instruments show that such great things are done and established not by our power but by the power and efficacy of God. Then also, so that he may break the pride of their enemies, when their vast power is overcome by our weakness, and the appearance of our foolishness is shown at last to be wiser than their wisdom, as it is said: "In quietness and in hope shall be your strength" (Isa. 30:15). For the Son of God destroys the works of the devil, snatching believers from the devil, remitting and taking away sin, beginning righteousness and eternal life, defending the Church, accusing and exposing the malice of its enemies, restraining and punishing them, and both now and in the future delivering the Church from all evils. And this he partly effects, and partly attests, through the miserable voices of men, even against the gates of hell, as it is said (2 Cor. 10:4–6): "Our weapons of warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God for the pulling down of strongholds, casting down counsels and every high thing that exalts itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ, and holding in readiness to avenge all disobedience, when your obedience is complete." Just as the cheapness of vessels takes nothing from the value of the wares they contain, so the smallness of the voice and the infancy of the one who speaks should not be regarded so lightly as to diminish in any way the weight of the most serious causes which urge you to ardent zeal for the Christian religion. But when I think that some of these must be reviewed at the start of this repetition of ours, I find myself so overwhelmed by the immense mass of the greatest matters that I can scarcely determine where to make a beginning.

units.la: Quia tamen aliquid istorum consi-derandum est, ea sane nobis prima sit, quæ omnes actiones & studia nostra debet regere, feria diuinæ maiestatis & perspicuis mandatis declarata voluntas. Colloquimur enim nunc, qui sumus ciues ecclesiæ, ac certò scimus prophetarum & apostolorum libros esse certissimas diuinæ mentis & voluntatis patefactiones. Passim autem in his tradita & repetita sunt præcepta, quæ iubent omnes homines diligenter inquirere & cognoscere doctrinam in illis libris comprehensam. Hoc est præceptum decalogi de sabbatho, hoc est illud, quod dicit Seruator Luc.10.42. Vnum[?] necessarium. Huius sapientiæ cognitionem ait esse vitam æternam:hanc,ut sæpe aliàs, ita scripturis eius quasi epitomen Dauid in primo Psalmo commendat, ea beatæ beatitudinis comitatu ornans.
units.tr: Yet since some of these must be considered, let the first be that which ought to govern all our actions and studies: the will of the divine majesty, declared in plain commands. For we who are citizens of the Church are speaking now, and we know for certain that the books of the prophets and apostles are the most certain disclosures of the divine mind and will. Throughout these books precepts are handed down and repeated, commanding all men to inquire diligently and to know the doctrine contained in those books. This is the precept of the Decalogue concerning the Sabbath; this is what the Saviour says (Luke 10:42): "One thing is necessary." Of the knowledge of this wisdom he says that it is eternal life; this, as often elsewhere, David commends in the first Psalm as an epitome of his Scriptures, adorning it with the company of blessed happiness.

units.la: Sed non satis hæc fuerunt [illegible, ~10 letters] & sollicito de nostra salute patri cœlesti. Addit etiam peculiaria mandata de summa doctrinæ, omnibus, præsertim verò iuuentuti proponenda, hoc est, de nostra institutione catechetica. Deuteronom.49.inquit: Docebis ea filios tuos. Et Deuteron.6.& 11. Ponite hæc verba in cordibus vestris & in animis vestris, & suspendite ea pro signo in manibus vestris, & ante oculos vestros collocate. Docete filios vestros, vt illa meditentur, quando sederis in domo tua, & ambulaueris in via[?], & accubueris atque surrexeris. Scri-bes ea super postes & ianuas[?] domus tuæ, vt multiplicentur dies tui & filiorum tuorum in terra. Præcipi audimus pa-rentibus, & quibus eorum partes commissæ sunt, vt do-ceant ac doceri curent: iuuentuti vt discat: utrisque ve[?] assiduè doctrinam inculcent, repetant, meditentur. Eam verò cùm liberis tradi, & in conspectu semper nobis esse vult, breuitatem & perspicuitatem requiri manifestum est, id est, catechefin seu summam doctrinæ cum explicatione nec prolixi, nec obscura. Sic Paulus 2. Tim. 1. 13. Habeas, inquit, hypotyposin sanorū sermonū, quos à me audisti, in fide & dilectione in Christo. Cū eius exercendæ ac tuedæ præcepto, definitionem nostræ catechescos audimus.
units.tr: But these were not enough [illegible, ~10 letters] and anxious about our salvation to the heavenly Father. He also adds special commandments about the sum of the doctrine, to be set before everyone, but especially before young people, that is, about our catechetical instruction. Deuteronomy 4.9 says: You shall teach them to your sons. And Deuteronomy 6 and 11: Put these words in your hearts and in your minds, and bind them as a sign on your hands, and place them before your eyes. Teach your sons to meditate on them, when you sit in your house, and walk on the way, and lie down and rise up. You shall write them on the doorposts and gates of your house, so that your days and the days of your sons may be multiplied in the land. We hear that parents, and those to whom their duties have been entrusted, are commanded to teach and to see that they are taught; that the young are to learn; and that both are to inculcate, repeat and meditate on the doctrine constantly. Now that it is to be handed down to the children and always kept before our eyes, it is plain that brevity and clarity are required: that is, a catechism or summary of the doctrine with explanation, neither long-winded nor obscure. So Paul, 2 Timothy 1:13: Hold fast, he says, the pattern of sound words which you heard from me, in faith and love in Christ. With this command to practise and maintain it, we hear the definition of our catechesis.

units.la: Hypotyposin & veras sententias de singulis doctrinæ partibus ordine & breuiter comprehensas ita vt quasi obiectæ sint: & genus seu formam docendi & loquendi propriam, perspicuam, congruentem cum sermone prophetico & apostolico significat. Ideo nominat sanos sermones à se traditos in fide, seu de fide & caritate in Christo, id est, in agnitione Christi, sicut passim totam pietatem ad fidem & caritatem reuocat. Est igitur catechesis summa doctrinæ de fide & caritate in Christo, ab apostolis & prophetis traditæ: seu summa doctrinæ Christianæ, breuiter, ordine & perspicue comprehensa. Non enim nostrum est, dogmata excogitare, sed necesse habemus, referre nos vt, Esa. 8. 20 dicitur, ad legem & ad testimonium. Explicatio autem addenda est, quæ sit recta partium & ordinis monstratio, & verborum ac phrasēos interpretatio.
units.tr: The hypotyposis, that is, the true statements about the individual parts of the doctrine, comprehended in order and briefly, set out as if before the eye, signifies both the kind and form of teaching and speaking, which is clear and agrees with prophetic and apostolic speech. Therefore he calls them sound words delivered by himself, in faith, or concerning faith and love in Christ, that is, in the knowledge of Christ, just as everywhere he refers all piety back to faith and love. Catechesis is therefore a summary of the doctrine of faith and love in Christ, delivered by the apostles and prophets; or a summary of Christian doctrine, comprehended briefly, in order and clearly. For it is not ours to devise doctrines, but we must refer ourselves, as Isaiah 8:20 says, to the law and to the testimony. An explanation, however, must be added, which shows the correct division and order of the parts, and interprets the words and phrases.

units.la: II. Salus nostra. DEVS adultos conuertit & saluat per doctrinam cognitam, tanquam organo vero: bi.
units.tr: II. Our salvation. God converts and saves adults through the doctrine known, as through a true instrument.

units.la: Hæc vna ratio, ad excitandum in non profanis mentibus doctrinæ sacræ studium, cuius est efficax. Illis enim Dei mandatum, instar omnium causarum est, etiam si nihil accedat. Sed cum Deus indulgens imbecillitati nostræ causas etiam huius præceptis indicet, reuerenter eas considerare necesse est. Affirmat autem Deus, ideo nobis discendam esse doctrinam, quia per eius cognitionem, & non aliter, omnes, qui per ætatem possunt intelligere, quique ex illis vitæ æternæ hæredes futuri sunt, velit convertere & saluos facere. Confidenter & mirificè dictum est à Paulo Rom. 1. 16. Euangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti Et 1. Cor. 1. 18. Sermo crucis pereuntibus quidem stultitia est, salvandis autem nobis potentia Dei est. Et ib. 23. Placuit Deo per stultam prædicationem salvos facere credentes.
units.tr: This is the one reason, effective for stirring up the study of sacred doctrine in minds that are not profane. For to those minds God's command stands in place of all causes, even if nothing else is added. But since God, indulgent to our weakness, also points out the reasons for these commands, it is necessary to consider them reverently. God affirms that this doctrine must be learned by us because, through its knowledge, and not otherwise, he wills to convert and save all who by their age are able to understand, and who are to be heirs of eternal life. Paul said it confidently and wonderfully, Romans 1:16: The gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes. And 1 Corinthians 1:18: The word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God. And ibid. 21: It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.

units.la: Verum hæc sententia, vt multis & gravibus Spiritus sancti testimoniis tradita & confirmata est, ita magnis diaboli conatibus oppugnatur. Nam paradoxon hoc de stulta crucis prædicatione, mentes humanas non mediocriter percellere videns mendaciorum pater, fanaticos homines inuitandi occasione arripit, vt nihil minus esse docendi officiu clamitet, quā organon, quo conuertantur homines, Deu se nobis immediate communicare, voce no strā [?] nos idolū facere. Fudunt illi quidem singularis cuiusdam illuminationis speciem habetia [?]. Sed quibus nitantur fudamentis, & quā diuino consilio sapientiā opponāt, audite, quæso, & cōsiderate. Nihil, inquiunt, omnipotes Deus indiget ad conuertendos homines istac voce, nihil istoc ministerio, lectione, meditatione. Non igitur hoc instrumento vtitur, nec saluādis vlla huius discēdi laboris necessitas imponenda est. Vos ego iam alloquor pueros, inter quos est ne aliquis tam infirmo, tamq. puerili iudicio, qui nō explodendum intelligat esse eum, qui sic vobis ratiocinetur? Facile Deus omnipotentia sua perficere potest vt quis absq. libris, absq. præceptoribus, absq. studio peritus sit literarū & doctrinæ, vt apostoli & alij in primitiua Ecclesia linguis vtebantur, quas nunquam di[?]iccrāt, potest fœcunda terram, & ex ea fruges edere sine agricolarū laboribus, potest naturam hominis sustentare absq. cibo, vt Moses & Christum quadraginta diebus: non igitur necessaria, nec earum, quas optamus & expectamus, rerum aliqua causa exsistens, opera sumitur, dū scholastici libros & studia tractant, præceptores & scholas adeunt, agricolę aratra, ligones, rastros, & falces terræ admouent, ac singuli vitæ tuendæ vitam impendimus. Videtis, in quos cæcitatis & infinitæ scopulos diabolus impellat infelices homines, qui cū nec fundamenta vel pietatis vel artium meliorum didicerint, nec discedi laborem ament, videri tamen quod minimè sunt, cupientes, extollere se aduersus scientiā Dei, & sapientiam æternam suæ sublimitate censuræ, non dubitant. Nec. n. plus mentis quā frontis habent, cū exempla eorum qui miraculo conuerti, vt Paulus, vel donis ornati sunt, vt apostoli in pentecoste: cū magna multitudine audientiū euangelium, nec tamen credentium, cū scripturæ sententias allegant, quæ de Spiritus sancti officio concionantur. Simi-mus Dei beneficio & fatemur, posse Deum sine hac docentium & discentium opera, quos vult, convertere, & hunc finē esse miraculorum, vt constet, ordine, quo in natura est efficax ab ipso conditū esse, & seruari liberrimè.
units.tr: But this doctrine, as it is delivered and confirmed by many weighty testimonies of the Holy Spirit, is so attacked by the great efforts of the devil. For the father of lies, seeing that this paradox about the foolish preaching of the cross strikes human minds not a little, seizes on the occasion of inviting fanatical men, so that he cries out that nothing is less the office of teaching than being an instrument by which men are converted; that God communicates himself to us immediately, and that we make an idol of our voice. They indeed pour forth the appearance of a certain singular illumination. But on what foundations they rest, and what wisdom they set against the divine counsel, hear, I beg you, and consider. Nothing, they say, does almighty God need to convert men by this voice, nothing by this ministry, reading, meditation. Therefore he does not use this instrument, and no necessity of this labour of learning is to be imposed for salvation. I now address you boys, among whom there is perhaps someone of so weak and so childish a judgment that he does not understand that the man who reasons like this to you must be rejected? God can easily by his omnipotence bring it about that someone without books, without teachers, without study, is skilled in letters and doctrine, as the apostles and others in the primitive Church used tongues which they had never learned; he can make the fertile earth bring forth fruits without the labours of farmers; he can sustain human nature without food, as he did Moses and Christ for forty days. Therefore labour is undertaken for no necessary cause, nor for any cause of the things we desire and expect, while scholars handle books and studies, go to teachers and schools, while farmers apply ploughs, hoes, rakes and sickles to the earth, and each of us spends his life in maintaining life. You see into what blindness and endless reefs the devil drives unhappy men, who, having learned neither the foundations of piety nor of the better arts, and not loving the labour of learning, yet, wishing to seem what they most certainly are not, do not hesitate to lift themselves up against the knowledge of God and eternal wisdom by the loftiness of their judgment. For they have no more mind than brazenness, when they allege the examples of those who were converted by a miracle, like Paul, or who were endowed with gifts, like the apostles at Pentecost, with a great multitude hearing the gospel, yet not believing, and when they cite the sentences of Scripture which preach concerning the office of the Holy Spirit. We agree, by God's kindness, and confess that God can, without this work of teachers and learners, convert whom he wills, and that the purpose of miracles is this: that it be evident that nature, in the order in which it was created by him, is effective, and is preserved most freely.

units.la: Scimus adeo conuersionem esse donum solius Dei, vt quanto perditum hominem saluti restituere, quàm nō existentem condere, maius opus & admirabilius est, tanto maioris impudentię sit ac furoris, illud, quàm hoc, efficacitati vocis humanæ tribuere. Sed illud etiam scimus, placuisse Deo, per stultam prædicationem saluos facere credentes. Cur sic ipsi visum sit, et si nihil necesse est, nobis rationem reddi, tamen huius etiam consilij causas ... Euangelium à se prædicatum nominet potentiam Dei ad saluandos credentes, Item Ephes.4.11. dicat: Dedit alios apostolos, alios prophetas, alios Euangelistas, alios pastores & doctores ad cogmetationé, sanctorū, ad opus ministerij in ædificatione corporis Christi, potéstne de officio dicedi vox gloriosior vlla proferri? Nō igitur plus Deo sapere nobis permittamus, nec omissis regula:ibus, irregularia sectemur, nec tanti sit apud nos cōtemnentium euangelij vocem superbia, contumacia & pernicies, vt ordinationis diuinæ fructum & efficientiam in organis misericordię minus amemus, ac veneremur, vt nec scholasticorum quorundam ignauia, & peruicacia, profectus omnis ac bonæ frugis impedimenta, cæteris persuadet, institutionem & studium ad doctrinam & virtute comparandam, atque augendam res non necessarias esse: sed potius obsequentibus & gratis animis fruamur dulcissima cōsolatione, qua nobis confirmatur & placere Deo nostros labores, & à nobis non frustra suscipi, iuxta hæc dicta: Eccles.11 1. Mitte panē tuum super aquas, quia post longū tempus eū reperies. 1.Corinth.15,58. Labor Vester nō est inanis in Domino. Matth.18.20. Vbicunque sunt duo vel tres congregati in nomine meo, in medio eorum sum. Hæ propositiones, nisi notæ & certæ essent in tantis diaboli furoribus & humani generis miseriis, de quibus nimis vere dicitur, οἱ πλάνοι κακοί [?], docentium optimus & publicæ salutis amantissimus quisque conditione esset infelicissima, locumque suum difficillimè teneret. Ego certè, qui nullo in numero sum, sic me affectū esse sentio, vt dolorem meum & consistere ad hoc pulpitum non mihi permissurum, & hanc vocem in ipsis præcordiis & fauci-bus inclusurum existimem, nisi in hoc nostro cœtu aliquos esse certò scirem, quorum pectora veram & salutarem doctrinam admittūt, & accēduntur Spiritu sancto, vt rectè Deum agnoscant & inuocent, ac viua Dei templa sint, ipsum celebratura in cœlesti consuetudine. Nec tamen hæc eo dicta sunt, quòd cognitionem ac lucem doctrinę parem, & eadem Spiritus sancti dona in omnibus expectemus. Iubet enim nos Paulus Rom.12. sapere iuxta mensurā fidei, quam singulis Deus attribuit. Fundamentum verò saluandos omnes idem tenere necessariŭ est,hoc est,quis sit Christus,& quid præstet singulis, scire & credere oportet,vt dicitur Iohan. 17.3. Hæc est vita æterna,vt cognoscant te solum esse verū Deum, & quem misisti Iesum esse Christum. Et Iohan.3.36. Qui credit in Filium habet vitam æternam. Ex his, aliisque similibus sententiis intelligimus,verum esse dictum, quod Dionysius,qui falso nominatur Areopagita, existimatur aute esse Corinthius,tribuit Bartholomæo Apostolo: Euangelium est breue & longum. Breuitas eius manifesta & multo maior est,quàm legis Mosaicæ, eáq. singulorum animis & cordibus infixa esse debet ac poterit,ideoq. toties in scriptis propheticis & apostolicis & tradita & repetita est euangelij summa,& symbolis coprehesa. Exhauriri vero euangelica sapientia multò etiā minùs, quàm legalis, per omne æternitatē poterit. Sed cum in hac mortalitate vitam æterna inchoāda esse certū sit: superinduemur enim,si nō nudi reperiemur: natura verae cōuerfionis ea est,vt nō resistere cōuerfos ad Deū in curriculo suo patiatur,sed perpetū in illis proficiēdi studiū ac desideriū accedat. Ideo præcipitur 2.Pet.3.18. Crescite in gratia & cognitione Domini nostri & saluatoris Iesu Christi. Et Eph. 2.19. dicitur: Non amplius estis hospites & aduenæ, sed cives sanctorum & domestici Dei. Superstructi fundamento prophetarum & apostolorum existente summo angulari lapide ipso Iesu Christo, in quo totum adificiū coagmentatum crescit in templum sanctum in Domino. Et Marc.9.24. orat ille: Credo domine, sed opem fer incredulitati mea: Et Luc.17.5. discipuli, Domine, adauge nobis fidē. Iubetur sancti & dicūtur proficere, & profectus petūt. Nō igitur sūt in eorū numero,qui proficiēdi studiū nō habēt. Sed nec illos animū despōdere oportet,qui lucis & vigoris in se minus inuenietes,imbecillitatē & sordes suas vero animi dolore agnoscunt atque deplorant. Sic enim dicit pater æternus de Filio Esaiæ 42.3. Calamum quassatum non conteret, & linum fumans non extinguet. Et filius de Patre, Matth.18.14. Non est voluntas patris mei, vt pereat vnus de paruulis istis: Et ipse de se, Ioph.6.37. Omne quod dat mihi pater, ad me veniet: & eum, qui venit ad me, non eiciā foras. Vbicunq; pietas nō simulata est, à Deo est & adiuuatur, cū eaque beneficia euangelij æterna & ἀμεταμέλη-λητα [?] indissolubili vinculo diuinæ veritatis coniuncta sunt,
units.tr: We know that conversion is the gift of God alone, so that to restore a lost man to salvation is a greater and more wonderful work than to create one who did not exist; and so it would be all the greater impudence and madness to ascribe the former, rather than the latter, to the power of the human voice. But we also know that it has pleased God to save believers through the foolish preaching of the Gospel. Why this has seemed good to him, although there is no necessity that we be given an account of it, let us nevertheless consider the reasons for this plan... The Gospel he calls the power of God for saving believers. Likewise Ephesians 4:11 says: "He gave some apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors and teachers, for the equipping of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the building up of the body of Christ." Can any more glorious voice concerning the office of teaching be uttered? Let us not therefore presume to be wiser than God, nor, having set aside the rules, pursue irregular ways; and let the pride, obstinacy and ruin of those who despise the voice of the Gospel carry such weight with us that we do not love and reverence less the fruit and efficacy of the divine ordinance in the instruments of mercy. Nor let the idleness and stubbornness of certain scholastics, which is the hindrance to all progress and good fruit, persuade others that instruction and study for acquiring and increasing doctrine and virtue are unnecessary. Rather let us enjoy, with compliant and willing minds, that most sweet consolation by which we are assured that our labours please God and are not undertaken by us in vain, according to these sayings: Ecclesiastes 11:1: "Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it." 1 Corinthians 15:58: "Your labour is not in vain in the Lord." Matthew 18:20: "Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them." These propositions, if they were not known and certain amid such great furies of the devil and miseries of the human race, of which it is only too true to say, "the wicked deceivers" [?], the best of teachers and each one most devoted to the public welfare would be in the most unhappy condition and would hold their place with the greatest difficulty. For my part, who am in no number, I feel myself so affected that I think I would not allow my grief to let me stand at this pulpit, and I would shut this voice up within my very heart and throat, unless I knew for certain that in this our assembly there are some whose hearts receive true and saving doctrine, and who are kindled by the Holy Spirit so that they rightly acknowledge and call upon God, and are living temples of God, destined to celebrate him in heavenly fellowship. Yet these things are not said because we expect the knowledge and light of doctrine to be equal, and the same gifts of the Holy Spirit, in all. For Paul bids us (Romans 12) to think soberly according to the measure of faith which God has assigned to each. But that all who are to be saved must hold the foundation in common is necessary: that is, one must know and believe who Christ is and what he accomplishes for each individual, as it says in John 17:3: "This is eternal life, that they know you to be the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent." And John 3:36: "He who believes in the Son has eternal life." From these and other similar sayings we understand that what Dionysius, falsely called the Areopagite, though thought to be a Corinthian, attributed to the apostle Bartholomew is true: "The Gospel is both brief and long." Its brevity is evident and much greater than that of the Mosaic law, and it ought and can be fixed in the minds and hearts of each individual; therefore the sum of the gospel has so often been handed down and repeated in the prophetic and apostolic writings and comprehended in the creeds. But the wisdom of the Gospel can be exhausted, through all eternity, much less than that of the law. But since it is certain that eternal life is to be begun in this mortal life (for "we shall be clothed upon, if we are found not naked"), the nature of true conversion is such that it does not allow the converted to stand still in their course, but a constant zeal and desire for progress comes upon them. Therefore it is commanded in 2 Peter 3:18: "Grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ." And Ephesians 2:19 says: "You are no longer strangers and sojourners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God, built upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles, Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone, in whom the whole building, being joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord." And in Mark 9:24 that man prays: "Lord, I believe; help my unbelief." And Luke 17:5, the disciples: "Lord, increase our faith." The saints are commanded and said to make progress, and they seek progress. Therefore they are not among those who have no zeal for progress. Nor ought those to despair who, finding little light and vigour in themselves, acknowledge and lament their weakness and filthiness with inward grief. For thus the eternal Father says of the Son, Isaiah 42:3: "A bruised reed he will not break, and a smoking flax he will not quench." And the Son says of the Father, Matthew 18:14: "It is not the will of my Father that one of these little ones should perish." And he himself says of himself, John 6:37: "All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will by no means cast out." Wherever piety is not feigned, it is from God and is helped by him, and since these benefits of the Gospel are eternal and irrevocable, they are joined by an indissoluble bond to the divine truth.

units.la: {*} Euangelium est breue & longum. sunt.Nisi enim ex sola & gratuita Dei misericordia, quia omnes credentes recipit, non autem ex nostrae renouationis gradibus, fidei & salutis nostrae certitudo pendet: nulla nostrae consolationis essent firmitas. Tria igitur hinc sumi possunt hominis Christiani quasi κεφάλαια: Fundamenti complexus, & perfici studium, quae singulos viuersali promissioni aeternae salutis includit: Et consolatio, quod propter donorum seu graduum inaequalitatem non simus perituri, quae consolatio indignitatis nostrae cogitationi opponenda est. Haec tria quae separari nunquam possunt, complexus est Paulus, inquies 1.Co. 3.11.
units.tr: {*} "The Gospel is both brief and long." For unless the certainty of our faith and salvation depended solely on the free mercy of God, who receives all believers, and not on the degrees of our renewal, there would be no firmness in our consolation. Three things, therefore, may be taken from this as the chief heads of the Christian man: the embrace of the foundation and the pursuit of perfection, which includes each one in the universal promise of eternal salvation; and consolation, that because of the inequality of gifts or degrees we shall not perish, which consolation must be set against the thought of our unworthiness. Paul has comprehended these three, which can never be separated, as you may see in 1 Corinthians 3:11:

units.la: Fundamentum aliud ponere nemo potest praeter id, quod positum est, qui est Christus. Si vero quis aedificat super fundamentum hoc, aurum, argentum, gemmas, lignum, fenum, calamum, cuiusque operum manifestum fiet: ipse autem salvus erit, sic tamen, tanquam per ignem. Ex his igitur, quae hactenus dicta sunt, manifestum est, mandatum Dei, & salutem propriam omnes homines, atque in his iuuentutem etiam magnam videlicet partem, & seminarium ecclesiae, ad discendum, cum primum per aetatem possunt, Christianae doctrinae fundamentum hortari & obstringere. Id quod omnes, quibus primae aetatis formandae provincia data est, grauissime seueriss imeque huius officij sui partis admonet.
units.tr: "For no one can lay any foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Now if anyone builds on this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one's work will become manifest; for the day will declare it, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. If anyone's work survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone's work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire." From what has been said so far, therefore, it is clear that all men, and especially a great part of youth, the seedbed of the Church, ought to be exhorted and bound, as soon as their age allows, to learn the foundation of Christian doctrine, both by God's command and for their own salvation. This all those are most seriously and sternly reminded of this part of their office to whom the task of forming the early age has been entrusted.

units.la: Docentes enim & discentes, diligentē & acrem pietatis curam non nobis solùm, sed nostris etiam & vniuersis posteritati debemus. Experimur autem doctrinae, cuius summa nō breuiter & perspicuè comprehensa, publicè nota, repetita, inculcata & peruulgata fit, quàm facilè, successu non longi temporis, obrepat obliuio, & multiplex deprauatio. Scimus etiā, quo tesla recens odore, siue bono, siue malo, semel est imbuta, illum tenacissimè seruare: cùm q. mala, si qua didicimus, plerūq. pertinacius adhaerescant, iuuenturę ad pietatem non institutam & assuefactā, cyclopica ac Dei, religionisque vniuersae cōtemtricem aetatem sequuturo seculo minari ac tradere: Ad bona vero cùm vix magnis conatibus & longa cura flectamur, operis difficillimi primo tempore principium faciendum esse, nemo sanae mentis non fatetur. Nō solū itaque ad puritatem & rectitudinem doctrinæ nobis & posteris conferuandam: sed etiam, cùm tradendam esse iuuentuti ostensum fit, ad iuuenile captü necessaria est institutio catechetica. Nam fi de cæteris artibus, huic ætati tradendis, rectè dictum est,
units.tr: For we teachers and learners owe a diligent and keen care for piety not only to ourselves but also to our descendants and to the whole of posterity. We know by experience how easily, in no long time, forgetfulness and manifold corruption creep in upon a doctrine whose sum is not briefly and clearly comprehended, publicly known, repeated, inculcated and widely spread. We also know that a vessel, once imbued with a fresh odour, whether good or bad, keeps it most tenaciously; and since the evil things we have learned usually cling more stubbornly, no one of sound mind denies that an age not trained and accustomed to piety threatens and hands down to the following century a Cyclopean age, contemptuous of God and of all religion. But since we are turned to what is good only with great effort and long care, that the beginning of this most difficult work must be made in the earliest time, no one of sound mind fails to admit. Therefore not only for preserving the purity and rectitude of doctrine for ourselves and for posterity, but also, since it has been shown that doctrine must be handed down to youth, catechetical instruction is necessary for the capacity of youth. For if what is rightly said of the other arts to be handed on to this age is true,

units.la: Quicquid præcipies, esto breuis, ut cito dicta Percipiant animi dociles, teneantque fideles:
units.tr: Whatever you prescribe, let it be brief, so that teachable minds may grasp quickly what is said and hold fast to it.

units.la: quanto magis in hac cœlesti & humanis mentibus peregrina sapientia, breuitas & facilitas quærenda & adhibenda est? præsertim sacris restimoniis hoftram experientiam approbantibus, vt Heb.5.13. Omnis particeps lactis imperitus est sermonis de iustitia: Puer enim est. Perfectorum autem est solida esca. Ideoque cùm Paulus de sua docendi ratione, 1. Corinth.3.2. sic loquitur: Lacte vos potaui, non cibo, nondum enim poteratis, ac ne tam quidem potestis cibo vescimini. Adhuc carnales estis.
units.tr: How much more, then, should brevity and ease be sought and employed in this heavenly wisdom, which is foreign to human minds! This is especially so since the sacred testimonies confirm our experience, as in Heb. 5:13: "Everyone who partakes of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is a child. But solid food is for the mature." And so when Paul speaks of his own method of teaching in 1 Cor. 3:2: "I gave you milk to drink, not solid food, for you were not yet able to receive it; indeed, you are still not able, for you are still fleshly."

units.la: Tu inde ab initio in ecclesia, doctrinæ hypotypofis aliqua nota, solemnis & propter breuitate & euidetia apprehenfu facilis extitit, & ad posteritate seruata est. Vt cum genere humano accreuerunt ipsius Dei voce traditæ sum mæ legis: Si bonus fueris, eris acceptus: & euangelij, Semé mulieris conteret caput serpentis: si postea Abrahæ repetita promissio & decalogus: tandem vero symbola & summæ in apostolicis libris passim sparsæ, accommodata nimirum forma confessionis ad singularum ætatum diuinas patefactiones. Et quidem nostrum hunc institutionis morem, qui catechesis nominatur, vsitatum fuisse tum in veteri tum in apostolica ecclesia, Paulus indicat Rom.2.verf.18. cùm nominat Iudæos [?]κατηχούμενοι ἐκ τοῦ νόμου[?], inde ab ineunte ætate legem edoctos: & Gal.6.v.6. cum inquit: [?]κοινωνείτω δὲ ὁ κατηχούμενος τὸν λόγον τῷ κατηχοῦντι ἐν πᾶσιν ἀγαθοῖς[?]. Item q. Luc. 1. cap. 4. [?]ἵνα ἐπιγνῷς περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης λόγων τὴν ἀσφάλειαν[?].
units.tr: From the beginning in the Church, some outline of doctrine has been in use, customary and easy to grasp because of its brevity and clarity, and it has been preserved for posterity. Thus, as the human race grew, there came first the voice of God himself declaring the chief points of his law: "If you do well, you will be accepted" (Gen. 4:7); and of the gospel: "The seed of the woman will crush the head of the serpent" (Gen. 3:15). Afterwards came the repeated promise to Abraham and the Decalogue; and finally the creeds and summaries scattered throughout the apostolic books, a form of confession, of course, adapted to the divine revelations of each age. That this custom of instruction of ours, which is called catechesis, was in use both in the ancient and in the apostolic Church, Paul indicates in Rom. 2:18, when he names the Jews as "those instructed (katēchoumenoi) out of the law", taught the law from their earliest age; and in Gal. 6:6, when he says: "Let the one who is being instructed (katēchoumenos) share all good things with the one who instructs (katēchounti) him" [katēchoumenos ... katēchounti]. Likewise in Luke 1:4: "that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught (katēchēthēs) [katēchēthēs]."

units.la: Hæc testimonia cùm omnibus anteponenda sint, ecclesiæ, apostolorum tempora sequuntur, exemplum non recito, tanquam ex historiis publicè notum. Illud potius addo, quod si tanta constantia morem hunc seu formam institutionis, non humano consilio, sed vt videmus, diuinitùs inducAam, recens adhuc & vrges ecclesia seruauit, sub deliram hanc mundi tenebras languescente indies ecclesia & maioribus subinde tenebris ingruentibus, accuenda magis est omnis in conseruanda & propaganda doctridoctrina diligentia,quàm quidquam de ea remittendâ. Hæc enim est ætas illa,de qua dictum est Matth.24.ver.23.Tunc si quis dixerit ἰδού[?]: Ecce hic est Christus,aut hic, ne credatis. Surgent enim pseudochristi & pseudoprophetæ, & edēt signa magna,& ostenta,st[?] seducantur etiā,si esset possibile,electi. Et prolixè cōcionatur Paulus 1.Tim.4.&2. Tim.3.Et Petrus 2.cap.2.ver.3.Hæ vero prædictiones calamitatū postremi temporis,nō tantum consolationis & confirmationis nostræ gratia scriptæ sunt,sed etiam ad vigilantiam,& quibus obuiam eatur erroribus,arma comparanda,nos hortantur. Sic enim orditur Christus hoc triste vaticiniū:Videte,ne quis seducat vos. Nō solos igi-tur ad docēdū accessuros,sed omnes,quib. salus sua cor-di est,veras sententias de singulis Christianæ doctrinæ partibus,animis infixas habere, & aduersus corruptelas, quā quisquè potest optimè munitos esse,necessariū existimemus,& omnes,quibus docendi & gubernandi partes datæ sunt,nisi tanquā curatores officij sui negligentes & infidi, de suorū pernicie malint rationes reddere, magna sedulitate sibi commissos rectè doceant,vel docendos curent. Ac parentum vestrorum voluntas merito laudanda est,quòd non domi tantùm & in templis, sed in scholis etiam, pietatis summam proponi vobis & in culcari volunt. Vident enim,quæ tenebræ sequuntur,& in his omnes detinendi,quanta diabolo facultas & occasio data sit,postquā amissa primitiuæ ecclesiæ catechumenos instituendi & audiendi consuetudine,in locū illius, ineptum & futile confirmationis papisticę spectaculum successit:vident,eadē nunc aut his deteriora, nisi Deus clementia singulari nos respiciat, esse metuenda. Quo periculo,vt vix quidquam piis omnibus maiorem tristitiam adferre possit, ita nec aliquid inuenire facile est piis parentibus optabilius aut iucundius, quàm si certò sibi polliceri possint,in eadē diuinæ veritatis luce, quæ nobis nunc accensa est,aliquantò post liberos & nepo-tes suos esse victuros. Quare si non sumus ἄξιοι[?], atque crudeles aduersus illos,qui nos plus quàm seipsos, diligunt:annitamur pro viribus,ne nostra negligentia hanc ipsorum spem labefactemus,ne his votis obsistamus:sed vt vna cum illis gratos Deo nos exhibeamus, qui etiam ex his mundi fœcibus æternam ecclesiam sibi collectu-rus, sole cœlestis doctrinæ reducto, regni Antichristiani caliginem ita discussit, ut nemo nisi pertinaciter aures & oculos obturas, aut agnitæ veritati repugnas, fraudes diabolicas, inuolucris, quibus sese veritabant, exutas nō animaduertat ac deprehendat. Quod si fecerimus, filius Dei beneficia in nos collata seruabit nobis & augebit iuxta promissionē: Habenti, i. volenti proficere, dabitur: sin diuersum egerimus poenę cōsequetur, quas minatur contraria sētētia: a nō habēte, etiā id, quod habet, auferetur. Certe quàm nō ferat Deus euangelij patefacti & mūdi cōtētū, & doctrina diuinitus inspirata, & mūdi tota historia clamat. Queritur Esa.5.v.4. Abiecerunt legem Domini exercituū, & verbū sancti Israel blasphemauerūt. Ideo iratus est furor Domini in populū suum, & extendit manum suā, & percussit eū. Et Amos 3.ii. minatur: Ecce dies venient, dicit Dominus, & mittā famē in terrā, nō famē panis, neq; sitim aquæ, sed audiēdi verbū Domini: Et cōmouebūtur a mari usq. ad mare, & ab aquilone usq. ad orientē: circumibunt quaerentes verbū Domini, & nō inuenient. Gete Israelitica, quā Deus tot insignibus titulis & priuilegiis, tantis successibus & miraculis ornauerat, & longe supra genus omne mortaliū extulerat, abiectā infrà omnes infimos homines videmus, & in meridiana prophetarū concionum luce tam turpiter & portentosè cæcutire, vt omnibus hominibus non dico iocum aut bile mouere, sed horrorem eius exēplū cōsideratum incutere possit. Causam tatorū [?] malorū esse cōtemtum & negligentiā sanæ doctrinæ de Deo & nostra salute audimus affirmare voce prophetarū, & ipsius Christi, Ioh. 5.43. Ego veni in nomine patris mei, & nō accipitis me: cū alius venerit in nomine suo, illū accipietis. Aliorū exemplorū recitatione supersedeo: sed vnū attingo, floretissimi paulò ante, ac felicissimi regni Angliæ, nō eo tantum, quòd est insigniter triste, sed etiā, quòd in hoc cætu nostro nullus adeò puer est, in cuius ætate nō inciderit. His enim temporibus, agniti one diuinæ veritatis donatā Angliæ, & regnante Eduardo VI. ecclesiis & scholis egregiè cōstitutis ac florētib°, rege vero nato annos sedecim, pietate, virtute ac doctrina lōgè, quàm pro modo ætatis, excellentius ornato,ita ut in regno pulcherrimo nihil esset ipso rege pulchrius, earegio nulli terrarum orbis parti, felicitate cedebat. Sed subito rebus humanis Eduardo summae spei principe exempto,regnum denuo pontificia tyrannis occupauit, carceribus, exiliis, flammis & ferro crudeliter vastatis pulcerrimis ecclesiis,hominibus eruditione & sanctitate antecellentibus,nulla nec aetatis,nec sexus,nec dignitatis ratione habita,aliis ad rogos & sequissima supplicia raptis : aliis versus omnes mundi angulos dissectis. Iam quintus dū hę calamitates illic durant,annus abiit. Ego nostra potius agnosco & deploro peccata, quàm de alienis iudicium mihi sumo. Sed nondum mihi penitus exciderunt voces Anglicorum exulum hisce à me acceptae auribus,quibus illi de suae gentis ingratitudine,securitate, & quae eā ceperat, euangelij satietate,conquerebantur. At videmur-ne re nostra nos melius agere? Utinam quidé agamus. Cum Pilatus Galilaeorum interfectorum saguinē admiscuisset victimis,inquit Christus Luc.13.3. Nisi pœnitentiā egeritis, omnes similiter peribitis. Versantur nobis ob oculos & minatur,imperiorum tumultus & ruinae,quibus duriter quassatur ecclesia. Inhiat nobis latrones Turcici, qui nobis magna vi conatur Christū eripere,suuq.[?] Mahometū obtrudere, quos audimus quotidie grassari latius in nobis cognatu sanguine,juvetutē Christianā ad suae turpitudinis & blasphemiae societate abstrahere, irruptione ad nos moliri. Exsecratur nos ac tollendos clamat universum βασίλευμα[?] regni Pōtificij: pullulat & sua crescit vndiq. tāquā hydrae capita,intra & extra ecclesiā haereses & veritatis corruptelę plures,quā numerari possunt. Ac plane nūc illud est,cū nisi Dominus feruet nobis semen,quin Gomorrhae & Sodomae similes reddamur,nihil restat. Ne sic tandem simus ferrei nec sic nos ipsos oderimus, ut ista nos nihil moveat. Quæramus Domini, dū inueniri potest. Suae quisq; salutis ratione secum ineat, quæq; ad eam pertinent, collecta & instructa corde teneamus, ut nos, si fractus illabatur orbis impauidos feriant ruinae.
units.tr: Since these testimonies must be placed before all others, the times of the Church and of the apostles follow; I do not recite examples, as they are publicly known from histories. I would rather add this: if the Church, still young and vigorous, has kept this custom or form of instruction with such constancy, introduced not by human counsel but, as we see, by divine guidance, then the Church, which is growing feeble day by day under the darkness of this world and is from time to time overtaken by still greater darkness, ought all the more to apply every diligence to preserving and spreading doctrine, rather than to relax anything concerning it. For this is that age of which it was said in Matt. 24:23: "Then if anyone says to you, 'Look, here is the Christ!' or 'There he is!', do not believe it. For false christs and false prophets will arise and will show great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect." Paul preaches at length on this in 1 Tim. 4 and 2 Tim. 3, and Peter in 2 Pet. 2:3. These predictions of the calamities of the last times were written not only for our consolation and confirmation, but also to exhort us to watchfulness and to prepare arms with which errors may be met. For Christ begins this sad prophecy in just this way: "Take heed that no one leads you astray." Therefore we should judge it necessary not only for those who are coming to be taught, but for all whose salvation is dear to them, to have true opinions on each part of Christian doctrine fixed in their minds, and to be well armed against corruptions, as far as each one can be; and all to whom the parts of teaching and governing have been given, unless they prefer, as negligent and faithless guardians of their office, to render accounts of the ruin of those under their care, should teach diligently what has been entrusted to them, or see that those to be taught are taught. And the will of your parents is rightly to be praised, in that they wish the sum of piety to be set before you and impressed upon you not only at home and in the churches, but in the schools as well. For they see what darkness follows, and how great an opportunity and occasion the devil has been given to ensnare all, now that the ancient custom of instructing and hearing catechumens has been lost in the primitive Church, and in its place the foolish and trifling spectacle of papal confirmation has taken over. They see that these same evils, or worse, are to be feared now unless God looks upon us with singular mercy. Nothing could bring greater sadness to all the pious than this danger; and yet it is hard to find anything more desirable or more pleasing to pious parents than being able to promise themselves with certainty that their children and grandchildren, in the same light of divine truth which now shines upon us, will live some time after us. Therefore, if we are not worthy and are cruel toward those who love us more than themselves, let us strive with all our strength not to undermine their hope by our negligence, nor to stand in the way of these wishes; but let us, together with them, show ourselves pleasing to God, who, to gather for himself an eternal Church even out of these dregs of the world, has, by bringing back the sun of heavenly doctrine, dispelled the darkness of the Antichristian kingdom to such an extent that no one who stubbornly stops his ears and eyes, or resists the truth once recognized, fails to notice and detect the diabolical frauds, now stripped of the wrappings in which they concealed themselves. If we do this, the Son of God will keep and increase for us the benefits bestowed upon us, according to his promise: "To one who has, more will be given" (that is, to one who is willing to make progress); but if we act otherwise, the punishment threatened by the opposite sentence will follow: "from one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away." Surely the whole history of the world cries out how little God endures the contempt of the revealed gospel and of divinely inspired doctrine. Isaiah complains in Isa. 5:24: "They have rejected the law of the Lord of hosts, and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. Therefore the anger of the Lord is kindled against his people, and he stretches out his hand and strikes them." And Amos threatens in Amos 8:11: "Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will send a famine on the land, not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the Lord. They will wander from sea to sea, and from the north to the east; they will run to and fro seeking the word of the Lord, and will not find it." We see the Israelite nation, which God had adorned with so many distinguished titles and privileges, with such successes and miracles, and had raised far above every kind of mortal, cast down below all the lowest of men, and blinding itself so shamefully and monstrously in the noonday light of the prophets' sermons that its example, when considered, can inspire not merely laughter or bile in all men, but horror. We hear, in the voices of the prophets and of Christ himself, that the cause of such great evils is contempt and neglect of sound doctrine concerning God and our salvation, as in John 5:43: "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me; if another comes in his own name, you will receive him." I pass over the recitation of other examples, but I touch on one, from the most flourishing and most fortunate kingdom of England shortly before us, not only because it is remarkably sad, but also because there is no child in this assembly of ours in whose lifetime it did not fall. For in those times, when the knowledge of divine truth had been granted to England, and while King Edward VI reigned, the churches and schools were excellently founded and flourishing, and the king, though only sixteen years old, was adorned with piety, virtue and learning far more excellently than his age allowed, so that in that most beautiful kingdom nothing was more beautiful than the king himself; in felicity that region of the earth yielded to no other part of the world. But suddenly, with Edward, a prince of the highest hope, taken from human affairs, the kingdom was again seized by papal tyranny. The most beautiful churches were cruelly laid waste with prisons, exiles, flames and sword; men preeminent in learning and holiness were carried off, with no regard for age, sex or rank, some to the stakes and to most unjust punishments, others were scattered to every corner of the world. Already a fifth year has passed while these calamities endure there. I recognize and deplore our own sins rather than presume to judge the sins of others. But the voices of the English exiles, which I heard with my own ears, have not wholly faded from my mind; in them they complained of the ingratitude of their nation, its complacency, and the satiety with the gospel that had taken hold of it. Yet do we seem to be doing better in our own affairs? Would that we were indeed doing well! When Pilate mingled the blood of the Galileans with their sacrifices, Christ said (Luke 13:3): "Unless you repent, you will all likewise perish." Before our eyes there hang the tumults and ruins of empires, by which the Church is harshly shaken. The Turkish robbers threaten us, who with great force try to snatch Christ from us and force Muhammad upon us; we hear that they daily rage more widely among our own blood-kin, drawing Christian youth into the fellowship of their shame and blasphemy, and they plan an assault upon us. The whole royal power of the papal kingdom curses us and cries out that we must be destroyed; on all sides, like the heads of the hydra, heresies and corruptions of the truth, more than can be counted, sprout up and grow, both within and outside the Church. And now the point is plainly this: unless the Lord preserves a seed for us, nothing remains but that we become like Gomorrah and Sodom. Let us not at last be so iron-hearted, nor so hate ourselves, that these things move us not at all. Let us seek the Lord while he may be found. Let each one take counsel with himself about the reason for his own salvation, and let us hold what pertains to it gathered together and well ordered in our hearts, so that, if the world should break apart and its ruins fall, they may strike us unafraid.

units.la: Omnes quidē haec, quae diximus, attingunt, sed nostrū præcipuè scholasticum ordinē. Consentiunt enim omnes, qui scholas unquam instituerunt, aut gubernarunt, aut in illis versati sunt,aut alios versari volunt,non doctiores tantùm,sed meliores etiam eos, qui in his educantur,effici debere.Quod cũ ita fit, scholā esse cõsitētur,cœtū ordinatione diuina docētiū& discētiū doctrinā generi humano necessariā,de Deo, & aliis rebus bonis, ne extinguatur notitia Dei inter homines, vt feruetur ecclesia,multi fiat hæredes vitæ æternæ,feruetur difcipli na,& homines habeat alias honestas vtilitates ex artibꝰ.
units.tr: Indeed, all these things we have said touch everyone, but they touch especially our scholastic order. For all who have ever founded schools, governed them, been engaged in them, or wish others to be engaged in them, agree that those who are educated in them ought to be made not only more learned but also better people. Since this is so, a school is a gathering, by divine ordinance, of teachers and learners, for the teaching of doctrine necessary to the human race: concerning God and other good things, so that the knowledge of God is not extinguished among men, so that the Church is preserved, so that many become heirs of eternal life, so that discipline is preserved, and so that men have other honourable advantages from the arts.
