For the properties of the divine nature, said of the whole person in the concrete, they apply to each nature: "Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age," they take as said of both natures; which is just the same as if it were said, "Christ was circumcised," and one should understand: "Christ was circumcised in deity and in flesh."

units.la: Inst. Tantum hoc addimus, illos articulos huc non perti-re. Respond. Hoc modo omnes sectæ omnia scripturæ testimonia possunt eludere. Imo vero duplici iure huc pertinent: 1. quia sunt scripti de corpore Christi. Corpus autem Christi pertinet ad coenam. Ergo etiam isti articuli huc pertinent. Docet enim quomodo corpus Christi sit manducandum. 2. quia nullus articulus fidei pugnat cum alio, & alius est regula, secundum quam alium oportet explicare. Sic huc pertinet doctrina de iustificatione, quia in coena non debet alia iustitia quæri, nisi per sanguinem Christi.
units.tr: Objection. We only add that those articles do not pertain here. Reply. In this way all sects can elude all the testimonies of Scripture. Indeed they pertain here by a double right: (1) because they were written about the body of Christ. But the body of Christ pertains to the Supper. Therefore these articles also pertain here, for they teach how the body of Christ is to be eaten. (2) because no article of faith fights against another, and one is the rule according to which the other must be explained. Thus the doctrine of justification pertains here, because in the Supper no righteousness is to be sought except through the blood of Christ.

units.la: VI. Modus non est definiendus. RESP. Dupliciter pec-cant, 1. Cum negant modum esse definiendum, & sic scripturæ contradicunt, quæ eum definit, & docet esse spiritualem, & unionem cum Christo fieri fide per Spiritum sanctum, 2. Ipsimet modum definiunt, ut ex eorum scriptis liquido constat.
units.tr: VI. The manner is not to be defined. REPLY. They sin in two ways: (1) when they deny that the manner is to be defined, and so contradict Scripture, which defines it, and teaches that it is spiritual, and that union with Christ is effected by faith through the Holy Spirit; (2) they themselves define the manner, as is clear beyond doubt from their writings.

units.la: VII. Verum est Durandi dictum: Verba audimus, mo-tum sentimus, modum nescimus, praesentiam credimus. Resp. Nihil facit nec pro vobis, nec contra nos, quia Durandus fuit papista. 2. Dictum recte intellectum possumus admittere: Verbū audimus, Hoc est corpus meum, non quod in pane corpus Christi ore comedamus. Motum sentimus, id est, panem ingredi in os, nō corpus Christi. Modum nescimus, scilicet perfecte, quomodo videlicet Spiritus sanctus sit ubique totus in Christo, & omnibus sanctis, & quomodo nos in Christo vniat. Praesentiam credimus, scilicet talem, qualis est esus, & qualis est vnio membrorum & capitis.
units.tr: VII. The saying of Durandus is true: "We hear the words, we feel the motion, we do not know the manner, we believe the presence." Reply. It helps neither you nor against us, because Durandus was a Papist. (2) The saying, rightly understood, we can admit: "We hear the words": "This is my body," not that we eat the body of Christ orally in the bread. "We feel the motion": that is, the bread enters the mouth, not the body of Christ. "We do not know the manner": namely, perfectly, how the Holy Spirit is wholly everywhere in Christ and in all the saints, and how he unites us to Christ. "We believe the presence": namely such as is the eating, and such as is the union of the members and the head.

units.la: VIII. Hoc tantum docemus, vere, substantialiter & naturaliter exhiberi corpus & sanguinem Christi. Resp. Cocedimus nos verum corpus Christi edere. Sic ergo inanis est disputatio[?]. 1. Quia fatentur nos fieri participes veri corporis Christi, & quod non fit agendum de modo. Illud autem & nos concedimus. 2. Quia rationes & refutationes quas adferunt nullius sunt momenti:
units.tr: VIII. We teach only this: that the body and blood of Christ are truly, substantially and naturally offered. Reply. We concede that we eat the true body of Christ. So then the dispute is empty: (1) because they confess that we become partakers of the true body of Christ, and that the manner is not to be treated; this we also concede. (2) because the arguments and refutations they bring are of no weight.

units.la: IV. Argumenta, quibus probatur, corpus Christi nec in, nec sub, nec ad panem coenae Dominicae adesse, nec sub, cum, in, ad eum corporaliter edi.
units.tr: IV. Arguments by which it is proved that the body of Christ is present neither in, nor under, nor at the bread of the Lord's Supper, and that it is not eaten bodily under, with, in, or at it.

units.la: 1, Quia assumfit naturam verè humanam. Hoc addendum, quòd non possumus eam aliter edere, quàm discipu-lis in prima coena.
units.tr: 1. Because he assumed a truly human nature. To this must be added that we cannot eat it otherwise than the disciples did at the first supper.

units.la: 2. Verè ascendit de terra in coelum.
units.tr: 2. He truly ascended from the earth into heaven.

units.la: 3. Talis est manducatio, qualis mansio.
units.tr: 3. Such is the eating as the dwelling.

units.la: 4. Omnes sancti, veteris & noui Testamenti habent eandem vnionem cum Christo.
units.tr: 4. All the saints of the Old and New Testament have the same union with Christ.

units.la: 5, Solus Christus potest se patri offerre. Necesse est autem in visu coenae petere à Deo remissionem peccatorum. Quare si ad panem adest, petendum est ab eo, & sic offerimus panem. In Nouo Testamento non licet orationem ad certum dirigere locum.
units.tr: 5. Only Christ can offer himself to the Father. Now it is necessary, in the act of the supper, to ask God for the forgiveness of sins. Therefore, if he is present at the bread, he must be asked for this, and so we offer the bread. In the New Testament it is not lawful to direct prayer to a certain place.

units.la: 6. Bona, quae solis piis promittuntur, spiritualia sunt.
units.tr: 6. The goods which are promised to the godly alone are spiritual.

units.la: His & aliis supra citatis accedit consensus Patrum, Ambrosij, Athanasij, Augustini, Basilij, Bedæ, Bertrami, Chrysostomi, Clementis, Alexandrini, Concilij, Nicæni, Cypriani, Cyrilli, Dionysij, Gelasij, Gregorij Magni, Gregorij Nazianzeni, Hesychij, Hieronymi, Hilarij, Irenæi, Iustini, Leonis, Macarij, Origenis, Procopij, Gazæ, Tertulliani, Theodoreti, &c.
units.tr: To these and the other arguments cited above is added the consensus of the Fathers: Ambrose, Athanasius, Augustine, Basil, Bede, Bertram, Chrysostom, Clement of Alexandria, the Council of Nicaea, Cyprian, Cyril, Dionysius, Gelasius, Gregory the Great, Gregory Nazianzen, Hesychius, Jerome, Hilary, Irenaeus, Justin, Leo, Macarius, Origen, Procopius of Gaza, Tertullian, Theodoret, etc.

units.la: V. Argumenta, quibus dogma Vbiquistarum refellitur, & sana doctrina veritas confirmatur.
units.tr: V. Arguments by which the doctrine of the Ubiquitarians is refuted and the truth of sound doctrine is confirmed.

units.la: Argumentum. 1. Marcionitæ & Manichæi finxerunt, Christum non fuisse vero & solido corpore humano præditum, sed speciem tantum corporis ostentasse, vt visus fuerit solum modo carnem & ossa habere cum reuera non haberet. Ipsam quoque [?]‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑‑, & omnes motus operationesque Christi in phantasia apparuisse, cùm in rei veritate nihil tale fieret. Sed Vbiquitatis & realis idiomatum communicationis dogma illud phantasticum delirium ex inferis reuocat. Ergo ipsum quoque, vt Manichæum ex Ecclesia Dei ad inferos relegandum est. Minor sic probatur: Sentiunt & docent Vbiquitarij, Omnes deitatis proprietates, ab ipso statim conceptionis momento, fuisse à deitate [?] in assumtam humanitatem Christi realiter effusas. Inde hæc absurda sequuntur, 1. Verè editus ex Virgine non erit Christus, si secundum humanitatis suæ naturam verè ac alienialiter extra vterum maternum fuit, antequam nasceretur, & post partum in illo ipso vtero non minùs verè ac substantialiter, quàm ante, secundum humanitatis naturam remansit. 2. Verè in sua natura humana infirmus & passionibus obnoxius non fuit Christus, si tunc etiam secundum eandem naturam diuinæ maiestatis & omnipotentiæ particeps fuit. 3. Verè mortuus non fuit, si etiam ipso mortis tempore, secundum animam & corpus essentialiter fuit vbique vnà cum deitate præsens. Non enim anima omni praesens a corpore omnipraesenti locorum spatio realiter separari, & proinde nec corpus moti potuit, nisi iuxta imaginationem. 4. Vere non ascendit in coelum: sed in nane tantum & imaginarium ac phantasticum spectaculum fuisse dicetur: si corpore suo substantialiter ibi fuit antequam visibiliter eo ascenderet: & postquam ascendit, substantiali eiusdem corporis praesentia non minus quam ante in terris, imo in ipsis etiam credentium corporibus manet. Haec si in rei veritate ita euenerunt, sequetur idem Christi corpus simul reipsa fuisse infirmum & omnipotens, humile & gloriosum: passibile & impassibile, mortuum & viuum, circumscriptum & incircumscriptum, quod horrendum est dicere.
units.tr: Argument. 1. The Marcionites and Manichaeans fabricated that Christ did not possess a true and solid human body, but only displayed the appearance of a body, so that he seemed to have flesh and bones when in truth he had none. Likewise [some words unclear], and all the movements and operations of Christ appeared in fantasy, since in the reality of the matter nothing of the kind took place. But the doctrine of ubiquity and of the real communication of attributes recalls that phantastic delirium from the dead. Therefore that doctrine itself, like the Manichaean, must be relegated from the Church of God to the dead. The minor premise is proved thus: The Ubiquitarians hold and teach that all the properties of the deity were really poured out from the deity into the assumed humanity of Christ from the very moment of conception. From this the following absurdities follow. 1. Christ would not be truly born of the Virgin, if according to the nature of his humanity he was truly and substantially outside the maternal womb before he was born, and after the birth remained in that same womb no less truly and substantially than before, according to the nature of his humanity. 2. Christ would not have been truly weak and subject to sufferings in his human nature, if at that time he also, according to the same nature, shared in the divine majesty and omnipotence. 3. He would not have truly died, if even at the very time of death, according to soul and body, he was essentially present everywhere together with the deity. For the soul, being everywhere present, could not be really separated from the body, which is omnipresent through the whole extent of places, and therefore the body could not have been moved either, except in imagination. 4. He would not truly have ascended into heaven, but it would be said that his ascent was only an empty, imaginary and phantastic spectacle, if he was substantially there in his body before he ascended visibly, and after he ascended the substantial presence of the same body remains no less than before on earth, indeed even in the bodies of believers. If these things happened so in the reality of the matter, it would follow that the same body of Christ was at once in fact weak and omnipotent, lowly and glorious, passible and impassible, dead and living, circumscribed and uncircumscribed, which is horrible to say.

units.la: Ad vitandas prodigiosas & impias istas absurditates excipiunt, Christum suo corpore non nisi circumscriptum, infirmum, passibilem & mortalem fuisse humiliationis tempore: quia exinaniuerit, & communicata corporis maiestate ante resurrectionem, exserere noluerit. Refp. Exinanitionem male interpretantur de occulta ad tempus assumptae humanitatis omni gloria & maiestate: cum respectu diuinae naturae τῶ λόγῳ sit accipienda, quatenus ille ferui formam, id est, naturae nostrae massam assumere & homo fieri voluit. Deinde sequeretur, Christum carnis suae potentiam & maiestatem communicatam exeruisse etiam tunc, quando vere fuit infirmus, & corpore circumscriptus: vt cum suis lachrymis resuscitauit Lazarum, & a Iudaeis comprehensus sanauit a Petro vulneratum Malchum. Iam quid est aliud Marcionitas[?] ex inferis excitare, aut in re omnium maxima impie blasphemare, si hoc non est?
units.tr: To avoid these prodigious and impious absurdities they object: Christ, in the time of his humiliation, had his body only circumscribed, weak, passible and mortal, because he emptied himself, and, the majesty of the body having been communicated, he was unwilling to display it before the resurrection. Answer: They wrongly interpret the emptying as a concealment, for a time, of the assumed humanity from all glory and majesty; it is rather to be understood with respect to the divine nature of the Word [τῷ λόγῳ], inasmuch as he willed to take the form of a servant, that is, to assume the lump of our nature and become man. Furthermore, it would follow that Christ displayed the power and majesty communicated to his flesh even when he was truly weak and circumscribed in body, as when with his tears he raised Lazarus, and when, seized by the Jews, he healed Malchus, who had been wounded by Peter. Now, if this is not so, what else is it than to raise up the Marcionites from the dead, or to blaspheme impiously in the most important of matters?

units.la: II. Argumentum. Samosateni, Arij, & recentium Antitrinitariorum blasphemia haec est: Hominem Christum non proprie & natura Deum esse, sed accidentali tantum proprietatum diuinarum, maiestatis, honoris, potentiae & virtutis participatione. Eandem quoque deitatis hominis Christi rationem statuunt Vbiquitarij, dum sola hac communicatione idiomatum, qua omnipotens & omni praesens fit effecta Christi caro, vnionem personalem definiunt: Ita vt homo ille fit & dicatur Deus, non quod proprie & natura Deus sit, sed quia ipsi diuinitus donata sic infinita potestas, maiestas gloria, & omnia spiritus sancti dona sine mesura in ipsum collata. Hæc vero accidentalis diuinitatis & omnium proprietatum collatio Christum minimè effecit proprie & naturâ Deum, sed tantùm per gratiam diuinam aut Deum improprie dictum: quia non est ipsa essentialis deitas τῷ λόγου [?], sed quædam eius participatio, secundum efficaciam. Ideo autem Arianis ab Orthodoxis fuit obiectum, quod tollerent veram & æternam Christi deitatem, cùm ipsum non natura, sed dignitatis tantùm & maiestatis participatione per gratiam Deum facerent. Ergo cum Vbiquitarii Immanuelē [?] nostrum solummodo proprietatum participatione Deo exæquantes, veram & æternam eius deitatem tollant, iure hanc eorum doctrinam, vt blasphemam & hæreticam, repudiamus & exsecramur. Testantur hoc ipsorum verba & sententiæ, vt Brentij in Recognit. pag. 20. Iacobi Andreæ. Thes. 20. disputation. Tubingensi. Item Thes. 15. & 26. Et Apolo. Ingol-stad. 26. Vnde statuitur eandem esse Vbiquitariorum, quæ Arianorum & Antitrinitariorū de hominis Christi deitate sententiam, id est, eum ab his omnibus haberi non natura Deum, sed participationis tantùm gratia, nouum, temporarium, creatum, adoptiuum. Hæc si vera sunt, Christus nō erit Θεάνθρωπος [?], sed Θεὸς ἄνθρωπος [?], qualis ab Vbiquitariis etiam habetur, qui, vt Seruetus lib. 1. de Trinit. sentiunt, Deum posse homini deitatis plenitudinem communicare, dare ei diuinitatem, maiestatem, potestatem & gloriam suam. At eandem vtrorumq. blasphemiam exsecramur & detestamur.
units.tr: Second argument. The blasphemy of Samosatenus, Arius, and the recent Antitrinitarians is this: that the man Christ is not God properly and by nature, but only by accidental participation in the divine properties, majesty, honour, power and virtue. The Ubiquitarians also hold the same account of the deity of the man Christ, while by this sole communication of attributes, by which the flesh of Christ is made omnipotent and omnipresent, they define the personal union, so that that man is and is called God, not because he is God properly and by nature, but because such infinite power, majesty, glory, and all the gifts of the Holy Spirit without measure have been conferred upon him divinely. But this accidental conferral of deity and of all properties has not made Christ God properly and by nature, but only God through divine grace, or God improperly so called, because it is not the essential deity of the Word [τοῦ λόγου], but a certain participation in it, according to its efficacy. The Orthodox objected to the Arians that they abolished the true and eternal deity of Christ, since they made him God not by nature but only by participation in dignity and majesty through grace. Therefore, since the Ubiquitarians, by equating our Immanuel with God through the participation of properties alone, abolish his true and eternal deity, we rightly reject and execrate this their doctrine as blasphemous and heretical. Their own words and opinions bear witness to this, as in Brenz, Recognitio, p. 20; Jakob Andreae, Thesis 20, Tübingen disputation; likewise Theses 15 and 26; and the Apology of Ingolstadt, 26. Hence it is established that the opinion of the Ubiquitarians about the deity of the man Christ is the same as that of the Arians and Antitrinitarians, namely that by all of them he is held to be God not by nature but only by the grace of participation: new, temporal, created, adoptive. If these things are true, Christ will not be a God-man [Θεάνθρωπος], but a man-God [Θεὸς ἄνθρωπος], such as the Ubiquitarians also hold him to be, who, as Servetus holds in book 1 of On the Trinity, think that God can communicate the fullness of deity to a man, giving him his divinity, majesty, power and glory. But we execrate and detest the blasphemy of both.

units.la: III. Argumentum. Docuit Nestorius sola æqualitatis se-cundum maiestatem, honorem, potestatem, virtutem & operationem participatione, vnionem Dei verbi ad hominem factam esse. Nec alia in re quàm in ipsis donis & gratiis àDeo in hominem collatis, discrimen inhabitationis τῷ λόγῳ [?] in homine assumpto & aliis sanctis constituit. Hoc ipsum quoque docent Vbiquitarij: quia clamant, nullum esse discrimen inter inhabitationem deitatis in Petro & in Christo, nisi à communicatione donorum seu proprietatum deitatis sumatur: & cõtendūt, hac ratione istum assumptū nomẽ Deum esse, quia verbum nihil sine ipso, sed per ipsum omnia agat. Hoc nihil aliud est, quàm Christum hominem tantum cōstituere Deum per accidens. Est igitur dogma Vbiquitatis prorsus Nestorianum.
units.tr: Third argument. Nestorius taught that the union of the Word of God with the man was made by the sole participation of equality in majesty, honour, power, virtue and operation. And in no other matter than in the very gifts and graces conferred by God upon the man did he establish a difference in the indwelling of the Word [τῷ λόγῳ] in the assumed man and in the other saints. The Ubiquitarians also teach this same thing, for they cry out that there is no difference between the indwelling of the deity in Peter and in Christ, unless it is taken from the communication of the gifts or properties of the deity; and they contend that on this account that assumed man is called God, because the Word does nothing without him, but all things through him. This is nothing other than to make Christ a man who is God only by accident. The doctrine of ubiquity is therefore altogether Nestorian.

units.la: Tertullianus, lib. de Trinitate, pag. 610. Si homo tātum-modo Christus, quomodo adest ubique invocatur, cū hac homi-nis natura nō sit: sed Dei, ut adesse omni loco possit? Hoc dicto refutatur naturæ humanæ in Christo Vbiquitas.
units.tr: Tertullian, book On the Trinity, p. 610: If Christ is merely a man, how is he invoked as present everywhere, since this nature is not of man but of God, so that it can be present in every place? By this saying the ubiquity of the human nature in Christ is refuted.

units.la: Obiect. Est tamen inseparabilis vnio diuinæ & humanæ naturæ in Christo. Ergo vbicūque est diuina, etiam est humana natura. Resp. Verum est quod dicitur, inseparabilem esse vnionem. λόγος nunquam deserit naturam semel assumtam. Sed λόγος non est in natura humana, sicut anima inclusa est in meo corpore. Vbicunque meum corpus est, ibi animam esse necesse est, nec anima simul est extra corpus. Non autem sic est λόγος in Christo homine, sed ita est in natura humana inseparabiliter & personaliter vt simul sit etiam extra naturam humanam in omnibus mundi partibus repletiuè, in sanctis hominibus & euangeli speciali præsentia. Nā vnio personalis duarum naturarum non euertit generalē actionem præsentiæ maiestatis: nec impedit specialem: quia λόγος est efficax in hominibus renatis.
units.tr: Objection: Nevertheless, the union of the divine and human natures in Christ is inseparable. Therefore wherever the divine nature is, the human nature is also present. Answer: It is true that the union is inseparable. The Word [λόγος] never abandons the nature once assumed. But the Word is not in the human nature as the soul is enclosed in my body. Wherever my body is, the soul must also be there, and the soul is never outside the body at the same time. It is not so with the Word in Christ the man; rather, it is in the human nature inseparably and personally, in such a way that it is also at the same time outside the human nature, in all parts of the world, by filling all things, and in holy men by a special presence. For the personal union of the two natures does not overturn the general action of the presence of majesty, nor does it hinder the special one, because the Word is effective in regenerate men.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: THESES THEOLOGICÆ DE PRÆCIPVIS ALIQVOT DOCTRINÆ CHRISTIANÆ CAPITIBVS.
units.tr: Theological Theses on Certain Chief Heads of Christian Doctrine.

units.la: A D. ZACHARIA VRSINO PARTIM PVBLICE in Academia Heidelbergensi, partim in collegio Sapientiæ ad disputandum propositæ.
units.tr: Proposed by Zacharias Ursinus, partly for public disputation in the Academy of Heidelberg, partly in the College of Wisdom.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: De doctrina ecclesiæ.
units.tr: On the doctrine of the Church.

units.la: I. Doctrina ecclesiæ seu religio Christiana, est doctrina legis diuinæ, & euangelij de Christo, integra & incorrupta, sicut in libris prophetarum & apostolorum tradita est, per quam solam Deus homines ad vitam æternam ducit.
units.tr: I. The doctrine of the Church, or the Christian religion, is the doctrine of the divine law and of the gospel concerning Christ, whole and uncorrupted, as it has been handed down in the books of the prophets and apostles, and through which alone God leads men to eternal life.

units.la: II. Vniuersa doctrina Christiana duabus partibus continetur, lege & euangelio.
units.tr: II. The whole Christian doctrine is contained in two parts, law and gospel.

units.la: III. Fundamentum religionis Christianæ est decalogus & articuli fidei recte intellecti.
units.tr: III. The foundation of the Christian religion is the Decalogue and the articles of faith, rightly understood.

units.la: IV. Idem [illegible, ~4 letters]
units.tr: IV. The same [illegible, ~4 letters]

units.la: IV. Idem intelligitur, si fundamentum dicatur doctrina de essentia & voluntate Dei.
units.tr: IV. The same is understood if the foundation is taken to be the doctrine of the essence and will of God.

units.la: V. Idem quoque intelligit Paulus 1. Cor. 3. cùm fundamentum dicit esse Christum.
units.tr: V. Paul also understands the same thing in 1 Cor. 3, when he says that the foundation is Christ.

units.la: VI. Necesse est, ecclesiae notum esse discrimen inter doctrinā ipsi à Deo traditā, & aliarū gentium religiones.
units.tr: VI. It is necessary for the Church to know the difference between the doctrine delivered to it by God itself and the religions of other nations.

units.la: VII. Primum discrimen est, quòd euangelium de Christo sonat in sola ecclesia, aliæ verò sectæ prorsus illud ignorant. Omnes hæretici defendunt errores aut de persona, aut de officio Christi.
units.tr: VII. The first difference is that the gospel concerning Christ resounds only in the Church, whereas other sects are altogether ignorant of it. All heretics defend errors either concerning the person or concerning the office of Christ.

units.la: VIII. Secundum, quòd ecclesia retinet integrā doctrinam legis divinæ: reliquæ autem sectæ, primam tabulam decalogi ignorant, de secundâ tantùm retinent particulam de disciplina externa.
units.tr: VIII. Second, the Church retains the whole doctrine of the divine law, whereas the other sects are ignorant of the first table of the Decalogue and retain only a small part of the second, concerning external discipline.

units.la: IX. Tertium, quòd ecclesia agnitionem & cultū Dei, non tantùm ex integro, sed etiam ex solo Dei verbo discit, nihil huic detrahēs, nec addens: sed aliæ religiones non modò veritatis divinæ maiorem partem adiiciunt, verùm etiam legis particulæ, quam retinēt, addunt idolatriam, multa concedunt, & approbant etiam cum secundā tabulā decalogi pugnantia.
units.tr: IX. Third, the Church learns the knowledge and worship of God not only in its entirety but also from God's Word alone, taking nothing away from it and adding nothing to it. But the other religions not only add a large part of their own to divine truth, but also, along with the small portion of the law that they keep, add idolatry, and concede and approve many things that conflict even with the second table of the Decalogue.

units.la: X. Etiam vera philosophia ab ecclesiæ doctrina est discernenda. Tantùm enim eius disciplinæ partem complectitur vera philosophia, quam secunda tabula præcipit: de integra verò dilectione proximi nihil docet, & pro vero Deo, sibi idolum fabricans, procul à vero veri Dei cultu aberrat.
units.tr: X. True philosophy also must be distinguished from the doctrine of the Church. For true philosophy embraces only that part of discipline which the second table prescribes; but it teaches nothing about the whole love of neighbour, and, fashioning an idol for itself in place of the true God, it wanders far from the true worship of the true God.

units.la: II. De scriptura sacra.
units.tr: II. Concerning Holy Scripture.

units.la: I. Summa scripturæ sacræ in decalogo & symbolo comprehensa est.
units.tr: I. The sum of Holy Scripture is comprehended in the Decalogue and the Creed.

units.la: II. Hoc idem manifestum est, quia tota continetur lege & euangelio.
units.tr: II. This same thing is clear, because the whole of Scripture is contained in law and gospel.

units.la: III. Quicquid enim traditur in ea, aut est de natura Dei, aut de voluntate Dei, aut de operibus Dei, aut de peccatis diabolorum & hominum.
units.tr: III. For whatever is delivered in it either concerns the nature of God, or the will of God, or the works of God, or the sins of devils and men.

units.la: IV. Voluntas Dei in præceptis, minis, promissionibus consistit.
units.tr: IV. The will of God consists in precepts, threats and promises.

units.la: V. Opera sunt vel beneficia Dei, vt creatio, conseruatio, gubernatio rerum, collectio & seruatio ecclesiæ, per filium mediatorem:vel iudicia,vt pœnæ peccatorum.
units.tr: V. The works are either the benefits of God, such as the creation, preservation and governance of things, and the gathering and keeping of the Church through the Son as Mediator; or his judgments, such as the punishments of sins.

units.la: VI. De his autem omnibus vel in lege, vel in euan-gelio,vel in vtroque docetur.
units.tr: VI. Now all these things are taught either in the law, or in the gospel, or in both.

units.la: VII. Idem ex diuisione totius scripturæ in vetus & nouum Testamentum seu fœdus,patet.
units.tr: VII. The same is evident from the division of all Scripture into the Old and New Testament, or covenant.

units.la: VIII. Fœderis enim nomè significat,in scriptura doceri,quid Deus,siue olim ante Christum exhibitū, siue nunc post exhibitū,hominibus præstet,aut promittat,& quid vicissim ab ipsis requirat, & propter quas rationes.
units.tr: VIII. For the name of covenant signifies that Scripture teaches what God either has given or promises to men, whether formerly before Christ was revealed, or now after he has been revealed, and what in turn he requires of them, and for what reasons.

units.la: IX. Idem vult scriptura, cùm Christum se docere profitetur.
units.tr: IX. Scripture wills the same thing when it professes that it teaches Christ.

units.la: X. Omnia enim,quæ in ea traduntur,vel ad personam, vel officium Christi recte agnoscendi pertinent.
units.tr: X. For all the things that are handed down in it pertain rightly to the knowing of the person or office of Christ.

units.la: XI. Discrimen inter eam,quæ in scriptura traditur, doctrinâ & religione & aliarū sectarū religiones, primum est:quòd in verę ecclesię doctrina euangelium de Christo integrum docetur: aliæ autem religiones,aut prorsus ignorant,aut aliquâ eius parte suis erroribus adiugunt, cuius tamen vsum neque norunt,neque percipiunt.
units.tr: XI. The first difference between the doctrine and religion that is delivered in Scripture and the religions of other sects is this: that in the doctrine of the true Church the gospel concerning Christ is taught in its entirety; but the other religions either are wholly ignorant of it, or with some part of it they join their errors, the use of which they neither know nor perceive.

units.la: XII. Alterū,quòd in doctrina prophetarum & apostolorum lex diuina integra,& rectè intellecta traditur: aliæ verò religiones præcipuas eius partes abiiciunt,videlicet veram agnitionem & verum cultū Dei,siue primam tabulam decalogi,& interiorem ac spirituale obedientiam secundæ tabulæ:ac tantū retinent ex ea parte præceptorum de disciplina secundæ tabulæ, siue externis ac ciuilibus officiis erga homines.
units.tr: XII. The second is that in the doctrine of the prophets and apostles the divine law is delivered whole and rightly understood; but the other religions reject its chief parts, namely the true knowledge and true worship of God, that is, the first table of the Decalogue, and the inner and spiritual obedience of the second table; and they retain from that part of the precepts only the discipline of the second table, that is, the external and civil duties towards men.

units.la: XIII. Etsi auté & ipsi de Deo vero eiusque cultu glo-riantur:tamen ab eo propter tres causas aberrant: Primo, quia testimonia naturalia de Deo non sufficiunt ad ve-rum Deum agnoscendum. Secundo, quia his affinguntur homines varios errores. Tertio, quia non accedente luce verbi diuini,etiâ illa quæ verbo tenus profitentur vera, nô rectè intelligūt,sed mala interpretatione corrupunt.
units.tr: XIII. Although they too boast of the true God and his worship, yet they go astray from him for three reasons: First, because natural testimonies concerning God are not sufficient to recognise the true God. Second, because men add various errors to these. Third, because, without the light of the divine Word, even those things which they profess in words to be true they do not rightly understand, but corrupt by a bad interpretation.

units.la: XIV. De affectibus quoque & inclinationibus cum secunda tabula pugnantibus vel tantum præcipiunt, quod ad frænationem eorum attinet, quæ disciplinæ pars est,vel non omnes,aut non, quantum ecclesiæ do-ctrina,eas accusant & damnant.
units.tr: XIV. Concerning affections and inclinations that conflict with the second table, they either enjoin only what pertains to the restraining of them, which is a part of discipline, or they do not condemn them all, or not as far as the doctrine of the Church does.

units.la: XV. Quin etiâ contra externam secundæ tabulæ obedientiā aliqua concedunt & approbant sectæ aliæ ab ecclesia, iuste Dei iudicio in sensu reprobū eos tradete.
units.tr: XV. Moreover, other sects outside the Church even grant and approve some things contrary to the external obedience of the second table; and by the just judgment of God he has given them over to a reprobate mind.

units.la: XVI. Doctrinam scripturæ sacræ veram esse, non propter ecclesiæ authoritatem statuimus, sed quia sci-mus à Deo esse traditam.
units.tr: XVI. We hold the doctrine of Holy Scripture to be true, not on account of the authority of the Church, but because we know that it has been delivered by God.

units.la: XVII. Diuinā autem esse scimus, ex testimonio spi-ritus sancti in cordibus piorū: ex liberatione à peccato & morte, quā hæc sola religio certam ostendit: ex puri-tate & integritate legis diuinæ, quæ in sola ecclesia re-peritur: ex vaticiniis & eorum impletione: ex miraculis ecclesiæ propriis: ex huius antiquitate & aliarum noui-tate: ex partium inter se in hac doctrina consensu & in aliis pugnantia: ex odio satanæ & malorum contra hanc religionem: ex eius mirabili conseruatione & defensione contra diabolum & mundum: ex pœnis hostium eam op-pugnantium: ex constantia martyrum & confessorum habentium consolationem firmam in morte: ex eorum sanctitate, per quos tradita & propagata est.
units.tr: XVII. We know that it is divine from the testimony of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the godly; from deliverance from sin and death, which this religion alone shows to be certain; from the purity and integrity of the divine law, which is found only in the Church; from prophecies and their fulfilment; from miracles proper to the Church; from its antiquity and the novelty of the others; from the agreement of its parts with one another in this doctrine, and the conflict of the others; from the hatred of Satan and of evil men against this religion; from its wonderful preservation and defence against the devil and the world; from the punishments of enemies who assail it; from the constancy of martyrs and confessors, who have firm comfort in death; and from the holiness of those through whom it has been delivered and propagated.

units.la: XVIII. Nullum dogma de Deo aut eius voluntate & cultu recipiendum est, quod in scriptura non est traditum: & eatenus aliis doctoribus ecclesiæ assentiendum est, quatenus doctrinam suam propheticis & apostolicis testimoniis confirmant.
units.tr: XVIII. No dogma concerning God, or his will and worship, is to be received which is not delivered in Scripture; and to other teachers of the Church assent is to be given only so far as they confirm their doctrine by the prophetic and apostolic testimonies.

units.la: XIX. Id nō solū ex scripturæ ipsiꝰ[?] testimoniis certū est, quib. ex ea sola pedere iubemur in rebus diuinis: sed etiā ex fidei & cultus Dei natura & definitione, quorū utrūque verbo Dei niti necesse est: itē ex perfectione doctri-nę pphetice[?] & apostolicę: & ex discrimine vocationis prophetarum & apostolorum & aliorū doctorum ecclesiæ.
units.tr: XIX. This is certain not only from the testimonies of Scripture itself, by which alone we are commanded to be taught in divine matters, but also from the nature and definition of faith and of the worship of God, both of which must rest on the Word of God; likewise from the perfection of the prophetic and apostolic doctrine; and from the difference between the calling of the prophets and apostles and that of the other teachers of the Church.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: De certitudine & authoritate sacræ scripturæ.
units.tr: Concerning the certainty and authority of Holy Scripture.

units.la: I. Solā hanc religionis doctrinā, quæ in libris prophe-ticis & apostolicis continetur, esse diuinitus traditā, nec solūm, nec principaliter ecclesiæ catholicæ, sed potissi-mum Dei, scripturæ ipsius testimonio niti, certum est.
units.tr: I. That this doctrine of religion alone, which is contained in the prophetic and apostolic books, has been divinely delivered, and that it rests not only nor principally on the Catholic Church, but chiefly on the testimony of God, of Scripture itself, is certain.

units.la: II. Primum & summum argumentum, quo ista sacræ scripturæ authoritas apud nos sancitur, est spiritus sancti testificatio in cordibus credentium.
units.tr: II. The first and chief argument by which this authority of Holy Scripture is established among us is the witness of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of believers.

units.la: III. Testimonium hoc ut sanctis peculiare est, ita solū efficit, ut prophetarum & apostolorum doctrinam vera fide amplectamur: cætera omnia possunt etiam à non renatis intelligi: & mètes quidem de veritate huius doctrinæ conuincunt, sed nisi hoc vnū accesserit, nūquam ad eam amplectendam animos humanos permouent.
units.tr: III. This testimony, as it is peculiar to the saints, so it alone brings it about that we embrace the doctrine of the prophets and apostles with true faith; all other things can be understood even by the unregenerate, and indeed reason may convince them of the truth of this doctrine, but unless this one thing is added, it never moves human minds to embrace it.

units.la: IV. Secundum testimonium est, quòd hæc sola doctrina causas malorum, & à peccato & morte liberationem hominibus ostendit, congruentem perfectæ Dei iustitiæ & bonitati, satisfacientem conscientiis.
units.tr: IV. The second testimony is that this doctrine alone shows the causes of evils, and deliverance from sin and death to men, agreeing with the perfect justice and goodness of God, and satisfying consciences.

units.la: V. Tertium, quòd sola doctrina prophetica & apostolica legem diuinam integram & puram retinet: aliæ verò religiones omnes fingunt sibi deos, & eorum cultus, absque autoritate diuina, & approbant aliquà etiam cum notitiis legalibus, natura notis, pugnantia.
units.tr: V. The third is that the prophetic and apostolic doctrine alone retains the divine law whole and pure; but all other religions devise gods for themselves and their worship without divine authority, and they approve some things which conflict with the legal notions known by nature.

units.la: VI. Quartum, sparsæ in sacris literis prædictiones, quibus euentū respondisse, historiæ & experientia testatur.
units.tr: VI. The fourth is the predictions scattered through the sacred writings, to which history and experience bear witness that the events corresponded.

units.la: VII. Quintum, miracula, quæ doctrinæ sunt addita.
units.tr: VII. The fifth is the miracles that have been added to the doctrine.

units.la: VIII. Sextum, antiquitas, quia & prima fuit hæc religio, & màsit [?] eadem inde ab initio mundi ad hūc usq. diem.
units.tr: VIII. The sixth is antiquity, since this religion was both the first and has remained the same from the beginning of the world until this day.

units.la: IX. Septimum, consensus omnium doctrinæ partium inter se, qui non est in aliis religionibus.
units.tr: IX. The seventh is the agreement of all the parts of the doctrine with one another, which is not found in other religions.

units.la: X. Octauum, Odium satanæ & impiorum aduersus hanc doctrinam.
units.tr: X. The eighth is the hatred of Satan and of the impious against this doctrine.

units.la: XI. Nonum, Diuina conseruatio & defensio eius aduersus omnes hostes.
units.tr: XI. The ninth is the divine preservation and defence of it against all enemies.

units.la: XII. Decimum, Poenæ hostium, qui hanc doctrinam persequuntur, aut corrumpunt.
units.tr: XII. The tenth is the punishments of those enemies who persecute or corrupt this doctrine.

units.la: XIII. Vndecimum, Constantia martyrum & cófessorum. Tertullian. Martyrū sanguis est semen ecclesiæ. Martyres ecclesiæ differunt ab aliis, 1. multitudine, 2. alacritate in adeundis periculis & ipsa morte, 3. impię doctrinę defensores patiuntur de suis erroribus conuicti, pij autem vi tyrannicà rapiuntur ad supplicia.
units.tr: XIII. The eleventh is the constancy of martyrs and confessors. Tertullian: the blood of martyrs is the seed of the Church. The martyrs of the Church differ from others: (1) in their number; (2) in their eagerness in facing dangers and death itself; (3) the defenders of an impious doctrine suffer when convicted of their errors, but the pious are dragged to punishment by tyrannical force.

units.la: XIV. Duodecimum, Sanctitas eorum, per quos tradita est & progata, longè superans virtutes Ethnicorum & alias religiones sectantium.
units.tr: XIV. The twelfth is the holiness of those through whom it has been delivered and propagated, far surpassing the virtues of the heathen and of adherents of other religions.

units.la: XV. Cùm igitur hæc sola doctrina de religione sit vera & diuina: nullum dogma ad credendum, vel obtepe-randam obligare potest conscientias, quod sacræ scripturæ testimoniis rectè intellecti non est stabilitum: cum verò pugnans, nullum omninò est recipiendum.
units.tr: XV. Since, therefore, this doctrine alone concerning religion is true and divine, no dogma can bind consciences to belief or to obedience which is not established by the testimonies of Holy Scripture rightly understood; and whatever conflicts with it is not to be received at all.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: De Deo & vera eius cognitione.
units.tr: Concerning God and the true knowledge of him.

units.la: i.Homo veraDei cognitione destitutꝰ est infelicissimꝰ.
units.tr: i. A man destitute of the true knowledge of God is most unhappy.

units.la: ii.Cognitio Dei vera non est, nisi congruit cum diui-nis patefactionibus, & cum vero Dei amore ac timore coniuncta.
units.tr: ii. The knowledge of God is not true unless it agrees with the divine revelations and is joined with a true love and fear of God.

units.la: iii. Patefactionis autem & notitiæ Dei in genere humano tres sūt gradus:ex operibus nimirum Dei in natura rerum lucentibus:ex verbo Dei ecclesiæ tradito: & ex spiritus sancti gratia per considerationem operum & verbi Dei,mentes renatorum illuminantis.
units.tr: iii. Of the revelation and knowledge of God in the human race there are three degrees: namely, from the works of God shining in the order of nature; from the word of God handed down to the Church; and from the grace of the Holy Spirit, which, through the consideration of the works and the word of God, illuminates the minds of the regenerate.

units.la: iv. Etenim esse Deum aliquem,sanos omnes,etiam ignorātes doctrinam ecclesiæ, fateri cogūt hęc testimonia:Ordo rerum sapientissimus in natura, Metis humanæ præstātia:Notitia principiorum: & in illis hæc notitia,quod fit Deus: Pauores cōscientiæ in sceleratis:Pœnæ scelerū in hac vita:Ordinis politici cōstitutio,& cōseruatio:Virtutes & motꝰ singulares in animis heroicis: Significationes futurorū:Destinatio rerū omniū ad fines certos: Series causarum non in infinitū progrediens.
units.tr: iv. Indeed, these testimonies compel all sane people, even those ignorant of the teaching of the Church, to confess that there is some God: the most wise order of things in nature; the excellence of the human mind; the knowledge of first principles, and in them this knowledge, that there is a God; the terrors of conscience in the wicked; the punishments of crimes in this life; the establishment and preservation of political order; the singular virtues and movements in heroic souls; the signs of future events; the ordering of all things to certain ends; a series of causes that does not proceed to infinity.

units.la: v. Deū etiam verum non nisi unum esse,præter verbi diuini testimonia,euincunt,unius tantum veri Dei patefactio:Summa veri Dei maiestas: Perfectio:Omnipotētia:Et quòd plures uno aut essent otiosi aut superflui.
units.tr: v. Apart from the testimonies of the divine Word, these same things also prove that the one true God is only one: the revelation of the one true God alone; the supreme majesty of the true God; his perfection; his omnipotence; and that several gods would be either idle or superfluous.

units.la: vi. DENIQVE fatentur etiam rectæ rationis iudicio non repugnantes, Deum essentiam spiritualem esse,intelligentem, æternā,aliam à cæteris rebus omnibus,incomprehensibilem,in se ipsa perfectissimam,immutabilem,immensæ potentiæ, sapientiæ & bonitatis,iustam, castam,veracem,misericordem,beneficam,liberrimam, irascentem peccatis,mundi gubernatricem.
units.tr: vi. Finally, they also confess, in agreement with the judgment of right reason, that God is a spiritual essence, intelligent, eternal, distinct from all other things, incomprehensible, most perfect in himself, immutable, of immense power, wisdom and goodness, just, pure, truthful, merciful, beneficent, most free, angered by sins, and the governor of the world.

units.la: vii.Sed sine luce verbi Dei,neque ista quæ fatentur de Deo, rectè intelligunt homines, neque norunt quicquam eorū,quæ addit huic notitiæ Dei vox doctrinæ cœlestis,de æterno patre,& filio, & spiritu sancto,de rerum creatione, missione filij,collectione ecclesiæ, universali iudicio,& vita æterna.
units.tr: vii. But without the light of the Word of God, men neither rightly understand those things which they confess about God, nor know any of those things which the voice of heavenly teaching adds to this knowledge of God: concerning the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; concerning the creation of things, the mission of the Son, the gathering of the Church, the universal judgment, and eternal life.

units.la: viii. Idcirco considerānda quidem sunt testimonia de Deo in natura:sed sine doctrina ecclesiæ quicunq;Deū quærunt,idolum in veri Dei locum substituunt.
units.tr: viii. Therefore, the testimonies about God in nature are indeed to be considered; but those who seek God without the teaching of the Church put an idol in the place of the true God.

units.la: IX. Quin etiam ex ipso Dei verbo, absque singulari spiritus S. gratia, vera Dei cognitio non potest hauriri.
units.tr: IX. Indeed, even from the Word of God itself, the true knowledge of God cannot be drawn without the special grace of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: X. Ac tandem quæcunque in hac vita est notitia Dei in hominibus, non nisi tenuis & inchoata est, nec nisi in cœlesti æternitate perficienda.
units.tr: X. And finally, whatever knowledge of God there is among men in this life is only slight and incipient, and it is to be brought to perfection only in heavenly eternity.

units.la: XI. Aeternus pater, filius, & Spiritus sanctus sunt tres personæ sive hypostases diuinæ:
units.tr: XI. The eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three divine persons or hypostases.

units.la: XII. Reuera à se invicem distinctæ:
units.tr: XII. Truly distinct from one another.

units.la: XIII. Æquales secundum omnes proprietates diuinitatis essentiales:
units.tr: XIII. Equal in respect of all the essential properties of deity.

units.la: XIV. Et unius essentiæ.
units.tr: XIV. And of one essence.

units.la: XV. Essentia diuinam ecclesia intelligit id, quod æternus pater, filius & Spiritus sanctus singuli, absolute sive secundum se aut naturam suam considerati sunt & dicuntur, ita ut tribus illis commune sit: Persona autem id, quod singuli horum trium ad alios collati, sive relatiue, sive secundum existendi modum cuiusque proprium considerati, sunt & dicuntur.
units.tr: XV. By essence the Church understands that which the eternal Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit each are and are said to be when considered absolutely, or according to themselves or their nature, so that this is common to all three; but by person, that which each of these three is and is said to be when compared with the others, whether considered relatively or according to the mode of existing proper to each.

units.la: XVI. Filium esse hypostasin diuinam, probatur, quia nominatur Filius Dei unigenitus & proprius, id est, natura his: dicitur in scriptura assumsisse naturam humanam, & ante eius assumtionem fuisse filius Dei: nominatur λόγος, qui à Iohane ὁ λόγος describitur: à Salomone describitur Sapientia Θεοῦ: est mediator inter Deum & homines, quæ necesse est semper fuisse: nominatur Angelus etiam ante incarnationem: Christus denique ex virgine natus describitur naturalis & verus Deus & Dei filius.
units.tr: XVI. That the Son is a divine hypostasis is proved because he is named the only-begotten and proper Son of God, that is, of the same nature; it is said in Scripture that he assumed human nature, and that before his assumption he was the Son of God; he is named the Word (λόγος), which John describes as ὁ λόγος; Solomon describes him as the Wisdom of God; he is the mediator between God and men, which must always have been so; he is named the Angel even before the incarnation; and finally Christ, born of the virgin, is described as natural and true God and the Son of God.

units.la: XVII. Spiritum sanctum esse hypostasin, constat, quia visibili specie apparuit: quia Deus in scriptura appellatur: quia in eius nomine baptizamur: quia personæ propria ei tribuuntur.
units.tr: XVII. That the Holy Spirit is a hypostasis is established, because he appeared in visible form; because he is called God in Scripture; because we are baptized in his name; because personal properties are attributed to him.

units.la: XVIII. Has personas inuicem verè distinctas esse, hinc est manifestum, quod pater, filius & Spiritus sanctus propter respectum ad se invicem dicuntur: quod scriptura dicit filium & Spiritum sanctum alium à patre, & Spiritum sanctum à filio: quod dicuntur esse plures quàm unus: quod uni tribuuntur propria, quæ alteri non competunt.
units.tr: XVIII. That these persons are truly distinct from one another is manifest from this: that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are named in relation to one another; that Scripture says the Son and the Holy Spirit are other than the Father, and the Holy Spirit other than the Son; that they are said to be more than one; that properties belong to one which do not belong to another.

units.la: XIX. Æqualitas deitatis in his trib. personis probatur expressis testimoniis scripturæ: proprietatibus personalibus, quod filius à patre, & Spiritus sancto à patre & filio, nō pars aliqua, sed tota diuina essentia communicata est: attributis seu proprietatibus naturæ diuinæ communi-bus: operibus diuinis: honoris, qui illis vindicatur, æqua-litate.
units.tr: XIX. The equality of deity in these three persons is proved by express testimonies of Scripture; by personal properties, namely that the Son is communicated by the Father, and the Holy Spirit by the Father and the Son, not some part, but the whole divine essence; by the attributes or common properties of the divine nature; by the divine works; and by the equality of honour which is claimed for them.

units.la: XX. ὁμοούσιος[?] esse certum est, quia sunt Iehouah, qui vnus est: quia describuntur in scriptura tanquam verus Deus, qui tantum vnus est: quia vnus est spiritus patris & filij: quia pater filio & spiritui sancto, & filius spiritui sancto non aliam, sed suam propriam essentiam communicat, eamque totam & indiuisam.
units.tr: XX. That they are consubstantial (ὁμοούσιος) is certain, because they are Jehovah, who is one; because they are described in Scripture as the true God, who is only one; because there is one Spirit of the Father and the Son; because the Father communicates to the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the Son to the Holy Spirit, not another but their own proper essence, and that whole and undivided.

units.la: XXI. Discrimina personarum diuinitatis alia interna, ab operationibus, quas erga se inuicem exercent: alia externa sunt, ab operationibus, quas erga creaturas exercent.
units.tr: XXI. The distinctions of the persons of the deity are of two kinds: some are internal, arising from the operations which they exercise toward one another; others are external, arising from the operations which they exercise toward creatures.

units.la: XXII. Discrimina interna sunt, quod pater est prima persona diuinitatis, nec nata nec procedens ab alio: sed a seipsa existens, quæ ab æterno genuit filium, & a qua procedit Spiritus sanctus: Filius est secunda persona diuinitatis, quæ ab æterno ex patre genita est, & a qua procedit Spiritus sanctus: Spiritus sanctus est tertia persona diuinitatis ab æterno procedens a patre & filio.
units.tr: XXII. The internal distinctions are these: the Father is the first person of the deity, neither born nor proceeding from another, but existing from himself, who from eternity begot the Son, and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds; the Son is the second person of the deity, who from eternity was begotten of the Father, and from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds; the Holy Spirit is the third person of the deity, proceeding from eternity from the Father and the Son.

units.la: XXIII. Opera, quæ diuinitas erga creaturas exercet, etiam sint tribus personis communia: tamen ordo, quem in illis perficiendis seruant tres personæ diuinæ, discrimen earum externum constituit: nimirum, quod pater a seipso, per filium & Sp. Sanctum, filius a patre, per Spiritum sanctum: Spiritus sanctus autem a patre & filio per se illa operatur.
units.tr: XXIII. The works which the deity performs toward creatures are common to the three persons; yet the order which the three divine persons observe in carrying them out constitutes their external distinction: namely, that the Father acts from himself, through the Son and the Holy Spirit; the Son from the Father, through the Holy Spirit; and the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, performs them by himself.

units.la: XXIV. Atque hinc est, quod quædam propria filij & Spiritus sancti beneficia dicuntur, non quod ab illis remoueatur pater, sed quod ea per filium aut Spir. Sanctum nobis præstat, vt quod filius dicitur sapientia, sermo, cõfiliarius, angelus, apostolus, imago patris, potentia patris, vniens sibi naturam humanam: ac proinde incarnatus & homo, & mediator, intercessor, sacerdos, redemptor, iustificator, pastor, caput, & rex ecclesiæ, sedens ad dextram patris, iudex viuorum & mortuorum, &c. Item, quod Spiritus sanctus dicitur sanctificator, hoc est, persona immediate nos illuminans, regenerans, vniens Deo, regens, consolans & confirmans.
units.tr: XXIV. And hence it is that certain benefits are said to be proper to the Son and the Holy Spirit, not because the Father is excluded from them, but because he bestows them upon us through the Son or the Holy Spirit. Thus the Son is called wisdom, word, counsellor, angel, apostle, image of the Father, power of the Father, the one who united human nature to himself, and therefore incarnate and man, and mediator, intercessor, priest, redeemer, justifier, minister, head and king of the Church, sitting at the right hand of the Father, judge of the living and the dead, etc. Likewise, the Holy Spirit is called sanctifier, that is, the person who immediately illuminates us, regenerates us, unites us to God, rules, comforts and confirms us.

units.la: V. De creatione mundi.
units.tr: V. On the Creation of the World.

units.la: I.Ordo in natura:mens humana: notitia principiorum: ordo politicus: causæ finales :feries causarum finita : ostendunt ab aliqua mente architectrice esse conditu.
units.tr: I. The order in nature, the human mind, the knowledge of first principles, political order, final causes, and a finite series of causes show that the world was constructed by some architectural mind.

units.la: II.Sed tamen propter obscuratam agnitionem Dei in hominibus per peccatum,propter vices corruptionũ & generationũ,propter absurditatem de creatore otioso,& propter amissam creationis & initiorum mundi historiam,extra ecclesiæ doctrinam nihil solidi ac certi de creatione mundi reperitur.
units.tr: II. But nevertheless, because of the obscured knowledge of God among men through sin, because of the cycles of corruption and generation, because of the absurdity of a idle Creator, and because the history of creation and the beginnings of the world has been lost, nothing solid and certain about the creation of the world is to be found outside the teaching of the Church.

units.la: III.Scriptura igitur sacra docet, omnes res per solum verum Deum,æternum patrem,filium & Spiritum sanctum,iuxta huius veri Dei æterni consilium & voluntatem,exsistere coepisse,& ab ipso esse creatas.
units.tr: III. Holy Scripture therefore teaches that all things began to exist through the one true God, the eternal Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, in accordance with the counsel and will of this eternal true God, and were created by him.

units.la: IV. Creavit autem æternus pater omnia per filiũ suũ & Spiritum sanctum,liberrimè, fine vlla sui mutatione aut labore,ex nihilo,sic ut omnia essent valde bona.
units.tr: IV. Now the eternal Father created all things through his Son and the Holy Spirit, most freely, without any change or labour on his own part, out of nothing, so that all things were very good.

units.la: V. Finis creationis mundi ultimus & principalis est celebratio Dei:huic subordinati fines sunt,patefactio & contemplatio divinæ sapientiæ,potetiæ & bonitatis in operibus Dei, providentia seu conservatio & moderatio perpetua omnium creaturarum , præsertim in ecclesiam beneficientia Dei: ac denique ut omnes aliæ res seruiant vitæ ac saluti hominum.
units.tr: V. The ultimate and principal end of the creation of the world is the celebration of God; subordinate to this are the following ends: the manifestation and contemplation of the divine wisdom, power and goodness in the works of God; the providence, that is, the continual preservation and governance of all creatures, especially of the Church, through the beneficence of God; and finally, that all other things serve the life and salvation of men.

units.la: VI. De creatione mundi.
units.tr: VI. On the Creation of the World.

units.la: I.Quicquid est,aut est creator,aut creatura.
units.tr: I. Whatever exists either is the Creator or is a creature.

units.la: II. Omnes aliæ res,quæ præter unum , solum , æternum,verum Deum,in ecclesia patefactum, exsistere coeperunt,ab illo uno vero Deo sunt creatæ.
units.tr: II. All other things, which began to exist besides the one, sole, eternal, true God made known in the Church, were created by that one true God.

units.la: III. Eo,quo creator voluit,temporis initio.
units.tr: III. At the beginning of time, when the Creator willed.

units.la: IV.Idque à patre æterno per filium & Spiritum sanctum.
units.tr: IV. And this by the eternal Father through the Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: V. Liberrimo divinæ 'voluntatis consilio & decreto.
units.tr: V. By the most free counsel and decree of the divine will.

units.la: VI.Sine ullo creatoris motu,aut mutatione, aut labore.
units.tr: VI. Without any motion, change, or labour on the part of the Creator.

units.la: VII. Idque ex nihilo.
units.tr: VII. And this out of nothing.

units.la: VIII. Et quidem ita,ut essent omnia in suo genere optima.
units.tr: VIII. And indeed in such a way that all things were in their own kind most good.

units.la: IX. Non vt ipse creator fieret inde melior aut perfectior.
units.tr: IX. Not so that the Creator himself might become better or more perfect thereby.

units.la: X. Sed vt suam bonitatem & laetitiam creaturis rationalibus, in creatione communicaret.
units.tr: X. But so that he might communicate his goodness and joy to rational creatures in the act of creation.

units.la: XI. Ac postea sua prouidentia res omnes creatas seruans, regens, sustentans, in aeternum illis benefaceret omnibus, praesertim vero suae ecclesiae.
units.tr: XI. And afterwards, by his providence preserving, governing and sustaining all created things, he would do good to all of them for ever, but especially to his Church.

units.la: XII. Et vt hominum saluti praesertim, alias omnes creaturas seruire volens,
units.tr: XII. And so that, willing that all other creatures should serve the salvation of men especially,

units.la: XIII. Suam illis sapientiam, bonitatem, potentiam, & laetitiam patefaceret:
units.tr: XIII. He might reveal to them his wisdom, goodness, power and joy:

units.la: XIV. Ex operibus suis agnitus, propter suam illam sapientiam, bonitatem, potentiam & laetitiam a creaturis rationalibus, in aeternitate celebraretur.
units.tr: XIV. Known from his works, on account of that wisdom, goodness, power and joy, he would be celebrated for eternity by rational creatures.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: De Angelis.
units.tr: On the Angels.

units.la: I. Angelos bonos & malos exsistere certum est.
units.tr: I. That good and evil angels exist is certain.

units.la: II. Et boni autem & mali angeli sunt spiritus, hoc est, substantiae incorporeae, non subiectae sensibus, viuae, intelligentes, robore & sapientia pollentes.
units.tr: II. Good and evil angels are spirits, that is, incorporeal substances, not subject to the senses, living, intelligent, and powerful in strength and wisdom.

units.la: III. Finiti essentia & proprietatibus.
units.tr: III. Finite in essence and properties.

units.la: IV. Creati a Deo ex nihilo tum, quando aliae res conditae sunt.
units.tr: IV. Created by God out of nothing at the time when the other things were made.

units.la: V. In vera sanctitate, iustitia & beatitudine.
units.tr: V. In true holiness, righteousness and blessedness.

units.la: VI. In qua boni singulari creatoris gratia confirmati sunt,
units.tr: VI. In which state the good were confirmed by the singular grace of the Creator,

units.la: VII. Vt ipsum in aeternitate agnoscant & celebrent,
units.tr: VII. So that they might acknowledge and celebrate him for eternity,

units.la: VIII. Et sint ministri Dei ad salutem electorum perficiendam, & reprimendos ac puniendos malos.
units.tr: VIII. And be ministers of God to bring the salvation of the elect to completion, and to restrain and punish the wicked.

units.la: IX. Mali autem propria & libera voluntate & sua i-[?] psorum[?] culpa a Deo defecerunt, & facti sunt hostes Dei & bonorum angelorum & generis humani.
units.tr: IX. But the evil ones fell away from God by their own proper and free will and by their own fault, and became enemies of God, of the good angels, and of the human race.

units.la: X. Itaque odio Dei impellunt homines ad peccata, & cupiunt eos perditos.
units.tr: X. Therefore, through hatred of God, they drive men to sin, and desire their destruction.

units.la: XI. Et immutabiliter sunt mali, & abiecti a Deo in aeternas poenas.
units.tr: XI. And they are evil immutably, and cast away from God into eternal punishments.

units.la: XII. Siuit autem Deus ipsos labi, & lapsos etiam conseruat, vt iram suam & iustitiam in ipsorum poenis ostendat, per eos puniat impios, & castiget, atque exerceat electos.
units.tr: XII. God, however, allows them to fall, and even preserves them when fallen, so that he may show his wrath and justice in their punishments, use them to punish and chastise the impious, and exercise the elect.

units.la: VIII. De creatione hominis.
units.tr: VIII. On the creation of man.

units.la: I. Homo est creatus à Deo,corpore terreno,& si homo peccaret,moriturò:anima verò non elementaris,sed spiritualis, hoc est,incorporeæ, intelligentis & immortalis naturæ,ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei.
units.tr: I. Man was created by God, with an earthly body, and if man had sinned, he would die; but the soul is not elemental but spiritual, that is, of an incorporeal, intelligent and immortal nature, according to the image and likeness of God.

units.la: II. Imago Dei in homine, post peccatum, in hac vita non est integra:neque in corpore, sed in anima:neq. in sola substantia animæ rationalis,videlicet intellectu & voluntate : & quidem animæ per Spiritum sanctum renatæ,spectanda est.
units.tr: II. The image of God in man, after the fall, is not whole in this life: not in the body but in the soul, nor in the substance of the rational soul alone, namely the intellect and will; and indeed it is to be regarded in the soul that has been reborn through the Holy Spirit.

units.la: III. Estque hac imago Dei,sapientia,iustitia, & beatitudo perfecta,in qua homo est conditus, & in quam beneficio mediatoris restituitur,hoc est, mēs recte agnoscēs Dei naturā,voluntate & operā:& voluntas libere Deo obtemperās, omniūq. inclinationū,appetitionū, & actionū,cū voluntate Dei,& cū recto iudicio metis cōgruētia: ac denique spiritualis & immortalis animæ natura,totiusque hominis puritas & integritas, perfecta beatitudo & lætitia acquiescens in Deo,& dignitas hominis ac maiestas,qua cæteris creaturis antecellit atq. dominat.
units.tr: III. This image of God is wisdom, righteousness and perfect blessedness, in which man was made, and into which it is restored through the benefit of the Mediator; that is, a mind rightly knowing the nature, will and works of God, and a will freely obeying God, and all inclinations, appetites and actions agreeing with the will of God and with the right judgment of the mind; and finally the spiritual and immortal nature of the soul, and the purity and integrity of the whole man, perfect blessedness and joy resting in God, and the dignity and majesty of man, by which he excels and rules over the other creatures.

units.la: IV. Finis hominis, ad quem est conditus, vltimus & principalis est æterna Dei celebratio: Huic subordinati sunt alij fines,vera agnitio Dei:declaratio misericordiæ Dei in electis,& iustitia in reprobis:societas humana: & mutua beneficentia.
units.tr: IV. The end of man, for which he was made, is ultimate and principal: the eternal celebration of God. Subordinate to this are other ends: the true knowledge of God; the declaration of God's mercy in the elect and of his justice in the reprobate; human society; and mutual beneficence.

units.la: IX. De providentia Dei.
units.tr: IX. On the providence of God.

units.la: I. Non tantùm doctrina prophetica & apostolica,sed etiam testimonia de Deo in rerum natura lucentia confirmant,mundū consecutari & regi Dei providentia,animarum Ordo in præcipuis naturæ partibus: Mens humana regens actiones hominum sua providentia:Lex naturæ, indita hominibus, ut sit regula vitæ : Præmia & pœnæ: Conscientia:Ordo politicus:Motus & virtutes heroicæ: Prædictiones futurorum eventuum : Fines,ad quos res ordinatæ sunt: Ac denique ipsa Dei omnipotentis, sapientissimi,iustissimi atque optimi natura.
units.tr: I. Not only prophetic and apostolic doctrine, but also testimonies concerning God shining forth in the nature of things, confirm that the world is sustained and governed by the providence of God: the order of souls in the principal parts of nature; the human mind directing human actions by its own foresight; the law of nature, implanted in human beings so that it may be the rule of life; rewards and punishments; conscience; political order; heroic movements and virtues; predictions of future events; the ends to which things have been ordained; and finally the very nature of God, who is almighty, most wise, most just and best.

units.la: II. Providentia Dei est consilium Dei æternū,liberrimum, immutabile, sapientissimum & iustissimum, secundùm quod Deus omnia in omnib. creaturis bona efficit, peccata autem fieri permittit: & bona ac mala vniuersa ad suam gloriam & electorum salutem dirigit.
units.tr: II. The providence of God is the eternal, most free, immutable, most wise and most just counsel of God, according to which God brings about all good things in all creatures, but permits sins to occur, and directs all good and evil things to his own glory and to the salvation of the elect.

units.la: III. Cōsilium hoc Dei nō tantùm est scientia in Deo, sed etiā decretum & Voluntas Dei efficax, qua ab aeterno cōstituit, quid ipse agere, & quid de operib. suis fieri velit, & quaecūq. decreuit, suo tempore atq. ordine efficit.
units.tr: III. This counsel of God is not only knowledge in God, but also the efficacious decree and will of God, by which from eternity he determined what he himself will do, and what he wishes to be done with his works, and whatever he has decreed, he brings about in its own time and order.

units.la: IV. Bona sunt, rerum omnium substantiae, proprietates & facultates ipsis à Deo inditae, motus item omnes omnium rerum & mutationes, actiones & euentus, quatenus sunt motus naturales, vel obedientia erga voluntatem Dei, vel beneficia Dei aut poenae malorum.
units.tr: IV. Goods are the substances, properties and faculties of all things, implanted in them by God, likewise all the motions and changes of all things, actions and events, insofar as they are natural motions, or obedience to the will of God, or benefits of God or punishments of evils.

units.la: V. Omnia haec immutabili & efficaci Dei voluntate fieri, cum plurima & clarissima scripturae testimonia, tū hae rationes confirmant: quod propter diuinam omnipotentiam, Deo simpliciter nolente, nihil in mundo potest fieri, ac proinde omnia quę fiūt, vel simpliciter, vel secundū quid eū velle necesse est: quod sapientissimus gubernator, qualis est Deus, nihil eorū, quae in sua potestate habet, praeter consilium & voluntatem suam finit euenire: quod qui fines omnium vult, etiam vult res & euentus omnes, quibus ad illos fines peruenitur siue simpliciter, siue secundum quid: quod consilia & decreta diuina non pendent ab actionibus causarum secundarum: quod praescientia Dei immutabilis, non nisi causa immutabili, hoc est, voluntate & decreto diuino potest niti: quod omnium bonorum naturalium in quibus sunt etiam omnes motus rerum, Deus est prima causa.
units.tr: V. That all these things come about by the unchangeable and efficacious will of God, both very many and very clear testimonies of Scripture confirm, and also these reasons: because, on account of the divine omnipotence, nothing in the world can happen if God simply were unwilling, and therefore all things that happen must necessarily be willed by him, either absolutely or in some respect; because a most wise governor, such as God is, permits nothing of those things that lie in his power to come about apart from his counsel and will; because whoever wills all ends also wills all things and events by which those ends are reached, either absolutely or in some respect; because the divine counsels and decrees do not depend on the actions of secondary causes; because the unchangeable foreknowledge of God can rest only on an unchangeable cause, that is, on the divine will and decree; because God is the first cause of all natural goods, in which are also all the motions of things.

units.la: VI. Malum cùm aliud sit culpae, aliud poenae, id autem quod est poena, cum sit exsecutio iustitiae ac proinde boni rationem habeat, etiam ad diuinam voluntatem tanquam ad causam principalem referri debet.
units.tr: VI. Since evil is one thing as guilt and another as punishment, and what is punishment, since it is the execution of justice and therefore has the character of good, must also be referred to the divine will as to the principal cause.

units.la: VII. Malum autem culpa siue peccatum, quatenus vel motus est, vel exploratio, vel exercitium, vel castigatio piorum, vel poena malorum cadit sub diuinam prouidentiam effectiue: quatenus vero peccatum est, non effectiue, sed permissiue.
units.tr: VII. Evil, however, as guilt or sin, insofar as it is a motion, or a testing, or an exercise, or a chastisement of the godly, or a punishment of the wicked, falls under the divine providence effectively; but insofar as it is sin, not effectively but permissively.

units.la: VIII. Permissio autē nō est prouidentiae & operationis diuinae in actionib. malorum cessatio, qua fiat, vt actiones illæ non ab alio principio, quàm à creaturis agenti-bus pędeant: sed est gratiæ diuinæ subtractio, qua Deus dum voluntatis suę decreta, per creaturas rationales ex-sequitur, aut voluntate suam, qua opus illud fieri velit, creaturæ non patefacit, aut voluntatem eius ad obtépe-rádū[?] in ea actione diuinæ voluntati nō flectit. Quod si fiat, necessario quidem, sed tamen voluntarie ac liberè, & iustissimo Dei iudicio peccat creatura, dum iustum & bo-nū opus suæ volutatis & prouidentiæ Deus per eā efficit.
units.tr: VIII. Permission, however, is not a cessation of divine providence and operation in the actions of evil men, by which those actions would come to depend on some other principle than the acting creatures; rather it is a withdrawal of divine grace, by which God, while carrying out the decrees of his will through rational creatures, either does not make known to the creature his will that the work be done, or does not turn his will, so that it might be restrained in that action, to the divine will. And if this happens, the creature sins necessarily indeed, but nonetheless voluntarily and freely, and by the most just judgment of God, while God through it brings about a just and good work of his will and providence.

units.la: IX. Actiones igitur & motus, quos diaboli aut homines peccādo efficiunt, Deus vult fieri, quatenus sunt motus & iusti iudicij diuini exsecutiones, quatenus autem peccata sunt, nec vult, nec approbat, nec efficit, sed quāuis eas prohibeat, oderitq.horribiliter & puniat, permittit tamen in diabolis & hominibus cum iustis suis operibus concurrere, dū propter optimas & iustissimas causas non efficit in illis suo spiritu, vt iuste, hoc est, secundum diuinæ voluntatis præscriptum actiones illas perficiat.
units.tr: IX. Therefore the actions and motions which the devils or men bring about by sinning, God wills to occur insofar as they are motions and executions of his just judgment; insofar as they are sins, however, he neither wills, nor approves, nor effects them; but although he forbids them, hates them with abhorrence and punishes them, he nevertheless permits them to concur in devils and men with his just works, while for the best and most just reasons he does not effect in them by his Spirit that they should perform those actions justly, that is, according to the prescription of the divine will.

units.la: X. Neque propterea Deus fit author confusionis, quæ est in actionibus malorum, siquidem quæ ipsi inordina-te, hoc est, contra Dei mandatum volunt & faciunt, Deus optimo & sapientissimo ordine vult fieri: Denique ipsa etiam peccata, quatenus peccata sunt, etsi non efficien-te, tamen permittente diuina prouidentia fiunt, eisque metas præfigente, & quò Deo visum est, ea dirigente.
units.tr: X. Nor on that account is God made the author of the disorder that is in the actions of evil men, since what they will and do in an disorderly way, that is, against God's command, God wills to happen in the best and wisest order. Finally, the sins themselves, insofar as they are sins, though they occur not by God's efficient causation but by his permissive providence, and he sets limits for them and directs them where it has seemed good to him.

units.la: XI. Neque author peccati per hanc doctrinam Deus constituitur: quandoquidem per accidens concurrit peccatum creaturæ vitiosæ, cum bono & iusto Dei opere, quod ipse in suo consilio instituit, & per creaturam peccantem exsequitur, ideoque respectu diuinæ voluntatis iustæ & rectæ sunt illæ actiones, quæ respectu malorum, per quos fiunt, peccata sunt.
units.tr: XI. Nor is God constituted the author of sin by this doctrine: since the sin of a vicious creature concurs by accident with the good and just work of God, which he himself has instituted in his counsel and carries out through the sinning creature; and therefore, with respect to the divine will, those actions are just and right, which with respect to the evil men through whom they occur are sins.

units.la: XII. Hæc manifesta sunt, primum ex vniuersali natura causarum & effectuum per se & per accidens. Quotiescunque enim eiusdem effectus plures causæ sunt, aliæ bonæ, aliæ vitiosæ, effectus ille respectu causarum bona-rū bonus est, respectu vitiosarū vero malus est: ac bonæ causæ sunt per se causæ boni, per accidens vero mali ac vitiosi effectus[?] siue vitij, quod est in effectu propter causam aliā vitiosā: & contrà, malæ causæ sunt per se causæ malæ, mali,per accidens autem boni quod est in effectu.
units.tr: XII. These things are made plain, first, from the universal nature of causes and effects, both per se and per accidens. For whenever several causes of the same effect exist, some good and some vicious, that effect is good with respect to the good causes, but evil with respect to the vicious ones; and good causes are per se causes of good, but per accidens of the evil and vicious effect, that is, of the vice which is in the effect on account of another vicious cause; and conversely, evil causes are per se causes of evil, but per accidens of the good which is in the effect.

units.la: XIII. Deinde patent etiam ex immutabili natura Dei & bonorum omnium fonte atque effectione. Aeque enim bona sunt opera Dei, siue per mala siue per bona instrumenta aliquid efficiat, & neque propter bona instrumenta fiunt meliora, neque propter mala fiunt deteriora cùm ipsorum bonitas & rectitudo non ab instrumentorum, sed à Dei vtentis illis natura pendeat: contrà verò, creaturæ nec esse nec manere bonæ, nec bene operari possunt, nisi Deo tales ipsas faciente ac seruante, & sic eas gubernante, vt bene operentur, cum ipso bene per eas quod vult operante.
units.tr: XIII. Secondly, they are also plain from the unchangeable nature of God and from him as the fount and author of all good things. For the works of God are equally good, whether he brings something about through evil or through good instruments; and they do not become better because of good instruments, nor worse because of evil ones, since their goodness and rectitude depend not on the instruments but on the nature of God who uses them. On the contrary, creatures can neither be nor remain good, nor act well, unless God makes and preserves them such, and so governs them that they act well, while he himself works through them what he wills.

units.la: XIV. Nec Deo tribuuntur voluntates contrariæ. Eadem enim opera vult & non vult diuersò respectu. Vult,quatenus cum iustissimo ipsius iudicio & ordine congruunt. nō vult autem,sed cùm serio oderit & detestetur,tamen fieri permittit,quatenus ordini & legi ipsius aduersantur,dū contra hanc à malis perpetrantur.
units.tr: XIV. Nor are contrary wills attributed to God. For he wills and does not will the same works in different respects. He wills them insofar as they agree with his most just judgment and order; but he does not will them, yet, since he seriously hates and detests them, he nevertheless permits them to occur, insofar as they oppose his order and law, while they are perpetrated by evil men against it.

units.la: XV. Neque necessitas consequentiæ, quæ euentibus accidit ex immutabili decreto diuinæ prouidentiæ,tollit contingentiam,quam habent ex mutabili natura causarum secundarum,vel etiam ex potentia & libertate diuina,qua Deus ab æterno sua decreta fecit: si modò re-ctè vtrumque definiatur: quòd videlicet sit ordo inter causam immutabiliter aut mutabiliter agentem. Ex eo enim apparet cuiuis,eundem effectum ex causis partim mutabilibus partim immutabilibus procedentem, respectu causarum mutabilium contingentem,respectu immutabilium verò necessarium esse & rectè appellari.
units.tr: XV. Nor does the necessity of consequence, which befalls events from the unchangeable decree of divine providence, abolish the contingency which they have from the changeable nature of secondary causes, or even from the power and freedom of God, by which God made his decrees from eternity: provided both are rightly defined, namely that there is an order between a cause acting immutably and one acting mutably. For from this it is plain to anyone that the same effect, proceeding from causes partly mutable and partly immutable, is rightly called contingent with respect to the mutable causes, but necessary with respect to the immutable ones.

units.la: XVI.
