Vita autem aeterna & alia Dei beneficia non effectus,seu merces ex merito data,sed consequēs seu merces gratuita sunt poenitentiae:sicut & fidei & bonorum operum. Psal.51.6. Tibi soli peccavi. Dan 9.7. Tibi Domine iustitia,nobis confusio faciei. Matt.3.9. Facite fructum dignum poenitentia. 1.Tim. 4.8. Corporalis exercitatio paululum habet utilitatis. Luc. 17.10. Cum omnia feceritis, dicite, serui inutiles sumus.
units.tr: The proper and perpetual effects of true repentance are the confession of one's unworthiness and of God's mercy, and all good works. Indifferent things, however, such as fasting, laying aside of ornament, etc., are aids or signs of repentance, not perpetual or simply necessary, but which may be undertaken according to the convenience and feeling of the pious. Eternal life and other benefits of God, however, are not effects or wages given from merit, but are the consequent and gratuitous reward of repentance, just as also of faith and good works. Ps. 51.6. Against you only have I sinned. Dan. 9.7. To you, O Lord, belongs righteousness; to us confusion of face. Matt. 3.8. Bring forth fruit worthy of repentance. 1 Tim. 4.8. Bodily exercise profits a little. Luke 17.10. When you have done all things, say: we are unprofitable servants.

units.la: XV.
units.tr: XV.

units.la: Vt igitur omnes electi in hac vita conuertuntur: sic nulli reprobi agunt veram poenitentiā: sed quanto magis mala conscientia,& sensu aut metu poenarū cruciatur,& ruentes in desperatione, contra Deum & iudicii eius fremunt: tanto magis à Deo auertuntur: & tato grauius peccant: & palam sunt blasphemi: aut aliquādo ex metu poenarum, aut cupiditate gloriae, vel aliorum commodorum huius vitae abiiciunt errores, amplectuntur & profitentur veritatem, abstinent à vitiis externis, & speciē sanctimoniae praeferūt, cūm tamē sint hypocritae sine fide, dilectione & timore Dei, ac proinde tandē deficiant. Exempla sunt: Cain, Esau, Iudas, Saul, Achab. Ies. 57.21. Non est pax impiis. Matt.21.44. Redit spiritus ne-quam. Hebr.6.6. Qui illuminati lubuntur[?], non denuò renocantur per poenitentiam, &c. 2. Pet. 2.10. Itaque si postquam inquinamenta mundi per agnitionem Domini, &c. effugerint, his rursum implicati superentur, facta est ultima eorum conditio deterior priore, &c.
units.tr: Just as all the elect are converted during this life, so no reprobate truly repent. Rather, the more an evil conscience torments them, with the feeling or fear of punishments, and the more they rush into despair and rage against God and his judgment, the more they turn away from God, sin all the more grievously, and openly become blasphemers. Or sometimes, out of fear of punishments, or desire for glory, or other advantages of this life, they cast off their errors, embrace and profess the truth, abstain from outward vices, and put on a show of holiness; yet they are hypocrites without faith, love and fear of God, and so in the end they fall away. Examples are Cain, Esau, Judas, Saul, Ahab. Isa. 57.21. There is no peace for the wicked. Matt. 21.44. The unclean spirit returns. Heb. 6.6. Those who have been enlightened, and have fallen away, cannot again be renewed through repentance, etc. 2 Pet. 2.10. Therefore if, after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord, etc., they are again entangled in them and overcome, their last state has become worse than the first, etc.

units.la: XVI.
units.tr: XVI.

units.la: Impia sunt dogmata pontificia de poenitentia, quod contritio posset & debeat esse sufficiens pro peccatis, & quod fit meritum remissionis peccatorum: quod necessaria sit ad remissionem omnium peccatorum apud ministrum confessio seu enumeratio: quod opera seu ritus, non a Deo, sed a ministris mandati, sint necessarij, & satisfactiones pro poenis peccatorum aeternis aut purgatorij. Psal. 90. 11. Quis novit magnitudinem irae tuae? Tit. 3. 5. Non ex operibus iustitiae, quae fecerimus nos: sed ex misericordia suâ servavit nos per lavacrum, &c. Psal. 19. 13. Delicta quis intelligit? ab occultis meis munda me. Isa. 29. 13. Matt. 15. 8. Frustra me colunt mandatis hominum.
units.tr: The Papist doctrines of repentance are impious: that contrition can and must be sufficient for sins, and that it is a merit of the remission of sins; that confession or enumeration before a minister is necessary for the remission of all sins; and that works or rites, commanded not by God but by ministers, are necessary, and satisfactions for the eternal or purgatorial punishments of sins. Ps. 90.11. Who knows the power of your anger? Titus 3.5. Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing, etc. Ps. 19.13. Who understands his errors? Cleanse me from my hidden faults. Isa. 29.13; Matt. 15.8. In vain do they worship me with the precepts of men.

units.la: XVI. De lege divina.
units.tr: XVI. On the divine law.

units.la: 1. Lex in genere est sententia praecipiens honestà, obligans naturam rationalem ad obedientiam, cum promissione praemij, si obedientia illi praestetur, & comminatione poenae si violetur.
units.tr: 1. Law in general is a statement commanding what is right, binding the rational nature to obedience, with a promise of reward if obedience is rendered to it, and a threat of punishment if it is violated.

units.la: II. Leges aliae divinae, aliae humanae sunt.
units.tr: II. Some divine laws and some human laws there are.

units.la: III. Humanae aliae politicae, aliae ecclesiasticae sunt.
units.tr: III. Of human laws, some are political and some ecclesiastical.

units.la: IV. Discrimina divinarum & humanarum hęc sunt praecipua: quod leges divinę partim ad angelos & homines, partim ad omnes, partim ad aliquos homines pertinet: Humanae tantum ad certos homines. Divinae praeter externas actiones, etiam internas qualitates & motus requirunt. Humanę certas actiones externas praecipiunt. Divinae non tantum corporalia & temporalia, sed etiam spiritualia & aeterna praemia & poenas proponunt: Humanae tantum corporalia & temporalia promittunt & minantur. Divinarum obedientia est finis legum humanarum: Humanae debent servire obseruationi divinarum. Divinae aliae aeternae, aliae mutabiles sunt: Humanę omnes sunt mutabiles. Divinae non nisi ab ipso Deo: Humanae, propter causas probabiles ab hominibus mutari & abrogari possunt.
units.tr: IV. The chief differences between divine and human laws are these: divine laws pertain partly to angels and men, partly to all, and partly to certain men; human laws only to certain men. Divine laws require, besides outward actions, also inward qualities and motions; human laws prescribe certain outward actions. Divine laws propose not only bodily and temporal but also spiritual and eternal rewards and punishments; human laws only promise and threaten bodily and temporal things. Obedience to divine laws is the end of human laws; human laws ought to serve the observance of divine ones. Some divine laws are eternal, others changeable; all human laws are changeable. Divine laws can be changed by God alone; human laws can be changed and abrogated by men, for probable causes.

units.la: XVII. De partibus legis Divinae.
units.tr: XVII. On the parts of the divine law.

units.la: I. Legis diuinæ, tres partes in scriptura sacra reperiuntur, Moralis, Ceremonialis, & Forensis.
units.tr: I. Three parts of the divine law are found in Holy Scripture: moral, ceremonial, and forensic.

units.la: II. Lex moralis, cuius summa est in decalogo comprehensa, est doctrina congruens cum æterna, & immota sapientia, & regula iustitiæ in Deo, discernens recta & non recta, natura nota, & insita creaturis rationalibus, in creatione, & postea sæpe repetita & declarata voce diuina, docés, quod sit Deus & qualis sit, obligans omnes creaturas rationales ad obedientiam perfectam, & conformitatem cum illa regula, externam & internam, & promittens fauorem Dei, & vitam æternam omnibus perfectam obedientiam præstantibus, & denuncians iram Dei, & pœnas æternas omnibus, qui non perfectè illi conformes sunt, nisi fiat remissio peccati, & reconciliatio propter filium Dei mediatorem.
units.tr: II. The moral law, whose sum is comprehended in the Decalogue, is a doctrine agreeing with the eternal and unchanging wisdom and the rule of righteousness in God, distinguishing right from not right, known by nature and implanted in rational creatures at creation, and afterwards often repeated and declared by the divine voice, teaching that there is a God and what kind of God he is, binding all rational creatures to perfect obedience and conformity with that rule, outward and inward, and promising the favour of God and eternal life to all who render perfect obedience, and denouncing the wrath of God and eternal punishments on all who are not perfectly conformed to it, unless remission of sin and reconciliation take place through the Son of God the Mediator.

units.la: III. Lex naturæ ante lapsum, fuit planè eadem cum lege diuina morali: post lapsum autem obscurata Dei agnitione in mentibus hominum, lex naturæ tantum pars decalogi est, præcipuè de agnitione & cultu Dei, obscura & mutila, quam etiam de causa Deus in ecclesia repetiuit & declarauit integram suæ legis sententiam:
units.tr: III. The law of nature before the fall was plainly the same as the moral divine law; but after the fall, with the knowledge of God obscured in the minds of men, the law of nature is only a part of the Decalogue, chiefly concerning the knowledge and worship of God, obscure and mutilated; for this reason God also repeated and declared in the Church the whole sense of his law.

units.la: IV. Leges cæremoniales sunt præcepta de cæremoniis, hoc est, actionibus, siue gestibus externis, solennib.[?] siue cum eorundem circunstantiarum obseruatione peragendis, in cultu Dei publico, institutis propter significationem, vel ordinem.
units.tr: IV. Ceremonial laws are precepts concerning ceremonies, that is, actions or outward gestures, to be performed solemnly or with observance of their circumstances, in the public worship of God, instituted on account of signification or order.

units.la: V. Leges forenses sunt de externa defensione disciplinæ, secundum utramque tabulam decalogi, siue de gubernatione politica in populo Iudaico, id est, de ordine & officiis magistratuum, iudiciorum, pœnarum, contrastuum[?], distinctione dominiorum.
units.tr: V. Forensic laws concern the outward defence of discipline according to both tables of the Decalogue, or the political government of the Jewish people, that is, the order and offices of magistrates, judgments, punishments, [contracts], and the distinction of domains.

units.la: VI. Hæc distinctio legum diuinarum retinenda est, tum propter ipsum discrimen harum legum, quo neglecto, non recte earum vis & sententia intelligitur, tum vt de abrogatione & vsu legis recte iudicari, & doceri possit.
units.tr: VI. This distinction of divine laws is to be retained, both because of the very difference between these laws, which, if neglected, leads to a wrong understanding of their force and meaning, and so that one may rightly judge and teach about the abrogation and use of the law.

units.la: VII. Discrimina inter legem moralem, & cæremoniales ac forenses leges, hæc sunt: Primùm moralia præcepta sunt natura nota: cæremonialia & forensia nō item.
units.tr: VII. The differences between the moral law and the ceremonial and forensic laws are these. First, moral precepts are known by nature; ceremonial and forensic ones are not.

units.la: VIII. Secundùm, moralia omnes creaturas rationales obligant, cæremonialia & forensia tantùm populo Iudaico præscripta fuerunt.
units.tr: VIII. Second, moral precepts bind all rational creatures; ceremonial and forensic ones were prescribed only to the Jewish people.

units.la: ix. Tertium, moralia sunt perpetua, cæremonialia & forensia non item.
units.tr: IX. Third, moral precepts are perpetual; ceremonial and forensic ones are not.

units.la: x. Quartum, moralia præcipiunt de obedientia interna & externa: cæremonialia & forensia de externa tantum, quę tamen cum interna morali obedientia coniuncta esse debet.
units.tr: X. Fourth, moral precepts command inward and outward obedience; ceremonial and forensic ones only outward obedience, which nevertheless ought to be joined with inward moral obedience.

units.la: xi. Quintum, moralia sunt generalia, non determinata certis circumstantiis: cæremonialia & forensia sunt specialia, id est, circumstantiarum determinatio.
units.tr: XI. Fifth, moral precepts are general, not determined by certain circumstances; ceremonial and forensic ones are particular, that is, a determination of circumstances.

units.la: xii. Sextum, cæremonialia & forensia sunt typi: moralia non sunt typi, sed per typos significata.
units.tr: XII. Sixth, ceremonial and forensic laws are types; moral ones are not types, but are signified by types.

units.la: xiii. Septimum, moralia sunt cultus Dei principalis, seu finis aliarum legum: cæremonialia & forensia seruire debent moralibus, vt hæc rite seruarentur.
units.tr: XIII. Seventh, moral precepts are the principal worship of God, or the end of the other laws; ceremonial and forensic ones ought to serve the moral ones, so that these may be duly observed.

units.la: xiv. Octauum, cæremonialia cedunt moralibus, moralia non cedunt cæremonialibus.
units.tr: XIV. Eighth, ceremonial laws yield to moral ones; moral laws do not yield to ceremonial ones.

units.la: XVIII. De usu & abrogatione legis diuinæ.
units.tr: XVIII. On the use and abrogation of the divine law.

units.la: i. Leges Mosaicæ cæremoniales & forenses abrogatæ sunt aduentu Messiæ, quod ad obedientiam attinet.
units.tr: i. The Mosaic ceremonial and judicial laws were abrogated by the coming of the Messiah, as far as obedience is concerned.

units.la: ii. Lex moralis autem, quod ad maledictionem, non autem, quod ad obedientiam attinet.
units.tr: ii. The moral law, however, is not abrogated as far as obedience is concerned, but only as far as the curse is concerned.

units.la: iii. Vsus cæremoniarum & iudiciorum Mosaicorum partim fuerunt, partim sunt isti, Padagogia ad Christū [?], id est, significatio seu adumbratio rerum spiritualium & cœlestium in regno Christi.
units.tr: iii. The uses of the Mosaic ceremonies and judgments were, and still are in part, a pedagogy to Christ [?], that is, a signification or foreshadowing of spiritual and heavenly things in the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: iv. Distinctio populi Dei ab aliis gentibus.
units.tr: iv. The distinction of the people of God from the other nations.

units.la: v. Exsecutio præceptorum moralium, quæ requirit multarum circumstantiarum determinationem in ecclesia & politia.
units.tr: v. The execution of the moral precepts, which requires the determination of many circumstances in the Church and the state.

units.la: vi. Testificatio obedientiæ erga Deum.
units.tr: vi. The testimony of obedience toward God.

units.la: vii. Obsignatio fœderis diuini per cæremonias, quæ erant sacramentalia signa.
units.tr: vii. The sealing of the divine covenant through the ceremonies, which were sacramental signs.

units.la: viii. Conseruatio politiæ Mosaicæ vsq; ad Christū per leges forenses, quæ erant neruus, & ipsa forma politiæ.
units.tr: viii. The preservation of the Mosaic polity until Christ, through the civil laws, which were the sinews and the very form of the polity.

units.la: ix. Confirmatio noui Testamenti per collationem impletionis cum typis.
units.tr: ix. The confirmation of the New Testament through the comparison of fulfilment with types.

units.la: x. Lex moralis, alios, quàm nunc, vsus habebat in natura nō corrupta, videlicet, conformationem integram vitæ hominum cum voluntate diuina, & bonā conscientiam, & fiduciam certam diuinæ beneuolentiæ.
units.tr: x. The moral law had a different use in uncorrupted nature than it has now, namely, the complete conformity of human life with the divine will, a good conscience, and a certain trust in divine goodwill.

units.la: xi. In natura corrupta hi sunt vsus: conseruatio disciplina in ecclesia & extra eam.
units.tr: xi. In corrupted nature these are its uses: the preservation of discipline in the Church and outside it.

units.la: xi. Agnitio peccati, qui duo usus ad omnes pertinent, & sunt etiam paedagogia legis ad Christum.
units.tr: xi. The recognition of sin; these two uses pertain to all, and are also the pedagogy of the law to Christ.

units.la: xii. Informatio ad verum Dei cultum, qui usus est renatorum proprius.
units.tr: xii. The instruction in the true worship of God, which is the proper use for the regenerate.

units.la: xiii. Atque hi sunt usus principales, praeter quos etiā alij sunt: Testimonii videlicet, quod sit Deus, & qualis sit.
units.tr: xiii. These are the principal uses, besides which there are also others: namely, as a testimony that God exists, and of what kind he is.

units.la: xiv. Nota ecclesia, qua discernitur integritate, & puritate legis, ab omnibus aliis sectis.
units.tr: xiv. As a mark of the Church, by which it is distinguished from all other sects by the integrity and purity of the law.

units.la: xv. Testimonium praestantiae naturae hominum, quae fuit ante lapsum, & quae per Christum nobis restituitur.
units.tr: xv. As a testimony to the excellence of human nature, which was before the fall and which is restored to us through Christ.

units.la: xvi. Testimonii de vita aeterna, in qua sit seruanda lex, cum in hac vita nō seruetur, nec Deus eā tulerit, vt proprium & principalem eius finem nunquam assequatur.
units.tr: xvi. As a testimony concerning eternal life, in which the law is to be kept, since it is not kept in this life, nor has God given it so that it should ever attain its proper and principal end.

units.la: XIX.
units.tr: XIX.

units.la: De expositione & partitione decalogi.
units.tr: On the exposition and division of the Decalogue.

units.la: 1. Decalogus, vt qui totius diuinae legis summā con-tiner, intelligendus est secundum declarationem per Mosen, prophetas, Christum & Apostolos traditam.
units.tr: 1. The Decalogue, as containing the sum of the whole divine law, is to be understood according to the explanation handed down by Moses, the prophets, Christ and the Apostles.

units.la: ii. Lex Dei requirit obedientiam integram, internam & externam in mente, voluntate, corde & actionibus, hoc est, dictis, factis, & gestibus externis.
units.tr: ii. The law of God requires complete obedience, inward and outward, in mind, will, heart and actions, that is, in words, deeds and outward gestures.

units.la: iii. Omnium aliorum praeceptorū obedientia, referenda est ad primum praeceptum, quia dilectio & gloria Dei debet esse impulsiva, & finalis causa totius obedientiae.
units.tr: iii. The obedience to all the other precepts is to be referred to the first precept, because the love and glory of God ought to be the impelling and final cause of all obedience.

units.la: iv. Sententia uniuscuiusque legis ex fine est sume-da, propter quem est lata.
units.tr: iv. The meaning of each law is to be taken from the end for which it was given.

units.la: v. Propter fines diuersos unum & idem opus in diuersis praeceptis praecipi sive contineri potest.
units.tr: v. On account of different ends, one and the same work can be commanded or contained in different precepts.

units.la: vi. Praecepta affirmativa sive imperativa includunt negativa sive prohibitiva; & contrà.
units.tr: vi. Affirmative or imperative precepts include negative or prohibitive ones, and conversely.

units.la: vii. Praecepta aut prohibita (specie aliquâ praecipua, species cognatae sive totū genus praecipitur aut prohibet.
units.tr: vii. Precepts either forbid or command some outstanding species, and in doing so command or forbid the related species or the whole genus.

units.la: viii. Vbi effectus praecipitur aut prohibetur, ibidem & causa praecipi, aut prohiberi intelligitur.
units.tr: viii. Where an effect is commanded or forbidden, there the cause is also understood to be commanded or forbidden.

units.la: ix. Cum relativis sanciuntur etiā correlativa, quandoquidem illa sine his nequeunt consistere.
units.tr: ix. Where relatives are enacted, correlatives are enacted too, since the former cannot exist without the latter.

units.la: x. Duae sunt tabulae decalogi, quarum prima quatuor praeceptis officia complectitur, quę immediatè erga Deum praestatur: secunda sex praeceptis docet, quae immediatè erga proximum, erga Deum verò mediatè praestantur, hoc est proximo præstatur propter Dei mandatū & gloriam.
units.tr: x. The Decalogue has two tables. The first, with four precepts, comprises the duties which are rendered immediately toward God; the second, with six precepts, teaches the duties which are rendered immediately toward the neighbour and mediately toward God, that is, a duty is rendered to the neighbour on account of God's command and glory.

units.la: XI. Præcepta secundæ tabulæ cedunt præceptis primæ tabulæ.
units.tr: XI. The precepts of the second table yield to the precepts of the first table.

units.la: XII. Rectior diuisio decalogi est, quæ præceptū secundum de statuis, & decimum de concupiscentia numerat.
units.tr: XII. A more correct division of the Decalogue is the one that counts the second precept as concerning images and the tenth as concerning concupiscence.

units.la: XX. De primo decalogi præcepto.
units.tr: XX. On the first precept of the Decalogue.

units.la: I. Prima tabula decalogi præcipit de officiis erga Deum, secunda de officiis erga proximum seu hominēs, sic tamen vt illa immediatē, hæc vero mediatē[?] ad Deum referantur.
units.tr: I. The first table of the Decalogue prescribes duties toward God, the second duties toward our neighbour or fellow men; yet in such a way that the former relate to God immediately, the latter mediately.

units.la: II. Primum præceptum, cùm iubeat nos solum verum, & in ecclesia patefactum Deum pro Deo nostro habere, cultum Dei internum præcipuè complectitur, qui in mente, voluntate, & corde consistit.
units.tr: II. The first precept, since it commands us to hold the one true God, made known in the Church, as our God, chiefly embraces the inward worship of God, which consists in the mind, the will, and the heart.

units.la: III. Huius cultus præcipuæ partes f[?]u capita sunt, vera Dei agnitio, fides, spes & dilectio Dei, timor Dei, humilitas coram Deo, & patientia.
units.tr: III. The chief parts or heads of this worship are: the true knowledge of God, faith, hope and love toward God, the fear of God, humility before God, and patience.

units.la: IV. Cognosci Deus à creaturis rationalibus aliquate-nus potest, nimirum quatenus ipse vnicuique se vult patefacere.
units.tr: IV. God can be known by rational creatures to some extent, namely insofar as he wishes to make himself known to each one.

units.la: V. Cognitio Dei alia est simpliciter & absolutè perfecta, quia solus Deus seipsum, hoc est æternus pater, & filius & spiritus sanctus, seipsos, & se invicem cognoscūt, infinitam essentiam suam totam & modum exsistendi, vniuscuiusque personæ divinæ totaliter, & perfectissimè intelligunt. Infiniti enim cognitionem perfectam non nisi infinitus intellectus capit. Alia est creaturarum, quæ angeli & homines totam quidem & integram, vtpote simplicissimam Dei naturam & maiestatem, sed non totaliter, hoc est eatenus tantum intelligunt, quatenus ipse illis revelat.
units.tr: V. The knowledge of God is of two kinds. The first is simply and absolutely perfect, because God alone knows himself, that is, the eternal Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit know themselves and one another, and fully and most perfectly understand his whole infinite essence and mode of existence, and each divine person entirely. For only an infinite intellect can grasp the perfect knowledge of the infinite. The second is that of creatures, which angels and men understand the whole and entire nature and majesty of God, since it is most simple, but not totally; that is, they understand only so far as he reveals himself to them.

units.la: VI. Quæ in creaturis est cognitio Dei, si ad eam, quā Deus seipsum intelligit, conferatur, imperfecta dicenda est: si autem gradus ipsius spectentur, etiam alia perse-cta, alia imperfecta est: non tamen simpliciter, sed collatione, hoc est, respectu gradus inferioris & superioris.
units.tr: VI. The knowledge of God that exists in creatures, if it is compared with that by which God knows himself, must be called imperfect; but if its degrees are considered, one kind is also called perfect and another imperfect. Yet this is not said absolutely but by comparison, that is, with respect to a lower and a higher degree.

units.la: Perfecta est, quæ beati angeli & homines in vita cœlesti Dei[?] mentis illustri intuitu cognoscunt, quantum ad conformitatem rationalis creaturæ cum Deo satis est.
units.tr: The perfect knowledge is that which the blessed angels and men have in the heavenly life, by a clear intuition of the mind of God; as far as the conformity of the rational creature with God requires, it is sufficient.

units.la: Imperfecta quæ homines Deum[?] in hac vita agnoscunt, minus quàm ex creationis beneficio poterant, ac propterea ex mandato diuino debebant.
units.tr: The imperfect knowledge is that by which men acknowledge God in this life, less than they could have from the benefit of creation, and therefore were bound to by the divine command.

units.la: VII. Imperfecta est duplex, Christiana (seu[?] theologica & philosophica. Christiana, quae ex doctrina prophetarum & apostolorum accipitur, Philosophica, quae est ex principiis naturae notis, & inspectione operum Dei in natura rerum.
units.tr: VII. Imperfect knowledge is twofold: Christian (or theological) and philosophical. Christian knowledge is that which is drawn from the teaching of the prophets and apostles; philosophical knowledge is that which comes from the principles of nature known to us and from the observation of God's works in the order of things.

units.la: VIII. Christiana etiam duplex est, Spiritualis, seu vera, viua, efficax, salutaris: & Literalis. Spiritualis est notitia de Deo, & eius voluntate in mentibus a spiritu sancto secundum verbum, & per verbum Dei accensa, efficiens in voluntate & corde inclinationem & studium ea magis magisque cognoscendi, credendi, & faciendi, quae Deus in verbo suo cognoscere, credere & facere nos iubet. Literalis est notitia de Deo, siue ex creatione retenta, siue deinceps a Spir.S. per verbum Dei effecta in mentibus, quam non comitatur ad ea se coformandi studiu.
units.tr: VIII. Christian knowledge is also twofold: spiritual, or true, living, effective, saving; and literal. Spiritual knowledge is the knowledge of God and of his will, kindled in minds by the Holy Spirit according to the Word and through the Word of God, producing in the will and heart an inclination and zeal to know, believe and do more and more those things which God commands us in his Word to know, believe and do. Literal knowledge is knowledge of God, either retained from creation or afterwards brought about in minds by the Holy Spirit through the Word of God, which is not accompanied by the zeal to conform oneself to it.

units.la: IX. Et spiritualis autem, & literalis, alia est immediata, quae fit per instinctum spiritus sancti sine mediis ordinariis, alia mediata, quae fit a spiritu sancto per vocem doctrinae coelestis auditam, lectam & cogitatam.
units.tr: IX. Both spiritual and literal knowledge are again of two kinds: one is immediate, which comes about through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit without the ordinary means; the other is mediate, which is effected by the Holy Spirit through the voice of heavenly doctrine heard, read and pondered.

units.la: X. Ordinarius Deum cognoscendi modus, & nobis a Deo praescriptus est per doctrinae coelestis studiu, & me-ditatione, ac proinde hac ad Dei cognitione via debe-mus cotendere, neq. a Deo extraordinaria & immediata illuminatione postulare, atq. exspectare, nisi hanc vltro ipse nobis offerat, & testimoniis certis confirmer.
units.tr: X. The ordinary way of knowing God, and the one prescribed to us by God, is through the study and meditation of heavenly doctrine; accordingly we ought to strive along this way of knowing God, and not demand or expect from God an extraordinary and immediate illumination, unless he himself offers it to us of his own accord and confirms it by certain testimonies.

units.la: XI. Etsi autem quantum in hac vita nobis constare de se Deus voluit, in verbo suo satis expositum, tamen testimonia naturalia de Deo, minime superuacanea sunt, quia reproborum impietatem coarguunt, electorum autem fidem confirmant, ideoque ab ipso Deo passim in scriptura allegantur, & a nobis consideranda sunt.
units.tr: XI. Although God has wished that as much of himself be known to us in this life as is set out sufficiently in his Word, nevertheless natural testimonies about God are by no means superfluous, since they convict the impiety of the reprobate and confirm the faith of the elect; therefore they are cited by God himself throughout Scripture and must be considered by us.

units.la: XII. Sed hoc de illis tenendum est, quod vera quidem & cum verbo Dei congruentia sint, sed ad veram Dei cognitionem non sufficiant.
units.tr: XII. But this must be held concerning them: that they are indeed true and agree with the Word of God, but they are not sufficient for the true knowledge of God.

units.la: XIII. Praeterea licet naturalia testimonia, nihil falsi de Deo doceant, homines tamen sine accedente luce verbi Dei non nisi falsas opiniones de Deo ex illis con-cipiunt, tum quia ista testimonia non tantum ostendunt, quantum in verbo traditum est, tum quia illa etiam, quae naturali iudicio intelligi possunt, homines propter innatam[?] tam ipsis caecitatem, & prauitatem perperam accipiunt & interpretantur, ac varie corrumpunt.
units.tr: XIII. Moreover, although natural testimonies teach nothing false about God, men nevertheless, without the added light of the Word of God, form from them only false opinions about God, partly because these testimonies do not show as much as is handed down in the Word, and partly because men, through the blindness and depravity innate in them, wrongly receive and interpret even those things which can be understood by natural judgment, and corrupt them in various ways.

units.la: XIV. Prohibetur itaq. & damnatur primo decalogi præcepto omnis eorum ignorantia, quæ Deus de se cognoscēda, nobis in verbo, & operibus suis, tam creationis, quàm redemtionis ecclesiæ proposuit : omnes itè errores fingentiū, vel nullū esse Deū, vt Epicureorū: vel plures esse deos, vt Ethnicorum: Manichæorū, inuocatiū angelos, homines mortuos aut alias creaturas, magorū, fuperftitioforū, fiduciā creaturarū nitētiū: vel diuersum ab eo, qui se patefecit in ecclesia, vt Philosophorū, Iudæorum, Mahometistarum, Sabellij, Arij, Samosateni, Pneumatomachorū & similium, qui Deum non agnoscunt, qui sit pater æternus cum coæterno filio & S.S.
units.tr: XIV. Therefore, by the first precept of the Decalogue, all the ignorance of those things which God has set before us to be known about himself, both in his Word and in his works, of creation as well as of the redemption of the Church, is forbidden and condemned; likewise all the errors of those who feign either that there is no God, as the Epicureans; or that there are many gods, as the heathens; of the Manichaeans; of those who invoke angels, dead men or other creatures; of the magicians and superstitious, who rely on confidence in creatures; or who think of a God different from him who revealed himself in the Church, as the philosophers, the Jews, the Mahometists, Sabellius, Arius, Samosatenus, the Pneumatomachi and those like them, who do not acknowledge God as the eternal Father with the coeternal Son and the Holy Spirit.

units.la: XXI. De sex prioribus decalogi præceptis.
units.tr: XXI. On the first six precepts of the Decalogue.

units.la: I. Primo præcepto cultus Dei immediatus, internus sacitur, cuius præcipuæ partes sunt vera Dei agnitio, fides, spes, dilectio Dei, timor Dei, humilitas coram Deo, patientia. Prohibentur & damnantur ignorantia Dei, errores de Deo, siue nullum siue plures vno fingentes, vt Ethnicorū, Manichæorū, creaturas inuocantium siue angelos, siue homines, siue alias magorum, superstitiosorum, fiducia creaturarum nitentium, siue aliū quā qui se patefecit fingentes, vt Philosophorū, Iudæorū, Mahometistarū, Sabellij, Samosateni, Arij, Pneumatomachorū. Item contemtus Dei, incredulitas, dubitatio de Deo, diffidētia, fides temporaria, apostasia, securitas carnalis, tentatio Dei, desperatio, dubitatio de vita æterna & liberatione, odiū Dei, amor sui aut creaturarum inordinatus, timor seruilis, superbia βαυκοπαθεια, impatientia, temeritas.
units.tr: I. The first precept requires the immediate, inward worship of God, whose chief parts are the true knowledge of God, faith, hope, love of God, fear of God, humility before God, and patience. Forbidden and condemned are ignorance of God and errors about God, whether by imagining that there is no God or many gods, as the heathens and Manichaeans do; by invoking creatures, whether angels, men, or other things; by the arts of magicians and superstitious people; by relying on trust in creatures; or by imagining a God other than the one who revealed himself, as the philosophers, Jews, Mahometans, Sabellius, Samosatenus, Arius, the Pneumatomachi, and others like them do, who do not acknowledge that the Father is eternal with the coeternal Son and the Holy Spirit. Likewise forbidden and condemned are contempt of God, unbelief, doubt about God, distrust, temporary faith, apostasy, carnal security, tempting God, despair, doubt about eternal life and deliverance, hatred of God, disordered love of self or of creatures, servile fear, pride, βαυκοπαθεια [a delicate, effeminate self-indulgence], impatience, and rashness.

units.la: II. Secundum præceptum est regula vniuersi cultus Dei, videlicet, ne vllo genere cultus Deū colere instituamus, nisi quo ipse coli se præcepit: ideoque verū Dei cultum præcipit & omnem cultum Dei fictitiū prohibet, præsertim statuas & imagines ad Deū repræsentādū, aut colendū factas: itē negligentiā potestatis publicæ, qua tolerantur in locis ipsis subiectis statuæ & instrumenta, quæ idololatriæ seruierūt, aut facile seruire possunt, ac multò magis earū cultūꝰté hypocrisin & profanitatem.
units.tr: II. The second precept is the rule of all worship of God: namely, that we should never set up any kind of worship of God except that by which he has commanded himself to be worshipped. Therefore it commands the true worship of God and forbids every fictitious worship of God, especially statues and images made to represent God or to be worshipped. It also forbids negligence on the part of the public authority, by which statues and instruments that have served idolatry, or can easily serve it, are tolerated in the very places under its control; and much more so their worship, hypocrisy, and profanity.

units.la: III. Tertium præceptum, cultum Dei extremum à singulis præstandū requirit, hoc est, veræ doctrinæ de Deo propapropagationem,iuramentum legitimum,zelu pro gloria Dei: vetat omissionē rædium & depravationē doctrinæ de Deo,neglectum celebrationis Dei, blasphemias, negationem,dissimulationem veritatis, & confessionem intepestiuam,abusum libertatis in adiaphoris, scandala in moribus,neglectum inuocationis,inuocationem praeuam[?], vel non ad verum Deum,vel non legitime factam: ingratitudinem,negationem,neglectum & abusum beneficiorum Dei,iuramenti necessarij recusationē, periurium,iuramenta idololatrica,illicita,temeraria : lenitatem in tuenda gloria Dei & zelum errantem.
units.tr: III. The third precept requires that the highest worship of God be rendered by each individual, that is, the propagation of the true doctrine about God, a lawful oath, and zeal for the glory of God. It forbids the neglect and corruption of the doctrine about God, neglect of the celebration of God, blasphemies, denial, dissimulation of the truth, and untimely confession; abuse of liberty in matters indifferent, and scandals in morals; neglect of invocation, and invocation that is either prior [?], or not addressed to the true God, or not lawfully made; ingratitude, denial, neglect, and abuse of the benefits of God; refusal of a necessary oath, perjury, and idolatrous, unlawful, and rash oaths; and leniency in defending the glory of God and misguided zeal.

units.la: iv. Quartum praeceptum continet cultū Dei externum publicum in ecclesia,seu coseruatione & usum ministerij,hoc est,publicā prædicatione & studium doctrinæ, administratione & usum sacramentorum: Inuocationem Dei publicā:honore & obedientiā ministerio debitam, hoc est,conseruatione ministerij & sabbatum spirituale,quod est obedientia erga doctrinā: vetat neglectum officij docendi:depravatione & mutilatione doctrinæ:negligentem hortationis ad usum sacramentorum,& administrationem eorum illegitimā: contemtum doctrinæ curiositatem in quærendis non necessariis:contemtum & profanationem sacramentorum:neglectum publicarum precum:hypocriticā in illis præsentiā, recitationem earum non seruienté vtilitati ecclesiæ:auocationem aliorum a ministerio:abolitionem ministerij,indignorum ad illud vocationē,errores de usu ministerij: contemtum ministrorum,inobedientiā erga ministerium,ingratitudinē vel acerbitatem erga ministros, neglectum scholarum.
units.tr: IV. The fourth precept contains the public external worship of God in the Church, or the preservation and exercise of the ministry, that is, public preaching and the study of doctrine, the administration and use of the sacraments; public invocation of God; and the honour and obedience due to the ministry, that is, the preservation of the ministry and spiritual Sabbath, which is obedience toward the doctrine. It forbids neglect of the duty of teaching; corruption and mutilation of doctrine; careless exhortation to the use of the sacraments, and their illegitimate administration; contempt of doctrine; curiosity in seeking what is not necessary; contempt and profanation of the sacraments; neglect of public prayers; hypocritical presence at them, and recitation of them that does not serve the benefit of the Church; the diversion of others from the ministry; the abolition of the ministry; the calling of unworthy persons to it; errors about the use of the ministry; contempt of ministers; disobedience toward the ministry; ingratitude or harshness toward ministers; and neglect of schools.

units.la: v. Quintum praeceptum sanctè ordinem politicum, seu mutua officia superiorum & inferiorum inter homines: quorum alia sunt propria parentū,vt nutritio, defensio, institutio & disciplina domestica liberorū: Præceptorum, institutio & disciplina scholastica. Magistratuum, præceptio disciplinæ totius decalogi, exsecutio præceptorum decalogi in defendendis innocentibus,& puniendis sontibus,constitutio legum positiua in politia,& earum exsecutio. Dominorum, imperare iusta familiæ,dare mercedem & regere disciplina domestica: Ætate vel authoritate præstantium, exemplo & consiliis præire aliis: Inferiorum[?], honor,id est reuerentia,amor,obedientia,gratitudo & [illegible, ~6 letters] erga superiores: Alia omnibus gradibus communia, videlicet iustitia vniuersalis, iustitia particularis distributiua, sedulitas, [illegible, ~6 letters] gratitudo, graui-ras, modestia, [illegible, ~6 letters]. Dinat igitur In parentibus neglectum aut luxum educationis, neglectum defensionis aut zelum pro liberis imprudentem: In parentibus & praeceptoribus neglectum institutionis, corruptelas, nimia indulgentiam aut seuitiam: In magistratibus ignauia & tyrannidem: In Dominis licentiae concessionem, iniusta imperia, mercedis fraudationem, asperitatem nimiam: In potentibus authoritate stultitiam cossiliorum, leuitatem aut prauitatem morum, neglectum iuniorum aut aliorum, quos possunt iuuare aut corrigere: In inferioribus, reuerentiae, amoris, obedientiae, gratificationis, [illegible, ~5 letters] defectum vel excessum, quo plus quam lex Dei permittit, illis tribuitur aut indulgetur. In omnibus vero, omissione officii, inobedientiam, [illegible, ~6 letters], errores aut [illegible, ~6 letters] in distribuendis officiis aut honoribus & praemiis, ignauiam, [illegible, ~6 letters], indulgentiam iniustam erga cognatos, ingratitudinem, gratificationem iniustam, leuitatem, fastum, immodestiam, arrogantiam, simulationem modestiae, rigore seu seueritate nimia, lenitatem.
units.tr: V. The fifth precept sanctions the political order, that is, the mutual duties of superiors and inferiors among men. Of these, some belong to parents, such as the nourishment, defence, instruction, and domestic discipline of children; to teachers, instruction and scholastic discipline; to magistrates, the prescribing of discipline across the whole Decalogue, the execution of the precepts of the Decalogue in defending the innocent and punishing the guilty, and the enactment and execution of positive laws in the commonwealth; to masters, to command what is just for the household, to give wages, and to govern domestic discipline; to those who excel in age or authority, to go before others by example and counsel; to inferiors, honour, that is, reverence, love, obedience, gratitude, and [illegible] toward superiors. Other duties are common to all grades, namely universal justice, particular distributive justice, diligence, [illegible], gratitude, gravity, modesty, [illegible]. Therefore, in parents there is neglect or extravagance in upbringing, neglect of defence or imprudent zeal for children; in parents and teachers, neglect of instruction, corruption, excessive indulgence or severity; in magistrates, sloth and tyranny; in masters, the granting of licence, unjust commands, defrauding of wages, and excessive harshness; in those who hold authority, foolishness of counsels, levity or perversity of morals, neglect of the young or of others whom they can help or correct; in inferiors, a defect or excess of reverence, love, obedience, and [illegible], by which more is granted or conceded to them than the law of God permits. In all, indeed: omission of duty, disobedience, [illegible], errors or [illegible] in distributing offices or honours and rewards, sloth, [illegible], unjust indulgence toward relatives, ingratitude, unjust favouritism, levity, pride, immodesty, arrogance, feigned modesty, excessive rigour or severity, and leniency.

units.la: v i. Sextum praeceptum
units.tr: VI. The sixth precept

units.la: vitam & incolumitatem corporis munit, propriam & alienam: ideoque praecipit iustitiam particularem neminem laedentem, mansuetudinem, [illegible, ~6 letters], iustitiam commutatiuam in poenis, fortitudinem, nemefin, humanitatem, misericordiam, amicitiam: Prohibentur, laesio iniusta vitae aut corporis nostri vel alieni, leuitas, iracundia, ira iniusta, vindicta, cupiditas, simultas, crudelitas, [illegible, ~6 letters], turbulentia, gratificatio iniusta pacis causa, calumnia, stricti iuris, vindicta priuata, timiditas, temeritas, inhumanitas, odium proximi, amor sui inordinatus, [illegible, ~6 letters] in aliena calamitate, leuitas in contrahendis & dissoluendis amicitiis, adulatio.
units.tr: It protects the life and bodily safety of oneself and of others. Therefore it commands particular justice that harms no one, gentleness, [illegible], commutative justice in punishments, fortitude, equity, humanity, mercy, and friendship. Forbidden are unjust injury to our own or another's life or body, levity, anger, unjust wrath, revenge, lust, enmity, cruelty, [illegible], turbulence, unjust favouritism for the sake of peace, calumny, strict right, private vengeance, timidity, rashness, inhumanity, hatred of one's neighbour, disordered love of self, [illegible] in another's calamity, levity in forming and breaking friendships, and flattery.

units.la: XXII.
units.tr: XXII.

units.la: De adiaphoris.
units.tr: On Adiaphora.

units.la: I. Actionum humanarum quaedam sunt suo genere bonae aut malae, quaedam adiaphorae siue indifferentes.
units.tr: I. Of human actions, some are good or evil by their own nature, and some are adiaphora, that is, indifferent.

units.la: II. Sue genere, siue per se, bonae sunt, quae expresse Dei mandato praecipiuntur, quas iuxta legis rectae intellectæ sententiam facere necesse est.
units.tr: II. Those are good by their own nature, or in themselves, which are expressly commanded by God's command, and which it is necessary to do according to the sense of the right law as rightly understood.

units.la: iii. Suo genere, siue per se, malæ sunt, quæ expressa lege diuina prohibentur.
units.tr: III. Those are evil by their own nature, or in themselves, which are expressly forbidden by the divine law.

units.la: iv. Adiaphoræ siue indifferentes sunt, quæ neque præceptæ, neque prohibitæ sunt à Deo.
units.tr: IV. Adiaphora, or indifferent things, are those which are neither commanded nor forbidden by God.

units.la: v. Hæ possunt cum peccato, aut sine peccato fieri, vel omitti.
units.tr: V. These can be done or omitted either with sin or without sin.

units.la: vi. Peccata sunt, quando vel à non renatis, vel à renatis cum scandalo facientis vel aliorum fiunt.
units.tr: VI. They are sins when they are done either by unregenerate persons, or by regenerate persons with scandal to others.

units.la: vii. Non sunt peccata, cum à renatis fiunt sine scandalo.
units.tr: VII. They are not sins when they are done by regenerate persons without scandal.

units.la: viii. Necessariæ autem factu sunt, quando sine scandalo non possunt omitti.
units.tr: VIII. They are necessary to do when they cannot be omitted without scandal.

units.la: ix. Itaque per se quidem licitæ & bonæ, sed tamen indifferentes ac liberæ sunt: per accidens autem malæ & illicitæ, vel necessariæ sunt.
units.tr: IX. Thus, in themselves they are indeed lawful and good, yet they are indifferent and free; but by accident they are evil and unlawful, or they are necessary.

units.la: XXIII. De iustificatione hominis coram Deo.
units.tr: XXIII. On the justification of man before God.

units.la: i. Iustitia, qua coram Deo iusti sumus, est legis diuinæ impletio.
units.tr: i. The righteousness by which we are righteous before God is the fulfilment of the divine law.

units.la: ii. Iustitia legalis est impletio legis, ab eo ipso præstita, qui iustus nominatur.
units.tr: ii. Legal righteousness is the fulfilment of the law, performed by him himself who is called righteous.

units.la: iii. Iustitia Euangelica, est poena nostrorum peccatorum, quam Christus pro nobis sustinuit credentibus, à Deo gratis imputata.
units.tr: iii. Evangelical righteousness is the punishment of our sins, which Christ endured for us, imputed freely by God to those who believe.

units.la: iv. Postquam genus humanum est lapsum, nemo hominum præter solum Christum in hac vita, legali iustitia est iustus coram Deo.
units.tr: iv. Since the human race has fallen, no one among men, except Christ alone, in this life is righteous before God with legal righteousness.

units.la: v. Iustificamur autem sola fide in Christum.
units.tr: v. We are justified, however, by faith alone in Christ.

units.la: vi. Et tamen legalem iustitiam in omnibus, qui salvantur, in hac vita inchoari necesse est.
units.tr: vi. Nevertheless, legal righteousness must necessarily begin in this life in all who are saved.

units.la: XXIV. De sacramentis, publicè disputatæ Heidelbergæ 23. Aug. anno 67.
units.tr: XXIV. On the Sacraments, publicly disputed at Heidelberg, 23 August 1607.

units.la: i. Deus inde ab initio promissioni gratiæ adiunxit signa siue ritus, qui vsitatè in ecclesia nominantur sacramenta.
units.tr: i. God, from the very beginning, joined to the promise of grace signs or rites, which are commonly called sacraments in the Church.

units.la: Probatio. Pro vetusto academiæ more ante disputationem à respondente recitata.
units.tr: Proof. According to the ancient custom of the university, this was recited by the respondent before the disputation.

units.la: Inde ab Adamo sacrificia fuerunt, quæ Deus instituerat, quia [?] ipsi placebant. Abrahamo circumcisio mandata fuit. Per Mosen sacrificiorum species et ritus aliti, et alia caremonia addita sunt: quae durarunt usque ad Christum: quo baptismum et coenam mysticam illis substituit.
units.tr: From Adam onward there were sacrifices, which God had instituted, because [?] they pleased him. Circumcision was commanded to Abraham. Through Moses the kinds of sacrifices and other rites were added, along with other ceremonies, which lasted until Christ, who substituted for them baptism and the mystical supper.

units.la: 11. Sunt autem sacramenta signa foederis aeterni inter Deum et credentes, hoc est, functi ritus divinitus ecclesiae mandati et additi promissioni gratiae, ut iis tanquam visibilibus ac certis testimoniis Deus significet ac testetur, se in vera fide haec symbola visurpantibus Christi & omnia ipsius beneficia communicare, iuxta promissionem euangelij, atque ita fiducia promissionis in ipsis confirmet, & ecclesia his visibilibus notis ab omnibus aliis sectis discernatur, suamque erga Deum fidem & graticudinem publice profiteatur, memoriam beneficiorum Christi conseruet & propaget, atque ad mutuam dilectionem sub uno capite Christo obligetur & excitetur.
units.tr: 11. Sacraments, moreover, are signs of the eternal covenant between God and believers, that is, sacred rites commanded by God to the Church and added to the promise of grace, so that by these visible and sure testimonies God may signify and attest that he, in true faith, communicates Christ and all his benefits to those who take up these symbols, according to the promise of the gospel; and thus, in them, he may confirm the confidence of the promise. And the Church, by these visible marks, may be distinguished from all other sects, publicly profess its faith and thankfulness toward God, preserve and propagate the memory of the benefits of Christ, and be bound and stirred up to mutual love under one head, Christ.

units.la: Probatio. Definitio hac expressa est Genes. 17. 11. Exod. 20. 10 et 31. 14. Ezech. 20. 12. Sabbatha mea observabitis, &c.
units.tr: Proof. This definition is expressed in Genesis 17:11; Exodus 20:10 and 31:14; Ezekiel 20:12: "My sabbaths you shall keep," etc.

units.la: Esse ritus mandatos ecclesiae a Deo patet indubitatione. Sic etiam, quod sint ritus additi promissioni tanquam eius visibilia signa: quia omnium sacramentorum ritus non tantum significant nostram erga Deum officia, sed primo et principaliter Dei erga nos beneficia: ut circumcisio remissione et mortificatione peccati. Deut. 30. 6. Colo. 2. 11. sacrificia et Pascha mactatione et maducatione Christi, 1 Cor. 5. 7. Ioh. 1. 19. Hebr. 8. 9. 10.
units.tr: That the rites are commanded to the Church by God is plain beyond doubt. So too, that they are rites added to the promise as its visible signs: because the rites of all sacraments signify not only our duties toward God, but first and chiefly God's benefits toward us: as circumcision signifies the remission and mortification of sin (Deut. 30:6; Col. 2:11); sacrifices and the Passover signify the slaying and eating of Christ (1 Cor. 5:7; John 1:19; Heb. 8:9, 10).

units.la: Nec tantum nos ea confitentes, et celebrantes significamus, sed primo ac principaliter Deus ea per ceremonias sacramentorum testificas et confirmas nobis significat. Ministri enim ta in sacramentorum administratione, quae in verbi praedicatione persona et voces Dei erga ecclesiam gerunt. Matt. 28. 19. Docete et baptizate omnes gentes. Ioh. 1. 33. Qui misit me baptizare, Ioh. 3. 22. et 4. 2. Iesus baptizabat, cum non ipse, sed discipuli ipsius nomine baptizarent. Sic de symbolo inaugurationis ad regnum, 1 Samuel 10. 1. Unxit te Iehova, cum tame Samuel ad Sengendum Saulem esset missus.
units.tr: Nor do we signify these things only by confessing and celebrating them, but first and chiefly God signifies them to us, testifying and confirming them through the ceremonies of the sacraments. For the ministers, in the administration of the sacraments, bear the person and voice of God toward the Church, just as they do in the preaching of the Word. Matt. 28:19: "Teach and baptize all nations." John 1:33: "He who sent me to baptize." John 3:22 and 4:2: "Jesus baptized," although it was not he himself, but his disciples, who baptized in his name. So too, the symbol of inauguration to the kingdom: 1 Samuel 10:1: "Jehovah has anointed you," although Samuel was sent to anoint Saul.

units.la: Fide igitur sacramenta confirmant, Quia scriptura testatur ea esse signa mutui atq. aeterni foederis inter Deum et credentes: Quia Deus per ea nobis collatione beneficiorum in evangelio promissorum significat, ac Deo, sive per symbola, sive per verba, sua ergo nos volutate significati, atque est credendi. Quia promissionem gratia, non tantum ut sacrificia et obedienobedientia nostra, Verum & signa gratia nobis à Deo tradita in [illegible, ~3 letters] legitimo habent addita: Ut Qui crediderit & baptizatus fuerit, salvus erit, Acceptabilis erit hostia ad expia dū illū. Quia denique scriptura ad confirmanda rerum significatarum acceptionem & privationem, allegat acceptio-ne vel privationem signorum, ut Psal.51. Asperges me Domine hyssopo & mundabor. Circumcidet Dominus cor tuum, &c. Quicunque baptizati sumus, in mortem illius baptizati sumus. Panis quem frangimus, nonne communio corporis Christi est?
units.tr: Sacraments therefore confirm faith, because Scripture testifies that they are signs of the mutual and eternal covenant between God and believers; because by them God signifies to us, by the conferring of the benefits promised in the gospel, and by his own will, that we are to believe, whether through symbols or through words. Because the promise of grace, unlike sacrifices and our obedience, has signs of grace given to us by God added to it in a lawful way: "He who believes and is baptized will be saved" (Mark 16:16); "the sacrifice will be acceptable to make atonement for him." Finally, because Scripture, to confirm the acceptance and rejection of the things signified, adduces the acceptance or rejection of the signs, as in Psalm 51: "Purge me with hyssop, O Lord, and I shall be clean" (Ps. 51:7); "The Lord will circumcise your heart" (Deut. 30:6), etc.; "As many of us as were baptized were baptized into his death" (Rom. 6:3); "The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" (1 Cor. 10:16).

units.la: Hinc alii fines accedunt. Discernunt ecclesiam ab aliis sectis: Hoc patet ex effectu: item testimonio, ut Omnis alienigena non comedet ex eo. Quae igitur vilitas circumcisionis? Multa. Credita sunt illis eloquia Dei. Vos gentes, qui dicebamini praeputium, quod eratis in illo tempore sine Christo, alieni a politia Israelis & hospites testamentorum, promissionis spem non habentes, & sine Deo in mundo: sunt confessio & gratiarum actio publica pro beneficiis Christi. Erit signum foederis inter me & vos: erit que pactum meum in carne vestra. Quotiescunque ederitis panem hunc, mortem Domini annunciate. Confirmant memoriam beneficiorum. Erit dies hic vobis in recordationem. Erit quasi signum in manu tua & appensum quid, ob recordationem ante oculos tuos. Hoc facite in mei recordationem. Sunt vinculum dilectionis. Quia enim in vtentes confederantur cum Deo, etiam inter se confederantur: Vnus Dominus, vna fides, vnum Baptisma, &c. Vnus panis, vnum corpus, multi fumus. Omnes enim de vno pane participamus.
units.tr: Hence other ends are added. They distinguish the Church from other sects: this is clear from the effect; likewise from the testimony, as in "No foreigner shall eat of it" (Exod. 12:43). What, then, was the value of circumcision? Great: "to them were committed the oracles of God" (Rom. 3:2). "You Gentiles, who were called uncircumcision, because at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants, having no hope of the promise and without God in the world" (Eph. 2:11, 12). They are a public confession and thanksgiving for the benefits of Christ. "It shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you, and my covenant shall be in your flesh" (Gen. 17:11, 13). "As often as you eat this bread, you proclaim the death of the Lord" (1 Cor. 11:26). They confirm the memory of the benefits: "This day shall be a memorial to you" (Exod. 13:9). "It shall be as a sign on your hand and as a thing bound between your eyes, for a remembrance" (Exod. 13:9, 16). "Do this in remembrance of me" (Luke 22:19). They are a bond of love. For as those who use them are bound together with God, so also they are bound together among themselves: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism" (Eph. 4:5). "One bread, one body, we who are many are one; for we all partake of one bread" (1 Cor. 10:17).

units.la: III. Ritus non mandati à Deo, vel non in hunc finem instituti, ut sint signa promissionum, non sunt sacramenta.
units.tr: III. Rites not commanded by God, or not instituted for this end, that they should be signs of promises, are not sacraments.

units.la: Probatio. Signum nihil confirmare potest nisi à consensu & promissione illius, à quo res promissa & significata exspectantur. Nulla igitur creatura potest signa & testimonia divinae voluntatis instituere.
units.tr: Proof. A sign can confirm nothing except by the consent and promise of him from whom the promised and signified thing is expected. No creature, therefore, can institute signs and testimonies of the divine will.

units.la: IV. Duo sunt in omnibus sacramentis consideranda. Signa visibilia, terrena & corporalia, quae sunt ritus sive caeremoniae, & res visibiles atque corporales, quas Deus nobis per ministros exhibet, ac nos corporaliter, hoc est, membris & sensibus corporis accipimus, & res significacæ, invisibiles, cœlestes & spirituales, hoc est, Christus ipse & omnia ipsius beneficia, quæ spiritualiter, hoc est virtute Spiritus sancti per fidem nobis a Deo communicantur.
units.tr: IV. Two things are to be considered in all sacraments. The visible signs, earthly and bodily, which are rites or ceremonies, and the visible and bodily things which God presents to us through ministers, and which we receive bodily, that is, with the members and senses of the body; and the things signified, invisible, heavenly and spiritual, that is, Christ himself and all his benefits, which are communicated to us by God spiritually, that is, by the power of the Holy Spirit, through faith.

units.la: Probatio. Distinctio manifesta est per inductionem. Item signorum acceptio corporalis, & externa: Res vero signata spiritualiter sive per fidem accipiuntur: Quia solis credentibus promittuntur: signa autem non aliter sunt rata, quam per promissiones quibus annectuntur. Item, quia signa idem nuntiant oculis, quod promissio nuntiat auribus. Sicut igitur promissio est inanis sonitus, sic est inanis ceremonia sine fide. Item, quia res signata sunt communio Christi & omnium eius beneficiorum. Hac vero non aliter, quam per fidem cuiusque potest contingere, sive in visu sive extra visum sacramenti.
units.tr: Proof. The distinction is evident by induction. Likewise the reception of the signs is bodily and external; but the things signified are received spiritually, or through faith, because they are promised only to believers. Signs, moreover, are not valid otherwise than through the promises to which they are attached. Likewise, because the signs announce to the eyes what the promise announces to the ears. Just as a promise without faith is an empty sound, so a ceremony without faith is empty. Likewise, because the things signified are the communion of Christ and of all his benefits; and this can happen to anyone only through faith, whether within the visible sacrament or outside it.

units.la: v. Mutatio symbolorum non fit, quod ad naturam, sed tantum, quod ad visum ipsorum attinet.
units.tr: V. The change of the symbols does not occur as regards their nature, but only as regards their outward appearance.

units.la: Probatio. Patet inductione & sensu. Item testimoniis.
units.tr: Proof. It is plain by induction and by sense. Likewise by testimonies.

units.la: Ego baptizo aqua. Panis quem frangimus est communio corporis Christi. Hic in visu nominantur aqua & panis.
units.tr: "I baptize with water." "The bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ." Here water and bread are named in their outward appearance.

units.la: vi. Coniunctio signorum & rerum significatarum non physica aut localis est, sed relativa, videlicet ordinatio divina, qua res invisibiles & spirituales per visibiles & corporales repræsentantur, tanquam per verba visibilia, & in visu legitimo unà cum signis exhibetur & percipiuntur.
units.tr: VI. The conjunction of the signs and the things signified is not physical or local, but relative: namely, the divine ordinance by which invisible and spiritual things are represented through visible and bodily things, as through visible words, and are exhibited and perceived in lawful use together with the signs.

units.la: Probatio. Talis est omnium signorum cum rebus significatis copulatio, ut res significata repræsentet & eorum acceptione confirment, siquidem pignora sive sigilla testificantia sunt, etiam si non in eodem loco sint cum signis: Ratio est: quia facere aliquid signum alterius rei, non est re ea signo includere, aut alligare, ut sint in eodem loco: sed ordinare signum ad rem, sive in eodem cum signo, sive in alio loco existenti significandam. Item, natura rerum significatarum per sacramenta hoc non patitur. Alia enim sunt spiritualia sub latia, ut Spiritus sanctus: alia accidentia non in symbolis sacramentalibus, sed in mentibus & cordibus hominum haeresia, ut Spiritus sancti dona: alia actiones divinae, ut remissio peccatorum: alia corporea, & in uno tantum loco, non autem ubicunque. Sacramenta usurpantur, localiter existentes, ut caro & sanguis Christi.
units.tr: Proof. Such is the joining of all signs with the things signified, that the signified thing is represented, and confirmed by their reception, since they are pledges or seals bearing witness, even if they are not in the same place as the signs. The reason is this: to make something a sign of another thing is not to enclose or bind that thing in the sign, so that they are in the same place; but to order the sign to the thing to be signified, whether that thing exists in the same place as the sign or in another place. Likewise, the nature of the things signified through the sacraments does not allow this otherwise. For some are spiritual and under no locality, such as the Holy Spirit; others are accidents that do not inhere in the sacramental symbols but in the minds and hearts of men, such as the gifts of the Holy Spirit; others are divine actions, such as the remission of sins; others are bodily and in only one place, not everywhere. The sacraments are used while existing locally, such as the flesh and blood of Christ.

units.la: vii. Nomina & proprietates rerum significatarum symbolis, & contrà, rebus symbolorum nomina & proprietates prietates tribuuntur: propter similitudinem siue propter significationem rerum per signa, & propter coniunctam rerum cum signis in legitimo vsu exhibitionem & perceptionem.
units.tr: vii. The names and properties of the things signified are attributed to the signs, and conversely the names and properties of the signs are attributed to the things of the signs, on account of the likeness, or rather the signification of the things by the signs, and on account of the conjoined exhibition and reception of the things with the signs in lawful use.

units.la: Probatio. Scriptura sic loquitur de sacramentis. Gen. 17. 10. Act. 7. 8. Circumcisio est foedus. Exod. 12. 11. Esus agni trāsitus. Exo. 31. 7. Sabbathum foedus aeternum. Exod. 24. 8. Sanguis testimonium sanguinis foederis. Et Leui. 17. 5. Expiatio animarum. Heb. 9. 5 operculum arca propitiatorium. Eph. 2. 26. Baptismus aqua, lauacrum mundans à peccato. Mat. 26. 26. 28. Panis & vinum corpus & sanguis Christi. Et 1. Corin. 10. 16. Communio corporis & sanguinis dicitur. Et sic seipsam exponit, Genes. 17. 11. Rom. 4. 11. circumcisio signum foederis. Exo. 12. 27. Pascha signum transitus. Exod. 31. 14. Sabbatum signū perpetuum gratia, & sanctificationis. Heb. 9. 14. Carnem eius ... sanctorum. Marc. 16. 16. Credens & baptizatus erit salvus. Luc. 22. 21. Panis coena dominica in recordationem Christi manducari iubetur.
units.tr: Proof. Scripture speaks thus of the sacraments. Gen. 17:10. Acts 7:8. Circumcision is a covenant. Exod. 12:11. The eating of the lamb is the passover. Exod. 31:7. The sabbath is an everlasting covenant. Exod. 24:8. The blood is the token of the blood of the covenant. And Lev. 17:5. The atonement of souls. Heb. 9:5 the mercy seat, the propitiatory cover of the ark. Eph. 2:26. Baptism is water, the washing that cleanses from sin. Matt. 26:26, 28. Bread and wine are the body and blood of Christ. And 1 Cor. 10:16. It is called the communion of the body and blood. And it explains itself thus, Gen. 17:11; Rom. 4:11: circumcision is the sign of the covenant. Exod. 12:27. The passover is the sign of the passing over. Exod. 31:14. The sabbath is a perpetual sign of grace and sanctification. Heb. 9:14. His flesh ... of the saints. Mark 16:16. He who believes and is baptized will be saved. Luke 22:19. The bread of the Lord's Supper is commanded to be eaten in remembrance of Christ.

units.la: viii. Vsus legitimus sacramentorum est, quando conuerti seruant eos ritus, quos Deus praecepit, in eos fines, propter quos à Deo sacramenta instituta sunt.
units.tr: viii. The lawful use of the sacraments is when the rites which God has commanded are observed for those ends for which God instituted the sacraments.

units.la: Probatio. Vsus legitimus is tantum est, qui cum institutio ne diuina congruit. Institutio autem has circumstantias personarum, ritūm & finium complectitur. His igitur violatis signa in abusum rapiuntur. Ief. 1. Ier. 7. Psal. 50.
units.tr: Proof. Lawful use is only that which agrees with the divine institution. The institution, however, comprises these circumstances: of persons, of rites and of ends. When these are violated, the signs are snatched into abuse. Isa. 1; Jer. 7; Ps. 50.

units.la: ix. In hoc vsu res significatae semper vna cum signis accipiuntur.
units.tr: ix. In this use the things signified are always received together with the signs.

units.la: Probatio. Hoc enim significat ritus, & cōtinet promissio ritibus addita: & Marc. 16. Qui crediderit, & baptizatus fuerit, saluus erit. Est autem Deus verax tam signis quam verbis nobiscum loquens. Ideo signa minime inania sunt, etsi aliter res, aliter signa accipiantur.
units.tr: Proof. For the rite signifies this, and the promise added to the rite contains it: and Mark 16: He who believes and is baptized will be saved. God, however, is true, speaking with us both by signs and by words. Therefore the signs are by no means empty, although things and signs are received in different ways.

units.la: x. Extra vsum vero institutum à Deo, qui sine conuersione non est, neque caeremoniae rationem sacramenti habent, neque beneficia Dei per eas significata cum signis accipiuntur.
units.tr: x. Outside the use instituted by God, which is not without conversion, neither does a ceremony have the character of a sacrament, nor are the benefits of God signified through them received together with the signs.

units.la: Probatio. Signa foederis nihil confirmantis, qui non seruat foedus, aut qui alia in eorum loca substituunt, aut qui ad fine alium ea referunt: At sacramenta sunt signa foederis, quo Deus se ad remissionem peccatorum & vita aeterna gratis, propter Christum, nobis donandam: nos vero ad fidem & nouam obedientiam prastanda obligat. Ergo non confirmàs eos de gratia Dei, qui sunt sine fide & pœnitentia, aut ritus alios, aut in alium finem surpant, quam Deus instituit.
units.tr: Proof. Those who do not keep the covenant, or who substitute other things in their places, or who refer them to another end, do not confirm the signs of a covenant that confirms nothing. But the sacraments are signs of the covenant by which God obliges himself to grant us, freely, for the sake of Christ, remission of sins and eternal life, and obliges us to faith and new obedience. Therefore those who are without faith and repentance, or who snatch at other rites, or at rites for another end than God instituted, do not confirm them concerning the grace of God.

units.la: Praterea superstitiosum - idololatricū est, sel externo operi sine promissione, sel ab hominibus excogitato, gratia diuina testificationem tribuere. Non igitur hic sacramentorum abusus gratiam Dei coniunctam habet, sel quenquā de ea confirmat, sicut dicitur Rom. 2. 15. Circumcisio prodest, si legem seruesiat si transgressor legis es, circumcisio tua præputium factà est.
units.tr: Moreover, to attribute divine testimony of grace to an external work without a promise, or to something devised by men, is superstitious, indeed idolatrous. Therefore this abuse of the sacraments does not have the grace of God conjoined with it, nor does it confirm anyone concerning it, as is said in Rom. 2:25: Circumcision profits if you keep the law; if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.

units.la: x'1. Signa pij ad salutem, impij ad condemnationem accipiunt: res vero significatas tantùm pij ad salutem possunt accipere.
units.tr: xi. The signs are received by the godly to salvation, by the ungodly to condemnation; the things signified, however, can be received to salvation only by the godly.

units.la: Probatio. Nos, inquit Petrus, videlicet, qui credimus, quibus ipse se annumerat, saluos facit baptisma, nòsordiū carnis ablutio, sed bonæ cõsciētiæ stipulatio erga Deū. Et Paulus Panis quem frangimus, est cōmunio corporis Christi. Cūque sacramenta sint organum externū, quo spiritus sanctus fouet & coseruat fidē, cōsequitur ea saluti credentiū seruire sicut verbū. Cōtra vero impij abusu sacramentorū, contempta Christi & beneficiorum eius, quæ illis in verbo & sacramētis offerūtur, & cossessione doctrina, quā vera fide non amplestuntur, ira Dei & pœnas sibi cumulat, iuxta dictā: Qui mactat boue, est quasi qui occidat virum, qui offert arietem, quasi qui canem iugulet, &c. Qui edit & bibit indignè, damnationem sibi edit & bibit, non discernens corpus Domini: propterea inter vos multi sunt debiles & inualidi, & dormiunt multi. Res autem significata, quia sola fide accipiuntur, suntque sel causa salutis propria, sel ipsa salus, sidelicet Christus & ipsius beneficia, nec ab impijs, nec nisi ad salutem possunt accipi: Vt docet Christus, Ioh. 6.
units.tr: Proof. Peter says, "We, that is, those who believe, among whom he counts himself, are saved by baptism, which is not the washing away of the filth of the flesh, but the pledge of a good conscience toward God." And Paul: "The bread which we break is the communion of the body of Christ." Since the sacraments are an external instrument by which the Holy Spirit nourishes and preserves faith, it follows that they serve the salvation of believers as the word does. On the contrary, the ungodly, by abusing the sacraments, despising Christ and his benefits which are offered to them in the word and the sacraments, and by rejecting a doctrine which they do not embrace with true faith, heap upon themselves the wrath of God and punishments, according to what is said: "He who slaughters an ox is as one who kills a man; he who offers a lamb, as one who breaks a dog's neck," etc. "He who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the body of the Lord. Therefore many among you are weak and sickly, and many sleep" (1 Cor. 11:29–30). The things signified, however, since they are received by faith alone, and are either the proper cause of salvation or salvation itself, namely Christ and his benefits, cannot be received by the ungodly, nor except to salvation: as Christ teaches, John 6.

units.la: xii. In eleētis tamen etiam indignè accepti sacramenti, postquam conuertuntur, fructus tandem consequitur.
units.tr: xii. Yet in the elect, even a sacrament received unworthily, after they are converted, at length bears its fruit.

units.la: Probatio. Promissio, & signa promissionis habetis addita conditione fidei, rata sunt: quādocūque præstatur cōditio. Talis autē est promissio quæ significatur, & cōfirmaturSa cramentis. Ergo siue in sua, siue post suum accedat fides, quæ credat promissioni & signis accipiūtur promissio & signifi cata res. Faciam tecū sicut fecisti, quæ contemnisti iuramentum. mentum, vt irritum faceret pactum: recordabor tamen pacti mei, quod pepigi tecum in diebus adolescentiae tuae, & confirmabo tibi pactum sempiternum.
units.tr: Proof. A promise, and the signs of the promise added with the condition of faith, are ratified whenever the condition is fulfilled. Such is the promise which is signified and confirmed by the sacraments. Therefore whether faith comes before or after, which believes the promise, the promise and the thing signified are received with the signs. "I will do with you as you have done, you who despised the oath so as to make the covenant void; yet I will remember my covenant which I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish with you an everlasting covenant" (Ezek. 16:59–60).

units.la: xiii. Sacramenta alia semel, alia sæpius accipienda: alia tantum adultis, alia etiam infantibus tribuenda sunt, prout fœdus semel sanciendo cum omnibus conuersis, & in ecclesiam recipiendis: vt circumcisio & baptismus: aut post lapsus & tentationum certamina renouando fœderi & ecclesiæ vnitati, & congressibus fouendis à Deo instituta sunt, vt area, pascha, & reliqua sacrificia, & cœna Domini.
units.tr: xiii. Some sacraments are to be received once, others more often; some are to be given only to adults, others also to infants, according as they were instituted by God either to ratify the covenant once for all with all who are converted and are to be received into the Church, as circumcision and baptism; or to be renewed after falls and the struggles of temptations, to foster the covenant, the unity of the Church, and fellowship, as the ark, the passover, and the other sacrifices, and the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Probatio. Circumcisionis & baptismi iteratio nusquam præcepta est. Nec obscura est ratio: quia instituta sunt illa sacramenta, vt sint initiatio seu receptio solennis in ecclesiam, quæ semper est rata pœnitentiæ agenti, aut in ea perseuerati. Aliorum vero sacramentorum usus iterari iubetur, vt de sacrificiis, de paschate, de adoratione ad arcā, de purgationibus, manifestum est. Item de cœna dicit: Quotiescūque feceritis, mortē Domini annūciabitis, &c. Causa est: quia sunt testimonia, & fœdꝰ in circumcisione & baptismo initum, sit ratū agenti pœni-tentiam. Hæc aute fidei exercitatio sæpe est necessaria.
units.tr: Proof. The repetition of circumcision and baptism is nowhere commanded. Nor is the reason obscure: those sacraments were instituted so that they might be an initiation, or solemn reception into the Church, which is always valid for one who repents, or who persists in it. The use of the other sacraments, however, is commanded to be repeated, as is clear concerning the sacrifices, the passover, the worship at the ark, and the purifications. Likewise concerning the supper he says: "As often as you do this, you will proclaim the death of the Lord," etc. The cause is that they are testimonies, and the covenant entered into in circumcision and baptism is ratified for one who repents. Yet the exercise of faith is often necessary.

units.la: xiv. Antiqui & noui fœderis sacramentis communia sunt ea, quæ in definitione sunt dicta. Eorum vero discrimina hæc sunt, quòd vetera exhibendum, noua exhi-bitum Christum cum suis beneficiis monstrant: Vetera erant alii, & plures ritus, vt circumcisio, sacrificia, ablu-tiones, pascha, sabbatum, adoratio ad arcam, &c. Noua itē alii, & tantum duo: baptismus & cœna domini: Ve-tera obscuriora, noua clariora sunt: Vetera posteris Abraham eorumque mancipiis præcepta erant: noua totī ecclesiæ ex Iudæis & gentibus eligendæ.
units.tr: xiv. The sacraments of the old and new covenant have in common those things which have been stated in the definition. Their differences, however, are these: the old showed Christ to be exhibited, the new show Christ exhibited with his benefits. The old were of other and more numerous rites, such as circumcision, sacrifices, ablutions, the passover, the sabbath, worship at the ark, etc. The new are of other kinds, and only two: baptism and the Lord's Supper. The old are more obscure, the new clearer. The old were commanded to Abraham's posterity and his servants; the new to the whole Church to be chosen from Jews and Gentiles.

units.la: Probatio. Definitione esse communè sacramentis veteribus, & novis, suprà est ostensum. In numero & ritūum forma esse differentia, patet inductione. Nā in novo testamento tantum duo esse constat: quia non sunt aliæ cæremoniæ à Christo mandatæ, habentes addita promissione gratiā. Vetera exhibendū, noua exhibitū Christi significare, constat ex eorum interpretatione in scriptura tradita, de qua in definitione dictum est. Claritate differunt, quia in novo pauciores sunt, & res iam completas significantes: In veteri plures ritus, & adumbrantes res futuras, quarum nondum erat omnes circumstāts expositā. Vetera Abrahami posteris tàtum fuisse præcepta & mâcipiis: noua omnibus, qui volunt esse membra ecclesiæ, patet inductio-ne: vt Genes. 17. Filius octo dierum circumcidetur in vobis omnis masculus in generationibus vestris, verna & emtus argeto ab omni filio alienigenæ, qui nō est de semine tuo. Exod. 12. Nullus alienigena comedet ex eo. Matt. 18[?] Docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos.
units.tr: Proof. That there is a commonality between the old and new sacraments by definition has been shown above. That they differ in number and form of rites is plain by induction. For it is established that there are only two in the New Testament, since no other ceremonies have been commanded by Christ which have a promise of grace added. That the old exhibited what was to be, and the new exhibit Christ, is established from their interpretation handed down in Scripture, of which it was said in the definition. They differ in clarity, because in the new there are fewer, and they signify things already completed; in the old there are more rites, foreshadowing things to come, of which not all the circumstances had yet been set out. That the old were commanded only to Abraham's posterity and servants, and the new to all who wish to be members of the Church, is plain by induction: as in Gen. 17: "The eight-day-old son shall be circumcised among you, every male in your generations, the home-born and the bought with money from any foreign son who is not of your seed." Exod. 12: "No foreigner shall eat of it." Matt. 28:19: "Teach all nations, baptizing them."

units.la: xv. Commune est sacramentis & prædicationi euangelicæ, quod sunt opus Dei, quod exercet erga ecclesiam per ministros, quòd docet, offerùt & promittit nobis eandem Christi & beneficiorum eius communionem, & sunt organa externa Spir. sancti, per quæ mouet corda ad credendum, ac proinde fidei respectu Christi & beneficiorum eius nos participes faciat: nec tamen Spiritus sancti operatio his alligata est: nec prosunt, sed nocet potiùs nō applicantibus sibi fide, id, quod verba & ritus significant.
units.tr: 15.
