What is common to sacraments and the evangelical preaching is that they are the work of God, which he performs toward the Church through the ministers: he teaches, offers and promises us the same communion with Christ and his benefits. They are the external instruments of the Holy Spirit, by which he moves hearts to believe, and so makes us partakers of Christ and his benefits with respect to faith. Yet the working of the Holy Spirit is not bound to these, and they do not profit, but rather harm, those who do not apply to themselves by faith what the words and rites signify.

units.la: Probatio. Quod agit ministri nomine Dei in administratione sacramentorum: quodque Deus per illa significet, hoc est, doceat, offerat, promittat nobis communionem Christi, ostensum est in probatione secunda. Ex hoc sequitur alterum, quod licet Spiritus sanctus per ea mouet corda ad credendum. Quia enim sacramenta sunt promissio visibilis, eadem confirmandi fidei in nobis authoritatem habent, quam promissio verbi fa-da[?]: Ex hoc sequitur tertium. Quod enim fidei in nobis accendenda vel suscitanda seruit, id communioni Christi percipiendæ seruit, quia hac nobis per fidem contingit. Ideo dicitur: Panis est communio corporis, Baptismus nos saluos facit, &c. Nec tamen semper fide per ea confirmat Spiritum sanctum: quia neque per verbum semper eam accedit: vt ostendunt Simonis Magi, & aliorum infinita exempla. Quod noceat eorum qui sine fide, probatum est in propositione decima[?].
units.tr: Proof. That the minister, in the administration of the sacraments, acts in the name of God, and that God through them signifies, that is, teaches, offers and promises us communion with Christ, has been shown in the second proof. From this follows the second point: that although the Holy Spirit through them moves hearts to believe. For since the sacraments are a visible promise, they have in us the same authority to confirm faith that the promise of the word has. From this follows the third point: what serves to kindle or raise up faith in us also serves to receive the communion of Christ, since this comes to us through faith. Hence it is said: "The bread is the communion of the body," "Baptism saves us," etc. Yet they do not always confirm the Holy Spirit's faith through them, since neither does he always approach it through the word, as the examples of Simon Magus and countless others show. That they harm those who lack faith has been proved in the tenth proposition.

units.la: xvi.

Differunt a verbo sacramenta, quod illud sermone, hæc gestibus, significant Dei erga nos voluntatem: illo fides & inchoatur & confirmatur, his confirmatur tantum inchoata: illud etiam sine sacramentis docet & confirmat, hæc autem non sine verbo: sine illius cognitione adulti non seruantur, sine sacramentorum usu autem si non contemtu omissus fuerit, & renasci homines & seruari possunt: illud etiam incredulis & impiis prædicandum est, ad hæc tantum eos admittere debet ecclesia, quos pro membris ecclesiæ Deus nos habere iubet.
units.tr: Sacraments differ from the word in that the word signifies God's will toward us by speech, the sacraments by gestures; by the word faith is both begun and confirmed, while by the sacraments it is only confirmed once begun. The word also teaches and confirms without the sacraments, but the sacraments not without the word: adults are not saved without knowledge of it, but without the use of the sacraments, if they are omitted not through contempt, men can be reborn and saved. The word is also to be preached to unbelievers and the wicked, but the Church ought to admit to the sacraments only those whom God bids us regard as members of the Church.

units.la: Probatio. Sacramenta sine Verbo praeunte nec docet, nec fidem confirmant: quia significatio eorum non intelligitur, nisi Verbo explicetur: nec signum confirmare aliquid, nisi prius promissum, poterit. Exemplo sunt Iudaei, qui seruabant, aut seruant ceremonias, abolita aut non intellecta promissione gratia & beneficiorum Christi.
units.tr: Proof. Sacraments without a preceding Word neither teach nor confirm faith, because their signification is not understood unless it is explained by the Word, nor can a sign confirm anything unless the promise has come first. The Jews are an example, who kept, or keep, ceremonies while the promise of the grace and benefits of Christ was abolished or not understood.

units.la: Sine Verbo adulti nō seruantur, siue per doctrinā, siue[?] ordinaria, siue per interna & extraordinariam revelationem, cognito: quia qui nō credit in filium, iā iudicatus est. Fides autē ex auditu: auditus per verbum Dei. Sine sacramentis vero seruari possunt, quia etsi his ex necessitate priuentur, credere tamen possunt, ut latro in cruce: aut si infantes sint, pro aetatis modo sanctificati, ut Iohannes in utero, & multi infantes, qui ante diem circumcisionis moriebantur.
units.tr: Without the Word, adults are not saved, whether by teaching, whether by ordinary means, or by internal and extraordinary revelation, which is known: because whoever does not believe in the Son is already judged. Yet faith comes by hearing, and hearing through the Word of God. But without the sacraments they can be saved, because although they are deprived of them out of necessity, they can still believe, as the thief on the cross; or if they are infants, they are sanctified according to the measure of their age, as John in the womb, and many infants who died before the day of circumcision.

units.la: Verbum etiam impiis est praedicandum, quia illis convertendis destinatum est.
units.tr: The Word is also to be preached to the wicked, because it is destined for their conversion.

units.la: Sacramenta his administranda, qui pro membris ecclesiae agnoscendi sunt: quia tantum in ecclesia ipsum instituta sunt, Actor. 8. 17. Licet tibi baptizari, si credis.
units.tr: The sacraments are to be administered to those who are to be acknowledged as members of the Church, because they were instituted only within the Church itself, Acts 8:17. "You may be baptized, if you believe."

units.la: XVII. Commune est sacramentis & sacrificiis, quod sunt opera a Deo mandata facienda in fide: Differt sacramentum a sacrificio, quod sacramento Deus nobis significat & testatur sua beneficia, quae ipse nobis praestat: sacrificio nos Deo nostram obedientiam praestamus & offerimus.
units.tr: XVII. What is common to sacraments and sacrifices is that they are works commanded by God to be done in faith. A sacrament differs from a sacrifice in that by a sacrament God signifies to us and attests his benefits, which he himself bestows on us; by a sacrifice we render and offer our obedience to God.

units.la: Probatio. Mandata esse a Deo in fide facienda, de sacramentis est ostensum prop. 1. 2. 3. & 10. De utrisq;[?] dicitur Heb. 11. 14. Abel per fidem maioris precij sacrificium obtulit Deo, quàm Cain, &c. Sacramenta esse voluntatis Dei signa erga nos, probatum est propositione secunda.
units.tr: Proof. That they are commanded by God to be done in faith has been shown of the sacraments in propositions 1, 2, 3 and 10. Of both it is said, Heb. 11:4: "By faith Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain," etc. That the sacraments are signs of God's will toward us has been proved in the second proposition.

units.la: XVIII. Ideoque eadem caeremonia sacramenti & sacrificij rationem habere potest, ut quâ Deus dando nobis symbola visibilia, suum erga nos beneficium: eâdem nos, accipiendo illa, nostrum erga ipsum officium testemur.
units.tr: XVIII. Therefore the same ceremony can have the character of both sacrament and sacrifice, since by giving us visible tokens God attests his benefit toward us, and by receiving them we likewise attest our duty toward him.

units.la: Probatio. Manifesta est ex paschate & reliquis sacrificiis: Item ex sabbatho: qua[?] erat obedientia a Deo praecepta, qua pij Deum colebat, & se ipsi gratos declarabat: & simul signa beneficiorum Dei quae per Messiā accipiebat. Sic baptismus est professio Christianismi, & signum, quo testatur Christus, nos ablui suo sanguine. Caena domini est gratarum[?] actio pro morte Christi, & admonitio, nos propter & per illiꝰ mortem significari, ipsius membra fieri, & in ipso mansuros in æternum.
units.tr: The proof is evident from the Passover and the other sacrifices, and likewise from the Sabbath: in which there was obedience commanded by God, by which the pious worshipped God and declared themselves grateful to him, and at the same time signs of the benefits of God which they received through the Messiah. Thus baptism is the profession of Christianity and a sign by which Christ attests that we are washed by his blood. The Lord's Supper is a thanksgiving for the death of Christ, and a reminder that we are signified through and because of his death, become his members, and will abide in him for eternity.

units.la: Obiectiones aliquot CONTRA THESES DE SACRAMENTIS, ET EARVNDEM BREVISSIMAS solutiones D.Zachariæ Vrsini.In publica disputatione exceptæ Anno 1567.
units.tr: Objections against some theses on the sacraments, with very brief solutions by Zacharias Ursinus, received in public disputation in the year 1567.

units.la: Obiect.1. Contra secundam partem: Sunt signa fœderis æterni. Fœderis æterni etiam signa sunt æterna. At signa non sunt æterna. Ergo nec fœdus æternum.
units.tr: Objection 1. Against the second part: They are signs of an eternal covenant. The signs of an eternal covenant are also eternal. But the signs are not eternal. Therefore neither is the covenant eternal.

units.la: Probatio maioris negatur: In relatiuis, sublato vno tollitur alterum.
units.tr: Proof of the major is denied: In relatives, when one is removed, the other is removed.

units.la: Resp. ad regulam per distinct. In relatiuis, quæ snum solum habent correlatiuum: vt pater, filius, sublato vno tollitur alterum: Non autem quæ plura, quale est fœdus Dei: quod habet correlatiuum non tantum signa, sed & confœderatos, qui in æternum manebunt, &c. Signa vero correlatiue se habent ad fœdus, non simpliciter, quatenus est fœdus, sed quatenus est fœdus signum confirmatum.
units.tr: Reply to the rule, with a distinction: In relatives which have only one correlative, such as father and son, when one is removed the other is removed. But this does not hold for those which have several, as is the case with the covenant of God, which has as correlatives not only the signs but also those who are bound by the covenant, who will remain for ever, etc. Now the signs stand in correlation to the covenant, not simply as it is a covenant, but as it is a covenant confirmed by a sign.

units.la: Nota. Quod in secunda theseos parte inter Deum & credentes, includantur etiam posteri & liberi credentium, tanquam pars in toto, licet actu ipso nondum credant vt infantes. Itaque definitio non est angustior definito.
units.tr: Note. That in the second part of the thesis, between God and believers, their posterity and children are also included, as a part in the whole, although as infants they do not yet actually believe. Therefore the definition is not narrower than the thing defined.

units.la: Obiect.2. Contra secunda partem: Atque ita fiducia promissionis in ipsis confirmet. Quod datur non habentibus fidem, id non potest confirmare fidem, cum nulla sit. Baptismus datur infantibus non habentibus fidem. Ergo baptismus non confirmat fidem. Non igitur omnia sacramenta confirmant fiduciam promissionis.
units.tr: Objection 2. Against the second part: And so the confidence of the promise is confirmed in them. What is given to those who do not have faith cannot confirm faith, since there is none. Baptism is given to infants who do not have faith. Therefore baptism does not confirm faith. Not all the sacraments, therefore, confirm the confidence of the promise.

units.la: Resp. 1. Ad maiorem per distinct. Non potest illu cōfirmare fidem, nēpe tum quando illis datur, & ipsi nullam habent fidem. Potest tamen confirmare, vbi adulti crediderint. 2. Minor etiam valde controuersa est, an infantes, præsertim renatorum omni fide sint destituti: cum ad ipsos quoque pertineant promissiones: Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui. Talium est regnum Dei, &c.
units.tr: Reply 1. To the major, with a distinction: It cannot confirm faith, namely at the time when it is given to them and they have no faith at all. It can, however, confirm faith where adults have believed. 2. The minor is also much disputed, whether infants, especially those of regenerate parents, are wholly destitute of faith, since the promises also pertain to them: "I will be your God and the God of your seed." "Of such is the kingdom of God," etc.

units.la: Obiect.3. Contra sextam. Exhibita signorum veritate desinunt signa. In nouo testamento exhibita est signorum veritas: Ergo in nouo testamento nulla sunt signa.
units.tr: Objection 3. Against the sixth thesis. Once the truth of the signs has been revealed, the signs cease. In the New Testament the truth of the signs has been revealed. Therefore in the New Testament there are no signs.

units.la: Resp. Conceditur totum de signis significantibus res futuras & exhibendas, qualia fuerunt veterum sacramenta: non autem de signis obsignantibus res exhibitas, cuiusmodi signa sunt sacrasacramenta noui testamenti.
units.tr: Reply. It is granted entirely of signs which signify things future and yet to be exhibited, such as were the sacraments of the old covenant; but not of signs which seal things already exhibited, of which kind the sacraments of the New Testament are.

units.la: Obiect. 4. Contra decimam partem: Qui sine conuersione est. Papistarum sacramenta fiunt sine regeneratione. Et tamen sunt sacramenta. Ergo etiam absque conuersione fieri possunt.
units.tr: Objection 4. Against the tenth thesis: Those who are without conversion. The sacraments of the Papists are administered without regeneration. And yet they are sacraments. Therefore they can also be administered without conversion.

units.la: Resp. Negari potest minor de non conuersis. His enim sacramenta non sunt sacramenta, hoc est, signa gratia: praesertim cum in mera idola ea conuertant. Fiunt autem eis sacramenta, hoc est, signa gratia, quando conuertuntur: Et si nunquam conuertantur, nunquam etiam eis fiunt sacramenta.
units.tr: Reply. The minor may be denied concerning those who are not converted. For to these the sacraments are not sacraments, that is, signs of grace, especially since they turn them into mere idols. But they become sacraments for them, that is, signs of grace, when they are converted; and if they are never converted, the sacraments never become sacraments for them.

units.la: Instantia ad absurdum: Qui deprauant verba & formam institutionis, ij euertunt substantiale baptismi. Papistae illud faciunt. Ergo etiam hoc. Proinde baptismus eorum non est baptismus: & nos qui sumus in papatu baptizati, sumus rebaptizandi.
units.tr: Instance to the absurd: Those who corrupt the words and form of institution overthrow the substance of baptism. The Papists do this. Therefore also this. Accordingly their baptism is not baptism, and we who were baptized in Papacy must be baptized again.

units.la: Resp. ad maiorem: Euertunt substantiale baptismi, nempe sibi, & iis, qui assentiuntur ipsis, neque conuertuntur: non autem iis, qui agnitis erroribus conuertuntur, & se ecclesiae Christi adiunguntur.
units.tr: Reply to the major: they overthrow the substance of baptism for themselves, and for those who assent to them and are not converted; but not for those who, having acknowledged their errors, are converted and join themselves to the Church of Christ.

units.la: Obiect. 5. Contra Vndecima partem: Signa pij ad salutem accipiunt: Tantum id, quod est salutiferum, ad salutem potest accipi a piis. Solae res significatae sunt salutiferae, & causa salutis. Ergo solae haec ad salutem accipiuntur a piis, & non etiam signa.
units.tr: Objection 5. Against the eleventh thesis: The godly receive the signs unto salvation. Only that which is salutary can be received unto salvation by the godly. Only the things signified are salutary and the cause of salvation. Therefore only these are received unto salvation by the godly, and not also the signs.

units.la: Resp. ad maiorem per distinct. Tantum quod est salutiferum, potest accipi ad salutem, nempe efficiendam siue conferendam: potest vero etiam, quod per se non est salutiferum, hoc est, salutis causa efficiens siue forma siue materia, accipi ad salutem, nempe confirmandam. Declaro. Et res & signa ad salutem accipiuntur: sed aliter haec, aliter illa. Res sunt causa salutis & eius pars quaedam. At signa non habent talem vim significandi in se, sed tantum, qua tenus coniuncta sunt cum rebus, salutem confirmant.
units.tr: Reply to the major, with a distinction: Only that which is salutary can be received unto salvation, namely to bring it about or to confer it; but that which of itself is not salutary, that is, which is an efficient cause of salvation, whether as form or as matter, can also be received unto salvation, namely to confirm it. I explain. Both the things and the signs are received unto salvation, but these in one way and those in another. The things are the cause of salvation and a certain part of it. But the signs do not have such power of signifying in themselves; they only confirm salvation, insofar as they are joined with the things.

units.la: Obiect. 6. Contra duodecimam. Quod affert condemnationem, non adfert fructum. Indigna sacramenti vsurpatio affert condemnationem: thesi 11. Ergo non affert fructum.
units.tr: Objection 6. Against the twelfth thesis. What brings condemnation does not bring fruit. Unworthy use of the sacrament brings condemnation: thesis 11. Therefore it does not bring fruit.

units.la: Resp. Conceditur totum ante conuersionem, post quam indigna vsurpatio fit digna.
units.tr: Reply. The whole is granted of the time before conversion; after conversion the unworthy use becomes worthy.

units.la: Instantia: Condemnatio non sequitur conuersionem. Fructus indigne accepti sacramenti est condemnatio: thesi 11. Ergo fructus non sequitur conuersos.
units.tr: Instance: Condemnation does not follow conversion. The fruit of a sacrament unworthily received is condemnation: thesis 11. Therefore the fruit does not follow those who are converted.

units.la: Resp. Concedimus de condemnatione: Nos vero hic loquimur de fructu indigne accepti sacramenti, qui ante conuersionem propter indignam acceptionem erat condemnatio: post conuersionem autem mutatur in bonum & salutarem, &c.
units.tr: Reply. We grant it concerning condemnation. But we are here speaking of the fruit of a sacrament unworthily received, which before conversion, on account of the unworthy reception, was condemnation; but after conversion it is changed into good and salutary, etc.

units.la: Obiect.7. Contra decimatertiam partem: Alia tantum semel. Quod facit ad confirmationem fidei, id saepius est vsurpandum. Omnia sacramenta faciunt ad confirmandam fidem. Ergo omnia sunt vsurpanda & per consequens, sape sumus baptizandi.
units.tr: Objection 7. Against the thirteenth thesis: Other things only once. That which serves to confirm faith must be used more often. All the sacraments serve to confirm faith. Therefore all the sacraments are to be used, and consequently we are to be baptized often.

units.la: Resp. ad maiorem: qua vera est: si Deus iterationem instituerit. At non vult iterari sacramenta receptionis in ecclesiam & regenerationis: quia tantum semel per ea nos gignit, ac foedus nobiscum init: Ut per circumcisionem & baptismum: sapius autem per alia foedus initum confirmat, ut per pascha & coenam.
units.tr: Reply to the major: which is true, if God had instituted repetition. But he does not will the sacraments of admission into the Church and of regeneration to be repeated, because through them he begets us only once and enters into covenant with us, as through circumcision and baptism; but he confirms the covenant entered into more often through other means, as through the Passover and the Supper.

units.la: Obiect.8. Contra secundum discrimen verbi & sacramentorum in thesi. 16. Qui admittendi sunt ad praesentius: non sunt arcendi ab eo, quod est minus praesens. Impij sunt admittendi ad verbum, quod est praestantius sacramentis: quod probatur ex dicto Pauli: 1.Cor.1.17. Non misit me Christus ut baptizarem, sed ut evangelizarem. Ergo a sacramentis impij non sunt arcendi.
units.tr: Objection 8. Against the second distinction of word and sacraments in thesis 16. Those who are to be admitted to the more excellent are not to be shut out from that which is less excellent. The wicked are to be admitted to the word, which is more excellent than the sacraments; this is proved from the saying of Paul: 1 Cor. 1:17. "Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel." Therefore the wicked are not to be shut out from the sacraments.

units.la: Resp. Negamus maiorem Sniuerfaliter acceptam: quia non Vbique, nec semper vera est.
units.tr: Reply. We deny the major as universally taken, because it is not true everywhere nor always.

units.la: Instantia: Ex quo consequi potest fructus: id non debet prohiberi. Ex acceptione coenae, quae fit ab impiis, consequi potest fructus: thesi 11. Ergo impij non sunt arcendi a coena.
units.tr: Instance: That from which fruit can follow ought not to be forbidden. From the reception of the Supper, which is made by the wicked, fruit can follow: thesis 11. Therefore the wicked are not to be shut out from the Supper.

units.la: Resp. ad maiorem. Non debet prohiberi: Deo non prohibente. At ecclesia habet mandatum Dei, ne faciat mala, ut eueniant bona.
units.tr: Reply to the major. It ought not to be forbidden, when God does not forbid it. But the Church has God's command not to do evil so that good may come of it.

units.la: Obiect.9. Contra eiusdem thefeos partem: Verbum etiam incredulis praedicandum. Christus vetat margaritas obiici porcis & canibus. Ergo impij etiam ad verbum non sunt admittendi.
units.tr: Objection 9. Against the other part of the same thesis: The word is also to be preached to unbelievers. Christ forbids pearls to be cast before swine and dogs. Therefore the wicked are not to be admitted even to the word.

units.la: Resp. ad antecedens: canes & porci non sunt simpliciter impij, sed hostes ridentes & persequentes doctrinam: allatrantes & impugnantes eam ut canes: & conculcantes eam ut porci. De his datur argumentum.
units.tr: Reply to the antecedent: dogs and swine are not simply the wicked, but enemies who mock and persecute the doctrine: who bark at it and attack it like dogs, and trample it underfoot like swine. An argument is given concerning these.

units.la: XXV. De Baptismo.
units.tr: XXV. Of Baptism.

units.la: 1. Baptismus est noui testamenti sacramentum, quo Christus fidelibus, aqua in nomine patris, filij & spiritus sancti baptizatis testatur omnium peccatorum remissionem, & spiritus sancti donationem, & in ecclesiam, & suum corpus insitionem, & ipsi vicissim profitentur, se haec beneficia a Deo accipere, & propterea deinceps viuere, & seruire velle & debere. Estque idem baptismus per Iohannem baptistam inchoatus, & per apostolos continuatus, nisi quod ille in Christum passurum & resuscitandum, hi vero in passum, & resuscitatum, baptizauerunt.
units.tr: 1. Baptism is the sacrament of the New Testament, in which Christ, through water, testifies to the baptized in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit that their sins are forgiven and that the Holy Spirit is given to them, and that they are grafted into the Church and into his body; and in turn they profess that they receive these benefits from God, and therefore wish and ought to live and serve from then on. This same baptism was begun by John the Baptist and continued by the apostles, except that he baptized in view of Christ who was to suffer and rise again, whereas they baptized in view of Christ who had suffered and risen.

units.la: II.[?] Finis instituti a Deo baptismi primus est, vt Deus per eū significet, & testetur, quòd sanguine & spiritu Christi mūdet baptizatos a peccatis, eósque corpori Christi inserat, & omnium eius beneficiorum participes faciat.
units.tr: II. The first purpose of baptism, as instituted by God, is that God, through it, signifies and attests that by the blood and Spirit of Christ he cleanses the baptized from sins, grafts them into the body of Christ, and makes them partakers of all his benefits.

units.la: III. Secundus, vt baptismus sit solennis receptio, seu ad-scriptio singulorum in ecclesiam visibilem, & eius di-stinctio ab omnibus aliis lectis.
units.tr: III. The second is that baptism be the solemn reception, or enrolment, of individuals into the visible Church, and their distinction from all other sects.

units.la: IV. Tertius, vt sit publica & solennis professio nostrę in Christum fidei, & obligationis ad fidem in ipsum & o-bedientiam erga ipsum.
units.tr: IV. The third is that it be a public and solemn profession of our faith in Christ, and of our obligation to faith in him and obedience toward him.

units.la: V. Quartus, vt sit admonitio de mersione in afflictiones & de emersione, ac liberatione ex iis.
units.tr: V. The fourth is that it be a reminder of our immersion into afflictions and of our emergence from them and deliverance out of them.

units.la: VI. Testandi autem seu obsignandi vim habet baptis-mus ex praecepto diuino, & ex promissione gratiae a Christo addita huic ritui legitimè usurpato. Christus enim per manum ministrorum, nos baptizat, sicut per os ipsorum nos alloquitur.
units.tr: VI. Baptism has the power of attesting and sealing by divine command, and by the promise of grace added by Christ to this rite lawfully used. For Christ baptizes us through the hands of his ministers, just as through their mouth he addresses us.

units.la: VII. Est igitur in baptismo duplex aqua: externa & visibilis, terrena, quae est elementaris: & interna, invisibilis, coelestis, quae est sanguis & spiritus Christi. Duplex ité[?] ablutio: externa, visibilis & significas, videlicet aquae aspersio, vel affusio, quae est corporalis, hoc est, membris & sensibus corporeis accipitur: & interna, invisibilis, & significata, videlicet, remissio peccatorum proprer effusu pro nobis Christi sanguine, & nostri per spiritum ipsius regeneratio, & in corpus ipsius insitio, quae est spiritua-lis, hoc est, spiritu & fide percipitur. Duplex denique administer baptismi: externus, qui est minister ecclesiae, manu sua baptizas nos aqua: internus, qui est ipse Christus, sanguine & spiritu suo nos baptizans.
units.tr: VII. There is therefore a twofold water in baptism: an external and visible water, earthly, which is elemental; and an internal, invisible, heavenly water, which is the blood and Spirit of Christ. There is likewise a twofold washing: the external, visible and signified washing, namely the sprinkling or pouring of water, which is bodily, that is, received by the bodily members and senses; and the internal, invisible and signified washing, namely the forgiveness of sins through the blood of Christ poured out for us, and our regeneration through his Spirit, and our grafting into his body, which is spiritual, that is, received by the Spirit and by faith. Finally, there is a twofold administrant of baptism: the external, who is the minister of the Church, who baptizes us with water by his own hand; and the internal, who is Christ himself, baptizing us with his blood and Spirit.

units.la: viii.Nec aqua in sanguinem, aut spiritum Christi mutatur, nec in aqua, aut in eodem loco cū aqua, adest sanguis Christi, nec eo perfunduntur inuisibiliter corpora eorum, qui baptizantur, nec Spiritus sanctus substantia, aut virtute sua in hac aqua magis est, quam alibi, sed in legitimo vsu baptismi operatur in cordibus eorum, qui baptizantur, & ea Christi sanguine spiritualiter aspergit & lauat, & hoc symbolo externo vtitur, tanquam instrumento, & tanquam verbo seu promissione visibili, ad fulciendam, & excitandam fidem baptizatorum.
units.tr: VIII. Neither is the water changed into the blood or Spirit of Christ, nor is the blood of Christ present invisibly in the water, or in the same place as the water, nor are the bodies of those who are baptized bathed in it; nor is the Holy Spirit, in substance or power, more present in this water than elsewhere. Rather, in the lawful use of baptism he works in the hearts of those who are baptized, and sprinkles and washes them spiritually with the blood of Christ; and he uses this external sign as an instrument, and as a visible word or promise, to support and stir up the faith of the baptized.

units.la: ix.Cum ergo baptismus dicitur lauacrū regeneratio-nis esse, aut nos saluos facere, aut peccata abluere, intelligitur baptismus externus esse symbolum interni, hoc est, regenerationis, salutis, & ablutionis spiritualis, & hic cum illo, in omni baptismi vsu legitimo coniunctus esse.
units.tr: IX. When therefore baptism is called the washing of regeneration, or said to save us or to wash away sins, it is understood that the external baptism is a sign of the internal, that is, of regeneration, salvation and spiritual washing, and that the one is joined with the other in every lawful use of baptism.

units.la: x.Sic tamen in baptismo peccatum aboletur, vt a reatu irae Dei, & poenarum aeternarum liberemur, & renouatio per Spiritum sanctum in nobis inchoetur, & reliquiae peccati, vsque ad finem huius vitae maneant.
units.tr: X. Yet sin is so put away in baptism that we are freed from the guilt of God's wrath and from eternal punishments, and renewal through the Holy Spirit is begun in us, while the remnants of sin remain until the end of this life.

units.la: xi.Legitimè autem accipiunt baptismum omnes, & soli renati aut renascentes, baptizati in eos fines, in quos baptismus à Christo institutus est.
units.tr: XI. Those receive baptism lawfully who alone are, or are being, reborn, and they are baptized to those ends for which baptism was instituted by Christ.

units.la: xii.Legitimè administrat ecclesia baptismum omnibus & solis, quos ipsa in renatorum & membrorum Christi numero habere debet.
units.tr: XII. The Church administers baptism lawfully to all and only those whom she ought to count among the reborn and the members of Christ.

units.la: xiii. Cùm etiam infantes Christianorum de ecclesia sint, in quam Christus recipi, & adscribi voluit per baptismum omnes ad se pertinentes, & proinde baptismus surrogatus sit circumcisioni, qua tam infantibus, quàm adultis ad semen Abrahami pertinentibus, iustificatio & regeneratio & in ecclesiam receptio obsignabantur, per & propter Christum futurum, sicut in baptismo per & propter exhibitum: ac denique nemo aquam prohibere possit, quo minus baptizentur ij, qui Spiritum sanctu[?], corda ipsorum purificantem, receperunt, infantes etiam eos baptizari est necesse, qui vel in ecclesia nascuntur, vel cum parentibus in eam transeunt.
units.tr: XIII. Since also the infants of Christians belong to the Church, into which Christ willed that all who pertain to him be received and enrolled through baptism, and therefore baptism has been substituted for circumcision, by which justification, regeneration and reception into the Church were sealed both to infants and to adults who belonged to the seed of Abraham, through and on account of Christ who was to come, just as in baptism they are sealed through and on account of Christ who has now been revealed; and finally, since no one can refuse water to those who have received the Holy Spirit purifying their hearts, it is necessary that infants also be baptized, both those who are born in the Church and those who pass into it with their parents.

units.la: xiv.Sicut promissio euangelij, sic baptismus etiam indigne, hoc est, ante conuersionem acceptus, poenitentiae agentibus est ratus & salutaris, atque vsus eius prius il-legitimus[?] legitimus,tunc eis fit legitimus.
units.tr: XIV. Just as the promise of the gospel, so baptism, even when received unworthily, that is before conversion, is valid and salutary for those who practise repentance; and its use, previously unlawful, then becomes lawful for them.

units.la: xv.Neque impietas ministri,irritum facit baptismum, si modo in fidem & promissionem Christi fiat,ac proinde etiam ab hæreticis baptizatos, ecclesia vera non rebaptizare,sed vera de Christo & baptismo doctrina informare debet.
units.tr: XV. Neither does the impiety of a minister render baptism void, provided it is performed in faith and in the promise of Christ; and therefore the true Church ought not to rebaptize those baptized by heretics, but to instruct them in the true doctrine concerning Christ and baptism.

units.la: xvi.Ac velut semel initum fœdus cum Deo etiam post peccata deinde commissa,perpetuò ratum est resipiscen-tibus,ita & baptismus semel acceptus,in omnem vitam, resipiscentes,de peccatorum remissione confirmat, ac proinde nec iterari debet, nec in finem usque vitæ differri, quasi sic demum à peccatis mundet, si nulla post cum acceptum committantur.
units.tr: XVI. Just as the covenant once entered into with God remains perpetually valid for those who repent, even after sins subsequently committed, so baptism, once received, confirms to repentant persons, throughout their whole life, the remission of sins; and therefore it ought neither to be repeated, nor deferred to the end of life, as though sins are cleansed only if nothing is committed after it has been received.

units.la: xvii.Neque autem omnes,qui baptizantur aqua, sive infantes,sive adulti,gratię Christi fiunt participes.Libera enim est æterna Dei electio,& ad regnum Christi vocatio.
units.tr: XVII. Yet not all who are baptized with water, whether infants or adults, become partakers of the grace of Christ. For the eternal election of God is free, and so is the calling to the kingdom of Christ.

units.la: xviii.Neque etiam,quicunque non baptizantur aqua, à gratia Christi excluduntur. Non enim privatio,sed contemtus baptismi, ex fœdere Dei, cum fidelibus, & eorum liberis inito, excludit.
units.tr: XVIII. Nor, again, are all who are not baptized with water excluded from the grace of Christ. For it is not the lack of baptism, but contempt for it, that excludes, according to the covenant of God entered into with believers and their children.

units.la: xix. Cumque sacramentorum administratio sit pars ministerij ecclesiastici, qui ad hoc non sunt vocati, ac præsertim mulieres,baptizandi sibi potestatem sumere non debent.
units.tr: XIX. Since the administration of the sacraments is part of the ecclesiastical ministry, and those who have not been called to it, especially women, ought not to assume for themselves the power of baptizing.

units.la: xx.Ritus ab hominib.assuti baptismo, ut aquæ conse-cratio,cerei,exorcismi, chrisma, sal, cruces, sputa, & si quę sunt similia,in ecclesia Christi,tanquam sacramenti depravatio,merito repudiantur.
units.tr: XX. Rites added to baptism by men, such as consecration of the water, candles, exorcisms, chrism, salt, crosses, spittle, and whatever else is similar, are rightly rejected in the Church of Christ as a corruption of the sacrament.

units.la: XXVI. De coena Domini.
units.tr: XXVI. On the Lord's Supper.

units.la: Disputata in collegio Sapientia[?] 23. Maij. anno 1575.
units.tr: Disputed in the college of Sapientia[?] on 23 May 1575.

units.la: I.Alterum Noui Testamenti sacramentum appellatur cœna Domini: non quòd vespertino seu cœnæ tempore in ecclesia celebrari illud oporteat, sed quòd à Christo in coena,quam cum discipulis ante mortem suâ habuit postremam,institutum fit.Mensa Domini: quia Christus in ea nos pascit:Sacramentū corporis & sanguinis Christi: quia hęc nobis in eo communicantur:Eucharistia,quia in ea pro morte & beneficiis eius Christo solenes agunturgratiæ.Synaxis, quia in cōgressibus ecclesiæ cęlebrari debet. Nominatur, etiam apud veteres sacrificiu, quia est sacrificij propitiatorij à Christo in cruce peracti repræsentatio, & pro eo gratiarum actio, seu sacrificium eucharisticum.
units.tr: I. The other sacrament of the New Testament is called the Lord's Supper: not because it ought to be celebrated in the church at evening or at suppertime, but because it was instituted by Christ at the supper which he held with his disciples before his death, his last. The Lord's table: because Christ feeds us at it. The sacrament of the body and blood of Christ: because these are communicated to us in it. The Eucharist: because in it solemn thanks are given to Christ for his death and benefits. Synaxis: because it ought to be celebrated when the church assembles. It is also called by the ancients a sacrifice, because it is a representation of the propitiatory sacrifice accomplished by Christ on the cross, and a thanksgiving for it, or a eucharistic sacrifice.

units.la: II. Cœna Domini est sacramentum Noui Testamenti, in quo, ex mandato Christi, panis & vinum in cœtu fidelium distribuitur & sumitur ad Christi recordationem: hoc est, vt Christus nobis testetur, se corpore & sanguine suo pro nobis tradito & fuso, nos ad vitam æternam pascere: & nos illi pro his beneficiis solennes gratias agamus.
units.tr: II. The Lord's Supper is a sacrament of the New Testament, in which, by the command of Christ, bread and wine are distributed in the assembly of the faithful and taken in remembrance of Christ: that is, so that Christ may testify to us that, with his body given and blood poured out for us, he feeds us to eternal life, and that we in turn give him solemn thanks for these benefits.

units.la: III. Finis siue vsus cœnæ dominicæ Primus & principalis est, vt Christus nobis testetur se pro nobis esse mortuum, & suo sanguine & corpore pascere nos ad vitam æternam, vt hac testificatione fidem nostram, ac proinde pastum hûc spiritualem in nobis foueat & augeat. Secu-dus, est gratiarum actio pro his beneficiis Christi, eorumque, & nostri erga Christum officij, publica & solennis professio. Tertius, est distinctio ecclesiæ ab aliis sectis. Quartus, vt sit vinculum dilectionis mutuæ inter Christianos: cùm sint omnes vnius corporis membra. Quintus, vt sit vinculum congressuum ecclesiæ, cùm Christus voluerit fieri vnius panis & poculi inter plures distributionem.
units.tr: III. The end or use of the Lord's Supper is, first and chief, that Christ may testify to us that he died for us, and feeds us with his blood and body to eternal life, so that by this testimony he may foster and increase our faith, and therefore the spiritual food in us. Second, it is a thanksgiving for these benefits of Christ, and a public and solemn profession of both his benefits and our duty toward Christ. Third, it is the distinction of the church from other sects. Fourth, that it may be a bond of mutual love among Christians, since they are all members of one body. Fifth, that it may be a bond of the church's assemblies, since Christ willed that there be one bread and one cup distributed among many.

units.la: IV. Primum illum vsum, qui est fidei nostræ in Christum confirmatio, inde habet cœna Domini, quia Christus ipse hunc panem & potum per manus ministrorum porrigit in sui memoriam, hoc est, vt nos hoc symbolo tanquam visibili verbo admoneat, se pro nobis esse mortuum, & se esse nobis cibum vitæ æternæ, dum nos sua membra facit, & quia promissione huic ritui addidit, se, edé-tes hoc panè in sui memoriâ, velle suo corpore & sanguine pascere, cùm dixit, Hoc est corpus meum: & quia Spiritus sanctus per hoc visibile testimonium animos & corda mouet ad firmius credendum promissioni euangelicæ.
units.tr: IV. The Lord's Supper has that first use, which is the confirmation of our faith in Christ, because Christ himself offers this bread and drink through the hands of his ministers, in remembrance of himself; that is, so that by this symbol, as by a visible word, he may remind us that he died for us, and that he is for us the food of eternal life, while he makes us his members. It also has it because, to this rite, he added a promise, when he said, "This is my body," that those who eat this bread in remembrance of him he wishes to feed with his body and blood; and because the Holy Spirit, through this visible testimony, moves minds and hearts to believe more firmly the gospel promise.

units.la: V. Est ergo in cœna Domini duplex cibus & potus: externus, visibilis & terrenus, videlicet panis & vinum: & internus, inuisibilis & cœlestis, videlicet corpus & sanguis Christi. Duplex item māducatio & sumtio: externa, visibilis & significas, quæ est sumtio panis & vini corporalis, hoc est, quæ manibus ore & sensibus corporis peragitur: & interna, inuisibilis & significata, quæ & fruitio mortis Christi, & in Christi corpº insitio spiritualis, hoc est, quæ nō manibus & ore corporis, sed spiritu & fide peragitur. Duplex denique administer huius cibi & potus: externus externi, qui est minister ecclesiæ, manu sua præbens nobis panem & vinum: internus interni, qui est ipse Christus corpore & sanguine suo nos pascens.
units.tr: V. In the Lord's Supper there is therefore a twofold food and drink: the outward, visible and earthly, namely bread and wine; and the inward, invisible and heavenly, namely the body and blood of Christ. Likewise there is a twofold eating and drinking: the outward, visible and signifying, which is the corporal taking of bread and wine, that is, what is performed by the hands, mouth and bodily senses; and the inward, invisible and signified, which is both the enjoyment of the death of Christ and the spiritual implanting into the body of Christ, that is, what is performed not by the hands and mouth of the body, but by the spirit and faith. Finally, there is a twofold minister of this food and drink: the outward minister of the outward food, who is the minister of the church, offering us bread and wine with his hand; and the inward minister of the inward food, who is Christ himself, feeding us with his body and blood.

units.la: VI. Non corpus & sanguis Christi, sed panis & vinum sunt symbola, quæ fidei nostræ confirmandæ serviunt: corpus n. & sanguis Christi sumuntur, ut vivamus in æternum. Panis autem & vinum sumuntur, ut de illa cœlesti alimonia confirmemur, & magis magisque ea fruamur.
units.tr: VI. It is not the body and blood of Christ, but the bread and wine, that are the symbols which serve to confirm our faith; for the body and blood of Christ are taken so that we may live forever. Bread and wine, however, are taken so that we may be strengthened by that heavenly nourishment and enjoy it more and more.

units.la: VII. Neque panis mutatur in corpus Christi, & vinum in sanguinem Christi: neq. illis abolitis succedit in locum eorum corpus & sanguis Christi: neq. in pane, aut sub pane, aut ubi panis est, substantialiter præsens est corpus Christi: sed in legitimo usu cœnæ Domini, Spiritus S. hoc symbolo utitur tanquam instrumento, ad excitandam in nobis fidem, per quam ipse magis magisque in nobis habitat, & nos Christo inserit, & facit, ut propter ipsum simus iusti, & ex eo hauriamus vitam æternam.
units.tr: VII. Neither is the bread changed into the body of Christ, nor the wine into the blood of Christ; nor, with them abolished, does the body and blood of Christ take their place; nor is the body of Christ substantially present in the bread, or under the bread, or wherever the bread is. But in the lawful use of the Lord's Supper, the Holy Spirit uses this symbol as an instrument to kindle faith in us, by which he dwells in us more and more, and joins us to Christ, and makes us righteous for his sake, and from him we draw eternal life.

units.la: VIII. Cū autē Christus dicit: Hoc, id est, hic panis, est corpus meum: & hoc poculū est sanguis meus, locutio est sa-cramentalis seu metonymica, qua symbolo tribuitur nomen rei significatæ, id est, docetur, panem esse sacramentum seu symbolum corporis Christi, hoc est, repræsentare, & testari corpus Christi pro nobis oblatum in cruce, & nobis in cibum vitæ æternæ datū, ac proinde instrumentum esse Spiritus sancti ad hunc passum in nobis conseruandum & augendum, ut Paulus ait: Panis est communio corporis Christi, id est, ea res per quam participes reddimur corporis Christi: & alibi: Omnes una potio-ne potati fumus in unum spiritum. Eadē sententia est cū dicitur, panem vocari corpus Christi per similitudinem rei significatæ cum signo, quod videlicet corpus Christi alit vitam spiritualem, sicut panis corporalem: & propter certo coniunctam perceptionem rei & signi in legitimo sacramenti usu. Atque hæc est sacramentalis unio panis & corporis Christi, quæ per locutionem sacramentalem indicatur: non autem illa secundum locum coniunctio, quæ à quibusdam fingitur.
units.tr: VIII. When Christ says, "This, that is, this bread, is my body; and this cup is my blood," it is a sacramental or metonymical expression, by which the name of the thing signified is given to the symbol; that is, it is taught that the bread is the sacrament or symbol of the body of Christ, that is, that it represents and attests the body of Christ offered for us on the cross and given to us as food of eternal life, and therefore is an instrument of the Holy Spirit for preserving and increasing this spiritual food in us. As Paul says: "The bread is the communion of the body of Christ," that is, the thing through which we are made partakers of the body of Christ; and elsewhere: "We have all been made to drink of one Spirit." It is the same meaning when the bread is called the body of Christ by a likeness of the thing signified to the sign, namely because the body of Christ nourishes spiritual life just as bread nourishes bodily life; and on account of the surely conjoined perception of the thing and the sign in the lawful use of the sacrament. This is the sacramental union of the bread and the body of Christ, which is indicated by the sacramental expression; but not that local conjunction which some invent.

units.la: IX. Ut igitur corpus Christi est & proprie dictū, & sa-cramentale, quod est panis eucharisticus: sic māducatio corporis Christi duplex est: sacramentalis, quæ est symboli, videlicet panis & vini externa & corporalis sumtio; & realis seu spiritualis, quę est ipsius corporis Christi: estque in Christum credere & per fidem, habitante in nobis ipsius spiritu, inseri ipsius corpori tanquam capiti membra, & viti palmites, atque ita mortis & vitæ Christi fieri participes. Unde patet, falso accusari sic docentes, quod in cœna Domini vel nuda signa constituat; vel solius mortis Christi, aut beneficiorum eius, aut Spiritus sancti participationem, exclusa vera, reali & spirituali ipsius corporis Christi communione.
units.tr: IX. Just as the body of Christ is both properly so called and sacramental, which is the eucharistic bread, so the eating of the body of Christ is twofold: sacramental, which is the outward and bodily taking of the symbol, namely of the bread and wine; and real or spiritual, which is of the very body of Christ. And this is to believe in Christ, and through faith, with his Spirit dwelling in us, to be implanted into his body as members into the head and branches into the vine, and thus to become partakers of the death and life of Christ. Hence it is clear that those who teach this are falsely accused of making the Lord's Supper either mere signs, or the participation only of the death of Christ, or of his benefits, or of the Holy Spirit, with the true, real and spiritual communion of the body of Christ excluded.

units.la: x. Vsus autem cœnæ legitimus est, quando fideles ritu hunc a Christo institutum seruant ad ipsius memoriam: hoc est, ad fidem & gratitudinem suam excitandam.
units.tr: X. The lawful use of the Supper is when the faithful observe this rite instituted by Christ in remembrance of him; that is, to kindle their faith and gratitude.

units.la: xi. Sicut in hoc vsu corpus Christi sacramentaliter & realiter editur: ita & extra hunc vsum, vtpote ab infidelibus & hypocritis sacramentaliter quidem, sed non realiter editur, hoc est, symbola quidem seu signa sacramentalia, panis & vinum, non autem ipsæ res sacramenti Christi, videlicet corpus & sanguis percipiuntur.
units.tr: XI. As in this use the body of Christ is eaten sacramentally and really, so outside this use, as it is eaten sacramentally but not really by unbelievers and hypocrites, that is, only the symbols or sacramental signs, bread and wine, are received, but not the things of the sacrament of Christ, namely the body and blood.

units.la: xii. Doctrina hæc de cœna Domini plurimis firmi-fimifq.[?] argumetis nititur. Confirmat ea omnia loca scripturæ, quæ de cœna Domini loquuntur. Et Christus non aliquid inuisibile in pane, sed illum ipsum visibilem & fractum panem vocat corpus suum pro nobis traditum seu fractum: quod cum proprie intelligi non posset: addit ipse declarationem, se panem illum velle in fui memoriam fumi, quod perinde est, ac si dixisset, panem fui corporis esse sacramentum. Item: Coenam dixit esse Nouum Testamentum quod spirituale, vnū & æternū est.
units.tr: XII. This doctrine of the Lord's Supper rests on very many and very firm arguments. All those passages of Scripture which speak of the Lord's Supper confirm it. Christ also does not call something invisible in the bread, but that very visible and broken bread he calls his body given, or broken, for us; and since this could not be understood literally, he adds an explanation, that he wishes that bread to be taken in remembrance of himself, which is just as if he had said that the bread is a sacrament of his body. Likewise: he called the Supper the New Testament, which is spiritual, one, and eternal.

units.la: Et Paulus dicit, esse κοινωνία[?] corporis & sanguinis Christi, quia omnes fideles sunt vnum corpus in Christo, & quæ cum dæmoniorum κοινωνία non potest consistere. Item, eandem in corpus Christi insitionem per vnū spiritum in baptismo & cœna sacra constituit. Confirmat eam tota doctrina & natura sacramentorum, quæ omnia eandem Christi communionem spiritualem, & fide accipiendam subiiciunt oculis, quam verbum seu promissio euangelij auribus nunciat: propterea rerum significatarum nominibus appellantur, nec nisi in legitimo vsu, rerum perceptionem adiunctam habent. Confirmant eam articuli[?] fidei, qui docent, Christi corpus esse vere humanu, non simul in plurib. locis præsens:iā in cœlū sublatū, & ibi mansurum, donec redeat Dominus ad iudicium: communionem sanctorum cum Christo fieri per Spiritum sanctum, non per ingressum corporis Christi in corpora hominum: idcirco & hanc sententiā tota purior ecclesiæ antiquitas maximo & manifestissimo cosensu pfitetur[?].
units.tr: And Paul says it is the fellowship [κοινωνία] of the body and blood of Christ, because all the faithful are one body in Christ, and it cannot coexist with fellowship with demons. Likewise, he establishes that the ingrafting into the body of Christ through the one Spirit takes place both in baptism and in the Lord's Supper. The whole doctrine and nature of the sacraments confirms this: all of them set before the eyes that same spiritual communion with Christ, to be received by faith, which the Word or promise of the gospel announces to the ears. For this reason they are named after the things they signify, and they carry the perception of those things with them only in lawful use. The articles of faith also confirm this, teaching that the body of Christ is truly human, not present in many places at once, but taken up into heaven and to remain there until the Lord returns to judgment; and that the communion of the saints with Christ takes place through the Holy Spirit, not through the entry of Christ's body into the bodies of men. Therefore the purer antiquity of the Church, with the greatest and clearest consensus, also professes this opinion.

units.la: XIII. Differt à baptismo cœna Domini. Ritu & significandi modo, quia mersio significat remissionē & expurgationem peccati per sanguinē & Spiritum Christi, & societatem afflictionum & glorificationis Christi. Distributio autem panis & vini, significat mortem Christi nobis ad remissionem peccatorum imputari, & nos Christo insitos membra eius fieri. Usu speciali, quod baptismus est testimonium regenerationis, initi fœderis cum Deo, & receptionis in ecclesiam: Cœna Domini autem testatur, nos perpetuo nutriendos esse Christo in nobis manente, semperque ratum nobis fore fœdus semel initum cum Deo, & semper nos maiores in ecclesia & corpore Christi. Personis, quibus tribui debent. Baptismus omnibus debetur, qui pro membris ecclesiæ sunt habendi, sive adulti, sive infantes sint: Cœna Domini non nisi iis, qui beneficia Christi intelligere, & celebrare, & seipsos probare possunt. Usurpationis frequentia. Baptismus semel tantum debet sumi, quia fœdus Dei semel initum semper est ratum pœnitentibus. Cœna autem Domini sæpe, quia fœderis illius renovatio, & in memoriam revocatio frequens fidei nostræ est necessaria. Ordine usurpationis. Quia baptismus ante Cœnam Domini: Cœna autem non nisi post baptismum accepti cuiquam dari debet.
units.tr: XIII. The Lord's Supper differs from baptism: in rite and mode of signifying, because immersion signifies the remission and cleansing of sin through the blood and Spirit of Christ, and fellowship in Christ's sufferings and glorification; but the distribution of bread and wine signifies that Christ's death is imputed to us for the remission of sins, and that we, ingrafted into Christ, become his members. In special use, because baptism is the testimony of regeneration, of the covenant entered into with God, and of reception into the Church; but the Lord's Supper testifies that we are to be nourished continually by Christ abiding in us, and that the covenant once entered into with God will always remain firm for us, and that we are always greater in the Church and in the body of Christ. In the persons to whom they ought to be given: baptism is owed to all who are to be regarded as members of the Church, whether they be adults or infants; the Lord's Supper is to be given only to those who can understand and celebrate Christ's benefits and examine themselves. In the frequency of use: baptism ought to be received only once, because the covenant of God once entered into always remains firm for the repentant; but the Lord's Supper often, because renewal of that covenant and frequent recalling of it to memory are necessary for our faith. In the order of use: because baptism comes before the Lord's Supper; and the Lord's Supper ought not to be given to anyone except one who has already received baptism.

units.la: XIV. Dignè accedunt ad Cœnam Domini, qui se ipsos probant, id est, vera fide & pœnitentia præditi sunt. Hanc qui in se non deprehenduntur, nec sine ea debent accedere, ne iudicium sibi edant & bibant, nec pœnitentiam cum qua accedant differre, ne indurationem & pœnas æternas sibi attrahant.
units.tr: XIV. Those come worthily to the Lord's Supper who examine themselves, that is, who are endowed with true faith and repentance. Those who do not find these in themselves ought not to approach without them, lest they bring judgment on themselves and eat and drink it; nor should they postpone the repentance with which they approach, lest they draw hardening and eternal punishments upon themselves.

units.la: XV. Admittere ad cœnam ecclesia debet omnes, qui fundamentum doctrinæ Christianæ se amplecti, & propositum huic obediendi se habere profitentur: arcere autem eos, qui vel ab erroribus, blasphemiis, vel à manifestis contra conscientiam peccatis admoniti ab eoclesia,& erroris conuicti,nolunt desistere.
units.tr: XV. The Church ought to admit to the supper all who profess that they embrace the foundation of Christian doctrine and have the purpose of obeying it; but it ought to exclude those who, having been admonished by the Church about errors and blasphemies, or about manifest sins against conscience, and convicted of error, are unwilling to desist.

units.la: xvi. Papa male ex ritu coenae sustulit fractionem panis,& vsum poculi ademit populo. Male item tot addi-tis caeremoniis, de quibus Apostoli non praeceperunt, Coenam Domini in missam theatricam,hoc est, in in κακο-ζηλίᾳ[?] Iudaicam & histrionicas praestigias deformavit. Sed magis impia & idololatrica figmenta sunt, missam esse sacrificium propitiatorium, in quo Christus a sacrificulis pro vivis & mortuis offeratur patri: & vi consecrationis substantialiter praesens sit & maneat tatisper, dum species illae maneant incorruptae, & gratiam Dei atque alia beneficia conferat iis, pro quibus offeratur: & a quibus ore corporis edatur,etiam sine bono ipsorum motu: atque etiam repositus & circumgestatus sub illis speciebus sit adorandus. Propter haec tetra idola necef-fe est missam in ecclesia Christiana aboleri.
units.tr: XVI. The Pope has wrongly removed from the rite of the Lord's Supper the breaking of bread, and has taken away from the people the use of the cup. Likewise he has wrongly deformed the Lord's Supper, by adding so many ceremonies, about which the Apostles gave no command, into a theatrical mass, that is, into a Jewish zeal [κακοζηλία] and histrionic trickery. But even more impious and idolatrous are the fictions that the mass is a propitiatory sacrifice, in which Christ is offered to the Father by little priests for the living and the dead; and that by the power of consecration he is substantially present and remains for as long as those appearances remain unspoiled, and confers grace and other benefits on those for whom he is offered; and that he is eaten by the mouth of the body even without the good motion of those who eat him; and that he is to be adored even when reserved and carried about under those appearances. Because of these foul idols it is necessary that the mass be abolished in the Christian Church.

units.la: IN OBITUM CLARISSIMI VIRI D. ZACHARIÆ VRSINI, FIDELISSIMI S. THEOLOGIÆ DOCTORIS, & PROFESSORIS in schola illustri Neapolitana apud Nemetas celeberrimi, ORATIO
units.tr: Funeral Oration for the Most Distinguished Man Dr. Zacharias Ursinus, Most Faithful Doctor and Professor of Sacred Theology in the famous Neapolitan school among the Germans

units.la: D. Francisci Iunij in eadem schola S. Theologiæ Professoris ordinarij.
units.tr: Of Dr. Francis Junius, ordinary Professor of Sacred Theology in the same school.

units.la: FIDELISSIMO Dei servo, Zacharia Vrsino, clarissimi viri & auditores ornatissimi, gravissimo illo tecte[?] Domini nostri Iesu Christi, viro optimo, & collega nobis suavissimo, ecclesiae apprime vili his diebus priuati sumus, & schola haec nostra orbata parente suo. Cuius in-commodi magnitudinem si vellemus explicare, affice-remus gravius iam valde affectam pietatem vestram, & abfuturi à rei dignitate essemus quam longissime. Etenim ut maxime vellem, atque ex animo cuperem, neq. illud mihi videtur salutare, si luctuosas mentes vestras candentibus dolorum facibus accumulavero; neq. posi-tū est in facultate mea, tū quia nec ingenio, nec diuturna tanti viri consuetudine, nec doctrina aut exercitatione aliqua huius rei praestandae commoditate me valere sentio: tum etiam, quòd, si qua in me vis dicendi effet (quae scio quàm sit exigua) hàc mihi grauitas oneris temporis an-guftiæ,& acerbitas doloris eriperent. Quàobrem volue-ram ego quidè nonnullis de collegio nostro persuadere, vt suam operam in hac re aliquantisper consumerent, studiúque & dolorem meum oratione sua alleuaret: sed eos mœror publicus,& amantissimus ipsorum dolor excu-sauit. An ergo si in hac publica ecclesiæ & scholæ nostræ calamitate indulgemus luctui, deserenda fuerit sanctæ illius animæ commendatio? At hàc fortasse inofficiosam mollitiè appellaret, qui doloris nostri nō vident vehementiā. Deinde (vt verbis vtar Ambrosij) etsi incremētum doloris est,id quòd doleas scribere: quoniam tamè plerumq; in eius, què amissum dolemus, commemoratione requiescimus; eò quòd in scribendo,dum in eum mentè dirigimus intentioneque defigimus, videtur no-bis in sermone reuiuiscere, omnino faciendum est, ne aut obliterasse silentio benemeriti de nobis pignoris memoriam videamur, atque inhonoratum reliquisse, aut refugisse incentiuum dolendi,cum doluisse plerumq; solatium fit dolentis.An laudatio hæc diutius differenda? quin potius excitandæ mentes, vt cùm in hoc tempore, tum in posteritatem omnè recolatur ὡς (vt Nazianzenus ait) [?] τῆς ἀξίων μάλιστα μνημονευτέον, καὶ ἐν τῷ μνήμῃ [?] ὅσιόν τι ὀμῶς καὶ ὠφέλιμον Quid ergo? audacissimus ego ex omnibus, qui in hac schola profitentur? minimè: at tanto officiosior quàm cæteri? ne istius quidem laudis ita cupidus, vt aliis eam præreptam velim. An imprudentissimus? prudentiam quidem mihi non arrogo, veruntamen hoc officium meum confido vacare culpa, neque huius rei solatur cogitatio. Quæ me igitur res præter cæteros impulit, vt habendam hanc oratio-nem reciperem? quia haberi quidem ab vno de nobis necesse est ex officio nostro: sed quod ab omnibus ac singulis nostrum officium postulat, id excusat in illis dolor: à me vero quòd æquè dolor excusare posset, id non solum flagitat, verum etiam extorquet necessitas.
units.tr: Most faithful servant of God, Zacharias Ursinus; distinguished gentlemen and most accomplished listeners: we have lately been deprived of that most serious servant of our Lord Jesus Christ, an excellent man and a most pleasant colleague to us, a loss the Church feels most keenly these days, and this school of ours is bereft of its parent. If I wished to explain how great this misfortune is, I would burden your piety, already gravely affected, and I would fall far short of the dignity of the subject. For although I would very much like, and sincerely desire, not to accumulate your grieving minds with burning torches of sorrow, that also does not seem wholesome to me; nor is it within my power, partly because I feel I am not equal to this task by talent, by long familiarity with so great a man, or by learning or practice of any kind; partly also because, even if I had some power of speech (which I know to be very small), the weight of the occasion, the shortness of time and the bitterness of grief would snatch it from me. Therefore I had indeed wished to persuade some of our colleagues to spend their effort on this matter for a while, and to relieve my grief and their own zeal with their speech; but the public mourning and their own most loving sorrow excused them. Shall we then, if in this public calamity of the Church and of our school we give way to lamentation, abandon the commendation of that holy soul? Perhaps those who do not see the vehemence of our grief would call this an unseemly softness. Furthermore (to use the words of Ambrose), although writing down what you grieve over increases the grief, nevertheless, since we usually find rest in remembering the one we have lost, because in writing, while we direct our mind and fix our attention upon him, he seems to us to come back to life in our speech, we must by all means act so that we do not seem either to have passed over in silence the memory of a pledge who deserved well of us, and so left it unhonoured, or to have shrunk from the incentive to grief; since, when we have grieved, the grieving person usually finds consolation. Shall this eulogy be postponed any longer? Rather, minds should be roused, so that his memory is recalled both now and in all posterity, as (in the words of Gregory Nazianzen) "of those worthy of memory above all, and in remembering him there is something holy and at the same time useful" [?]. What then? Am I the most daring of all who lecture in this school? Not at all. But am I more dutiful than the rest? I am not so eager for that praise either, that I would wish it snatched away from others. Am I the most imprudent? I do not claim prudence for myself; yet I trust that this duty of mine is free of blame, and the thought of it brings no consolation. What then drove me, beyond the rest, to undertake giving this oration? Because it is indeed necessary, by virtue of our office, that it be given by one of us; but what our office requires of all of us and each of us, grief excuses in them; whereas in my case, what grief could equally excuse, necessity not only demands but even extracts.

units.la: Primum enim iusti illius & sancti collegæ nostri benedictæ memoriæ,debeo, quod debent alij,honorificà illius recordationem. Deinde id à nobis officij,eoq. amplius debetur huic scholæ nostræ,quæ nostram operam æquè in hac re,atque in aliis,sibi optimo iure vendicas.
units.tr: For first, I owe to the memory of that just and holy colleague of ours, of blessed memory, the honourable remembrance of him, as others also owe it. Second, this is owed by us as a duty, and all the more to this school of ours, which rightly claims our labour in this matter just as in others.

units.la: Accedit illa quoque causa, quòd in hac re & vtilitati publicæ consulitur, & existimationi nostræ: quis enim non esset de nobis cogitaturus Sophocleum illud & plenis buccis obiecturus,
units.tr: There is also this further reason: that in this matter both the public benefit and our own reputation are being consulted. For who would not think of us and, with cheeks full, bring forward that line of Sophocles:

units.la: Φεῦ, ἕ ξενόν τος ὡς ταχεῖα [?] τῆς βέβηκας [?] Χαῖρε [?] διαρρεῖ [?] ἀλίσκεται [?]
units.tr: Alas, stranger, how swiftly... [the Greek lines are corrupt in the transcription and cannot be restored with certainty]

units.la: Summi autem illi viri, qui adsunt, homines clarissimi, in hoc dolore nostro id habent commodi, quòd illud dicendi onus salvo officio subterfugere se posse hoc tempore arbitrantur: à me vero functionis meæ flagitat necessitas, vt aut de altero videam, qui hic commodius quàm ego dicat, velitq; dicere, aut ipse aleam iudiciorum subire cogat. Me occupationes plus satis distinet, me tenuitatis meæ depellit conscientia, me huius rei deterret amplitudo. Sed in occupationibus iniicit manū scholæ authoritas, conscientiæ vim facit exemplum, & publicū ecclesiç documentum: ut sepositá rei gravitate atq; maiestate aliquid in hac corona dicã me trudit necessitas.
units.tr: Those most distinguished men who are present, however, have this advantage in our grief: they think they can avoid the burden of speaking on this occasion without failing in their duty; but for me the necessity of my office demands that either I look for another who speaks here more fittingly than I do, and is willing to speak, or that I myself submit to the hazard of judgment. Occupations keep me busy quite enough; the awareness of my own slightness drives me back; the greatness of the matter deters me. But the authority of the school lays its hand upon my occupations, the example of conscience does violence to me, and the public instruction of the Church compels me, setting aside the gravity and majesty of the subject, to say something before this assembly.

units.la: Fretus itaque humanitate & æquanimitate vestra, clarissimi viri & auditores ornatissimi, à vobis peto rogó-que: primùm vt æquis auribus atque animis audiatis oratione meâ imparé veritatis amplitudini, vestræ ex-pectationi, & officio nostro, sed parem tamen facultati meæ: deinde verò, vt me pauca quædã de optimæ illius & sanctissimæ arboris fructu decerpentem amanter ex-cusetis, si neque tabulam istam iustis coloribus, neque mensam dapibus illis multis lautisque instruxero, quæ in hoc penu extiterunt, sed res ab insciente prætermissas suppleatis, & imprudenter, si forte, effusas condone-tis tempori & dolori meo. Non enim constitui dicere de iis rebus omnibus, quas in hoc tanto viro præsentes sumus admirati, & sublatas desideramus, (omnia illa [?] ec scio, nec possum.) Non de multis agere, quæ noui & [?]uę mihi sæpenumero in mentem veniunt, (illud enim [?] infinitum prope futurum esset, ac incredibile plerique viderètur.) Sed quanquam bonorum descriptione summam, quæ ante vidimus, ereptáque deflemus, quàm breuissime perstringere, & acceptũ à nobis damnum ex præmatura summi illius viri morte adûbrare, vt iis velut facibus ad certam fidem feriãque respiscentiam accendamur, & ad imitationem huius testis idonei for[?]issimique militis nos ipsos magis ac magis comparemus.
units.tr: Relying therefore on your kindness and fairness, distinguished gentlemen and most accomplished listeners, I ask and beg of you: first, that you hear with fair ears and minds my speech, which is unequal to the greatness of the truth, to your expectation and to our duty, yet equal to my ability; and then, that you kindly excuse me if, plucking a few things from the fruit of that best and most holy tree, I do not furnish that panel with fitting colours, nor that table with those many rich and elegant dishes which were present in this storehouse, but that you supply what I have passed over through ignorance, and pardon, if by chance I have poured out anything carelessly, my time and my grief. For I have not resolved to speak about all those things which we admired in this great man while he was present and now miss now that he is taken away (I neither know all of them nor am able to); nor to deal with many things which I know and which often come to my mind (for that would be almost endless and would seem incredible to most). But although I want to sketch as briefly as possible the sum of the good qualities which we saw before and now lament as lost, and to set forth the loss we have suffered by the premature death of that great man, so that by these torches we may be kindled to a sure faith and a steadfast repentance, and so that we may prepare ourselves more and more to imitate this trustworthy and most valiant soldier of Christ.

units.la: Zacharias igitur Vrsinus Vratislaviæ ex honesta familia natus est, anno à salute parta MDXXXIV. Firmo fuit à natura corpore, firmiore animo, in primis autem ex quo ad naturam illam artes, scientiæ, eximiæque è cœlo dotes accesserunt. Ac de corporeis quidem rebus prædicari multa non videtur opus, quarum aliæ omnium hominum inter se communes sunt, aliæ præter hominem brutarum animantium. Nam etsi commodæ sunt illæ & optandæ homini cuique ad laudabilium rerum adiumentum, nihil tamen ad veram laudem faciunt eorum hominum, quibus adsunt: nobis vero placet de hoc tanto viro, non qua homo fuit, sed qua Theologus instructissimus, cognoscere.
units.tr: Zacharias Ursinus was therefore born at Breslau, of an honourable family, in the year of salvation 1534. He had a body strong by nature and a mind still stronger, especially since, in addition to that natural gift, arts, sciences and extraordinary gifts from heaven were added. Now, concerning bodily matters, there seems no need to say much: some of them are common to all men, others belong to brute animals beyond man. For although those things are pleasant and to be wished for by every man as an aid to praiseworthy deeds, they contribute nothing to the true praise of those men who possess them; but we wish to know about this great man not as a man, but as a most accomplished theologian.

units.la: De virtutibus autem animi, quæ bonorum [?]onsensione ipsæ per se sunt expetendæ, perpetuámque possident veræ laudis fructum, quid dicturi sumus? Unde initium? quando finem facturi? Si de hoc sanctissimo, lectissimóque vase, ad gloriam Dei comparato, conaremur dicere quæcunque afferri possunt? Tempus me profecto citius, quam oratio in causa ista deficeret. Itaque video, quid agam: certos mihi fines terminosque constituam, extra quos egredi non possim, si maxime velim: ut & mihi sit propositum, de quo dicam, & vos etiam, clarissimi viri, & auditores ornatissimi, iam ante animo possitis prospicere, quibus de rebus sitis audituri. Dicimus primum, Vrsinum hunc nostrum maximis ingenii facultatibus, plurimis ac summis fuisse instructissimum. Deinde illud dicimus, ad summas illas & præstantissimas, & incredibiles dotes ingenii sanctissimum vitæ institutum, & accuratissimam rationem morum, qui ad publicum Ecclesiæ bonum fuerunt opus, accessisse. Postremo dicimus sanctæ illius morte certissimum nobis esse documentum politissimi illius ingenii, & vitæ accuratissimæ. Hos mihi cancellos ipse de industria circumdabo, ut rem facilius totam recolligatis, si hæc memineritis, & me quoque facile, si extra hos conabor egredi, vestra exstimatione revocetis. Ac mihi quidem videtur, quod de ingenio dicebamus: optimum hunc virum quàm plurimis, iisque maximis & cœlestibus ingenii virtutibus fuisse cumulatissimum: Id sine cuiusquè iniuria offensaque dici à nobis posse, & citra invidiam petimus accipi. Has n. vires ingenii, quæ à natura sunt, cum animo meo reputans, nihil in ullo deprehendi posse existimo, quod in hoc exi-mio viro iure 'desideraueris : sin virtutes illas,quibus ex-coli ingenia, & confirmari ad humanitatem ac pietatem solent, omnia pene in hunc unum præstantem virum di-sinitùs fuisse collata, testes sunt huiùs sermonis nostri, quicunque vel uno illius congressu incredibilem eius vir-tutem experti sunt, testes familiares, testes amici, testes consultores innumeri,maximi & principes viri,qui hunc suorum consiliorum authorem, hunc scriptorum suorum Aristarchum anteposuerunt cæteris,testes literæ innume-rabiles,testes populi,gentes,ecclesiæ,denique testes libri, quorum varia & multiplice eruditione populus Christi pascitur,& recreatur iamdiu, quamuis hi germani parétis sui voluntati modestissimæ obsequentes, ut pudici liberi, nomen illius dissimulent. Quæ cùm ita sint,quid optimi huius,& longè maximi ingenij ingentes facultates,me at-tinet proloqui?quid minutatim exponere? Etenim si na-turalem quandam ingenij illius sapientiâ cum animo meo expendero,ecce repente sese confertim exhibent,& densa ac velut stipata procedunt agmina sermonû,literarum,lec-tionum, concionû,scriptorum, librorû,indices & offici-næ quædã sapientiæ.Si ad illam vim ingenij quæ in exco-gitando versatur,animû meû & cogitationem conuertero, quid acriore acuminatum(ut cum poeta loquar) acie? quid promptius ac velocius? quid magis solers & industrium venire in mente potest, quàm illa vis fuit,quâ Deus Opt. Max.in hoc sanctimoniæ vase ingenerauerat? Si ad magnitudinem animi attendero,aciémque illam, qua res omnes humanæ percipiuntur atque superantur,quis homo facilius ad nistum(quod aiunt)oculi, quis aptius res istas omnes, quæ cœlestibus illis mentibus sordescere videtur, transuolauit?Si ad memoriæ fidé,quæ ingenij comes est, oculos aduertero, hîc immortale video memoriæ boni-tatê.Sed postquam uberrimû illud ac felix ingeniû, disci-plinarum humaniorû cultura subactû & expolitum est,tû uero eximiam illam vim naturæ suæ, supra omnes alios ad perfectionē quandam visus est attollere.Nam quarum artium,aut scientiarũ notitiam non assecutus est, ut lauda-tam illam à ueteribus Philosophis, celebratámque ἐγ-κλοπαιδίαν[?] possideret?Disciplinas sermonis puri,perspicui, elegantis,ueri,tàm probè tenuit,quàm quì maxime. Sin[?]gulas partes philosophiæ studiosè & artificiosè tractauit, vt non discipulum esse hunc philosophiæ, sed huius alumnam dicas Philosophiam. Mathese[?]n fuit peritissimus: quæ ad naturalem cognitionem spectant, novit absolutis-simè, quæ ad mores publicè priuatimque beneinformandos pertinent, sic ad vnguem tenuit, vt singulare hac memoria miraculum mundi merito dici possit.
units.tr: As for the virtues of the mind, which by common consent are to be sought for their own sake and possess the lasting fruit of true praise, what shall we say? Where shall we begin? When shall we make an end? If we were to try to say everything that can be said about this most holy and most chosen vessel, prepared for the glory of God, time would fail me far sooner than my speech would fail in such a cause. Therefore I see what I must do: I shall set for myself certain limits and boundaries, beyond which I could not go even if I wished. In this way the subject I am to speak about will be clear to me, and you too, distinguished gentlemen and most accomplished listeners, may already in your minds foresee on what matters you are about to hear. We say first that our Ursinus was furnished with the greatest and most numerous and highest faculties of talent. Next we say that to those high and outstanding and remarkable gifts of talent there were added a most holy manner of life and a most careful order of conduct, which were a work for the public good of the Church. Lastly we say that by the death of that holy man we have a most certain proof of his most refined talent and most exact life. These limits I shall draw around myself deliberately, so that you may more easily gather up the whole matter if you keep these points in mind, and so that you may easily recall me, by your judgment, should I try to go beyond them. And indeed it seems to me that what we said about his talent is true: that this best of men was endowed with the greatest number of talents, and those the greatest and heavenly gifts of intellect. We ask that this may be said by us without wrong or offence to anyone, and that it be accepted without envy. For when I weigh in my own mind these powers of talent which come from nature, I think nothing can be found in any man that you could rightly miss in this distinguished man. But if those virtues by which talents are usually cultivated and strengthened towards humanity and piety were almost all bestowed by God on this one outstanding man, the witnesses of this speech of ours are: whoever experienced his incredible virtue even in a single meeting; family witnesses, friends, countless advisers, the greatest and princely men, who placed this one first among their counsellors, this one as the Aristarchus of their writings, above all others; countless letters are witnesses, the people are witnesses, nations and churches are witnesses; finally the books themselves are witnesses, by whose varied and manifold learning the people of Christ has long been fed and refreshed, although these brothers, obedient with the most modest obedience to the will of their father, like chaste children, hide his name. Since these things are so, what need have I to set forth the great powers of this best and by far greatest talent? Why should I explain them piece by piece? For if I weigh with my mind some natural wisdom of his talent, behold, at once they present themselves all together, and there come forward dense and, as it were, crowded columns of discourses, letters, lectures, sermons, writings, books, and storehouses of wisdom. If I turn my mind and thought to that power of talent which is occupied in inventing, what could be more sharpened, as the poet says, with a keener edge? What could be quicker and swifter? What could come to mind more clever and more diligent than that power with which God, the Best and Greatest, had endowed this vessel of holiness? If I attend to greatness of mind, and to that keen sight by which all human things are perceived and surpassed, what man has more easily flown over (as they say) the eye's grasp, and more aptly over all those things which seem base to those heavenly minds? If I turn my eyes to the reliability of memory, which is the companion of talent, here I see an immortal goodness of memory. But after that abundant and happy talent was trained and polished by the cultivation of the humane studies, then indeed it seemed to lift that remarkable power of its nature above all others to a certain perfection. For what arts or sciences did he fail to attain, so as to possess that encyclopaedia so praised by the ancient philosophers? He mastered the disciplines of pure, clear, elegant and true speech as thoroughly as anyone. He treated each part of philosophy diligently and skilfully, so that you would call philosophy not this man's pupil, but his foster-child.
