He was most skilled in mathematics: what pertains to natural knowledge he knew most perfectly, and what pertains to forming morals both publicly and privately he held so exactly that he may rightly be called a unique wonder of the world for this memory.

units.la: Deinde (vt discedentes ab arte progrediamur longius) quos, quot, quàm magnos & præstantes viros omni studio prosecutus est dispendio rei familiaris suę, vt animum suum in notitia iflarū rerum confirmaret, atque imitatione attentissima elaboratum redderet? Nam V Vittembergę, Lipsię, Lutetię Parisiorum, Tiguri, clarissima illa & lucentissima Europę lumina, quę tum circumfulgebant, inuisit, audiuit, non oculis, & auribus solùm, sed animo quoq; sitientissima. Itaque ab illis omnibus, tanquam frugalis apes, prouida atque benefica, mel suauissimū eruditionis comportauit: cuius mellis faui nobis qui hic in hac schola sumus, Germaniæ patriæ ipsius carissimæ, & toti ecclesiæ Dei (quę nostra communis mater est omnium) salutares extant, infidelibus vero, impiis & hæreticis exitiabiles. Sed quid ego de exercitatione dicam? cuius amore maximus ille Dei seruus & sanctæ ecclesiæ administer tanto opere affectus est, vt præ seueriore & rigidiore animi sui occupatione, qua se mancipabat totū, & exercitamentis addicebat, omnem sui corporis recordationem abiiceret. Atq; hoc quidem tum effecit maximè, cùm animu suu ex parte humaniorum disciplinarum scientia explcuisset[?]: ne idem forte sibi contingeret, quod athletis solet imperitioribus, qui diu multumq; aere verberat, nō attingentes corpora, sumtáq; inani operâ tandem occubunt victi certamine. Nam magnum quidem & laudabile est illis naturalibus ingenij facultatibus viribusq; omnes aemulari[?] alios: maius est, si valē-tissimū illū succū ingenij florentissimā iucundissimáq; literaturæ humanioris cortina in iueri[?]s:id vero maximū omniū est, & imprimis præstabile, si quādo hic succus & color vniuersꝰ in sacris fontib. cœlestis huiꝰ diuinæq.doctri-næ, immergitur atq; eluitur: non id quidem eo vt noster animus, quasi dibapha Tyria olim amplius coloretur, sed vt in spiritu metis suæ quisq; renouetur, ad imaginem illius q; gressit ipsu[?]. Hoc aut si quisquá memoria nostra, fortissimꝰ hic athleta Christi fecit, elaborauit, perfecit studiosissi- me. Primum enim vidit, & optime vidit, amplissima ista humanitatis ornamenta ancillari verbo Dei & scripturæ sanctæ oportere. Deinde id quoque statuit, seipsum non sui iuris, sed alieni esse. Præterea, quicunque Deo se mancipauerint, hos salutem ab eo sentire adipisci: qui vero se de manu eius seduxerint, eos de salute plane decidere.
units.tr: Next (to move on a little further from the arts): whom, how many, and how great and outstanding men did he not pursue with every effort, at the cost of his own private means, so that he might strengthen his mind through knowledge of these things and make it, by the most attentive imitation, polished? For he visited and heard, at Wittenberg, Leipzig, Paris, and Zurich, those most famous and brilliant lights of Europe which then shone around, and he took them in not only with his eyes and ears but with a mind most thirsty. And so, like a thrifty, provident and beneficial bee, he gathered from all of them the sweetest honey of learning. The honeycombs of this honey are wholesome for us who are here in this school, for Germany, our most dear fatherland itself, and for the whole Church of God (which is the common mother of us all), but deadly for unbelievers, the impious and heretics. But why do I speak of his exercise? By love of which that greatest servant of God and minister of the holy Church was so greatly moved that, because of the more severe and rigid preoccupation of his mind, to which he gave himself wholly and devoted himself to his studies, he cast off all recollection of his body. And indeed he achieved this most of all when he had, in part, filled his mind with knowledge of the humane disciplines, lest perhaps the same thing should happen to him that often happens to less skilled athletes, who beat the air long and hard, not touching their opponents' bodies, and at last fall defeated in the contest after vain effort. For it is indeed great and praiseworthy to rival others in those natural faculties of the mind and its powers; greater if one dips that most vigorous juice of the mind into the flourishing and most pleasant purple of the more humane literature; but this is the greatest of all and especially to be prized, if this juice and colour is, at last, immersed and washed in the sacred fountains of this heavenly and divine doctrine: not indeed so that our mind may be dyed more deeply, as Tyrian purple was once, but so that each may be renewed in the spirit of his mind, according to the image of him who created him. If anyone in our memory has done this, this most valiant athlete of Christ did so, laboured at it and accomplished it most diligently. For first he saw, and saw rightly, that those splendid ornaments of humanity ought to be handmaids to the Word of God and Holy Scripture. Then he also determined that he himself was not his own master but belonged to another. Moreover, that those who have given themselves to God obtain salvation from him, but those who have drawn away from his hand plainly fall from salvation.

units.la: Tum autem, Deus bone, quatum studium in sanctissima Christiani huius pugilis anima generauit, effecitque istarum rerum cogitatio? quem metum? quod desiderium? quæ zelum? Hinc nata est in Christum fides, spes, & perfectionis vinculum, charitas, cœlestes plantæ, quæ vbi a Deo patre fuerunt insitæ, nunquam ratione illa eradicari, aut corrumpi tentatione, violentia, fraude, rebus secundis, aduersisque potuerunt. Quid? quod ne hæc quidem illi fuerunt satis, nisi de seipso vindictam indies sumeret homo innocentissimus? nam strenuè suum ipsius corpus sugillauit, ut in seruitutem Christi abriperet. Incredibile est, quanta sollicitudine & religione vidit, ne quid altius demenso saperet: semper Christo captiuam dedidit naturalem illam, qua valebat plurimum, sapientiam: nihil unquam nisi ex diserto & perspecto Dei verbo ausus est statuere: nihil pronunciare voluit, nisi quod certissima fide a spiritu Dei accepisset: Denique de receptis rebus atque sententiis nihil mutandum, nisi imperante & vim (vt ita dicamus) afferente in re ineluctabili Dei veritate iudicauit. Hæc autem omnia vt assequeretur certius, exactissimam linguarum peritiam habuit, commodissimum præter alia Theologi veri instrumentum: habuit autem ad dexteram suam (vt cum sapiente loquar) & ad omnia, quæ fuerunt opus, est visus commodissime ac sapientissime. Vir rebus iudicandis sapientissimus, præuidendis prudentissimus, excogitandis solertissimus, inuestigandis sagacissimus, eruditis laboriosissimus, discutiedis acutissimus, percipiendis promptissimus, tradendis veris fidelissimus, depellendis falsis potentissimus, a vanitate alienissimus, ad omnia diligentissimus, iustis veri Theologi armis præsidiisq. instructissimus, certissimum falsi ἀμυντήριον, veritatis propugnaculum. Hunc doctrina Theologum reipsa pugilem Christi amantissimus, clarissimi viri, & auditores ornatissimi, amantissimus pez voluntatem Dei acerrimum hunc veritatis
units.tr: Then, good God, how great a zeal did the thought of these things generate and effect in the most holy soul of this Christian fighter? What fear, what desire, what zeal? From this was born faith in Christ, hope, and charity, the bond of perfection, heavenly plants which, once they had been implanted by God the Father, could never be uprooted by that reasoning, nor corrupted by temptation, violence, fraud, prosperity or adversity. What more? Since not even these things were enough for him, did this most innocent man not daily take vengeance on himself? For he vigorously bruised his own body so as to snatch it into the servitude of Christ. It is incredible with what care and scruple he watched lest he should think anything above measure: he always surrendered to Christ as a captive that natural wisdom, in which he was most strong; he never ventured to lay down anything except from the eloquent and carefully examined Word of God; he wished to pronounce nothing except what he had received with most certain faith from the Spirit of God. Finally, he judged that nothing in the received matters and opinions should be changed, unless the truth of God, which cannot be resisted, commanded it and (so to speak) forced it. Now, to attain all these things more surely, he had the most exact skill in languages, a most convenient instrument, among others, of a true theologian; and he had, at his right hand (to speak with the wise man), and for all things that were needed, he seemed most conveniently and wisely equipped. A man most wise in judging matters, most prudent in foreseeing, most skilful in devising, most sagacious in investigating, most laborious in learning, most acute in discussing, most ready in grasping, most faithful in delivering the truths, most powerful in repelling falsehoods, most remote from vanity, most diligent in all things, most fully furnished with the just arms and defences of a true theologian, a most certain bulwark against falsehood, a rampart of truth. This theologian, a fighter of Christ in deed as well as by doctrine, most beloved of Christ, most distinguished sir and most honoured listeners, most beloved of the will of God, this most fierce defender of divine truth, most powerful foe of Satan, the refuter and judge most faithful to the frauds and false witnessings which that one is wont to weave, this most brave conqueror and overthrower of heresies, we have seen snatched from our number; this most grievous blow has been struck at our school, and a double wound inflicted on the whole Church of Christ.

units.la: ἀμυντήριον ... [Greek word; the scan is too small here to read it letter by letter, so the Greek is marked as illegible below.] veritatis diuinæ defensorem, hostem satanæ potentissimum, fraudum & ψευδομαρτυρίων[?], quæ ille solet nectere, ἐλέγχον[?] atque iudicem fidelissimum: hunc fortissimum hæreseon[?] expugnatorem euersoremq; è numero nostro ereptum vidimus: hanc grauissimam plagam inflictam scholæ nostræ, vulnusque toti ecclesiæ Christi,geminus impositum. Sed quid ago? Iamne videtis, clarissimi viri, & ornatissimi auditores, nos sensim ad secundum locum, de quo instituimus dicere, delapsos esse? Ante enim illud docuimus, hunc Doctorem nostrum, bonitate ingenij, eruditione, fide & diuinarum rerum intelligentia fuisse conditissimum, Theologorum doctissimum, & doctorum σχολαστικῶν[?]. Nunc secundum illud caput, quo de sanctissimæ huius arboris fructu nos acturos promisimus, videre paucis necesse est, vt theoricæ practicæ virtus adiungatur.
units.tr: [Greek word: the scan is too small here to read it letter by letter, so the Greek is marked as illegible below.] ... [Greek word; illegible in the scan] truth of divine doctrine, ... Yet what am I doing? Do you already see, distinguished sirs and most honoured listeners, that we have slipped gradually to the second point, about which we set out to speak? For before, we showed that this our teacher was most richly endowed in goodness of mind, learning, faith and understanding of divine things, the most learned of theologians and of learned scholastics [Greek word]. Now, as to the second head, in which we promised to speak of the fruit of this most holy tree, it is necessary to see briefly how the practical virtue is joined to the theoretical.

units.la: Illud autem est huiusmodi: alterum hunc Zachariam in-stum[?] fuisse coram Deo, & omnem operam navasse, vt ad amplissimas illas dotes ingenij à natura, arte, & cœlesti gratia collatas, sanctissimum vitæ institutum sibi adiungeret. Vos appello, qui hoc homine vti estis coram & familiariter: quicquid à natura habuit, nonne id doctrina humanarum artium elaboratum quàm fidelissimè, infusaq; è cœlo gratia perfectum, in studiis atque officiis pietatis, charitatis, humanitatisque occupauit? Hi fortassis incredibile, illi insidiosè dictum putauerint: perpaucos ta-men hac memoria nostra inueniri arbitror, quorum studio-sus animus aut officiosa mens cum huius mente & animo coparari possit. Atq; hæc non eò dicitur à me, quòd assentari placeat: Nam quid assentari fuerit[?]? non quòd amicitiæ indulgeam, aut couersationis familiari nostræ nā mihi à tanto viro pene semper abfuisse[?] molestum fuit admodum, nunc verò spe etiā exoptatæ couersationis hoc casu ademtam esse mihi videtur acerbissimum. Veritate dico, & ex animo dico vt sentio, me in hoc vno viro tantam studiorum vim[?], tantam officiorum gratiam animaduertisse, vt æquari ab vllo homine difficillimè potuerit, nedum exsuperari queat. Quî hoc intelligi potest? quia pietate omni, charitate, ac humanitate, cæteris satisfecit omnibus, sibi ipse nunquam satisfecit. At quis, obsecro, his rebus testis est? nemo non testis est, qui vel Vrsini nomé audiuerit. Audiuerit autem? imo eos ipsos testes si lubet appellare,qui nomen ipsius nescierunt, quamplurimi hac memoria nostra extiterunt, qui tanquam de ignota arbore suavissimes & saluberrimos fructus laborem eius avidissime rapuerunt, & nobiscum aquâ de huius riuo atq. visceribus à Christo profusam sitiuerunt. Atque hæc quidem exéplis, testimoniis, & argumentis confirmare longum esse: addo etiam, fortasse nonnullis vestrū inutile, aliis onerosum. Veruntamen ex multis decerpemus pauca, & velut frugalem mensam de uberrimo huius viri penu, & promptuario instruemus. Primum igitur pietatis studium ab ineunte ætate imbiberat: magnum quiddam est. Tempore procedente auxit fouitq. cumulatissimè: & hoc maius. Quod autem omnium maximum est ac nobilissimū, proiectā[?] iam ætate (si proiecta ætas quasi annorum quadraginta nouem dicenda est, cum hanc lucem ad illius veræ lucis testimonium accensam nobis eripuit & extinxit Deus) veruntamen proiectā ætate studium illud pietatis, vt cum maxime, confirmauit.
units.tr: Now the matter is of this kind: that this Zachariah was, as I say, just before God, and took every pains to join to that most ample endowment of mind, given by nature, art and heavenly grace, a most holy manner of life. I call upon you who are familiar with this man and have known him closely: whatever he had from nature, did he not, trained by the teaching of the humane arts most faithfully, and made perfect by grace poured from heaven, devote to studies and duties of piety, charity and humanity? Some may think this incredible, others may think it said with guile; yet I believe that in our memory only very few can be found whose zealous spirit or dutiful mind could be compared with his mind and spirit. And I do not say this from a wish to flatter: for what would be the point of flattering? Nor because I indulge in friendship, or in our familiar conversation; for it has been very troublesome to me that I was almost always away from so great a man, but now, by this chance, I seem to have been deprived of even the hope of the longed-for conversation, which is most bitter. I speak in truth, and I speak from my heart, as I feel: that in this one man I have noticed so great a force of study, so great a grace of duties, that it could hardly be matched by any man, much less surpassed. How can this be understood? Because he satisfied all others in every piety, charity and humanity, yet never satisfied himself. But who, I beg you, is a witness to these things? Everyone is a witness who has so much as heard the name of Ursinus. Heard it? Nay, if it please to call those very witnesses who did not know his name, very many have arisen in our memory who most eagerly snatched up his labour, as from an unknown tree, as most sweet and most wholesome fruits, and with us have thirsted for the water poured out from Christ in the stream and inward parts of this man. And indeed to confirm these things by examples, testimonies and arguments would be long; I add also that it might be useless to some of you, burdensome to others. Nevertheless, from many I will pick out a few, and, as from the rich storeroom and pantry of this man, I will set out a plain table. First, then, he had drunk in the zeal for piety from his earliest age: that is something great. As time went on, he nourished and cherished it most abundantly: and this is greater. But what is the greatest and most noble of all: in advanced age (if an advanced age is to be called about forty-nine years, since God snatched from us and extinguished that light, kindled as a witness to that true light), nevertheless in advanced age he strengthened that zeal for piety, as much as ever.

units.la: Deniq. omni tempore (vt paucis complectar, si possum, omnia) sine modo, sine fine, in pietatis & reuerentiæ Dei studium abreptus est, seque ipse in illud abdidit, vt à principiis sapientiæ facta indies progressione maxima ad perfectionem illam contenderet, qua ipsum iustissimus index coronauit Deus. Sanctissimi huius studij quod optimè nouit, & summopere probauit Deus, idoneos testes si non alios procurauit aut adhibuit ipse quâ summū illum καταλογισμῷ[?] Deum, & Dominum Iesû Christū, cui seruiebat in spiritu mentis suæ: duo tamen certissima istius rei documenta afferre possum, nimirum oratione fidei, & sacram meditationem. Quid ergo? dixerit quispiam, tuus illeic Vrsinus testes aduocauerit, ad habendas orationes suas? tanquam in theatro & non in conclaui, spectandum sese, & exaudiendum præbuit? minimè omnium. Homo simplicissimus, & ab omni specie humanæ istius vanitatis & κενοδοξίας alienissimus semper satis habuit, quod se à patre, qui in abdito videt, in abdito videri cognosceret: ab aliis videri cauit diligentissimè: Christiana sese oratione pie sustentauit, non ratione Pharisaica ostentauit. Diuinamus igitur, an ex coniectura dicimus? nequaquâ: sed ex certissima rei notitia confirmamus. Omninò ita fuit homo Dei, veritatis, ecclesiæ, fratrū afflictorū, omniū deniq; studiosissimus,& in erationem fidei intentissimus,qua tanqua alte losua die & noctem in luce rerum diuinarū versatus fer-uētissimis[?] precibus seruabat suos,& fidei aduersarios gladio verbi diuini profligabat. Sed quid ego de meditatione dicā ? illud quidem à te verissime, mi Vrsine, animaduersum esse cōperimus,quod olim Demosthenes, sermone & facto coprobauit, [illegible, ~45 letters]: adeo nihil meditatione indignum esse iudicasti. Nam quæ res facilis hunc virum effugit,quæso?quid difficile non assecutus est?Quidquid æternus ille Dei spiritus in libris scripturæ sacræ, per suos Prophetas & Apostolos exarauit,id totum summa fide accepit, maxima peruestigauit diligentia & attentissima meditatione ad miraculū vsque consecutus est.Hanc enim dignissimam esse operā statuebat, quæ in studiis illis sanctiorib.consumitur.Quod meditationis studium,quoties in eo homine tā graue, laboriosum, pertinax fuisse cogito(id autem non possum quin sæpe multùmq.cogitè) toties mihi elegantissimæ illius sententiæ in mentem venit, quam Basilius magnus pronunciauit, [illegible, ~30 letters], &c. Id est, cum difficilis sit peruestigatu veritas, hæc nobis omni ex parte inuestiganda est: nam si quemadmodum martium, ita etiam pietatis & religionis verę perceptio iis augetur accessionibus , quæ paulatim adhibentur,nihil est omnino, quod ij qui ingrediuntur in cognitionem illius, debeant possintve despicere. Quid vero, quod nihil à summis illis viris & Philosophorum principib. olim profectum est, quod hic noster [illegible, ~10 letters] collega non sit meditando assecutus,quamuis spinosum, arduum, abstrusum? Nonne moralia præcepta Aristotelis atque aliorum opt me tenuit? annon huic plana fuit rerum naturalium doctrina?non peruia?non expo-sita? Organi illius Aristotelei vim naturámq. non calluit absolutissime? cuius operisacumen alij tanquam spinas refugiunt obtinendi desperatione, alij vt Scyllam aut Charybdim tanquā iuuentuti ineluctabilem,ac perniciosam præcipite iudicio damnant, huius operis subtilitatem acerrimè,vtilitate facilimè Vrsinus vidit,& videndā aliis,tanquam in tabella spectandam,recognoscedámq.præbuit.Quid matheses?quatum fundamenta imaginatione mentis studiosa, documenta vero axiomatis, sue (ut illi vocant) postulatis ni[?] tuntur plurimum. Ne harum quidem abdicissima[?] præcepta fugerunt Vrsinum, quia meditatione seria, ac non volatica, aut leui quadam vellicatione ista omnia pertentauit. Nunc age, videamus, quos testes ad hunc rem simus productu-ri. De testibus aliis post videro, quàm ipsum sui ipsius testem adhibebo. Ipse Vrsinus toto perbreuis istius vitæ curriculo testis suarum meditationum exstitit locupletissimus, earumque virtutum omnium, quas ante percurrimus. Etenim quæ pietatis officia? quæ Christianæ charitatis? quæ humanitatis ab hoc tâto viro om-ssa sunt?
units.tr: Finally, at all times (to sum up everything briefly, if I can), without restraint and without limit, he was carried away into the zeal for piety and the reverence of God. He immersed himself in it, so that, advancing day by day with the greatest progress from the beginnings of wisdom, he strove toward that perfection with which the most just Judge, God, crowned him. As for this most holy zeal, which God knows best and has most highly approved, if God did not himself provide or bring forward other witnesses, to whom the supreme God and the Lord Jesus Christ, whom he served in the spirit of his mind, would be recognized, I can nonetheless offer two most certain proofs of this matter: namely, prayer offered in faith, and holy meditation. What then? someone may say, did your Ursinus summon witnesses to see his prayers? Did he present himself to be watched and heard, as on a stage and not in a private room? By no means. Being a most simple man, and entirely free from every form of human vanity and empty glory, he was always content that he was seen in secret by the Father who sees in secret; he took the greatest care not to be seen by others. He sustained himself piously by Christian prayer; he did not display himself by Pharisaical show. Are we then guessing, or speaking from conjecture? Not at all: we affirm it from the most certain knowledge of the matter. He was altogether a man of God, most devoted to the truth, to the Church, to the afflicted brethren, and in short to all; and he was most intent on prayer of faith, by which, as one standing high in the light of divine things, day and night, he kept his own safe with most fervent prayers and struck down the adversaries of the faith with the sword of the divine Word. But why should I speak of meditation? It has been most truly observed by us, my Ursinus, what Demosthenes once confirmed by word and deed, [illegible]: so greatly did you judge nothing unworthy of meditation. For what task, I ask, did this man find too easy to avoid, or what difficult thing did he not achieve? Whatever that eternal Spirit of God wrote in the books of holy Scripture through his Prophets and Apostles, he received with the greatest faith, investigated with the utmost diligence, and mastered with the most attentive meditation, even to a marvel. For he judged that work most worthy which is spent on those more holy studies. As often as I think how grave, laborious and persistent that study of meditation was in this man (and I cannot help thinking of it often and much), so often there comes to my mind that most elegant saying which Basil the Great pronounced, [illegible], etc. That is: since the truth is difficult to investigate, it must be investigated by us on every side; for if the perception of piety and true religion is increased, as the arts are, by additions gradually applied, then there is nothing at all which those who enter upon the knowledge of it ought or can despise. Moreover, is there anything that was ever achieved by those great men and princes of the philosophers which our colleague here did not attain by meditation, though it was thorny, arduous and abstruse? Did he not master the moral precepts of Aristotle and of others, the best? Was the doctrine of natural things not plain to him? Not accessible? Not set out? Did he not know most thoroughly the power and nature of that Aristotelian Organon? The keenness of that work others flee as thorns, despairing of mastering it; others condemn it with hasty judgment as a Scylla or Charybdis, an unavoidable and pernicious thing for youth; Ursinus saw most keenly the subtlety of this work, most readily its usefulness, and he presented it to be seen by others, as if on a tablet, and recognized and reexamined. What of the mathematical sciences? Their foundations rest greatly on the zealous imagination of the mind, and their proofs on axioms or, as they call them, postulates. Not even the most abstruse precepts of these escaped Ursinus, because he tested all these things with serious meditation, not fleetingly or by some light touch. Come now, let us see what witnesses we are going to bring forward for this matter. I will consider the other witnesses afterward; first I will call upon himself as a witness of himself. Ursinus himself, in the whole brief course of this life, was a most abundant witness of his meditations and of all those virtues which we have just run through. For what offices of piety, what of Christian charity, what of humanity were omitted by this great man?

units.la: Ac pietatem quidem in Deum ipse vidit, & agnouit, & obsignauit, & nunc demum etiam muneratus est Deus.
units.tr: And as for piety toward God, he himself saw it, and acknowledged it, and sealed it, and now at last God has also rewarded it.

units.la: Sed quia ex fructu ratio cognoscendarum arborum est commodissima, paulisper modo, si placet, ad fructus am-plissimæ illius pietatis animum aduertamus. Equidem vberiimos esse illos pietatis fructus ex sacris scripturis iudico, qui ad veritatis diuinæ illustrationem pertinent.
units.tr: But since the method of knowing trees is most convenient from their fruit, let us, if you please, pay attention for a little while to the fruits of that most ample piety. Indeed I judge those fruits of piety from the holy Scriptures to be most abundant which pertain to the illustration of divine truth.

units.la: Ecquando autem suas partes sanctissima hæc anima desiderari passa est in hoc argumento? quando non id egit, non sategit, non elaborauit, ut facem veritatis magis ac magis accenderet, præferrétque iis quibuscum agebat: ut tenebras errorum discuteret? Atque hæc pietatis officia charitate sunt coniunctissima, cùm ad ecclesiæ ædificationem proximorumque saltem occupentur. Quamobrem coniunctè iam dicturi sumus de vtroque officiorum genere, & demonstraturi, quàm strenuè hi miles Christi sermone, scriptis, animo toto laborauerit, ne vel latu pede ab officio suo discederet. Pietatis igitur & charitatis officia, ut apta inter se atque connexa sunt, ita in hoc viro vixerunt, processerunt, & præexerunt coniunctissimè. Nam si exercitationes spectemus ad hæc officia comparatas, Deum immortalem, quæ fides? quæ diligentia? quæ iniu-nia? quæ peruigilia? Nam harum omnium testificationem non fructus solum consecuti, nobis perhibere possunt: sed illa quoque corporis macerationi, illa domitura carnis, illa homo exterior ex antegressi laboribus confectus præmatura morte. Vtinam vero te, mi Vrsine, immani labore tuo non vsque adeo confecisses, & diutius nobis, diutius scholæ, diutius ecclesiæ profecisses! Sic enim habuisti rationem Dei, ut non haberes tui. Mi Vrsine, maximum Germaniæ lumen, ecclesiæ columen, singularis scholæ no-stræ parens, & Palatinatus immortale decus, utinam id nobis per te licuisset, ut te tibi ereptum aliquando, & ab assiduis tuis occupationibus avulsum diutius & nobis, & scholæ, & ecclesiæ toti vindicavissemus! Sic mihi elim[?] monenti respondebas, exercitationem corporis esse pa-rum utilem: ad quæ ego, igitur utilem esse, igitur esse hu-ius exercitationis cum illa vicissitudinē[?], hoc populo An-tiocheno elegantissimè à Chrysostomo demonstrari: ten-tatum frustra. Sed quid ago? facta est voluntas Domini: ta-cere præstat, quàm obloqui. Huius ergo tanti viri & tot modis exerciti officia, quis in sermone aut scripto un-quam demonstret defuisse, dum potuit? Ego profiteor[?] nescio, utrum me iam dolore magis afficiat commemoratio invidiæ illius diligentiæ, qua indefessenter in his officiis præstandis usus est, an juvet eorum fructuum perceptio[?], quos in omne, posteritate abiecta sui cura placuit transmittere: & si dolorem delet tempus, fructus tempora omnia superabit. Sermones privatos si specto, salutaris fuit officina mentis tuæ: si publicos, locupletissimum Dei (ut in rebus humanis extare potest) oraculum: & utrosque simul, divina illa quædam œconomia mysteriorum Dei perstringit aciem, & oculos mentis meæ. Tu vir Dei, tu sanctis quibusque rerum divinarum præsidiis instructissime Theologe, ac potius Θεολογώτατε, ecquando tandem supersedebas à veritate serio pronunciandā? Ecquando confertissimam illam mysteriorum vim penes te in armamentario tuo, id est, in mente conditam prolatabas? Ecquando nihil agebas? Admirabile quidem illud est quod dico, sed tamen verissimum, nunquam me præsente inane verbum excidit ex ore illius: adeò accurata, librata, expensa, explorata ab eo manabant omnia. De publicis verò sermonibus quid dicturi sumus? concionum accuratio, quas Heidelbergæ primùm habuerat, omnibus fuit admiratione: varia & multiplex lectionum eius eruditio multorum ingenia coluit, exornavit, provexit, fœcundavit, qui nunc longè latèque in orbe Christiano plantant, serunt, rigant hortum & agricolationem Dei, qui domum Dei viventis ædificant, qui deniq. vicariâ operâ suâ hunc fidelissimum præceptorem suum quasi redivivum exhibent. Quin illa ipsa ordinaria mensa, quæ in domo sapientiæ olim vtebatur, sic strata fuit floribus amœnissimis fructibúsque variis sanctioris illius philosophiæ, sic instructa commeatu vetere & nouo, vt non aliquod triclinium Philosophiæ vulgaris, sed penetraл ipsum esse sapientiæ diuinæ videretur. Ibi vox scripturæ personabat, quæ sola nuncia est atque interpres sapientiæ, aderant alumnæ eius honestas & modestia, nec minus (vt verbis vtamur Euftachij apud Macrobium) cū sobrietate pietas. Aderat historia multiplex, naturalis, gesta: assidebant scientiæ omnes, & aliæ ex aliis interdu ctu suo coronam totam velut interspiratione facta recreabant. Hæc in numero sermonum si qui volet reponere, per me licet: verumtamen has iustas fuisse lectiones scio, insignes scientiæ notis, & gratia adspersas admirabili. Atque hæc quidem sermonum virtutes amplissimæ. Quis autem non miretur, has omnes virtutes stylo, optimo illo & præstantissimo dicendi effectore ac magistro, indies limatas & ornatas esse? Placebat enim tanto huic viro, non modo orationis, sed ingenij quoque vbertatem stylo depascere: quod omnibus dicendi docendique studiosis faciendum præcepit Tullius. Scribebantur itaque illius lectiones, commentationes, animadversiones, notæ: & cum ipsi ad memoriam, tum aliis ad doctrinam instrumenta de scripto parata habebantur. Ex omnibus tamen scriptionibus iste nihil tacere mihi videtur mirum, quàm quod deripiebat & suffurabatur de eis tempus, quo ad quæstiones plurimas grauissimasque respondere. Aperiebat rerum intelligentiam, consiliorum demonstrabat vias consulentibus, tum denique erat officiosissimus, quum nihil minus quam de faciendo officio suo cogitare putabatur. Testes huic rei sunt viri docti, indocti, proceres, tenues, propinqui, longinqui, amici, aduersarij: quorum nemo iure queri possit, aut se ab hoc neglectu, aut sibi non satisfactum admirabiliter. Adeo studebat comiter, clementer, fideliterque omnibus benefacere, vt lucraretur omnes, & Domino Christo adiungeret. Hæc priuata sunt, dixerit fortasse quispiam: at vbi publica illius pietatis & charitatis argumenta? hæc publice ita sunt testata, vt lucerent meridie clarius. Nam quæ scripta elegantissima olim Heydelber-gę [?] vidimus, ea pleraque ex officina hac prodierunt: quæ hic, hic, apud nos ab hinc annos quinque emanarunt, ex eadem sunt manu: quam manum hic duxit virtute sua, illic iam certissima quiete donauit Deus. Quid tu, o noue Euthyches, grauius hac manu expertus es, si a Dei manu, quae te vexat, agitat, cruciat, urit, profligat, diiscessertis? Qui Bellerophontes chimaeram tuam, qui Hercules hydram valentiore verberauit ictu? quis cerberum illud ubiquitatis monstrum contudit vehementius? Sed ne in publica & peruulgata re insistamus diu, ne tu quoque iam, Arie Sarmata, huius herois nostri, quamuis a nobis professi, dexteram effugies. Hic idem nobis curauit, limauit, polivit, acuit & aptauit arma ad scelerati tui dogmatis perniciem comparata: quorum vires de industria visum est tibi indicere, ut ad Deum tandem respicias, aeternumq. Dei aeterni filium, qui cum patre unum est, fuit, & futurus est in sempiterna secula, venerariis: sin minus, ab hoc tanto viro euictionem impietatis tuae, a Deo casum, ruina, ex[?]tiumq. Tuum denunciari intelligas: Quam igitur fidem & diligentia in hoc sanctissimo fuauissimoq. animo patemus exti[?]tisse, qui nullam diei horam, nullum momentum frustra abire passus est? In his duab. potissimum causis spectantur pietatis charitatisq. documenta, si vera doctrina propugnatur, si oppugnatur & expugnatur falsa. Quis sanctius, doctius, aptius, pressius, vehementius, fidelius, diligentius, fortius insanam doctrinam queat excutere? quis falsae grauius obsistere? De humanitate vero ut dicamus paucis, quae maior est illius gratia, quam ea ipsa, de qua ante diximus, in quaestionibus explicandis consiliisque dandis accuratior? quae quidem hoc in viro semper tam elaborata fuit, ut omnes nodos expediuerit euidentissime, non sapientiae humanae verbis, sed efficacitate spiritus, omniaq, sophismata argutissime, promptissime, summa cum dexteritate & agilitate retexerit. Quid ergo hic mihi quisquam morosum fuisse hominem, difficilemque obiiciat? scilicet ut ignauis pueris, aetiosis & iis qui nuces pro pugillaribus habent, morosi sunt ij, qui studiis suis dant operam: sic vanis hominib. morosi sunt quiq. diligentissimi. Nam mihi quidem & vitis bonis, qui norunt ipsum, nihil magis come, nihil blandius visum est. Quod si quando ipsi religio fuit ab instituto opere discedere, mihi certe non minus religioni fuisset auoca-[?] quia aut premebatur occupatione, aut detinebatur ad uersa valetudine. De occupationibus,ego, inquit Tullius,animi pendere solco,quâ semel quid orsus tradu-cor alio:neque tàm facilè interrupta contexo,quàm ab-solùo instituta.De valetudine nemo tam bardus est,quin, duce natura,ab experimento suo,si mihi non credit, do-ceatur.Itaque sucus est,qui laboriosæ negotium facessit [illegible, ~4 letters]pi:Morosus est,ineptus,importunus,qui officij loco du-xerit tam damnosam diligentiâ.Cuiusmodi homines ple-rosque videas tam ineptos atque iniquos viris bonis , ut eos præ se homines esse negent,nisi diserte ( quod aiunt) secum saltare velint. Quid?quod summos quosque viros graujssimè de ea re videmus conquceri ? se à sanctis gra-uioribúsq.studiis,& cũ functione sua conuenientib. teme-rè abripi,se in rebus nihili & sermonibus otiosis conse-nescere inuitos,ac pene sordescere maximo cum dolore suo & publico ecclesiarum damno.Nazianzenus,Ambro-sius,Augustinus quoties & quàm indignè testantur à se hæc auocamenta accipi? Prudetius certè faciunt, modò ne quid nimis,qui magnum illum Basilii & Chrysostomi imitantur.Hi.n. ad commendandam functionè suam ita se abdiderunt, ut caverent sibi ab auocationibus eiusmodi, quæ aut temere,aut præter officium literatis viris ac celeberrimis obtrudi solent. Videbant si importunes salutatores istos principio admiseris,eos & sibi ius illud indignissimè vindicare,ut viris bonis molesti sint , & alios exemplo suo ad importunitatem eandè accersere:optimè autem prospectû esse,si à principio caueris & inofficiosa hæc officia averteris.In hûc igitur modum Deo & ecclesiæ hæc sanctissima anima ministrauit,aut affectæ valetudini.Morosus es,ô importune , qui id inofficiose postulas,quod officiosè denegare Ursinos potuit, & ex officio debuit.Res ecclesiæ agentem non excusare, imprudentia est:curantem corpus,inhumanitas:utrumq. verò repugnat charitatis legi. Etsi ne hoc quidem pacto (ut ad postremum sermonis nostri caput veniamus) hic noster fuit impeditus,quin iam deiectis manibus,titubante lingua , & præclusis prope faucibus animus anhelus in studia illa officiaque incumberet. Nam quoties de schola hac nostra defectus viribus,exsacco & exsangui corpore, cogitauit?quoties otiari se in acerbissimo ille inualetudinis negotio conquestus est:quàm infractè in sua illa scriptione ptione instituta perstitit,donec animus ille inuictus atque indomitus ab afflictionib.ex fracto, victo, edomitoque corpore euolauit. O beatum illum,fidelem & prudentem seruum,quem veniés Dominus eius reperit ita facie-tem!beatum cui Dominus est Deus! Atq.hunc quidem optimum virum,& nobis coniunctissimum,in illo Sionis monte in ciuitate Dei viui,in caelesti Hierusalem inter myriadas angelorum,in conuentu & ecclesia primogenitorum,qui conscripti sunt in caelis,apud iudicem vniuersorum, Deum spiritusq.iustorum cõsummatorũ,apud Noui Testamenti mediatorem Iesum , & sanguinem aspersionis salutarem versari, cum antecedentes illae res, nimirum caelestes ingenij dotes,fides,spes,studium pietatis, charitatis,humanitatisque & officia omnia confirmat euidentissimè, tu exitus ille felicissimus demonstrauit. Nam, vt illud taceam,iamdiu animu illius vixisse Deo, & huic detestabili incertóq.mundo fuisse mortuum(sic.n.sanctè cum Apostolo Christi de re sancta loquimur,) quum eam sermones de fide,spe,carnis resurrectione, vita,gloria,& felicitate aeterna habebantur,vt annuebat! vt acclamabat!vt arridebat blande! vt oculos sursum ad redemptorem nostrum erigebat! cui vt seipsum iam diu commendauerat,ita animam suam tandem reddidit placidissimè,& ex profundo in amoenissimum salutis & tranquillitatis portum ad optimi parentis vnas translatus est. Quis obsecro,hic no exclamet sanctissimè atq.exoptet mecum?Moriar ego morte iustorum,& sit finis meus similis illius. Vidit.n.profectò vidit certa fide caelum sibi apertum,Christum principem & consummatorem fidei suae sedentem ad dexteram maiestatis in caelis, gloriam ineomparabilem sibi constitutam, chorum coelestis ecclesiae sibi gratulantem,denique ad salutem omnia,cum adeo placide lenitérque sua ipsius anima creatori Deo, & patri spirituum tradidit, vt in aeternum cum eo viueret. Haec igitur illa est anima, clarissimi viri & auditores ornatissimi,illa,inquam,anima sanctissima, & Deo accepta, quae his diebus nobis erepta est magno malo nostro:etsi (quemadmodum olim Cyprianus & Ambrosius dixerunt) non amissimus eam,sed praemissimus suo tempore secuturi:non amissimus,sed reddidimus,vt Epictetus monet: is enim qui dederat, repetiit, & recepit ad se. Quid[?] ergo lugemus eum, si non amisimus? Lugemus receptum à nobis tam suaue & commodum ad Dei gloriam instrumentum: lugemus iam malorum impendentium & iam iam instantium praesignificationem: lugemus praesentissimam impietatis, iniustitiae omniisque perfidiae inundationem: quae eo vehementius fere inualescit, quo magis subtrahi à Deo videt haec curationis & salutis armamenta. Quid enim? an non lugere mus id nobis instrumentum eripi de quo si vlla encomia satis praedicari possunt, nefas dissimulare est? At vos quidem, clarissimi viri, qui hic adestis, plura scio posse praestare in hac causa quam adhuc fecerim, aut quicquam facere. Nam & diuturna illa familiaritas, quae cum nostro VRSINO vobis intercesserit, materiam vobis contulit, & doctrina multiplex eloquentiam. Sed quia vobis huius rei primas ex officio & veritate defero, & vos mihi secundas tribuistis: hoc mihi aequo animo (spero) condonabitis, si Theologum de instrumentis hoc nostro Theologo dicturum subdidero in locum meum, eaque ipsa quae de Athanasio fortissimo illo veritatis propugnatore errorumque antagonista dicebat, huic tribuero. Hic fidelis Domini operarius, vir Dei, conciliator omnium, tuba veritatis, ecclesiae columen, patrus athleta Dei, & firmus secundum fidem, quae est in Christum defensioni aduersus venenatas haereses accommodatissimus: qui etsi pacificus erat moderatusque in rebus omnibus, id tamen nunquam animo aequo pertulit, vt propter pacem praederetur Deus, sed bellator fuit in hac causa vehemens & heros inuictissimus: hos laudans, illos moderate verberans: horum frigus excitans, illorum compescens ardorem: his ne ruerent prospiciens: illi vt[?] ercigerentur prostrati curans: simplex moribus, multiplex administratione, sapiens sermone, sapientior mente: hic ergo sic vixit, sic institutus est, sic alios instituit, vt cum vita moresque ipsius, quasi terminos ponant iustae administrationi, cum ipsius dogmata quasi leges orthodoxae fidei habeantur. Haec nos de Theologo nostro, vt olim Theologus de Athanasio. An vero instrumentum eiusmodi adempturus nobis & ecclesiae fuisset Deus, nisi peccatis nostris infestus esset? Nonne Deus Enochum recipiens & assumens ad se, improbitatem mundi condemnauit: non totus Israel Elisæo sublato
units.tr: Yet when did this most holy soul ever allow its duties to be missed in this subject? When did it not strive for this, not labour at it, not toil, so that it might kindle the torch of truth more and more and hold it up before those with whom it dealt, and dispel the darkness of errors? These duties of piety are most closely joined with charity, since both are occupied at least with the building up of the Church and the good of our neighbours. Therefore we shall now speak of both kinds of duty together, and show how vigorously this soldier of Christ laboured, by speech, by writings and with his whole mind, lest he depart from his office even by a hair's breadth. The duties of piety and of charity, as they are fitted and connected with one another, so in this man they lived, advanced and went before one another most closely. For if we consider the exercises prepared for these duties, immortal God, what faith! what diligence! what labours! what sleepless nights! Of all these, not only the fruits they gained can bear witness for us, but also his body's wasting, his body's mortification, and that outer man worn out by the labours that went before, by his untimely death. Would that you, my Ursinus, had not worn yourself out so greatly by your immense labour, and had made progress for us, for the school and for the Church for a longer time! For you so regarded the honour of God that you had no regard for yourself. My Ursinus, greatest light of Germany, pillar of the Church, unique parent of our school and immortal glory of the Palatinate, would that it had been granted to us through you, that we might at some time have claimed you for ourselves, snatched back from yourself and torn away from your constant occupations, and kept you longer for us, for the school and for the whole Church! For when I advised you, you answered that bodily exercise is of little use; to which I, on the contrary, say that it is useful, and that the value of this exercise, together with that alternation of work and rest, was demonstrated most elegantly by Chrysostom to the people of Antioch: this was attempted in vain. But what am I doing? The will of the Lord is done: it is better to be silent than to complain. Who, then, could ever show, in speech or writing, that the duties of so great a man, exercised in so many ways, were lacking while he was able to perform them? I confess I do not know whether the recollection of that remarkable diligence, with which he tirelessly used himself in performing these duties, now grieves me more, or whether the enjoyment of those fruits pleases me, which he chose to hand down for all posterity, setting aside care for himself; and if time removes the grief, the fruits will surpass all times. If I look at his private discourses, they were a healthful workshop of your mind; if at his public ones, the richest oracle of God (so far as such a thing can exist among human affairs); and both together, that divine economy of God's mysteries, strikes the edge of my sight and the eyes of my mind. You, man of God, most thoroughly equipped theologian with all the holy resources of divine things, or rather most God-taught theologian, when did you ever shrink from speaking the truth seriously? When did you bring forth that very dense force of the mysteries stored in your armoury, that is, in your mind? When did you do nothing? What I say is admirable, yet most true: never, while I was present, did an empty word fall from his mouth; so exact, balanced, weighed and tested were all the things that flowed from him. But what shall we say about his public sermons? The accuracy of the sermons, which he first delivered at Heidelberg, was a wonder to all; the varied and manifold learning of his lectures cultivated, adorned, advanced and made fruitful the minds of many, who now far and wide in the Christian world plant, sow and water the garden and cultivation of God, who build up the house of the living God, and who, by their own work in his place, display this most faithful teacher of theirs as if restored to life. Indeed, that very ordinary table which once he used in the house of wisdom was so spread with lovely flowers and various fruits of that more holy philosophy, and so furnished with provisions old and new, that it seemed not the dining-room of common philosophy but the very inner sanctuary of divine wisdom. There the voice of Scripture sounded, which alone is the messenger and interpreter of wisdom; there were present her companions, honesty and modesty, and no less (to use the words of Eustathius quoted by Macrobius) piety together with sobriety. There was history in many forms, natural and of deeds; all the sciences sat by; and some, in their turn, refreshed the whole company as if by a single breath of inspiration. If anyone wishes to count these among the sermons, I permit it: yet I know that these were just lectures, distinguished by the marks of learning and sprinkled with a wonderful grace. And these are the very great virtues of his sermons. Who, however, would not marvel that all these virtues were daily polished and adorned by the style, that best and most excellent maker and master of speaking? For it pleased this great man to feed not only the richness of his speech but also of his mind with the pen; which Tully prescribed should be done by all who study speaking and teaching. Thus his lectures, commentaries, observations and notes were written down, and written records were kept both as aids to his own memory and as tools for the learning of others. Yet of all his writings, this one thing seems to me remarkable: the time he snatched and stole from them to answer very many and most weighty questions. He opened up understanding of things, showed the paths of counsel to those who consulted him, and finally he was most obliging exactly when he was thought to be thinking least about performing his duty. Witnesses to this are learned and unlearned men, nobles and commoners, near and distant, friends and opponents; none of them could justly complain either that he was neglected by this man or that he was not satisfied, to a remarkable degree. So eagerly did he strive to do good to all courteously, mercifully and faithfully, that he gained them all and joined them to the Lord Christ. These are private matters, someone perhaps will say: but where are the public proofs of that piety and charity? These were attested publicly in such a way that they shone clearer than midday. For the most elegant writings we once saw at Heidelberg came mostly from this workshop; those which have issued here, here among us, for the past five years, are from the same hand: a hand which here he guided by his virtue, and there God has now granted him most certain rest. What, O new Eutyches, have you suffered more grievously from this hand, if you have departed from the hand of God, which vexes, troubles, torments, burns and crushes you? Which Bellerophon struck your chimera, which Hercules struck the hydra with a stronger blow? Who crushed that monster of ubiquity, Cerberus, more violently? But lest we dwell long on a public and widely known matter, lest you too, Aries the Sarmatian, escape the right hand of this our hero, though we have professed you as our own. This same man took care to file, polish, sharpen and fit the weapons prepared for the destruction of your wicked doctrine; it has been your wish to challenge their strength on purpose, so that at last you may look back to God and worship the eternal Son of the eternal God, who is one with the Father, who was, and will be, for everlasting ages: otherwise, understand that the overthrow of your impiety, your fall, ruin and destruction from God, will be announced by this great man. What faith and diligence, then, do we see this most holy and sweet-natured soul to have shown, who allowed no hour of the day and no moment to pass in vain? In these two chief causes the proofs of piety and charity are seen: if true doctrine is defended, and if false doctrine is attacked and overthrown. Who could shake off mad doctrine more holily, more learnedly, more aptly, more closely, more forcefully, more faithfully, more diligently or more bravely? Who could withstand false teaching more gravely? As for his humanity, to say a few words: what greater grace is there than that same quality of which we spoke before, greater accuracy in explaining questions and giving counsel? This was always so carefully wrought in this man that he unravelled all knots most clearly, not with the words of human wisdom but by the efficacy of the Spirit, and most keenly, readily and with the greatest skill and agility unwove all sophisms. Why, then, may anyone object that this man was a fussy or difficult person? Just as those who devote themselves to their studies seem fussy to idle boys, to the affected and to those who take nuts for writing-tablets, so the most diligent are fussy to empty men. For to me, and to good men who knew him, nothing seemed more courteous or more pleasant than he. But if ever it was a scruple for him to turn aside from the work he had undertaken, it certainly would have been no less a scruple for me, when he was weighed down by business or held back by poor health. Tully says: "I usually depend on the state of my mind, from which, once I have begun something, I am drawn to another; nor do I weave together things once interrupted as easily as I finish what I have begun." As for poor health, no one is so stupid that, guided by nature, he cannot be taught it by his own experience, if he does not believe me. Therefore he is a fool who causes trouble to one busy at work; he is fussy, foolish, unseasonable, who counts as a duty such a harmful diligence. You may see most people so foolish and unjust towards good men that they deny that they themselves are human beings, unless, as they say, they wish to dance with them openly. What then? When we see the greatest men complaining most bitterly about this matter, that they are rashly dragged away from holy and weightier studies and from tasks fitting their office, and that against their will they grow stale among trifles and idle talk, becoming almost sordid, to their great grief and to the public loss of the churches. How often and how unworthily do Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose and Augustine bear witness that these distractions are imposed upon them? The Prudentius certainly do this, provided they do not overdo it, who imitate that great Basil and Chrysostom. For these men so withdrew themselves in order to commend their office that they took care to guard themselves against interruptions of this kind, which are usually forced upon learned and very famous men, either carelessly or contrary to their duty. They saw that if you admit these importunate visitors at the start, they will most unworthily claim for themselves the right to be a nuisance to good men, and by their example they will draw others into the same importunity; but that it was best to look out from the beginning, and to turn away these unseasonable duties. In this way this most holy soul served God and the Church, or served his weakened health. You are fussy, O importunate one, who ask unseasonably for what Ursinus could have refused courteously and was bound to refuse as a duty. To fail to excuse a man who is busy with the affairs of the Church is imprudence; to fail to care for the body is inhumanity; and both are opposed to the law of charity. Yet not even in this way (so that we may come to the last part of our discourse) was this man of ours so hindered that, with his hands now sunk down, his tongue faltering and his throat almost shut, his panting spirit did not still bend itself to those studies and duties. For how often, when weakened in strength, emptied and bloodless in body, did he think of this school of ours? How often did he complain that he was idle in the bitter business of his poor health: with what unbroken perseverance he kept to his undertaken writing, until that unconquered and untamed spirit flew out from the body broken, defeated and subdued by afflictions! O blessed faithful and wise servant, whom his master, coming, finds so doing! Blessed is he whose Lord is God! And this best of men, and most closely joined to us, is now, we are most clearly assured, in that Mount Zion, in the city of the living God, in the heavenly Jerusalem, among the myriads of angels, in the assembly and Church of the firstborn who are written in heaven, before the Judge of all, God, and the spirits of the just made perfect, before Jesus the mediator of the New Testament, and the sprinkled blood that speaks salvation; since those former things, namely his heavenly gifts of mind, faith, hope, zeal for piety, charity, humanity and all his duties, confirm this most clearly, that most happy end of his has shown it. For, to pass over the fact that long ago his soul lived to God and was dead to this detestable and uncertain world (for so we speak holily of a holy matter with the apostle of Christ), when discourses on faith, hope, the resurrection of the flesh, life, glory and eternal happiness were held, how he nodded assent! how he cried out! how he smiled sweetly! how he raised his eyes upward to our Redeemer! To whom, as he had long since committed himself, so at last he gave up his soul most peacefully, and was carried from the depths into the most lovely harbour of salvation and tranquillity, into the arms of the best of fathers. Who, I beg you, would not here cry out most holily and wish with me: "Let me die the death of the righteous, and let my end be like his." For he certainly saw with sure faith heaven opened to him, Christ the prince and perfecter of his faith sitting at the right hand of majesty in the heavens, incomparable glory laid up for him, the choir of the heavenly Church rejoicing with him, and finally all things for salvation; so calmly and gently did he give up his soul to its Creator God and the Father of spirits, that he might live with him for ever. This, then, is that soul, distinguished men and most adorned hearers, that soul, I say, most holy and acceptable to God, which in these days has been snatched from us to our great harm: although (as Cyprian and Ambrose once said) we have not lost it, but sent it on ahead, to follow us in its time; we have not lost it, but given it back, as Epictetus advises: for he who gave it has asked for it again and taken it back to himself. Why then do we mourn him, if we have not lost him? We mourn the instrument, so sweet and useful for the glory of God, that has been received back from us; we mourn the foretoken of evils hanging over us and now already at hand; we mourn the very present flood of impiety, injustice and all faithlessness, which grows strong almost in proportion as it sees these armaments of healing and salvation withdrawn from God. For what? Do we not mourn that this instrument has been taken from us, of which, if any praises can be sufficiently spoken, it is wrong to be silent? But you, distinguished men, who are here present, I know can do more in this cause than I have yet done or can do. For that long familiarity which you had with our Ursinus gave you the material, and your manifold learning gives you eloquence. But since I offer you the first place in this matter, as is due to you by duty and truth, and you have assigned me the second, I hope you will pardon me in good spirit if I put in my place a theologian who will speak about the instruments of our theologian, and I shall assign to him what was said about Athanasius, that most brave defender of truth and opponent of errors. This faithful worker of the Lord, man of God, reconciler of all, trumpet of truth, pillar of the Church, the Father's athlete of God, and firm according to the faith which is in Christ, most fitted for defence against poisonous heresies: who, although he was peaceable and moderate in all things, never bore it with an even mind that God should be betrayed for the sake of peace, but was a vehement fighter in this cause and an unconquered hero: praising some, moderately lashing others; stirring up the coldness of some, restraining the heat of others; watching to prevent some from rushing into ruin; caring that others, cast down, should be raised up; simple in morals, manifold in administration, wise in speech, wiser in mind. He, then, so lived, was so formed, and so formed others, that his life and morals are held as bounds for just administration, and his doctrines as the laws of orthodox faith. These things we say of our theologian, as once the theologian said of Athanasius. Would God indeed have taken away such an instrument from us and from the Church, unless he were hostile to our sins? Did not God, when he received and took Enoch up to himself, condemn the wickedness of the world? Did not all Israel, when Elisha was taken up, burn ... not after the extinction of Josiah was Judah miserably harried and overthrown? Did not ... Stilicho say, as a companion...

units.la: [?] The line "illi vt ercigerentur" is uncertain; the scan reads roughly "vt[?]ercigerentur", probably "vt[?]" for "vt" plus a word such as "percigerentur" or "exterrigerentur". sublato conflagrauit? non extincto Iosia fuit exagitatus miserè & euersus Iuda? non comitem Stiliconem dixisse legimus, Ambrosio tanto viro recedente de corpore, interitum Italiae imminere? non sublato Augustino Africa, Luthero Germania, Bucero Anglia diuexata est? Ac mihi quidem videtur Dominus & aliorum clarissimorum hominum, & huius lectissimi instrumenti morte praesentem ira pergrauem explicare, seuerūmque iudicium ingratissimae huic generationi portendere. Sed quid si mentes [illegible, ~9 letters] ad istarum rerum cogitationem salubremque terrorem non sermone solum, verum etiam opere excitauit frequentissime? Legimus profecto, vidimus, animaduertimus, quam magna Deus variaque signa Coelo & Terra edere soleat, priusquam sanctis illas luces ex humano genere eximat: quam vehementer coelum & terra quasi luctu induat, quā gravibus miscere omnia minetur incendiis. Nimirum ut nos quamplurimis testificationibus ad bonam frugem reuocet: ostendat a se ira suam in alia potius omnia degenerari, quam ut genus humanum feriat: tandem vero quum prope est, ut in nostra ipsorum capita sagittas irae suae iaculetur propter laesam saepius patientiā suam, ut demonstret summos illos viros, quos in deliciis tanquam peculiū habet, ex incendio communi, malorumque diluvio iā exundante eripi. Haec sunt igitur quae lugemus, clarissimi viri & auditores ornatissimi, haec deflemus, his commouemur atque percellimur: ferrei fumus, nisi gravissimis illis & seuerissimis illis castigationum praedictis portentisque frangimur, ut Deo Opt. Max. obsequamur. Aliud quiddam praeterea video summopere lugendum & lamentabile. Quid aliud est? quod si iudicia minas non sequantur proximè, tantis viris sublatis mundus insolescit, veritatem cuniculis & apertas vi appetit, haereses excitat, se confirmat in omni malo, sibi gratulatur eos e medio tolli, qui rationibus suis aduersantur, ecclesias pessumdat, pastoribus suis, doctoribus & custodibus fidelissimis destitutas. Haec immania periscula, haec asperrima incommoda, haec mala turpissima piae mentes verberant, torquent, conficiunt: horum metus, (ut aliquid de me ipso dicam) non tam suauissimi & continentissimi collegae nostri, doctoris potentissimi, animae beatissimae exitum flere iubet, quam nostram omnium destitutionem & malorum praesagitionem, quae gratiose auertat Dominus. Habetis à me, Clarissimi viri & auditores ornatissimi, penicillo rudi adumbratam vitam Vrsini illius nostri, cuius memoria in æternum benedicta futura est. Scimus neque illum diu lugendū esse, neq; memoriam eius prosequendam commiseratione. Si cuius dolore hac oratione nostra refricauimus, is quǫso mecū recordetur, quantum boni ab illo hauserimus superstite. Quicquid ab eo accepimus boni, eo non accepimus, vt ipsius inuideamus bono. Id potius singuli videamus, vt quemadmodum ille bonus in omnes fuit, sic in bona illa spiritualia incumbamus, quibus efficiamur boni. Studiis bonis optime incubuit: studeamus & nos. Optimum illum the-saurum, quem studia comparauerant, & gratia Dei e cœlo infuderat, prolixè omnibus expo-suit: & nos exemplum illius imitati conseruis [?] nostris vtenda fruenda bona, si qua sunt in nobis per Dei gratiam, concedamus: pietati charitati, humanitati, paci, publico bono consulamus, & earam Deo in hac schola, velut theatro lectissimo, studiosam iuuentutem doctrina & opere ad eundem finem perducamus, nosque & alios in fide, quae est in Christum, conser-uemus. Tu quoq. iuuentus charissima, tu corona iucundissima, quae doctorem illum tuum tibi, nobis, scholae, ecclesiae, mundo, fuisse diutius seruatum cupis incolume: ne defleto amplius absente, quem tibi exemplo vitae fuisse prae-sentem gratularis, & quo nunc etiam vteris percepta adeo illustrium scriptorum, quae exaraauit [?], side. Da potius operam, vt de numero tuo plures Vrsinos suscites. Vnum ex carne hæredem habet, quem futurum quoque sperɑmus hæredem pietatis: at vobis omnibus via pietatis ad hæreditatem hanc adeundam & percipiendam aperta est. Agedū, iam satis creuistis, adite, atque in possessionem hæreditatis illius pedem ponite. Non deest vobis ingenium: non studiorum adiumenta, non via deficit: vnum restat, nec vobis voluntas desit, ne vos destituatis ipsi. Voluntatem igitur vestram, adeoque vos ipsos ad eiusmodi studia sedulo adhibete, ad officia pietatis, charitatis, humanitatis optima fide diligentiaque maxima: in his desudate & elaborate: alterum VRSINUM quisque nobis officio vestro sistite. Quod si non omnes illud VRSINI aurum, argentum, gemmas ad huius tabernaculi ædificationem potestis apportare, ne continuo animum abijcite, etiam ferrum, aes, lignum, dignum,lana caprina,netum,Deo accepta sunt. Qui du- ces aut primani nequitis esse,ne desperate:& secundanis, tertianis,quartanis,decumanis,vicesimanis opus est:his quoque stationem esse testatur Christus in domo patris sui. Ne ianitorem quidem eff: vertetur vitio in Dei vi- uētis domo : hoc enim Dauidem illum (qui vir erat se- cundum cor Domini) nequaquam pudu̅t. Neque iam pudet,neque poenitebit vnquam,si vos in hanc arenam, in hæc studia in hæc officia intendatis, si exempla hæc persequamini. Altius (inquit Fabius) ibunt,qui ad sum- ma nitetur,quàm qui præsumpta desperatione quò ve- lint euadendi,statim circa ima subsiterint. Quid autē? neq; nos qui dicimus absumus prope ab illius viri ex- emplo (de me ipse loquor,collegarum dona admiror,& ex officio colo) neque vos id poteritis assequi vestra ip- sorum industria. At Vrsinus ille,vir ille recordatio- nis Dei,( nam hoc nomen Hebraeum sonat) nobis ere- ptus est: iam tāti illius viri sola nobis adest recordatio. Quid igitur facturi sumus? Ille Iah,Deus ille fortis, qui Zachariam suum recordatus ad tantum fidei,pietatis,do- ctrinae culmen euexerat, Christus propheta ille & rex noster vnicus nobis est praesentissimus tū æterna maie- state sua,tum sancti spiritus communicatione. Huc prae- ceptorem adeamus, huncconsulamus magistrum, hunc sequamur duce: huius gratia & ope freti ad studia illa, ad quae vocati sumus, & ad officia constantissimè per- tendamus.Ne glorietur haereticorum impietas.neq. in- tumescat aduersantiu pectus,quod confracta fuerit vir- ga percutientis ipsos: nam e radice serpentis prodi-ura potiusest vipera,& fructus illius futurus praeteruolans (quod olim Esaias vaticinatus est) quàm vt à Deo no- stro deseramur,& violentis insanorum hominum furiis, aut ludicris amentium omniis , quibus ( proh dolor) inuaduntur plus satis ecclesiae,permittamur.
units.tr: The passage opens with a note on the scan itself, which is not part of the book's text. Here the Latin is translated: Ah, but what if he [illegible] roused their minds to the thought of these things and to a wholesome terror, not by speech alone but also, very often, by deeds? Surely we have read, we have seen, we have observed how great and various signs God is wont to display in heaven and on earth before he takes those holy lights from the human race; how vehemently heaven and earth clothe themselves as in mourning, how they threaten to mingle all things in grievous conflagrations. Doubtless it is so that he may recall us to good conduct by very many testimonies; that he may show his anger is more inclined to fall on anything else than on the human race; and finally, when it is near that he is about to hurl the arrows of his wrath upon our own heads, because his patience has been offended so often, so that he may show that those most eminent men, whom he holds as his special treasure, are snatched out of the common conflagration and the flood of evils now overflowing. These, then, are the things we mourn, most distinguished sir and most accomplished hearers; these are what we bewail, by these we are moved and struck down. Unless we are broken by those most grave and severe castigations and portents foretold, we are, as iron smoke, ... so that we may obey God, Best and Greatest. Besides this, I see another thing that is greatly to be mourned and lamentable. What else is it? That if judgments do not closely follow the threats, with such men taken away the world grows insolent, seeks the truth by stealth and openly, stirs up heresies, confirms itself in every evil, and rejoices that those who oppose its reasoning are removed from the midst; it ruins the churches, left destitute of their ministers, teachers and most faithful guardians. These immense perils, these very harsh inconveniences, these most shameful evils strike, torment and wear down pious minds; the fear of these things (to say something of myself) bids us weep not so much for the death of our most sweet and most continent colleague, that most powerful teacher, and the most blessed end of his soul, as for the loss of all of us and the foreboding of evils, which the Lord graciously turn away. You have from me, distinguished sirs and most accomplished hearers, the life of that Ursinus of ours, sketched with a rough brush, whose memory will be blessed forever. We know that he is not to be mourned long, nor is his memory to be pursued with pity. If anyone has by this speech of ours reopened a wound of grief, let him, I beg, remember with me how much good we drew from him while he lived. Whatever good we received from him, we did not receive so that we should envy his good. Rather, let each of us see to it that, as he was good to all, so we apply ourselves to those spiritual goods by which we may be made good. He devoted himself excellently to good studies: let us too be eager. He set out fully to all that excellent treasure which his studies had gathered and the grace of God had poured down from heaven; and let us, imitating his example, grant to our fellow servants the goods to be used and enjoyed, if there are any in us through the grace of God; let us have regard for piety, charity, humanity, peace, and the common good, and let us lead studious youth, in this school as in a most choice theatre, by teaching and by deed, to the same end; and let us preserve both ourselves and others in the faith which is in Christ. You too, dearest youth, you most delightful crown, who wish that teacher of yours to have been kept alive longer for you, for us, for the school, the Church, and the world: do not mourn further for one who is absent, whom you rejoice to have been present to you as an example of life, and whose most illustrious writings, which he set down, you now also use and hold in trust. Rather, take care that from your number you raise up more Ursinuses. He has one heir in the flesh, whom we also hope will be an heir of piety; but for all of you the way of piety is open to enter upon and receive this inheritance. Come on, you have grown enough; go forward, and set your foot in possession of that inheritance. Talent is not lacking to you, nor the aids of study; the way is not wanting; one thing remains, that your will not be lacking either, lest you desert yourselves. So apply your will, and yourselves, diligently to such studies, to the duties of piety, charity and humanity, with the best good faith and the greatest diligence: toil and labour at these; let each of you present to us, by your duty, another Ursinus. But if you cannot all bring that gold, silver and gems of Ursinus for the building of this tabernacle, do not cast down your spirit at once: iron, bronze, wood, stone, and goat's hair and linen are also acceptable to God. You who cannot be leaders or first-rank, do not despair; there is need also of those of the second, third, fourth, tenth and twentieth rank: Christ attests that there is a station for these too in the house of his Father. Not even the doorkeeper is to be counted a fault in the house of the living God; for David himself, who was a man after the heart of the Lord, was in no way ashamed of this. Nor shall you be ashamed or ever repent, if you strive in this arena, in these studies and these duties, if you pursue these examples. Those who aim at the heights (says Fabius) will go higher than those who, by presumptuous despair of escaping where they wish, straightaway stop near the bottom. But what then? Neither we, who say we are far from the example of that man (I speak of myself, I admire the gifts of my colleagues and I cultivate them as my duty), nor you will be able to attain it by your own industry. But that Ursinus, that man of the memory of God (for this name sounds Hebrew), has been snatched from us; now only the memory of so great a man is with us. What then are we going to do? That Iah, God the strong, who lifted up his Zechariah to such a height of faith, piety and learning, Christ, that prophet and our only king, is most present to us both by his eternal majesty and by the communion of the Holy Spirit. Let us go to this teacher, let us consult this master, let us follow this leader; relying on his grace and help, let us persevere most constantly in those studies to which we are called and in those duties. Let the impiety of heretics not glory, nor the breast of our adversaries swell because the rod of those who strike them has been broken; for out of the root of the serpent a viper rather will come forth, and its fruit will be a flying serpent (as Isaiah once prophesied), rather than that we should be forsaken by our God and given over to the violent furies of mad men, or to the playful follies of the insane, by which (alas) the Church is assailed more than enough.

units.la: Omnipotens aeterne Deus,misericors pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi,qui tum illius serui tui, tum aliorū, quos huic scholae praeficis,salutari doctrina iuuentutem imbuere voluisti, & nostras singulorum mentes promis- sionis veritatisque spiritu obsignare:Nunc toto pectore agnoscimus , quòd seruū illū tuū e medio nostrū sustu- leris, te non mediocriter nobis infensi m esse,neq. im-
units.tr: Almighty, eternal God, merciful Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who wished to imbue the youth with saving doctrine both through your servant and through the others whom you set over this school, and to seal our individual minds with the Spirit of promise and truth: we now acknowledge with our whole heart that in taking your servant from our midst you have been not a little hostile to us, and not

units.la: Et quibus est lusus dominorum fallere dextras, Iuratámque thori contemerare fidem: Crimine quo Tityus, terra omniparentis alumnus, Et lust Ixion, hic iecur, ille rotam: Sunt hostes patria, pulsatoresque parentum: Et quibus impietas pectore tanta sedet, Instar Aloidum ut, vel si quid sauius istu[?], In superas acuant ora manusque domos. Demententque novis incautum erroribus orbem, Splendida quos bilis dictat, & ambitio. Quin hos, ô Parca, celeri compescitis ira? Et venit hic prima luce suprema dies? Parcitis: ha pestes hominum, hae sunt Vlcera mundi, Fulmine digna Iouis, sugeribusque[?] nouem: In magnos Virtute Viros, quibus inclita cura est Et patria, & Vera religionis honos: Ni prius exacti grandaevi Nestoris anni Sint, liceat Vobis iuris habere nihil. Hanc Vtinam Parcae mihi fas sit condere legem, (Suggerit haec iustus nam mihi Vota dolor) Na pro bissenis, VRSINE, tot integra lustris Vita indulsisset secula cana tua. Altius è caelo sic purior illa tulisset Religio, summo de Ioue nata, caput: Sic tibi crevisset Virtutum laude tuarum Immenso aeternum nominis orbe decus, Esset & antiquis aui cum patribus aurei, Et Voce & scriptis, aequiparatus honos. Sed ter Magne iaces communi morte peremtus: Et iacet heu nostra spesque nitorque schola: Siue ea Parcarum est, quae nent fatalia, culpa, Inuidit que auram numinis ira tibi: Seu potius Vita posuisti sponte labores, Tristitia Vt nobis causa dolenda foret: En lacrymis profusa genas dulcissima coniux Ad tibi succensos stat gemebunda rogo.: Stansque fuer cum matre, tua spes Vnica gentis, Ter, pater, heu quo tu, Sociferatur, abis? Qualis, ab indomito Priameius Hector Achille Moenia ter circum cum raperetur, erat Parvulus Astyanax tristi cum matre, sub alta
units.tr: And to whom it is sport to deceive their masters' right hands, and to defile the marriage faith sworn: for whose crime Tityus, nursling of the all-parent earth, and Ixion, the one on his liver, the other on his wheel... They are enemies of their country and beaters of their parents; and those in whose breast such great impiety sits, like the Aloidae, so that, or if anything is fiercer than these, they sharpen their mouths and hands against the heavenly abodes. They drive the unwary world mad with new errors, those whom splendid bile and ambition dictate. Why, O Fates, do you not check them with swift wrath? And does the last day come at the first light? You spare them: these are the plagues of men, these the ulcers of the world, worthy of Jove's thunderbolt and of nine ... In great men, men of virtue, to whom illustrious care belongs for country and the true honour of religion: unless first the years of aged Nestor have been completed, let it not be lawful for you to have any right. Would that the Fates might allow me to establish this law (for my grief suggests this prayer to me), for Ursinus, your whole life of twice six lustra would have granted your grey years. Thus that purer religion, born of supreme Jove, would have raised its head higher from heaven; thus to you would have grown, by the praise of your virtues, an everlasting glory in the immense orb of your name, and there would be honour equal to the golden ancestors of old, both in voice and in writings. But you lie, thrice great one, destroyed by common death; and alas, our hope and brightness of the school lies dead. Whether it is the fault of the Fates who spin what is fated, or the wrath of the deity has envied you the breath of life; or rather you, of your own accord, laid down your labours in life, so that sorrow would be a cause for us to grieve. Behold, your dearest wife, dissolved in tears, stands weeping by the pyre kindled for you. And standing with your mother, the only hope of your race, she cries: "Thrice, father, alas, where are you going?" As once, when Hector was dragged thrice around the walls by untamed Achilles, there was the little Astyanax with his sad mother, under the lofty ...

units.la: Ter frustra ingeminans Hectora, turre puer:
units.tr: Again and again, in vain, the boy calls on Hector from the tower.

units.la: Heu, ait, hunc tulimus nuper te dante nitorem,

units.la: Hunc tibi pro maestis reddimus inferiis.

units.tr: You could and were worthy, Ursinus, to draw out the threads of the whirling heavens in an everlasting spin.

units.tr: For what is more worthy than your learning and such great acuteness of intellect, to remain forever?

units.tr: But how much more he was admired by you! He is to be honoured, and the hearer of the liberal arts, whatever he was,

units.tr: whether the heavenly teachings of the Word were to be handled by you, or whichever enemy was to be refuted by skill.

units.tr: Many things flow from a full breast to no purpose, and the crowd approves cleverness through chatter.

units.tr: You, by contrast, would match many things of others with three words; nothing was obscure while you taught.
