units.tr: She saw too, with the ingenuous youth crowding around,

units.la: Vidit & ingenuam circumglomerante iuventam
units.tr: The loquacious Gultus imitating the bold lion. How quickly, alas, has he lost his feigned trappings!

units.la: Agmine, Gorgonei lumina mille iugi.
units.tr: How far does wicked Gulpes differ from brave Orsus? By the command of Mars she dared to join the leaders in battle,

units.la: Tunc rata res quod erat, charos morientis amicos
units.tr: and, talkative, to pretend to be a bold lion. But how quickly she lost her false disguise!

units.la: In cineres luctus pignora ferre sui,
units.tr: But, Ursinus, your merits were harmed by an unhappy day, as fate, whirling all things, turns them about.

units.la: Tristis adit, lacrymasque premens inita fluentes,
units.tr: Whether Nicer had wiped out his labours from the exhausted mind, or the fates under your auspices rolled on,

units.la: Cum gemitu soluit talibus ora modis:
units.tr: to found new homes for the exiled Muses and their father Phoebus, the bright halls of the Neapolitan school,

units.la: Ille hominum Diuumque Vrsinus gloria, Amici,
units.tr: where Casimir, powerful in virtue and famous in arms, reigns and turns the honoured years to the front.

units.la: Heu iacet, immerita succubuitque neci:
units.tr: (Keep him, Christ, gracious Lord, for his country, for the Muses, for the honour of religion, for the empire, this leader.)

units.la: Tu poteras & dignus eras, VRSINE, perenniTurbine currentis ducere fila coli.
units.tr: Here, then, the most cultivated band of the Aonian goddesses had sat down with you, glad in their new lodging.

units.la: Ingenio quid enim doctrina & acumine tanto Dignius, aeternum quam superesse fuit?
units.tr: And now the holy work was boiling; now a great youth had come here from the Hyperborean regions;

units.la: Et tibi nil pietas, nil rara modestia, summi Virtutumque latrix profuit alma fides?
units.tr: Gaul, rich in its own learning and cleverness, had come, and dukes famed for their nobility.

units.la: Ni Gerear sanctos aliquà tibi ladere manes, Cui bene, dum Sixti, cura latere fuit:
units.tr: Then, when you were scarcely in your better years, cruel fates hurried you to a wretched death,

units.la: Nonne tuis explere queam Virtutibus orbem, Si modo sint faciles in mea Vota Dea,
units.tr: and they laid waste the harvest flowering in the grass. So, alas, how briefly a single hour destroys great honour!

units.la: Maxima Slesiadum te Vratislauia matrum Progenuit: maius nomen & inde tulit.
units.tr: As when the field, luxuriant in stalks, or grazed by the blow of hail, dries up; or as when a tiny breeze, let in through the cracks of a nocturnal vault, puts out a bright torch.

units.la: Viderat Agricolam schola Lotichium que poetam. Quà Vitreus Rhenì se Nicer abdit aquis:
units.tr: O vain hopes of men! O vain labour! Glory, if it comes at all, comes scarcely won.

units.la: Strigelio audierat nil dulcius hactenus, & nil Tremelio lingua doctius Aramica:
units.tr: What use is it to strive by merit toward the steep heights of virtue, or to stand on the highest summit?

units.la: At quanto magis est re demirata? colendus Artibus auditor seu foret ingenuis:
units.tr: Let scabies and the useless crowd seize the last place, if it is nothing to have cultivated the learned goddesses.

units.la: Seu tibi caelestis tractanda didagmata Verbi: Arte refutandus sive quis hostis erat.
units.tr: Or let the impious man love the cruel altars of Busiris, or let him keep his faith sworn with piety:

units.la: Multa superuacue pleno de pectore manant, Vulgus & ingenium garrulitate probat,
units.tr: the just Aristides, and the Lapiths and Ixion's sons are carried in one boat to the Stygian waters.

units.la: Tu tribus aquabas aliorum plurima verbis: Obscurum nil te praecipiente fuit:
units.tr: Am I mistaken? Or as lofty things are blown by hostile winds, does the breeze strike the slight huts more lightly?

units.la: Tu poteras Gnus, Lyrica quod in arte docentes Perspicua Flaccus de brevitate monet.
units.tr: So the best men are sought by a hastened death, and the wicked one, untouched, goes through six changes of fortune?

units.la: Vidi ego tota leues Virgere theatra sophistas: Sed patuit te Six ora movente dolus.
units.tr: Hector, the bravest of the Trojans, is laid low before the others; a Danaan soldier falls by an infamous enemy.

units.la: Sensit & Vtopici male felix dogmatis author, Sensere Abbates, molliculique Patres,
units.tr: The world nurses a thousand plagues under both poles; a band no less than the Furies and worthy of flight, whom the cross, whom the wheel with its spokes, if Jupiter is held just, or why does not the Fate suddenly slay?

units.la: Improba quid Gulpes animoso distet ab Orso: Ausa erat huic iussu Marte coire Ducum,
units.tr: He fears nothing, practising illicit arts in filth, the miser who offers no help to the wretched;

units.la: Audacémque loquax Gultu simulare leonem: Quàm cito sed fictas perdidit exuvias?
units.tr: But for you, Ursinus (thus fortune whirls all things in a storm), the unhappy day, Gna, stood in the way of your merits.

units.la: Ast, VRSINE, tuis (sic turbine cuncta rotat fors) Infelix meritis obfuit Gna dies:
units.tr: Whether Nicer had wiped away the labours exhausted from the mind, or the fates turned under your auspices

units.la: Seu Nicer exhaustos delerat mente labores, Fata sub auspicio seu Voluere tuo
units.tr: To found new homes for the exiles and for the Phoebus-father's Muses, the bright buildings of the Neapolitan school,

units.la: Exulibus Phoebóque patri nova condere Musis Tecta, Neapoleos candida tecta schola,
units.tr: Where Casimir, mighty in virtue and famous in arms, reigns and in advanced years turns honoured years aside. (Him, the fatherland, him the Muses, him the honour of religion, him, kind Christ, preserve as leader for the empire.)

units.la: Qua Virtute potens CASIMIRVS & inclytus armis Regnat, honoratos anteque Vertit anuos. (Hunc patria, hunc Musis, hunc religionis honori, Hunc serua[?] Imperio, Christe benigne, Ducem,) Hic ergo Aonidum cultissima turba Dearum Lata nouo tecum sederat hospitio: Iamque sacrum feruebat opus: iam plurima pubes Huc ab Hyperboreis venerat usque plagis: Ipsa domi studijs et acumine Gallia diues Venerat, et magni nobilitate Duces: Tum tibi, Vix actis aui melioribus annis, Praecipitant miseram fata seuera necem, Florentemque ipsa messem populantur in herba: Sic breuis heu quantum subruit hora decus! Vt cum luxurians culmis Vredine[?], vel cum Verbere depastus grandinis, aret ager: Aut si fulgentem nocturno in fornice rimis, Admissa exilis deleat aura facem. O vanas hominum spes! o vanumque laborem! Quo vix, si qua venit, gloria parta venit. Quid meritis niti virtutis ad ardua tantis Culmina, quid summo vertice stare iuuat? Occupet extremum scabies, et inutile vulgus, Si nihil est doctas excoluisse Deas. Seu quis amet crudas Busyridis impius aras: Iuratamue colat cum pietate fidem: Iustus Aristides, Lapithaque, Ixionidesque Ad Stygias vna puppe feruntur aquas. Fallor? an infestis perflantur ut ardua ventis, Leuius exiles impetit aura casas: Optima sic hominum properata morte petuntur: Intactaque subit sex scelerata vices? Sternitur ante alios Troum fortissimus Hector: Infami Danaus miles ab hoste cadit. Mille fouet pestes sub cardine mundus utroque: Nec minor est furiis et fuga digna cohors, Quos cruce, quos radiisque rota, si iustus habetur Iuppiter, aut cur non Parca repente necat? Nil timet, illicitas exercens sordibus artes, Qui miseris nullam praestat auarus opem: Utque homines iugulent, surgentes nocte latrones, Aut quos ex rapto nutris adunca manus: meritò: Agnoscimus, ô Deus, accusamus, damnamus nos & peccata nostra, quibus tu pestilente gladiū superiore anno visum fuerat immittere, tum hoc succedente anno lumē illud præstantissimum, quod in illustri celebris huius scholæ candelabro statueras (prout minatus eras iadiu) extinguere. Oramus te, ô Deus & pater miserationum, ne porro sœvias in hunc pusillum gregem nostrum, neque rationem nobiscum ineas, aut cum peccatis nostris, ut ira tua amplius exardescente de via iusta pereamus.
units.tr: Here then the most cultivated throng of the Aonian goddesses had settled, joyful, with you in the new hospice; and now the sacred work was glowing; now a great crowd of youth had come here from the Hyperborean regions; Gaul, rich in her own studies and sharpness, had come, and the nobility of great leaders. Then, as you had scarcely reached your better years, cruel fates hasten your wretched death, and they ravage your flourishing harvest in the grass: so briefly, alas, does an hour overthrow how much glory! As when the field, lush in its stalks, or grazed by the blow of hail, dries up; or as when a thin breeze, let in through the chinks of a night-time vault, destroys a shining torch. O vain hopes of men! O vain labour! For which glory, if it comes at all, comes scarcely won. Why does it help to strive by merits towards such steep heights, why to stand on the highest summit? Let the scab and the useless crowd seize the last place, if it is nothing to have cultivated the learned goddesses. Or whether an impious man loves the cruel altars of Busiris, or cultivates a faith sworn with piety: the just Aristides, and the Lapiths and Ixion's sons, are carried in one boat to the Stygian waters. Am I mistaken? Or as lofty things are blown upon by hostile winds, a light breeze strikes the humble huts more gently: so the best of men are sought by a hastened death, and the untouched wicked man goes through six changes? Hector, the bravest of the Trojans, falls first of all; a soldier of the Danai falls by an infamous enemy. The world nourishes a thousand plagues under either pole; and no less a band, worthy of flight and of the furies, whom the cross, whom the wheel with its spokes... if Jupiter is considered just, or why does not the Fate suddenly kill them? He fears nothing, practising illicit arts in filth, the avaricious man who gives no help to the wretched; and as robbers rising at night slay men, or those whom your hooked hand feeds on plunder: deservedly. We acknowledge, O God, we accuse, we condemn ourselves and our sins, for which you had seen fit to send a pestilential sword in the previous year, and then in this following year to extinguish that most excellent light, which you had set in the famous candelabrum of this celebrated school (as you had long threatened). We beseech you, O God and Father of mercies, that you not rage further against this little flock of ours, nor enter into reckoning with us or with our sins, lest, with your anger flaring more fiercely, we perish from the just way.

units.la: Sed potius quandoquidem vexillū filii tu hic constitui gratiosissimè voluisti, fideq. dedisti beatos fore qui sese ad te receperint: rege nos, ô Deus, tuo spiritu, ut osculemur filii dilectionis tuæ, & salute omne[?] ab eo expectemus: Satanæ consilia & conatus perde: populum tuum coferua, ecclesiæ huic, scholæ, & regioni toti bonos fidelesque pastores, doctores & administros confer:tuere quos dedisti, & auge omni benedictionum genere, populares atq. studiosos in officio iusto, sanctimonia, charitate, & pace continue, omnia denique in nobis perfice, ut Deus omnipotens & pater optimus noster, quæ ad gloriam tui nominis, communem ædificationem, & salutem nostram pertinebunt in Christo Iesu Domino nostro, qui tecum vivit regnatque in unitate spiritus, æternus Deus in secula, Amen.
units.tr: But rather, since you have most graciously willed to set up here the banner of your Son, and have pledged that those will be blessed who have received themselves to you: rule us, O God, by your Spirit, that we may kiss the sons of your love, and from him expect salvation from all things: destroy the counsels and attempts of Satan; preserve your people, grant to this Church, this school, and the whole region good and faithful ministers, teachers and deacons; keep those whom you have given, and increase them with every kind of blessing, and preserve the common people and the students in just duty, holiness, charity and peace; in short, perfect all things in us, so that the almighty God and our most good Father may bring about those things which pertain to the glory of your name, to our common edification, and to our salvation, in Christ Jesus our Lord, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Spirit, the eternal God, for ever and ever, Amen.

units.la: Neapoli Nemetum obdormiuit in Christo placidis-sime die 6. Mart. hora vesper. 6. anno 1583. cum vixisset annos 48 menf. 6. horas 11. sepultus 8. Mart. in templi choro.
units.tr: He fell asleep in Christ most peacefully at Neapolis of the Germans, on the 6th day of March, at the sixth hour of evening, in the year 1583, having lived 48 years, 6 months, 11 hours. Buried on 8 March in the choir of the church.

units.la: EXEQUIIS D. ZACHARIÆ URSINI, PRÆCEPTORIS SUI COLENDISSIMI,
units.tr: FUNERAL RITES FOR D. ZACHARIAS URSINUS, HIS MOST REVERED TEACHER

units.la: DAVID PAREVS.
units.tr: DAVID PAREUS.

units.la: OURSINE sacros inter celeberrime Vates, Quos modo sincerus numinis ardor agit, Siccin' abit? ô & iuuenum[?] ter maxime cultor, Quo fugis? ô nostra lux que decusque schola: Cur nos tam dubio rerum sub turbine linquis, Ceu rate si mediis nauita cedat aquis[?]
units.tr: Ursinus, most famous among the sacred poets, whom the sincere ardour of the divine power now drives: do you depart so? O cultivator of the young, greatest of all, whither do you flee? O our light and the glory of our school: why do you leave us under so doubtful a whirlwind of affairs, as a sailor leaves his ship in the midst of the waters?

units.la: Te, te prisca fides, Verique clientula mater Religio, ô adsis portus & aura, vocant: Ne turpes agitent nostra de clade triumphos, Qui nunc de superum prælia sede movent. Sed nec ades, nec abis: quia te mors invida terris Eripuit, gelido composuitque sinu, Haud ideo ereptus nobis. Tua conscius orbis Edita mutato nomine scripta legit, Plurimaque Ursini sub nomine posthuma, lucem Si modo contigerint, quam meruere, leget, Arte laborata, & niveum testantia pectus: Non his livor edax, non nigra bilis inest, Qua modo Cadmæos rapiens in prælia fratres Scripta Lycambæo tincta cruore vomit: Næve tuis desint meritis qui congrua reddant Præmia, ut æternus nominis exstet honos: Surget in hoc olim, doctis pro cultibus, arvo Docta tibi Libyca fertilitate seges. Tunc (liceat plausus isti modo tollere) victrix Causa triumphabit robore justa suo. Et prius Ursinos uno pro mille dabit, quàm Exul ab æthērio culmine Christus eat, Lustret & humano terras stygiamque paludem Corpore: quod finxit conditor Utopia. Credimus, ille equidem præsenti numine complet Cuncta: sed & cœlo carne receptus agit. Carne, inquam, superósque locos & regna sequestrans, Nostrum sibi nunc certa stat πολιτευμα[?] fide. Carneque quem nobis tandem sine fraude reducet Conspicuum aeria nube suprema dies. At nos, clare tuam vir, quo decorabimus urnam Carmine? sic habeat qui tegit ossa lapis: Hac cubat Ursini funus lacrymabile tumba: Mens fruitur cœlo: fama sed orbe viget.
units.tr: You, you, ancient faith and Religion, the true mother who is your client, call you to the harbour and the breeze. Lest shameful triumphs stir up from our calamity those who now stir up battles from the seat of the heavens. But you neither remain nor depart: for envious death has snatched you from the earth and laid you in a cold bosom. Yet you have not been snatched from us on that account. The world, aware of you, reads your published writings under a changed name, and many posthumous works under the name of Ursinus, which, if only they come to light, as they deserve, it will read: works laboured with skill and attesting a snow-white breast. In these there is no gnawing envy, no black bile, with which, lately, seizing the Cadmean brothers for battle, he vomits writings steeped in the blood of Lycambes. And lest your merits lack the fitting rewards, so that the eternal honour of your name may stand: in this field, once cultivated by learned care, a learned harvest will rise up for you from Libyan fertility. Then (let it be allowed to raise this applause for now) the just cause, victorious by its own strength, will triumph. And sooner will it give a thousand Ursinuses for one, than Christ, exiled from the ethereal height, will go forth and traverse the lands and the Stygian marsh in a human body, which the creator of Utopia invented. We believe, indeed, that he fills all things with his present divinity; but also, received into heaven in the flesh, he acts. In the flesh, I say, separating the heavenly and the royal places, he now stands firmly in our own citizenship by a sure faith. And in the flesh, which at last the final day, in an aerial cloud, will restore to us without fraud, conspicuous. But we, illustrious man, with what song shall we adorn your urn? Let the stone that covers the bones have this: Here lies the mournful funeral of Ursinus in the tomb: his mind enjoys heaven, but his fame flourishes in the world.

units.la: EPICEDION IN OBITVM EIVSDEM D. ZACHA-RIAE URSINI, EODEM DAVIDE Pareo authore.
units.tr: EPICEDIUM ON THE DEATH OF THE SAME D. ZACHARIAS URSINUS, BY DAVID PAREUS AS AUTHOR.

units.la: SI quid ab extremo foret inviolabile fato, Tristeque Parcarum sisque retardet opus:
units.tr: If anything could be inviolable against the final fate, and might delay the sad work of the Fates:

units.la: Maximus ingenio nostri in montibus ille Concidit: Actiaco proximus ille patri: Quo nemo excoluit summi pia iussa Tonantis Candidiore fide, candidiore manu. Spes erat, hunc meritum, & multa Viribus artis Spernere lethaas posse Charontis aquas, Vtque erat indignus Parcarum immanibus ausis, Flectere lanificas in sua Vota Deas. Nec tamen, Vt Vobis opus immortale parantem Videre, extremas continuere manus. Scilicet illa animum spes Vobis sed rat[?] olim: Nunc premit attonitos, spe fugiente, dolor. Non ego, quicquid id est Vestru[?] tam sletibus obsto, Ipsa haud cum leuius pectore Vulnus alam: Est pietatis opus tanta indoluisse ruina, Credite quaseipsa[?] tempore maior erit: Non Aganippaeam qui funderet Hippocrenen, Sat lachrymis dignas ille litabit aquas. Sed quia nec lacrymis tres exorare sorores, Nec datur Elysium slectere Voce Iouem: Membra quidem VRS NI merito tumulemus honore: Lege sed & noster non sine luctus eat. Quin potius memores animis nunc indite, Vestri Quàm generis Varia sint fuerintque Vices. Maximus ille fuit: maior quoque dignus haberi: Sed fuit & terra debita massa simul. Non si transsierint decies centesima patrum Secula, primaevus quos tulit orbis, homo, Cum sit humus, sixam poterit transcendere metam, Omnia quà sistit mortis auara manus. Non adeo Vlla duos concordia iunxit amantes, Alterius quin sit funere ruptus amor. Ipsa parens rerum quid nobiliore ligauit Fœdere, quàm Vestrum hoc corpus, & hanc animam: Sed breue connubium est: labentéque molliter auo, Soluitur hoc tandem corpus, & haec anima. Sic nullo rapitur discrimine Croesus & Irus, Sunt quia mortalis Croesus & Irus humus. Nec tamen ingenio (quod fert insania Vulgi) Est coluisse nouem numina docta nihil.
units.tr: That greatest man has fallen among our mountains, that one next to Actiacus his father, whom no one has cultivated the pious commands of the Thunderer with a purer faith, with a purer hand. There was hope that he, by his merit and by the many powers of his art, could scorn the Lethean waters of Charon, and, as he was unworthy of the cruel deeds of the Fates, bend the wool-spinning goddesses to his prayers. Nor, however, while he was preparing for you an immortal work, did the final hands hold back. Surely that hope once nourished your spirit: now grief, with hope fleeing, oppresses the astonished. I do not, whatever it is, obstruct your tears, nor will I nourish a wound less keen in my own heart. It is a work of piety to have grieved at so great a ruin; believe that it will be greater in time. He who would pour out Aganippean Hippocrene will offer waters sufficiently worthy of tears. But since neither can three sisters be implored with tears, nor is it granted to bend Jove with a voice from Elysium: let us indeed bury the limbs of Ursinus with due honour; but let our mourning also go forth, not without reading. Nay rather, now, remembering, consider in your minds how varied the changes of our kind are and have been. That man was greatest: yet he was also deserving of being considered greater; but he was at the same time a mass owed to the earth. If the hundred-times-tenth ages of the fathers, whom the first-born world bore as men, had passed over, since they are earth, they could not go beyond the fixed boundary at which the greedy hand of death halts all things. Indeed no concord has joined two lovers so closely that love is not broken by the death of the other. The very parent of things has bound together nothing by a nobler compact than this body of yours and this soul; but the bond is brief, and as the age gently glides away, this body and this soul are at last dissolved. Thus Croesus and Irus are seized without any distinction, because Croesus and Irus are mortal earth. Nor, however, is it nothing, by genius (which the madness of the crowd bears), to have cultivated the nine learned goddesses.

units.la: Aut indefessis adisse laboribus arcem, Qua pietas regnat, justitiaque decor. Quisquis Hiantaas[?] trahit in commercia Musas, Et nostro afflatum numine pectus habet, Nec falsi pravique tenax male transigit ævum: Huic pulcra aeternus laude paratur honos. Omnia mors abolet: sola est sine funere virtus, Effugit extremos ingeniumque rogos: Felicesque animae terrena mole soluta, Aeternum summo cum Jove numen habent: Nocte carent atra: diroque silentis averni Termine, quod Lapithae Pirythoúsque luunt. Ergo ter es felix, caelo dignissime Vates: Te beat aetherium pro pietate tuba: Nunc penitus vivis: te vastus Olympus & orbis Laudibus in sera posteritate vehent: Docta per ora virum volitas: nil morte peremptum est, Ossa nisi, & tenuis, quae tegit ossa, cutis. Vos etiam laudis decus immortalis, Amici, Quarite: sic pariter vita perennis erit: Nec lacrymis porro tumulos aspergite: quisque Carmina sed Vati, dona suprema, date, Dicat ut aspiciens olim monimenta viator Funeris: VRSINI mollitor ossa cubent.
units.tr: Or to have approached the citadel, where piety reigns and the grace of justice, by tireless labours. Whoever draws the gaping Muses into his dealings, and has a breast inspired by our divinity, and does not cling to what is false and wicked, passes his age badly: for him an eternal honour is prepared by a fine praise. Death abolishes all things: virtue alone is without funeral, and genius escapes the final pyres. And happy souls, loosed from the earthly mass, possess the eternal divinity with the supreme Jove: they lack dark night and the dread boundary of silent Avernus, which the Lapiths and Pirithous pay for. Therefore you are thrice happy, poet most worthy of heaven: the ethereal trumpet blesses you for your piety. Now you live fully: vast Olympus and the world will carry you in praises into late posterity. You fly through the mouths of learned men: nothing is destroyed by death except the bones, and the thin skin that covers the bones. You also, friends, seek the immortal glory, the honour of praise: thus likewise a perennial life will be yours. Nor further sprinkle the tombs with tears: but give to the poet songs, the last gifts, so that the traveller, looking upon the monument of the funeral, may one day say: "May the bones of Ursinus rest softly."

units.la: D. Opt. Max. S.
units.tr: To God, Best and Greatest

units.la: VRSINVM dederas Vnum[?], Deus optime, nobis, Sufficeret nobis tua qui pene omnia solus, Siue homines ille humana ratione doceret, Artibus excultus cunctis: sive enim heus[?] illum Spiritus arcanos depromere pectore sensus Jusserat: & sacri quatientem lampada verbi, Discutere errorum nebulas: cuneosque ruentum Divinis fretum telis hinc inde luporum Rumpere tutantem Christi divinitus agnos. Ergo quid VRSINO properata morte peremto, Crediderim superesse gregi, qui sicut in uno[?] Cuncta habuit quondam, sic cuncta amisit in uno? Sic ego multa gemens & planctibus aera complens, Tum[?] Deus excelsa miseratus ab arce gementem, Qu[?]one modum lacrymis, inquit, Vobisque sibique Appositque thymum,& passos de vite racemos, Si quando miseras premeret penuria victus, Non illum pictus squallentia terga lacertus, Non fucus latuit,non stellio, lucifugaque Blatta,non merops,non Progne Veris amica, Et manibus dirum pectus signata cruentis. Non etiam pecori, Siuo Damone, Chelydrus Formidandus erat,sacro nidore fugatus, Non sub praesepi latitans mala Vipera tactu, Non anguis qui Sarmaticis in saltibus errat Conspurcans loca Ariano Vicina Veneno, Inficiensque herbas Virides aspergine tabi: Hunc convoluentem sublato pectore terga Squamea,tollentemque minas & colla tumentem Deiecturus erat divini fulmine Verbi, Interpellasset sanctum nisi sæva laborem Uis morbi,atque alio calamum avertisset acutum Importuna hominum rabies, quos nosse cuiuis In promptu est:cantu proprio dignoscitur ales. Ut tacite,credo, pertentant gaudia eorum Pectora,terrori quibus huic fuit ante molossus: Iam sibi despondent palmam,hoc custode remoto: Forsan & ex illis caput altum in pralia tollit Unus,& extinctum crudele Voce lacessens Provocat ad pugnas,& verberat ictibus auras. Sic potis est timidus lepus insultare leoni Ex animo:sic Priamidem petiere iacentem, Teloque AEacida confossum Dorica pubes, Quem Siuum armigeri duro in certamine Martis Fugerat & Ventis, & fulminis ocyor alis. Nil tamen efficient,qua fundamenta locavit Artifici studio Damon,excisa fodinis Omnia Apostolicis,aeternum immota manebunt, Non secus ac cautes tumidis qua tunditur olim Fluctibus,hybernis turbantur Ubi aquora Coris. Sic erit Alphesibœe:alio nos plura canemus Tempore Damoni,rumpantur Ut illa Codro Invidia;ut clam se cum Mopso maceret AEglon.
units.tr: You had given us Ursinus, the one (God most good), and he alone was nearly enough for us in all things. Whether he taught men by human reason, having been trained in every art, or whether the Spirit had ordered him to draw forth the hidden meanings from his breast and, shaking the sacred lamp of the Word, to scatter the clouds of errors, and to break through the ranks of the attacking wolves, defending the lambs of Christ divinely with the divine weapons: so, with Ursinus snatched away by hasty death, what am I to believe the flock has left, which, as it once had all things in the one man, so has lost all things in the one man? Thus I, groaning much and filling the air with laments, then God, pitying the groaning man from his lofty citadel, said: "In what manner do you weep, and do you season with thyme for yourselves and for others, and grapes plucked from the vine, if sometimes penury of food should press you wretchedly? Neither the painted lizard with its squalid back, nor the fly, nor the stellion, nor the light-shunning beetle, nor the bee-eater, nor Progne the friend of spring, nor the dire breast marked with bloody hands, escaped notice. Nor even for the flock, for Damon, was the dreaded hydrus, put to flight by the sacred smoke, nor the evil viper lurking under the manger by touch, nor the snake that wanders in the Sarmatian thickets, polluting the places near with Arian poison and infecting the green herbs with its foul spray. This one, coiling its scaly back with raised breast and lifting threats and a swollen neck, was about to be cast down by the thunderbolt of the divine Word, had not savage force of disease interrupted the holy labour, and had not unseasonable human rage turned the sharp pen aside, those whom it is easy for anyone to know: the bird is recognised by its own song. As, I believe, the hearts of those for whom the mastiff was once a terror secretly test their joys: now, with this guardian removed, they promise themselves the palm. Perhaps even one of them lifts his high head into battle and, provoking the dead man with cruel voice, challenges him to fight and beats the air with blows. Thus the timid hare can insult the lion from its spirit; thus the Dorian youth attacked Priam's son lying prostrate, and the son of Aeacus, pierced with a spear, whom the armour-bearer had fled in the hard contest of Mars, and the winds, and swifter than the wings of lightning. Yet they will accomplish nothing: the foundations which Damon laid with his artful zeal, and all that was hewn from the apostolic quarries, will remain unshaken for ever, just as the cliffs that are beaten by swelling waves once upon a time, where the seas are troubled by winter Coros. So it will be: Alphesiboeus, we shall sing more at another time for Damon, so that that envy may burst for Codrus, and that Aeglon may pine away secretly with Mopsus."

units.la: Mortifero gregibus corrumpere pabula tabo. Dira per incautum &[?] serpant contagia vulgus, Corripiatque ardens vel singula corpora morbus. Ille quidem felix: nos contra quanta malorum Circumstat series! miserabile fundite carmen Custodes pecudum, & tumulo superaddite carmen; Hic situs est Damon, hinc usque ad sidera notus, Sic decus omne suis, Viti velut sua, gregique Taurus, & ut pingui seges aruo, laureaque horto. Omnia nunc lugent: colles quando hosce reliquit AEquiparans Damon calamis & voce magistros Quos Rhodani ad ripas mirata & ad Al[?]dos undas Cantantes, nostra longe felicior atas: Ad quos obstupuit Tigurinus Limagus olim, Ad quorum voces cursus retraxit aquarum Sequana Parrisios fecundans molliter agros. Omnia muta tacent: quis nunc erit alter ab illo? Argutumque canet sub montibus hisce cicuta Terribilique lupis & furibus? hanc simul ore Inflauit: subito sunt facta silentia in agris Omnibus: ipsa etiam rana tacuere palustres. Testis erit Viadrus, cumque albi flauus Elister, Testis erit Sala cum Nicro Rhenoque perenni: Nullus ad hos fluuios pastorum, nullius opinor Damoni voluit contendere: quin etiam si Communes operas vel sex conferre parárent, vel plures, vel tres, vel quatuor, haud tamen ausi Damonis certare, quod iis symphonia discors Ex templo fieret, risumque audita moueret. Carpite, quos mittit varios humus humida flores, Lilia, narcissos, ferrugineosque hyacinthos, Intyba cum violis, casiaque, rosisque, thymoque, Et breue Damonis magni conspergite bustum, Cuius in his terris nomen laudesque manebunt, Dum cythiso pascentur apes, dum fronde capella, Dum fluuius piscis gaudebit, rore cicada. Lenta inter quantum sese Siburna cupressus Erigit, ac humilis inter procera myricas Alnus, tantum inter reliquas caput extulit urbes Patria Damonis, quae sit pulcerrima quamuis Rebus opima bonis, multa munita vi[?]rum Si:
units.tr: To corrupt the pastures for the flocks with deadly pestilence. Dire contagions creep through the unwary crowd, and disease seizes and burns the individual bodies. He indeed is happy; but we, how great a series of evils surrounds us! Pour out a wretched song, guardians of the flocks, and add a song to the tomb. Here lies Damon, known from here even to the stars; thus he was the glory of all his people, as the vine is to Vitus, as the bull is to the herd, as the crop is to the rich field, and the laurel to the garden. Now everything mourns: since he left those hills, equalling the masters with his reeds and voice, whom the banks of the Rhone admired, and the waters of the Aldus, singing, our age far happier than ours: at whom Limmat of Zurich was once astonished, and at whose voices the Seine, fertilising the Parisian fields gently, drew back the course of its waters. All things are silent and mute: who now will be another like him? Who will sing with sharp voice under these mountains, and to the fearful wolves and thieves? He breathed upon it with his mouth, and suddenly there were silences in all the fields, and even the marsh frogs fell silent. The Oder will be witness, and the yellow Elster with the white one, the Saale will be witness with the Necker and the perennial Rhine: no one, I think, wished to contend with Damon at these rivers of the shepherds. Indeed, even if they had prepared to bring together their common works, six, or more, or three, or four, they still did not dare to vie with Damon, because from their discordant harmony there would be made a disturbance in the temple, and the hearing of it would move laughter. Scatter the various flowers which the moist earth sends: lilies, narcissi, and iron-coloured hyacinths, endive with violets, and cassia, and roses, and thyme, and sprinkle the small tomb of great Damon, whose name and praises will remain in these lands as long as bees feed on the cytisus, as long as the goat feeds on the foliage, as long as the fish of the river will rejoice, the cicada in the dew. As far as the slow cypress of Siburna raises itself, and the low alder among the tall tamarisks, so far above the other cities has the fatherland of Damon raised its head, which is most beautiful though rich in goods, and fortified with many men.

units.la: Nil tamen hoc habuisse Viro praclarum in se, Nec sanctum magis,& mirum,doctumque videtur. Quantum oleis salices, quantum saliunca rosetis, Quantum ulula cygnis, Philomela cedit hirundo: Tantum indicio nostro tibi cedere fas est, Damon, quotquot habet pastores Teutonis ora, Aurea Brettani damnantes scripta Philonda, Romanamque suis centonibus Artolatriam Firmantes, totumque novis erroribus orbem Turbantes: scabiem pecoris pestemque redemti Sanguine Christe tuo: cuius sex impia carnem Implere humanam duro nimis asserit ore, Terrasque tractuque maris, coelumque profundum. Delicia nostra, Damon, dum fata sinebant; Dulces delicia: quis te felicius unquam Lappasque, tribulosque, interque nitentia culta Infelix lolium, & steriles euulsit avenas? [?] Quando te latuit, si forte horreret in aruis Carduus, & segetis non utilis herba subiret? Runcina ubi tua nunc? ubi rastrum & mystica vannus. Pectien ubi? rutrumque, irpexque, teresque cylindrus? Quo complanatur creta solidanda tenaci Area, ne mures subeuntes horrea ponant, Neu fodiant in ea sibi grata cubilia talpa, Neue canis latitet bufo, neu farris aceruum Curculio populet, collectis frugibus hostis. Omnia nunc squallent in agris, sinetaque moesta Excipiunt actos magnis aquilonibus imbres, Subsistuntque nova lacrymosa in palmite gemma, Falx quoniam Damonis abest, qua doctius uti Nemo ipso potuit: quoties resecare fluentes Vidimus hunc ramos? quoties compescere frondes Luxuria nimia crescentes, latior inde Surgeret ut cultis hortis propaginis ordo? Non agri tantum, non vinea sola requirit Solertem Damonis opem: sed apes quoque dulci Ante suas solita distendere nectare cellas, Iam tristes languent, sacuisque examina ducunt Rara fauis, tractimque sonant graviore susurro, Ag minibus pigris ad pabula nota volantes, Damonis desiderio, qui defuncta sape Vixit, qui Vitam impendit Vobisque mihique. Ergo, VRSINE, absit nobisque, tibique, Deoque Vt te Viuentem, demceps [?] ceu lumine cassum Ploremus stulti, quem tot tantique labores, Æternum æterna consecrauere saluti. Et quibus hosce lupos tecum Vi strictibus armis Fregimus, in media, nobis quum morte relinquas, Nempe etiam nobis Vere post funera, Viuis, Et Viues donec cœlorum regia tecum Felici excipiat functos certamine cunctos.
units.tr: Yet it seems that this has not made the man any more famous, holy, marvellous or learned in himself. As far as willows yield to olives, as far as the marjoram yields to the roses, as far as the owl yields to the swans, and the swallow yields to the nightingale: so far, Damon, it is right for you to yield, by our judgment, to all the pastors whom the Teutonic mouth has, those who condemn the golden writings of the Briton Philonda, and who uphold the Roman Artolatry with their patchwork cento, and who disturb the whole world with new errors: the scab and pestilence of the flock, redeemed by your blood, O Christ, whose impious doctrine asserts with too hard a mouth that he fills human flesh, the lands, the sea's expanse and the deep heaven. Our delight, Damon, while the fates allowed; sweet delight: who ever tended you more happily? Who uprooted the burdock, the thistles, and among the shining crops the unhappy darnel, and the barren oats? Whenever did it escape you if a thistle bristled in the fields, and a useless weed crept under the crop? Where is your weeding hook now? Where is your rake and your mystic winnowing fan? Where is your comb? Your spade, your rake and your smooth roller, by which the threshing floor is levelled with tenacious clay to be bound, lest mice creeping in place their granaries, or moles dig their pleasant dens in it, or the toad hide in the dog's lair, or the weevil plunder the heap of spelt, an enemy of the gathered crops. Now everything is squalid in the fields, and the sad hedges receive the showers driven by the great north winds, and the new tearful buds stand still on the vine-shoot, since the sickle of Damon is absent, which no one could use more skilfully than he himself. How often have we seen him cut back the flowing branches? How often restrain the fronds growing from excessive luxuriance, so that from there a wider row of shoots might rise in the cultivated gardens? Not only the fields, not the vineyard alone, lacks the skilful help of Damon; but the bees too, which were used to fill their cells with sweet nectar, now languish sadly, and lead out their swarms rarely to the combs, and sound with a heavier hum, and fly with sluggish wings to their familiar pastures, longing for Damon, who often lived, who gave his life for you and for me. Therefore, Ursinus, let it be far from us, and from you, and from God, that we, foolish, should weep for you as one lost to the light, as if you were living; whom so many and great labours have consecrated eternally to eternal salvation. And with you we broke these wolves by force of arms, and yet, leaving us in the midst of the fight by death, indeed you will also live for us after the funeral, and you will live, until the royal house of heaven receives you together with all the departed in a happy contest."

units.la: ZACHARIÆ VRSINO SILESIO, VIRO IN OMNI DISCIPLINARVM GENERE EXERCITATISSIMO, THEOLOGO SVMMO, VITÆ INCVLPATÆ, IVDICIO ADMIRABILI, LABORE INDEFESSO, TH. BEZA CHARISSIMO IN CHRISTO FRATRI, P. EPITAPHIVM D. ZACH. VRSINO SCRIPTVM A LAMBERTO LVDOLPHO PITHOPOEO, Dauentriensi.

units.la: Hic Vrsine iaces, Vbi parua Neapolis amplas De Nemetum paruo flumine fundit opes. Inclyta progenuit te Vratislauia, mentem Artibus erudiit Leucoris alma tuam, Lipsia, Parrisij, Tigurum, Basilea, Geneua, Largiter has donis excoluere suis, Estelberga [?] decem, septemque Neapolis annos, Quinque est ingenii dotibus aucta tui: Consilio, dextra, sonuere & voce diserta Sincere Christus, templa scholaque tua. Immodico tandem studij Vitaque labore Ereptus nobis, conderis hoc tumulo. Magnus eras totum, dum Sixti, Vrsine, per orbem, Sed tua post mortem gloria maior erit. Pestis eras viuens: moriens, damnosa Papatus Mors eris antiqui, & certa ruina noui. Cum lacrymis, pietas, doctrina, modestia, candor, Corporis exuuias hic posuere tui.
units.tr: Here you lie, Ursinus, where little Naples pours out its wide wealth by the small river of the Nemetes. The renowned Breslau bore you; kindly Leucoris, Leipzig, Paris, Zurich, Basel and Geneva trained your mind in the arts, and generously adorned it with their gifts. Naples held you for seven years and ten, and was enriched by the gifts of your talent for five. By your counsel, your hand and your eloquent voice you sounded forth sincerely for Christ, for his churches and his school. At last, worn out by immoderate study and labour of life, you were taken from us and laid in this tomb. You were great throughout the whole world, while you stood, Ursinus, among the Sixtus; but your glory after death will be greater still. While living, you were a plague to the Papacy; dying, you will be a ruinous death to the old and a sure downfall to the new. With tears, piety, learning, modesty and candour have laid the remains of your body here.

units.la: Aliud de eodem.
units.tr: Another on the same.

units.la: Clarius VRSINO Germania, MARTYRE tellus Itala, CALVINO Gallia nomen habet?
units.tr: Which has a greater name, Germany for Ursinus, Italy for the martyr, or Gaul for Calvin?

units.la: Aliud.
units.tr: Another.

units.la: Curia, templa, schola, te stante, VRSINE, virebant, Téque iacente, arent[?], curia, templa, schola.
units.tr: While you stood, Ursinus, the court, the churches and the school flourished; with you lying low, the court, the churches and the school wither.

units.la: ECLOGA IN OBITVM REVERENDI ET CLARISS. VIRI, ZACHARIAE VRSINI, Vratislauiensis, S. Theologiae Doctoris & Professoris celeberrimi, deque Ecclesia optimè meriti, Scripta à Simone Stenio Lomacensi.
units.tr: ECLOGUE ON THE DEATH OF THE REVEREND AND MOST DISTINGUISHED MAN, ZACHARIAS URSINUS, of Breslau, most celebrated Doctor and Professor of Holy Theology, and one who deserved very well of the Church, written by Simon Stenius of Lomza.

units.la: PALAEMON. ALPHESIBOEVS.
units.tr: PALAEMON. ALPHESIBOEUS.

units.la: ESse quid hoc dicam, quòd tristior, Alphesibæe,
units.tr: Is it something I should call this, that you walk more sadly than usual, Alphesiboeus?

units.la: Incedis solito? quòd turgent lumina fletu?
units.tr: That your eyes swell with weeping?

units.la: Quòd tua singultu vox interrupta quiescit?
units.tr: That your voice, broken by sobbing, falls silent?

units.la: Incustoditum num depraedatus ovile
units.tr: Has a wolf plundered the unguarded fold,

units.la: Est lupus? aut tenero num de grege rapta capella?
units.tr: or has a goat been snatched from the tender flock?

units.la: Pracipites rupes conscendere prima sueta,
units.tr: Have you stopped climbing the steep rocks as you used to,

units.la: Et data Victori nuper, ringente Menalca?
units.tr: and given the prize recently to Victor, while Menalcas grumbled?

units.la: De grege nil periit: nec rapta capella, Palamon,
units.tr: Nothing has perished from the flock, nor has a goat been snatched away, Palaemon;

units.la: Sunt & oves salvæ, Pastorum gloria Damon
units.tr: the sheep too are safe. Damon, the glory of the shepherds,

units.la: Occidit: hunc lacrymis, queis udos[?] cernis ocellos,
units.tr: has died. I adorn him with the tears by which you see my eyes wet.

units.la: Condecoro: ante horam morbóque laboréque fructum
units.tr: A short while ago, having laboured and suffered illness, we laid his body in the earth, a body worthy of marble

units.la: Condidimus terra corpus, vel marmore dignum
units.tr: of Tenarus, or of your famous tomb, Mausolus.

units.la: Tenario, vel clare tuo Mausole sepulcro.
units.tr: So Damon too has been snatched from us, and the white swan

units.la: Ergo etiam Damon nobis ereptus, olorque
units.tr: has fallen silent, while the crows caw and the unwelcome starlings

units.la: Candidus obticuit, coruis crocitantibus atque
units.tr: chatter? So recently Acanthis has ceased

units.la: Ingratis sturnis? sic nobis nuper Acanthis
units.tr: to pour out her song from her throat in the brambles;

units.la: Desiit in dumis depromere gutture carmen:
units.tr: so too the finch was silenced a while ago. Yet meanwhile

units.la: Sic etiam dudum fringilla obmutuit: atqui
units.tr: the owl, a dreadful omen to mortals,

units.la: Interea bubo, dirum mortalibus omen,
units.tr: shrieks sluggishly, and the chattering crow does not stop

units.la: Ignauum stridet, nec cessat garrula cornix
units.tr: making noise, while the cuckoos swell their horrid-sounding songs.

units.la: Obstrepere, horrisonas cuculis augentibus odas.
units.tr: But now Damon marvels at the seat of shining Olympus,

units.la: Sed nunc fulgentis sedem miratur olympi,
units.tr: and sees the clouds and stars beneath his feet,

units.la: Sub pedibusque videt nubes & sidera Damon,
units.tr: and, looking down, laughs at his enemies whom he once hated;

units.la: Despectánsque suos ridet, quos oderat hostes:
units.tr: for they are enemies of God and of truth, to whom their only care is

units.la: Quippe Dei veríque hostes: queis unica cura est[?]
units.tr: about power. [?]

units.la: Aliud de potentia. [?]
